Intensive versus standard blood pressure targets (fictional trial)
sets.introHtml: Study summary (fictional). In a randomized, open-label trial, 8,000 adults aged 50 years or older with hypertension and high cardiovascular risk, but without diabetes or prior stroke, were assigned to a systolic target of less than 120 mm Hg (intensive) or less than 140 mm Hg (standard). After a median of 3.5 years, mean systolic pressure was 122 mm Hg in the intensive group and 136 mm Hg in the standard group. The primary composite outcome (myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure or cardiovascular death) occurred in 6.0% of the intensive group and 8.5% of the standard group (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.60–0.82). Acute kidney injury occurred in 4.0% and 2.4%, and syncope in 2.6% and 1.9%, respectively.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with known moderate mitral regurgitation comes to the clinic because of 3 weeks of fevers to 38.3°C (101°F), night sweats and fatigue. Pulse is 96/min and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. A grade 3/6 holosystolic apical murmur is heard, unchanged from her last visit. There are splinter hemorrhages in two fingernails. She appears well and is not in distress. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Start oral amoxicillin and see her again in 1 week

options.label: B
options.html: Start IV vancomycin and ceftriaxone, then obtain blood cultures

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain three sets of blood cultures from separate venipunctures

options.label: D
options.html: Order transesophageal echocardiography before any other test

options.label: E
options.html: Order a chest CT to look for septic emboli

items.explanationHtml:
Subacute fever in a patient with a regurgitant valve and splinter hemorrhages suggests infective endocarditis. In a hemodynamically stable patient, the first step is to draw at least three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics. Positive cultures identify the organism, guide narrow therapy and are a major diagnostic criterion; even one dose of antibiotic can make cultures negative.

Takeaway: suspected IE in a stable patient → blood cultures first, then echo, then antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Oral antibiotics without cultures would mask the diagnosis and are never empiric therapy for suspected endocarditis.
whyNot.B: Empiric antibiotics before cultures fit septic shock or acute, destructive disease, not a stable patient with a weeks-long course.
whyNot.D: Echocardiography is needed, but TTE usually comes first, and cultures should not wait for imaging.
whyNot.E: Septic lung emboli come from right-sided disease; chest CT does not establish this diagnosis.

items.objective: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics in a stable patient with suspected endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve placed 4 years ago has fever and malaise for 10 days. Two of three blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. He had a cystoscopy 3 weeks ago. Transthoracic echocardiography shows normal prosthetic valve function with no vegetation, but the images are of limited quality. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.html: No further imaging; treat for 2 weeks for bacteremia

items.explanationHtml:
Enterococcal bacteremia in a patient with a prosthetic valve is endocarditis until proven otherwise. TTE is insensitive for prosthetic valve vegetations and perivalvular abscess because the prosthesis casts acoustic shadows. Transesophageal echocardiography is the next step; cardiac CT or PET-CT can be added if TEE is inconclusive.

Takeaway: a negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis on a prosthetic valve: get a TEE.

whyNot.B: Waiting 2 weeks delays diagnosis while complications such as abscess can develop.
whyNot.C: Cardiac MRI is poor at imaging valves and prosthetic material and is not the standard test.
whyNot.D: Coronary angiography assesses coronary disease and does not evaluate vegetations.
whyNot.E: A short course for uncomplicated bacteremia would undertreat probable prosthetic valve endocarditis.

items.objective: Choose TEE when TTE is negative or limited in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 37-year-old man who injects drugs is admitted with 5 days of fever. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), pulse 110/min and blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn and results are pending. Local rates of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus are high. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
This patient probably has tricuspid valve endocarditis, most likely caused by S. aureus. With MRSA common, empiric therapy must cover it: IV vancomycin (often combined with a β-lactam until susceptibilities return). Once cultures show methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, switch to an antistaphylococcal β-lactam, which kills MSSA faster and more reliably than vancomycin.

Takeaway: empiric therapy for native valve endocarditis in a person who injects drugs must cover MRSA: vancomycin.

whyNot.A: Oral linezolid is bacteriostatic and is not appropriate empiric therapy for endocarditis.
whyNot.B: Nafcillin is the drug of choice for MSSA, but alone it leaves MRSA uncovered while results are pending.
whyNot.C: Ceftriaxone covers streptococci but not MRSA.
whyNot.E: Gentamicin alone is not adequate therapy for staphylococcal endocarditis.

items.objective: Select empiric antibiotics that cover MRSA for suspected endocarditis in a person who injects drugs.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man is being treated for viridans streptococcal endocarditis of the aortic valve. On hospital day 4 he becomes acutely short of breath. Pulse is 124/min, blood pressure 96/40 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 86% on room air. There is a new loud early diastolic murmur and bilateral crackles. Echocardiography shows a perforated aortic leaflet with severe regurgitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add gentamicin to the antibiotic regimen

options.label: E
options.html: Continue antibiotics and repeat echocardiography in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
Heart failure caused by valve destruction is the most important indication for early (urgent) surgery in infective endocarditis. Acute severe aortic regurgitation is tolerated poorly because the ventricle has not had time to dilate; medical therapy alone has high mortality. Surgery should not wait for completion of antibiotics.

Takeaway: endocarditis + heart failure from valve dysfunction → urgent surgery.

whyNot.A: The organism is already being treated; more antibiotic does not fix a perforated leaflet.
whyNot.C: β-blockers slow the heart, lengthen diastole and increase regurgitant volume in acute aortic regurgitation.
whyNot.D: An intra-aortic balloon pump is contraindicated in significant aortic regurgitation because it worsens diastolic backflow.
whyNot.E: Waiting a week risks death from cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema.

items.objective: Recognise heart failure from valve destruction as an indication for urgent surgery in endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A dentist asks for advice about five patients scheduled for tooth extraction next week. Which of the following patients should receive antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis before the procedure?

options.label: A
options.html: A 34-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse and mild regurgitation

options.label: B
options.html: A 52-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and mild stenosis

options.label: C
options.html: A 45-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without obstruction

options.label: D
options.html: A 70-year-old man with coronary stents placed 1 year ago

options.label: E
options.html: A 61-year-old woman with a transcatheter aortic valve implanted 2 years ago

items.explanationHtml:
Prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue is reserved for patients at highest risk of a poor outcome from endocarditis: any prosthetic valve (surgical or transcatheter) or prosthetic material used in valve repair, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy. A single oral dose of amoxicillin 30–60 minutes before the procedure is standard.

Takeaway: prophylaxis = prosthetic valve, prior IE, specific congenital disease, transplant valvulopathy; not native valve disease.

whyNot.A: Mitral prolapse, even with regurgitation, is no longer an indication.
whyNot.B: A native bicuspid valve, with or without stenosis, does not warrant prophylaxis.
whyNot.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not a prophylaxis indication.
whyNot.D: Coronary stents are not an indication for endocarditis prophylaxis.

items.objective: Identify which patients need endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man completed 4 weeks of IV ceftriaxone for Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis of the mitral valve. Repeat blood cultures are negative and his fever has resolved. He has no abdominal symptoms and his last screening colonoscopy was 9 years ago and was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

items.explanationHtml:
S. gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis is associated with colonic adenomas and adenocarcinoma in a large share of patients, so every patient needs a colonoscopy regardless of symptoms or prior screening.

Takeaway: S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy, whatever the screening history.

whyNot.A: Stool testing is a screening tool for average-risk people and can miss adenomas; this patient needs direct visualisation.
whyNot.C: CT does not detect polyps or early cancers reliably.
whyNot.D: CEA is not a diagnostic or screening test for colon cancer.
whyNot.E: Skipping evaluation ignores a strong, actionable association.

items.objective: Order colonoscopy after Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man from Massachusetts has had fatigue and two episodes of light-headedness over 3 days. Six weeks ago he had a large expanding red rash on his back after hiking. Pulse is 48/min and blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. ECG shows a PR interval of 340 ms with intermittent nonconducted P waves (Mobitz type I). He is alert and well perfused. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Hospital admission with cardiac monitoring and IV ceftriaxone

items.explanationHtml:
Second-degree AV block with a PR over 300 ms weeks after erythema migrans is Lyme carditis. Patients who are symptomatic or have a PR of 300 ms or more, or second- or third-degree block, should be admitted for continuous monitoring because block can progress suddenly, and given IV ceftriaxone. Oral therapy completes the course once the block improves. A temporary pacemaker is used if block becomes unstable.

Takeaway: Lyme carditis with high-grade block → admit, monitor, IV ceftriaxone; a permanent pacemaker is rarely needed.

whyNot.A: Outpatient oral therapy suits only mild first-degree block (PR under 300 ms) in an asymptomatic patient.
whyNot.B: Lyme block usually resolves with antibiotics; a permanent device is premature.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids are not standard therapy for Lyme carditis.
whyNot.D: Vancomycin and gentamicin treat staphylococcal or enterococcal infection, not Borrelia.

items.objective: Manage Lyme carditis with high-grade AV block.

items.stemHtml:
A 60-year-old man is on day 6 of IV cefazolin for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of a native aortic valve. He still has fevers. Results of daily monitoring are shown.

Day 1Day 3Day 6
Temperature (°C)39.438.938.8
Blood culturesMSSA 3/3MSSA 2/2MSSA 2/2
PR interval (ms)170210290
Leukocytes (/mm3)16,20015,80016,900

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent bacteremia and fever despite appropriate therapy, together with a progressively lengthening PR interval, indicate extension of aortic valve infection into the annulus: a perivalvular (root) abscess that is reaching the AV node and His bundle. The next step is TEE and early surgery; abscess is an indication for operation.

Takeaway: aortic valve endocarditis + persistent bacteremia + new AV block = root abscess → TEE and surgery.

whyNot.A: The isolate is methicillin-susceptible, so it is susceptible to cefazolin; resistance does not explain new heart block.
whyNot.B: Drug fever does not cause persistently positive cultures or AV block.
whyNot.D: Lyme carditis causes AV block but not S. aureus bacteremia.
whyNot.E: Septic lung emboli arise from right-sided disease and do not lengthen the PR interval.

items.objective: Recognise perivalvular abscess from persistent bacteremia and new AV block in aortic valve endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of chest pain that is worse lying down and with deep breaths, followed by dyspnea. A week ago he had fever and diarrhea. Pulse is 112/min. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with diffuse ST elevation. Troponin I is markedly elevated. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with global hypokinesis. Coronary CT angiography shows normal coronary arteries. Which of the following is the best test to confirm the diagnosis noninvasively?
items.explanationHtml:
Chest pain and heart failure after a viral illness, high troponin, global dysfunction and normal coronaries suggest acute myocarditis (here with pericardial involvement, myopericarditis). Cardiac MRI is the best noninvasive confirmation: it shows myocardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a subepicardial or midwall (non-coronary) pattern. Endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for fulminant or atypical cases.

Takeaway: suspected myocarditis with normal coronaries → cardiac MRI.

whyNot.B: Exercise testing is unsafe in acute myocarditis and does not confirm it.
whyNot.C: Perfusion imaging looks for coronary ischemia, which has been excluded.
whyNot.D: Follow-up echocardiography tracks recovery but does not confirm the diagnosis now.
whyNot.E: ASO titers support acute rheumatic fever, which follows streptococcal pharyngitis and causes valvulitis.

items.objective: Use cardiac MRI to confirm suspected acute myocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman who injects fentanyl comes to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse 116/min, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. There are track marks on both forearms. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increases with inspiration. Chest radiograph shows multiple round opacities in both lower lobes, two of them cavitated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Tricuspid valve endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli

items.explanationHtml:
A person who injects drugs with fever, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign) and multiple peripheral cavitating nodules has right-sided endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli. Fragments of the tricuspid vegetation lodge in the pulmonary arteries and form infarcts that cavitate.

Takeaway: multiple cavitating lung nodules + inspiratory-increasing murmur in a person who injects drugs = tricuspid endocarditis.

whyNot.A: Pneumococcal pneumonia causes lobar consolidation, not multiple round cavitating nodules, and does not explain the murmur.
whyNot.B: Reactivation TB favours the apices, and a subacute course over weeks would be expected.
whyNot.C: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis can cause cavitating nodules but brings sinus and kidney disease, not a new murmur with fever after injection use.
whyNot.E: Choriocarcinoma can metastasise to the lung as nodules but would not cause a new tricuspid murmur and acute fever.

items.objective: Diagnose tricuspid endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.

items.stemHtml: The patient with tricuspid valve endocarditis was started on IV vancomycin after blood cultures were drawn. Two days later all cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus that is susceptible to oxacillin. She has no penicillin allergy. Kidney function is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her antibiotic therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
For methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, an antistaphylococcal β-lactam (cefazolin, nafcillin or oxacillin) is superior to vancomycin: it kills faster, clears bacteremia sooner and is associated with lower mortality. Vancomycin should be stopped once susceptibility is known in a patient without β-lactam allergy.

Takeaway: MSSA → switch from vancomycin to cefazolin or nafcillin.

whyNot.A: Vancomycin is inferior to β-lactams for MSSA and should not be continued when a β-lactam can be used.
whyNot.B: Rifampin is added for prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection, not native valve endocarditis.
whyNot.C: Initial oral TMP-SMX is not an established therapy for S. aureus endocarditis.
whyNot.E: Combining daptomycin with vancomycin adds toxicity without a role in MSSA.

items.objective: Narrow therapy to an antistaphylococcal β-lactam for MSSA endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 4 days of high fever, rigors and pleuritic chest pain. He injects heroin daily. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse 118/min, and blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg. A holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border and becomes louder with inspiration. Chest CT shows multiple peripheral nodules, several with central cavitation. Which of the following best describes the organism most likely responsible?

options.label: A
options.html: Catalase-negative, alpha-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains

options.label: B
options.html: Catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci in clusters

options.label: C
options.html: Catalase-positive, coagulase-positive gram-positive cocci in clusters

options.label: D
options.html: Catalase-negative, gamma-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in pairs

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur (holosystolic, left lower sternal border, louder with inspiration) and cavitating septic lung emboli in a person who injects drugs point to right-sided infective endocarditis. The leading cause is Staphylococcus aureus: gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase- and coagulase-positive. Its fibrinogen- and fibronectin-binding adhesins let it infect previously normal valves.

Takeaway: injection drug use + tricuspid murmur + cavitary lung nodules = S. aureus tricuspid endocarditis.

whyNot.A: This describes viridans streptococci, which cause subacute endocarditis of already abnormal left-sided valves, usually after dental bacteremia.
whyNot.B: This describes S. epidermidis, which causes endocarditis mainly on prosthetic valves and devices.
whyNot.D: This describes enterococci, which follow GU or GI procedures in older patients.
whyNot.E: Pseudomonas can cause endocarditis in people who inject drugs, but it is much less common than S. aureus.

items.objective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus as the leading cause of tricuspid endocarditis in people who inject drugs, and its laboratory features.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has had low-grade fevers, night sweats and a 4-kg weight loss over 6 weeks. Two months ago she had two molars extracted. She has known mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation. Three blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant gram-positive cocci in chains. Which of the following properties of this organism most directly allows it to colonise her mitral valve?

options.label: A
options.html: Production of extracellular dextran that binds fibrin–platelet deposits

options.label: B
options.html: Production of a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis

options.label: C
options.html: Secretion of an exotoxin that lyses valvular endothelial cells

options.label: D
options.html: Expression of protein A that binds the Fc portion of IgG

options.label: E
options.html: Production of coagulase that converts fibrinogen to fibrin

items.explanationHtml:
Subacute endocarditis on a previously damaged valve after dental work, with alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant streptococci, is caused by viridans group streptococci (for example S. sanguinis or S. mutans). They synthesise dextrans (glucans) from sucrose; these sticky polymers attach the organism to the sterile platelet–fibrin nidus that forms where a regurgitant jet has injured the endothelium.

Takeaway: viridans streptococci need a damaged valve and use dextran to adhere to its fibrin–platelet deposit.

whyNot.B: A capsule is the key virulence factor of S. pneumoniae, which is also alpha-hemolytic but optochin-sensitive.
whyNot.C: Viridans streptococci do not destroy valves with a cytolytic exotoxin; that destructive picture fits S. aureus.
whyNot.D: Protein A is a virulence factor of S. aureus, not of streptococci.
whyNot.E: Coagulase is produced by S. aureus; streptococci are coagulase-negative.

items.objective: Explain how viridans streptococci adhere to damaged heart valves.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man is admitted with fever and a new diastolic murmur. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 9-mm vegetation on the aortic valve. In addition to antibiotic therapy, which of the following conditions should most specifically be looked for in this patient?
items.explanationHtml:
Bacteremia or endocarditis caused by Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I) is strongly associated with colonic adenomas and adenocarcinoma. The tumour's disrupted mucosa is thought to let this gut commensal enter the blood. Colonoscopy is indicated even without GI symptoms.

Takeaway: S. gallolyticus in the blood → colonoscopy.

whyNot.A: Lung cancer is not linked to S. gallolyticus bacteremia.
whyNot.B: Prostate procedures are associated with enterococcal, not S. gallolyticus, endocarditis.
whyNot.C: Dental disease is the source of viridans streptococci, a different group.
whyNot.E: GU obstruction or instrumentation is linked to enterococci and gram-negative rods.

items.objective: Associate Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteremia with colonic neoplasia.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with a bicuspid aortic valve has had fever and fatigue for 5 weeks. Examination shows several tender, raised, violaceous nodules on the pads of her fingers and toes and an early diastolic murmur. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the finger and toe lesions?

options.label: A
options.html: Septic microemboli forming small dermal abscesses

options.label: C
options.html: Direct invasion of digital arteries by organisms

options.label: D
options.html: Vasospasm of digital arterioles triggered by cold

items.explanationHtml:
Tender nodules on the finger and toe pads in a patient with endocarditis are Osler nodes. They are attributed to immune complex deposition with a small-vessel vasculitis, the same immunologic process that produces Roth spots and glomerulonephritis in endocarditis.

Takeaway: painful nodules (Osler) are immunologic; painless macules on palms and soles (Janeway) are embolic.

whyNot.A: Septic microemboli with microabscesses explain Janeway lesions, which are painless, flat and on the palms and soles.
whyNot.C: Organisms are not seeded in digital arteries to form these nodules; invasion of an arterial wall produces a mycotic aneurysm.
whyNot.D: Cold-triggered vasospasm is Raynaud phenomenon, which causes colour change rather than nodules.
whyNot.E: Antiphospholipid thrombosis can cause digital ischemia but does not explain tender nodules in a febrile patient with a valve lesion.

items.objective: Distinguish the immunologic and embolic mechanisms of the peripheral signs of endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old sheep farmer has had intermittent fevers and fatigue for 4 months. He had aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthesis 3 years ago. Several sets of blood cultures show no growth after prolonged incubation. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a small vegetation on the prosthesis. Serology shows high antibody titers against the phase I antigen of the causative organism. Which of the following is the most likely route by which he acquired this infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Bite of an infected tick while working outdoors

options.label: B
options.html: Ingestion of unwashed vegetables grown in manure

options.label: C
options.html: Bite of a body louse living in clothing seams

options.label: D
options.html: Scratch from an infected cat on the farm

options.label: E
options.html: Inhalation of aerosols from animal birth products

items.explanationHtml:
Culture-negative endocarditis on a prosthetic valve in a livestock worker, with antibodies to phase I antigen, indicates chronic Q fever caused by Coxiella burnetii. The organism is shed heavily in placentas and birth fluids of sheep, goats and cattle, survives in the environment as a resistant small-cell form, and is inhaled. No arthropod vector is needed, unlike most other rickettsia-like organisms.

Takeaway: livestock + culture-negative endocarditis = Coxiella, acquired by inhalation.

whyNot.A: Ticks transmit Rickettsia rickettsii and Borrelia; Coxiella does not need a tick to infect humans.
whyNot.B: Food-borne infection does not fit; unpasteurised milk is a minor route, not unwashed vegetables.
whyNot.C: Body lice transmit Bartonella quintana, another cause of culture-negative endocarditis, in people experiencing homelessness.
whyNot.D: Cat scratches transmit Bartonella henselae.

items.objective: Recognise Coxiella burnetii as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis and describe its transmission.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who has lived in shelters for several years is admitted with fever and a new aortic regurgitation murmur. His clothing is infested with lice. Three sets of blood cultures are negative after 5 days. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the aortic valve. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Bartonella quintana, transmitted by the human body louse, causes trench fever, bacillary angiomatosis and culture-negative endocarditis, especially in people experiencing homelessness or alcohol use disorder. Diagnosis is by serology or PCR of valve tissue.

Takeaway: body lice + culture-negative endocarditis → B. quintana.

whyNot.A: Louse-borne relapsing fever (B. recurrentis) causes recurring febrile episodes, not endocarditis.
whyNot.C: Epidemic typhus (R. prowazekii) is also louse-borne but causes a rash and encephalopathy, not valve vegetations.
whyNot.D: Coxiella causes culture-negative endocarditis after livestock exposure, which this patient lacks.
whyNot.E: Cardiobacterium is a HACEK organism from the oral flora; it grows slowly but is not tied to lice.

items.objective: Associate Bartonella quintana with louse exposure and culture-negative endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man who moved from rural Bolivia 10 years ago has progressive exertional dyspnea and difficulty swallowing solids and liquids. ECG shows right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an apical aneurysm. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely way he acquired the underlying disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Bite of an infected sand fly at night

options.label: B
options.html: Bite of an infected tsetse fly by day

options.label: D
options.html: Skin penetration by larvae in moist soil

options.label: E
options.html: Feces of a blood-feeding bug rubbed into a bite

items.explanationHtml:
Dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm, RBBB with left anterior fascicular block and megaesophagus in someone from rural Latin America is chronic Chagas disease. Trypanosoma cruzi is passed in the feces of triatomine (reduviid) bugs, which feed at night and defecate near the bite; scratching rubs the parasite into the wound or conjunctiva. Destruction of myocytes and of enteric ganglion cells explains the heart and gut findings.

Takeaway: cardiomyopathy + megaesophagus/megacolon + Latin America = Chagas, spread by triatomine feces.

whyNot.A: Sand flies transmit Leishmania, which causes skin or visceral disease, not cardiomyopathy with megaesophagus.
whyNot.B: Tsetse flies transmit T. brucei (African sleeping sickness), a disease of lymph nodes and the CNS.
whyNot.C: Undercooked pork transmits Taenia solium and Trichinella; trichinellosis can cause myocarditis but not megaesophagus.
whyNot.D: Soil larvae that penetrate skin are hookworms and Strongyloides, which cause anemia or lung and gut disease.

items.objective: Identify the transmission and organ involvement of chronic Chagas disease.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has progressive dyspnea. He was treated for a genital ulcer in his 20s with an unknown regimen. Examination shows a decrescendo diastolic murmur at the right upper sternal border and bounding pulses. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum with linear calcification of the ascending aorta. Treponemal antibody testing is positive. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of his aortic disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Cystic medial degeneration from abnormal fibrillin

options.label: B
options.html: Atherosclerotic plaque weakening the intima and media

options.label: C
options.html: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum

options.label: D
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic media

options.label: E
options.html: Immune complex deposition in the aortic adventitia

items.explanationHtml:
Tertiary syphilis causes syphilitic aortitis: inflammation and obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the thoracic aorta. Ischemia of the outer media destroys smooth muscle and elastic tissue, leaving scars that wrinkle the intima (“tree-bark”) and allowing aneurysmal dilation of the ascending aorta and root. Root dilation causes aortic regurgitation; ostial involvement can narrow the coronaries.

Takeaway: ascending aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation + positive treponemal test → vasa vasorum endarteritis.

whyNot.A: Cystic medial degeneration from abnormal fibrillin explains aortic root disease in Marfan syndrome, usually in younger people.
whyNot.B: Atherosclerotic aneurysms favour the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries, not the ascending aorta.
whyNot.D: Granulomatous aortitis is the lesion of giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis.
whyNot.E: Immune complex deposition is not the mechanism of luetic aortitis.

items.objective: Explain the pathogenesis of syphilitic aortitis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman from Connecticut is evaluated for light-headedness and palpitations. Five weeks ago she noticed an expanding red rash with central clearing on her thigh after a camping trip. Pulse is 42/min. ECG shows P waves that bear no relationship to the QRS complexes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her conduction disorder?

options.label: C
options.html: Intracellular gram-negative rod transmitted by a Dermacentor tick

options.label: D
options.html: Flagellated protozoan transmitted by a triatomine bug

options.label: E
options.html: Nonenveloped RNA virus spread by the fecal–oral route

items.explanationHtml:
An expanding annular rash after a camping trip in New England is erythema migrans. Weeks later, dissemination of Borrelia burgdorferi can cause Lyme carditis, which typically presents as AV block (here complete heart block). The spirochete is transmitted by Ixodes ticks.

Takeaway: erythema migrans followed by heart block = Lyme carditis.

whyNot.B: Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin can cause myocarditis with heart block, but it follows a pharyngeal pseudomembrane, not a rash.
whyNot.C: Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a petechial rash spreading from wrists and ankles, with vasculitis rather than isolated heart block.
whyNot.D: T. cruzi causes conduction disease in people from Latin America, and its rash is not erythema migrans.
whyNot.E: Coxsackievirus B causes myocarditis with heart failure; it does not follow a tick-associated rash.

items.objective: Recognise Lyme carditis as AV block after erythema migrans.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man develops chest pain and dyspnea 10 days after an illness with fever, sore throat and diarrhea. Troponin is elevated, and echocardiography shows a globally reduced ejection fraction. Coronary angiography is normal. Endomyocardial biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate with adjacent myocyte necrosis. Which of the following best describes the virus most commonly associated with this condition?

options.label: E
options.html: Enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus with reverse transcriptase

items.explanationHtml:
A viral prodrome followed by heart failure, raised troponin, normal coronaries and lymphocytic myocarditis on biopsy is viral myocarditis. Classically it is caused by coxsackievirus B, an enterovirus (picornavirus): small, nonenveloped, icosahedral, with a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome that acts directly as mRNA.

Takeaway: coxsackievirus B (picornavirus: naked, + ssRNA) is the classic cause of viral myocarditis.

whyNot.A: Herpesviruses are enveloped dsDNA viruses; HHV-6 is found in some biopsies but is not the classic agent.
whyNot.B: Influenza is an enveloped, segmented negative-sense RNA virus; it can cause myocarditis but less typically.
whyNot.C: Rotavirus is a nonenveloped dsRNA virus that causes diarrhea, not myocarditis.
whyNot.E: Retroviruses such as HIV carry reverse transcriptase; HIV cardiomyopathy is a chronic process.

items.objective: Describe the virus most associated with viral myocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has fever 7 weeks after mechanical mitral valve replacement. Two sets of blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive and coagulase-negative. Which of the following best explains this organism's ability to persist on the prosthetic valve despite host defenses?

options.label: A
options.html: Protein A binding to the Fc region of antibodies

options.label: D
options.html: Production of an extracellular polysaccharide biofilm

items.explanationHtml:
Early prosthetic valve endocarditis is most often caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis. These skin commensals produce an extracellular polysaccharide matrix (biofilm) that attaches to plastic and metal, protects organisms from phagocytes and antibodies, and blocks antibiotic penetration. This is why device infections often need removal of the device.

Takeaway: S. epidermidis + prosthetic material = biofilm infection.

whyNot.A: Protein A is a virulence factor of S. aureus, which is coagulase-positive.
whyNot.B: Superantigen toxins (such as TSST-1) belong to S. aureus and group A streptococci and cause toxic shock, not device persistence.
whyNot.C: A hyaluronic acid capsule is a feature of Streptococcus pyogenes.
whyNot.E: Penicillinase inactivates penicillin, not complement, and does not explain adherence.

items.objective: Explain biofilm production by coagulase-negative staphylococci in prosthetic valve endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old boy was diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever 2 weeks ago, with migratory polyarthritis and carditis. Echocardiography now shows moderate mitral regurgitation. His arthritis has resolved with naproxen, and he completed eradication therapy for group A streptococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

options.label: A
options.html: No further antibiotics unless he has a sore throat

options.label: B
options.html: Oral amoxicillin before dental procedures only

options.label: C
options.html: IM benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks for at least 10 years

options.label: E
options.html: Annual throat cultures with treatment if positive

items.explanationHtml:
After acute rheumatic fever, secondary prophylaxis prevents recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis and the new valve damage each recurrence causes. The preferred regimen is IM benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks where risk is high). With carditis and residual valve disease, it continues for 10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer, sometimes for life.

Takeaway: rheumatic fever with valve disease → monthly benzathine penicillin for at least 10 years (or until 40).

whyNot.A: Treating only symptomatic pharyngitis misses asymptomatic infections, which can also trigger recurrences.
whyNot.B: Rheumatic valve disease without a prosthesis is not an indication for dental endocarditis prophylaxis, and that would not prevent rheumatic fever.
whyNot.D: Azithromycin is an alternative only for penicillin allergy, and 1 year is too short.
whyNot.E: Throat culture surveillance does not prevent infection and is not an accepted strategy.

items.objective: Choose secondary prophylaxis and its duration after rheumatic fever with carditis.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl has had a sore throat and fever to 38.9°C (102°F) for 2 days. She has tonsillar exudates and tender anterior cervical nodes, and no cough or rhinorrhea. A rapid antigen test for group A streptococci is positive. She has no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Supportive care only; antibiotics do not change outcomes

items.explanationHtml:
Confirmed group A streptococcal pharyngitis is treated with penicillin V or amoxicillin for a full 10 days (or a single IM dose of benzathine penicillin G). Antibiotics shorten symptoms, reduce spread and suppurative complications, and, if started within about 9 days of onset, prevent acute rheumatic fever.

Takeaway: strep throat → 10 days of amoxicillin or penicillin (primary prevention of rheumatic fever).

whyNot.B: Antibiotics do prevent rheumatic fever, so withholding them is not appropriate for confirmed infection.
whyNot.C: Azithromycin is for penicillin allergy, and macrolide resistance is increasing.
whyNot.D: Cephalexin is also a second-line choice for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy, and 3 days is too short.
whyNot.E: IV therapy is not needed for uncomplicated pharyngitis.

items.objective: Treat group A streptococcal pharyngitis to prevent rheumatic fever.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl has had 3 weeks of clumsiness, sudden jerky movements of her arms and face, and new episodes of crying. Her mother recalls a sore throat about 3 months ago. Temperature is normal. Neurologic examination shows irregular, purposeless movements that disappear during sleep and a "milkmaid" grip. No murmur is heard. ESR is normal and antistreptolysin O titer is mildly raised. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Purposeless choreiform movements with emotional lability months after pharyngitis are Sydenham chorea, a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever. Chorea appears late, often alone, when inflammatory markers have normalised. Echocardiography with Doppler is indicated in every suspected case, because subclinical carditis is common and changes the duration of penicillin prophylaxis.

Takeaway: Sydenham chorea → echocardiogram for silent carditis, then secondary prophylaxis.

whyNot.A: CT is not needed for typical chorea without focal deficits.
whyNot.B: EEG does not diagnose chorea, which is not epileptic.
whyNot.C: Wilson disease can cause movement disorders, but the timing after pharyngitis and the age favour rheumatic chorea.
whyNot.E: There is no sign of CNS infection to justify a lumbar puncture.

items.objective: Order echocardiography to detect subclinical carditis in Sydenham chorea.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has had worsening dyspnea and orthopnea for 2 weeks. She had rheumatic fever as a child in Ethiopia. Pulse is 118/min and regular, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. There are bibasilar crackles, an opening snap and an apical diastolic rumble. Echocardiography shows severe mitral stenosis with a valve area of 1.0 cm2 and pliable, noncalcified leaflets. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Pregnancy increases heart rate and plasma volume; in mitral stenosis a faster rate shortens diastole, so the left atrium cannot empty across the narrow valve and pulmonary venous pressure rises. A β1-selective blocker such as metoprolol slows the heart, prolongs diastolic filling and relieves congestion; a diuretic is added for pulmonary edema. Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy is an option if symptoms persist despite medical therapy.

Takeaway: symptomatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy → β-blocker (plus a diuretic).

whyNot.A: Digoxin controls rate mainly in atrial fibrillation and does little for sinus tachycardia during exertion.
whyNot.C: Afterload reduction does not help a fixed inflow obstruction and can cause hypotension.
whyNot.D: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because they cause fetal renal damage.
whyNot.E: An inotrope raises heart rate and worsens filling across a stenotic mitral valve.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic rheumatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy with a β-blocker.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus had a left middle cerebral artery stroke. Echocardiography shows small sterile vegetations on the mitral valve. Blood cultures are negative. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies are positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to prevent recurrent stroke?
items.explanationHtml:
Stroke with Libman–Sacks vegetations and persistent triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies is thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome. Long-term anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) is recommended. Direct oral anticoagulants had more arterial events than warfarin in high-risk APS and are avoided, especially in triple-positive patients and after arterial events.

Takeaway: antiphospholipid syndrome with arterial thrombosis → warfarin, not a DOAC.

whyNot.A: Aspirin alone is inadequate for secondary prevention after an APS-related stroke.
whyNot.B: DOACs such as apixaban were inferior to warfarin in high-risk APS.
whyNot.C: Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent and does not replace anticoagulation in APS.
whyNot.D: The vegetations are sterile; antibiotics have no role.

items.objective: Choose warfarin for secondary prevention in antiphospholipid syndrome with Libman–Sacks endocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the lung presents with sudden left leg pain and a cold, pulseless foot; two days earlier she had transient right-sided weakness. Blood cultures are negative. Transesophageal echocardiography shows small mobile vegetations on the aortic and mitral valves without regurgitation. After vascular surgery restores flow to the leg, which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Sterile vegetations with emboli to the brain and leg in a patient with advanced adenocarcinoma are nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis. The underlying cancer-associated hypercoagulability responds best to heparin (low-molecular-weight or unfractionated); warfarin and DOACs appear less effective at preventing recurrent emboli in this setting. The cancer itself should be treated where possible.

Takeaway: NBTE with emboli → full-dose heparin.

whyNot.A: Aspirin does not prevent fibrin-rich thrombi in cancer-associated hypercoagulability.
whyNot.C: Warfarin has a high failure rate in cancer-associated thrombosis and NBTE.
whyNot.D: Dabigatran has not been shown to be effective for NBTE.
whyNot.E: Untreated NBTE carries a high risk of recurrent embolism.

items.objective: Treat nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis with heparin.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman has had a new right-sided headache for 2 weeks, pain in her jaw when chewing and, since this morning, intermittent blurring of vision in her right eye. Her right temporal artery is tender with a reduced pulse. ESR is 92 mm/h. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Low-dose prednisone and rheumatology referral in 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
New headache, jaw claudication, temporal artery tenderness and a very high ESR in a patient over 50 indicate giant cell arteritis. Visual symptoms mean the ophthalmic circulation is threatened, so high-dose glucocorticoids (IV methylprednisolone when vision is affected) must start immediately. Temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound should follow within 1–2 weeks; findings persist despite treatment.

Takeaway: suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms → steroids now, biopsy later.

whyNot.A: Waiting for a biopsy risks permanent blindness; biopsy can be done after steroids begin.
whyNot.B: Brain MRI does not diagnose giant cell arteritis and delays treatment.
whyNot.C: Low-dose prednisone is used for isolated polymyalgia rheumatica, not for arteritis threatening vision.
whyNot.D: Aspirin may be added but cannot replace glucocorticoids.

items.objective: Start glucocorticoids immediately in suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had fatigue, night sweats and aching in both arms with use for 3 months. Blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg in the right arm and 104/72 mm Hg in the left. The left radial pulse is weak, and bruits are heard over both subclavian arteries and the abdomen. ESR is 48 mm/h. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

options.label: C
options.html: MR angiography of the aorta and its branches

items.explanationHtml:
A young woman with constitutional symptoms, arm claudication, unequal arm pressures and multiple bruits most likely has Takayasu arteritis. The diagnosis is made by imaging the aorta and its primary branches: MR or CT angiography shows wall thickening and long, smooth stenoses or aneurysms. Biopsy of large vessels is rarely possible.

Takeaway: suspected Takayasu arteritis → MR or CT angiography.

whyNot.A: Temporal artery biopsy diagnoses giant cell arteritis in patients over 50.
whyNot.B: Nerve studies do not evaluate arterial stenoses causing limb claudication.
whyNot.D: ANCA testing evaluates small-vessel vasculitis, which spares the aorta.
whyNot.E: Echocardiography can show aortic root dilation but cannot map arch branch stenoses.

items.objective: Diagnose Takayasu arteritis with vascular imaging.

items.stemHtml:
A 61-year-old man has had flushing of the face and neck, watery diarrhea and increasing leg swelling for 8 months. He has a soft holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration, an elevated jugular venous pressure and a palpable liver edge. Laboratory results are shown.

TestResult
Hemoglobin13.9 g/dL
AST36 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase164 U/L
Albumin3.6 g/dL
Glucose, fasting92 mg/dL

CT of the abdomen shows several hypervascular liver masses. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the suspected syndrome?
items.explanationHtml:
Flushing, diarrhea, tricuspid regurgitation with right-sided heart failure and liver metastases indicate carcinoid syndrome with carcinoid heart disease. The best confirmatory test is the 24-hour urinary excretion of 5-HIAA, the main metabolite of serotonin (plasma 5-HIAA is an alternative). Foods rich in serotonin and some drugs must be avoided before collection.

Takeaway: flushing + diarrhea + right-sided valve disease → urine 5-HIAA.

whyNot.B: Gastrin is measured for Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (ulcers and diarrhea, not flushing with valve disease).
whyNot.C: Metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, which causes episodic hypertension and pallor more than flushing.
whyNot.D: VIPoma causes profuse watery diarrhea with hypokalemia but not right-sided valve fibrosis.
whyNot.E: Calcitonin is a marker of medullary thyroid carcinoma, which can cause diarrhea and flushing but not carcinoid heart disease.

items.objective: Confirm carcinoid syndrome with 5-HIAA testing.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after 6 days of fever up to 39.8°C (103.6°F) that has not responded to acetaminophen. He is irritable. Examination shows bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge, red cracked lips, a red tongue with prominent papillae, a blanching maculopapular rash on the trunk, swollen red hands and feet, and a single 2-cm tender node in the right neck. Rapid streptococcal antigen test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Fever for at least 5 days plus at least 4 of the 5 principal features (bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, oral changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes and cervical lymphadenopathy of 1.5 cm or more) defines complete Kawasaki disease. This child has all five.

Takeaway: 5+ days of fever + conjunctiva, mouth, rash, hands and feet, neck node = Kawasaki disease.

whyNot.A: Scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash and exudative pharyngitis with a positive strep test, and the conjunctivae are usually spared.
whyNot.B: Measles brings cough, coryza and exudative conjunctivitis, with a rash that spreads from the head down.
whyNot.C: Adenovirus causes exudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis, typically with lower inflammatory markers and without extremity changes.
whyNot.E: Scalded skin syndrome causes tender erythema with superficial blistering and no mucosal or conjunctival involvement.

items.objective: Diagnose complete Kawasaki disease from the clinical criteria.

items.stemHtml: The child is diagnosed with Kawasaki disease on day 6 of fever. Baseline echocardiography shows mild dilation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Standard initial therapy for Kawasaki disease is IV immunoglobulin (2 g/kg as a single infusion) plus aspirin, given as early as possible within the first 10 days of fever. IVIG lowers the rate of coronary aneurysm from about 25% to a few per cent. Echocardiography is repeated at 1–2 and 4–6 weeks; children at high risk of aneurysm may also receive glucocorticoids with IVIG.

Takeaway: Kawasaki disease → IVIG + aspirin, then serial echocardiography.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids alone are not first-line; they are an adjunct for high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases.
whyNot.B: Ibuprofen antagonises the antiplatelet effect of aspirin, and observation leaves the coronary risk untreated.
whyNot.C: There is no evidence of bacterial infection to justify broad-spectrum antibiotics.
whyNot.E: Infliximab is used for IVIG-resistant disease, not as sole initial therapy.

items.objective: Treat Kawasaki disease with IVIG and aspirin.

items.stemHtml: The child received IV immunoglobulin and aspirin, became afebrile within 24 hours and is now on low-dose aspirin. At discharge, his parents ask about vaccines; his 15-month measles-mumps-rubella vaccine was due next week. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Give the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine as scheduled

options.label: C
options.html: Give a double dose of measles-mumps-rubella vaccine now

options.label: D
options.html: Give the live intranasal influenza vaccine this season

options.label: E
options.html: Defer the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine for about 11 months

items.explanationHtml:
High-dose IVIG contains antibodies against measles and other viruses that can neutralise live attenuated vaccine viruses. Live vaccines such as MMR and varicella should be deferred for about 11 months after IVIG for Kawasaki disease (sooner if exposure risk is high, followed by a repeat dose). He should receive inactivated influenza vaccine while on aspirin to lower the risk of Reye syndrome.

Takeaway: after Kawasaki IVIG, delay live vaccines about 11 months; give inactivated flu vaccine during aspirin therapy.

whyNot.A: Giving MMR now risks a poor immune response because passive antibody neutralises the vaccine virus.
whyNot.B: There is no reason to withhold MMR permanently; it is only deferred.
whyNot.C: A double dose is not effective and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: The live intranasal influenza vaccine is contraindicated in children taking aspirin because of the Reye syndrome risk.

items.objective: Defer live vaccines after IVIG for Kawasaki disease.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl has had fever and pain moving from her knees to her ankles and then to her wrists over 10 days. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat that was not treated. A new holosystolic apical murmur is heard. Antistreptolysin O titer is elevated. Antibodies against which bacterial component most likely cross-react with her cardiac tissue?
items.explanationHtml:
Migratory polyarthritis and new mitral regurgitation weeks after untreated pharyngitis is acute rheumatic fever. Antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve proteins (molecular mimicry, a type II hypersensitivity reaction).

Takeaway: rheumatic fever = anti–M protein immunity cross-reacting with heart (molecular mimicry).

whyNot.A: Lipoteichoic acid helps streptococci adhere to epithelium but is not the main mimic of cardiac antigens.
whyNot.B: Streptolysin S is a nonimmunogenic hemolysin, so it cannot provoke the cross-reacting antibodies.
whyNot.D: The hyaluronic acid capsule resembles host connective tissue, which makes it poorly immunogenic, not a target.
whyNot.E: Streptokinase activates plasminogen and is not the cardiac cross-reactive antigen.

items.objective: Explain molecular mimicry between the streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue in rheumatic fever.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy with acute rheumatic fever dies of heart failure despite treatment. At autopsy, the myocardium contains foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes and large macrophages with a central, wavy ribbon of nuclear chromatin. Which of the following is the name of these macrophages?
items.explanationHtml:
The lesion described is an Aschoff body, the hallmark of rheumatic carditis. Its activated macrophages, Anitschkow cells, have slender, wavy central chromatin ("caterpillar" nuclei) and can fuse into multinucleated Aschoff giant cells.

Takeaway: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells = rheumatic carditis.

whyNot.B: Langhans giant cells have peripheral horseshoe nuclei and occur in tuberculous granulomas.
whyNot.C: Reed–Sternberg cells are the neoplastic cells of Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyNot.D: Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages of atherosclerotic plaques and xanthomas.
whyNot.E: Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages in chronic pulmonary congestion.

items.objective: Identify Anitschkow cells within Aschoff bodies in rheumatic carditis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman who emigrated from Nepal is 26 weeks pregnant and has progressive dyspnea and palpitations. She had a long febrile illness with joint pains as a child. Examination shows a loud first heart sound, an early diastolic opening snap and a low-pitched apical diastolic rumble. Which of the following best describes the structural change in her affected valve?

options.label: B
options.html: Calcification of the annulus with normal leaflets

options.label: D
options.html: Fusion of the commissures with thickened leaflets

options.label: E
options.html: Perforation of a leaflet by infection

items.explanationHtml:
Opening snap plus diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, and in a woman from a high-prevalence region with a childhood febrile arthritis it is rheumatic. Healing of repeated valvulitis causes leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and fused, shortened chordae, giving a "fish-mouth" orifice. Pregnancy unmasks it by raising heart rate and blood volume.

Takeaway: rheumatic heart disease → commissural fusion → mitral stenosis.

whyNot.A: Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse with a midsystolic click, not stenosis.
whyNot.B: Mitral annular calcification occurs in older adults and seldom causes significant stenosis in a young woman.
whyNot.C: Congenital fusion of two leaflets describes a bicuspid aortic valve.
whyNot.E: Leaflet perforation from endocarditis causes acute regurgitation.

items.objective: Describe the valve pathology of chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old boy is diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever. His family asks what infection caused it, because he also had skin sores 2 months ago. Which of the following infections most likely triggered his condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngeal infection with group A Streptococcus. Streptococcal skin infection (impetigo, pyoderma) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis but is not an established trigger of rheumatic fever, probably because skin strains and the local immune response differ.

Takeaway: throat → rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis; skin → glomerulonephritis only.

whyNot.A: Impetigo can precede post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.
whyNot.C: S. aureus does not cause rheumatic fever.
whyNot.D: Viral pharyngitis does not induce cross-reactive anti–M protein immunity.
whyNot.E: Group B streptococci cause neonatal sepsis and do not trigger rheumatic fever.

items.objective: Identify group A streptococcal pharyngitis as the trigger of rheumatic fever.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a transient episode of right arm weakness. Blood cultures are sterile. Echocardiography shows small vegetations on both the atrial and ventricular surfaces of the mitral leaflets with mild regurgitation. Which of the following laboratory findings is most strongly associated with this valve lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
Sterile vegetations on both surfaces of the mitral leaflets in a patient with lupus are Libman–Sacks endocarditis. It is strongly linked to antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I), which also explain the embolic stroke risk.

Takeaway: Libman–Sacks = lupus/antiphospholipid, vegetations on both sides of the leaflet.

whyNot.A: Anti-centromere antibodies mark limited systemic sclerosis.
whyNot.B: ANCA are linked with small-vessel vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyNot.C: Rheumatoid factor can be positive in infective endocarditis and rheumatoid arthritis, not specifically Libman–Sacks.
whyNot.D: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are found in myositis with interstitial lung disease.

items.objective: Associate Libman–Sacks endocarditis with antiphospholipid antibodies.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the pancreas has sudden aphasia. MRI shows acute infarcts in several vascular territories. Three blood cultures are negative. Echocardiography shows small vegetations along the closure lines of an otherwise normal mitral valve. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the valve lesions?

options.label: A
options.html: Deposition of immune complexes on the valve

items.explanationHtml:
Small sterile vegetations on a normal valve in a patient with a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma are nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis. Tumour mucin and tissue factor create a hypercoagulable state, and bland fibrin–platelet thrombi form where leaflets meet. They embolise easily, causing infarcts in several territories.

Takeaway: cancer + sterile vegetations + multiple emboli = NBTE from hypercoagulability.

whyNot.A: Immune complex deposition fits Libman–Sacks endocarditis in lupus, which places vegetations on both surfaces.
whyNot.C: Negative cultures and a normal valve argue against infective endocarditis.
whyNot.D: Cross-reacting antibodies cause rheumatic valvulitis after streptococcal pharyngitis.
whyNot.E: Serotonin-induced plaques define carcinoid heart disease, which affects right-sided valves.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis in advanced cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour of the ileum and multiple liver metastases has episodic facial flushing, watery diarrhea and leg swelling. Echocardiography shows thickened, retracted tricuspid and pulmonic valves; the mitral and aortic valves are normal. Which of the following best explains why her left-sided valves are spared?

options.label: A
options.html: The left ventricle generates higher pressures that prevent plaque formation

options.label: B
options.html: The liver metastases secrete serotonin only into the portal vein

options.label: D
options.html: Bronchial vessels filter out tumour cells

options.label: E
options.html: Monoamine oxidase in the lungs inactivates serotonin

items.explanationHtml:
In carcinoid heart disease, serotonin and related products from liver metastases enter the hepatic veins and reach the right heart, where they stimulate fibroblasts to lay down endocardial plaques that fix the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. Blood then passes through the lungs, where monoamine oxidase degrades serotonin, so left-sided valves are usually spared unless there is a bronchial primary or a right-to-left shunt.

Takeaway: carcinoid heart disease is right-sided because the lung inactivates serotonin.

whyNot.A: Pressure differences do not explain the sparing; serotonin-driven fibrosis depends on exposure.
whyNot.B: Hepatic metastases release products into the hepatic veins, bypassing first-pass metabolism; that is why the syndrome appears.
whyNot.C: Serotonin receptors such as 5-HT<sub>2B</sub> are present on valves of both sides of the heart.
whyNot.D: Bronchial vessels do not filter tumour cells; the protection is metabolic, not mechanical.

items.objective: Explain why carcinoid heart disease affects mainly right-sided valves.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated after 7 days of fever. He has bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, a diffuse maculopapular rash, swollen hands and a 2-cm unilateral cervical lymph node. Without treatment, which of the following is the most serious complication of his condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Fever for 5 or more days with conjunctival injection, oral changes, rash, extremity swelling and cervical adenopathy is Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis with a predilection for the coronary arteries. Transmural inflammation weakens the wall, and coronary artery aneurysms develop in about a quarter of untreated children; thrombosis and myocardial infarction follow.

Takeaway: Kawasaki disease → coronary artery aneurysm, the reason for IVIG and serial echocardiography.

whyNot.A: Glomerulonephritis is a feature of small-vessel vasculitides; sterile pyuria is common in Kawasaki, but renal failure is not.
whyNot.B: Intussusception is linked with IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura).
whyNot.D: Aortic dissection is not a typical complication of Kawasaki disease.
whyNot.E: Transaminases can rise mildly, but liver failure is not a feature.

items.objective: Recognise coronary aneurysm as the major complication of Kawasaki disease.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman of Japanese ancestry has had fatigue, low-grade fevers and pain in her left arm when she combs her hair. The left radial pulse is weak, blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg in the left arm and 132/80 mm Hg in the right, and a bruit is heard over the left subclavian artery. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely in the affected artery?

options.label: A
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation of the media and adventitia

options.label: B
options.html: Fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles with neutrophils

options.label: C
options.html: Cystic degeneration of the media with pooled mucoid material

options.label: D
options.html: Lipid-laden macrophages in a fibrous intimal plaque

options.label: E
options.html: Onion-skin concentric thickening of the arteriolar wall

items.explanationHtml:
A young woman of Asian ancestry with arm claudication, unequal arm pressures and a subclavian bruit has Takayasu arteritis, a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches. Inflammation of the media and adventitia (with giant cells) is followed by fibrosis and intimal thickening that narrow the lumen.

Takeaway: granulomatous aortitis in a woman under 40 = Takayasu; over 50 = giant cell arteritis.

whyNot.B: Fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils in small vessels fits small-vessel vasculitis or malignant hypertension.
whyNot.C: Cystic medial degeneration causes aortic root aneurysm and dissection (Marfan syndrome), not stenosis with inflammation.
whyNot.D: Atherosclerotic plaque would be unusual at 27 and would not cause systemic symptoms.
whyNot.E: Onion-skinning is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of malignant hypertension.

items.objective: Identify the histology of Takayasu arteritis.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with biopsy-proven giant cell arteritis has had two relapses whenever prednisone is tapered below 15 mg/day. A monoclonal antibody is added to allow a faster taper. The drug binds the receptor of the cytokine most responsible for her systemic inflammation and acute-phase response. Which of the following drugs was most likely added?
items.explanationHtml:
IL-6 drives the fever, high CRP and ESR and vessel inflammation of giant cell arteritis. Tocilizumab, a humanised monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor, lowers relapse rates and cumulative glucocorticoid dose. Because it suppresses CRP, CRP is no longer a reliable marker of infection or flare on treatment.

Takeaway: giant cell arteritis steroid-sparing therapy = tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor).

whyNot.A: Infliximab blocks TNF-α and did not prevent relapse in trials in giant cell arteritis.
whyNot.B: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells and is used for ANCA-associated vasculitis.
whyNot.C: Ustekinumab blocks the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23 and is used for psoriasis and Crohn disease.
whyNot.E: Anakinra is an IL-1 receptor antagonist used for autoinflammatory diseases and gout.

items.objective: Identify tocilizumab as an IL-6 receptor antagonist used in giant cell arteritis.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man is readmitted 3 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction with fever and sharp chest pain that improves when he sits forward. A pericardial friction rub is heard. ESR is elevated. Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion and no new wall motion abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Extension of transmural necrosis to the pericardium

options.label: B
options.html: Bacterial seeding of the pericardium from a catheter

options.label: C
options.html: Rupture of the ventricular free wall

options.label: D
options.html: Autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens exposed by the infarction

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, pericarditis and effusion weeks after a myocardial infarction is post-MI (Dressler) syndrome. Necrotic myocardium releases antigens that trigger an autoimmune response with antibodies to myocardial proteins, leading to pericardial (and sometimes pleural) inflammation.

Takeaway: pericarditis 1–6 weeks after MI = autoimmune Dressler syndrome; pericarditis in the first few days = direct extension of necrosis.

whyNot.A: Extension of transmural necrosis causes early pericarditis within 1–4 days of the infarction.
whyNot.B: Purulent pericarditis would cause a sicker patient with sepsis and is uncommon after MI.
whyNot.C: Free-wall rupture occurs in the first 2 weeks and causes tamponade and shock, not a small effusion with fever.
whyNot.E: Uremic pericarditis needs renal failure, which is not described.

items.objective: Explain the autoimmune mechanism of post-myocardial infarction pericarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman is diagnosed with a 4-cm pedunculated left atrial mass attached to the fossa ovalis after an episode of transient visual loss in the right eye. She is in sinus rhythm. Cardiac MRI is consistent with a myxoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Long-term warfarin therapy and repeat echocardiography in 3 months

options.label: C
options.html: Surgical excision of the mass in the near term

items.explanationHtml:
A left atrial myxoma should be surgically excised soon after diagnosis, because it can embolize (as it already has) or cause sudden obstruction of the mitral orifice and death. Excision includes the stalk and a margin of the atrial septum to reduce recurrence.

Takeaway: diagnose myxoma, then remove it; there is no medical treatment.

whyNot.A: Anticoagulation treats thrombus; it does not prevent fragments of tumor from embolizing.
whyNot.B: Balloon valvotomy treats rheumatic mitral stenosis; passing a balloon across a myxoma could fragment it.
whyNot.D: Surveillance is wrong for a tumor that has already embolized; the risk of further embolism or obstruction is ongoing.
whyNot.E: Myxoma is benign; chemotherapy has no role, and percutaneous biopsy risks embolization.

items.objective: Choose prompt surgical excision for cardiac myxoma.

items.stemHtml: A 1-day-old boy is examined after a prenatal ultrasound showed three small echogenic masses in the ventricular walls. He is feeding well. Vital signs are normal. Echocardiography confirms three 6- to 9-mm intramyocardial masses with no inflow or outflow obstruction and normal ventricular function. An ECG shows sinus rhythm. In addition to evaluation for an associated genetic syndrome, which of the following is the most appropriate management of the cardiac masses?

options.label: A
options.html: Surgical resection during the neonatal period

options.label: C
options.html: Oral propranolol until the masses resolve

items.explanationHtml:
Multiple ventricular masses in a newborn are almost always rhabdomyomas, usually associated with tuberous sclerosis. They are hamartomas that typically regress during infancy, so asymptomatic, non-obstructive tumors are observed with serial echocardiography (and ECGs for arrhythmia). Intervention is reserved for obstruction, heart failure or refractory arrhythmia.

Takeaway: asymptomatic infant rhabdomyomas are watched, not removed.

whyNot.A: Surgery carries real risk and is unnecessary for tumors that usually regress; it is for hemodynamically significant obstruction.
whyNot.B: Transplant is not considered for asymptomatic tumors with normal function.
whyNot.C: Beta-blockers are not a treatment for rhabdomyoma and he has no arrhythmia.
whyNot.D: Radiation has no role for benign cardiac hamartomas in a newborn.

items.objective: Manage asymptomatic cardiac rhabdomyomas in infancy with observation.

items.stemHtml:
A 37-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue, intermittent fevers to 38.2°C (100.8°F) and a 4-kg weight loss. She has had two episodes of fingertip pain with discoloration. She takes no medications. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 88/min and regular, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. In the left lateral position there is a low-pitched early diastolic sound and a soft apical diastolic rumble, both of which are fainter when she lies supine. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Hemoglobin10.4 g/dL
MCV84 fL
Leukocytes8,900/mm3
ESR81 mm/h
Antinuclear antibodiesNegative
Blood cultures (3 sets, before any antibiotics)No growth at 5 days

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman-Sacks endocarditis

items.explanationHtml:
Constitutional symptoms, anemia and a high ESR with negative blood cultures, digital embolic events, and auscultatory findings of mitral obstruction that change with position in a patient in sinus rhythm point to a left atrial myxoma. The early diastolic sound is the tumor plop. Transthoracic echocardiography is the next test.

Takeaway: a culture-negative endocarditis picture with positional mitral findings is a myxoma until echocardiography says otherwise.

whyNot.A: Culture-negative endocarditis is usually explained by prior antibiotics or fastidious organisms, and its murmurs are regurgitant and do not vary with posture.
whyNot.C: Rheumatic mitral stenosis causes an opening snap and rumble that do not change with position and does not cause fever or a very high ESR.
whyNot.D: Lupus is unlikely with a negative ANA, and Libman-Sacks vegetations rarely obstruct the valve.
whyNot.E: Polyarteritis nodosa causes renal, neural and gut ischemia but not a diastolic sound or positional mitral obstruction.

items.objective: Diagnose left atrial myxoma from constitutional, embolic and positional auscultatory findings.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man had a left atrial myxoma excised 1 year ago; at that time a second, smaller myxoma was found in the right atrium. He has numerous small dark macules on his lips and eyelids and had a breast myxoma removed at age 20. Echocardiography today shows no recurrence. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: No further cardiac imaging because the tumors were fully excised

options.label: B
options.html: Lifelong warfarin to prevent tumor embolism

options.label: C
options.html: Prophylactic replacement of the mitral valve

options.label: D
options.html: Annual chest CT to screen for pulmonary metastases

options.label: E
options.html: Genetic counselling, testing for the familial variant, and screening of first-degree relatives

items.explanationHtml:
Multiple, recurrent or unusual-site myxomas in a young patient with spotty pigmentation suggest Carney complex (autosomal dominant, usually PRKAR1A). Patients need lifelong surveillance (cardiac imaging and endocrine screening), and relatives should have genetic counselling and testing, with echocardiography for those affected or untested.

Takeaway: familial myxoma syndromes require surveillance of the patient and screening of the family.

whyNot.A: Familial myxomas recur and new tumors appear, so imaging surveillance continues for life.
whyNot.B: Anticoagulation does not prevent tumor embolism and adds bleeding risk.
whyNot.C: The valve is not diseased; removing it does nothing to prevent new myxomas.
whyNot.D: Myxomas are benign and do not metastasize; chest CT screening is not indicated.

items.objective: Recommend genetic evaluation and family screening for suspected Carney complex.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man has a transient episode of left-sided weakness that resolves within 30 minutes. Brain MRI shows a small right frontal infarct. He is in sinus rhythm, and 30-day ambulatory monitoring shows no atrial fibrillation. Carotid imaging is normal. Transesophageal echocardiography shows an 11-mm mobile, frond-like mass on the aortic surface of the aortic valve without regurgitation. Blood cultures are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone for 6 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Observation with repeat echocardiography in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
A mobile, frond-like mass on the aortic valve of an older adult is most likely a papillary fibroelastoma. Because this one has already embolized (and is mobile and larger than 1 cm), surgical excision, usually with valve-sparing technique, is recommended to prevent further stroke.

Takeaway: excise a papillary fibroelastoma that is symptomatic or mobile.

whyNot.B: Negative cultures and the absence of fever or valve destruction make infective endocarditis unlikely; empiric antibiotics would not treat a tumor.
whyNot.C: Anticoagulation does not remove a tumor and has not been shown to prevent its emboli.
whyNot.D: Observation is reserved for small, immobile, asymptomatic lesions; this one has caused a stroke.
whyNot.E: The valve itself functions normally; excision of the tumor usually spares the valve.

items.objective: Choose excision for an embolizing papillary fibroelastoma.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer comes to the emergency department with 3 days of progressive dyspnea. Pulse is 124/min, blood pressure is 84/60 mm Hg and respirations are 26/min. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H2O. Heart sounds are faint. The systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mm Hg during inspiration. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low QRS voltage and beat-to-beat alternation of QRS amplitude. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypotension?

options.label: D
options.html: Pericardial tamponade from a malignant effusion

items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension, raised jugular pressure and muffled heart sounds with pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic fall greater than 10 mm Hg), low voltage and electrical alternans indicate cardiac tamponade. In a patient with lung cancer, the usual cause is malignant pericardial effusion from pericardial metastasis.

Takeaway: cancer + hypotension + JVD + pulsus paradoxus + electrical alternans = malignant tamponade; drain it.

whyNot.A: Constriction raises venous pressure but usually develops over months, causes a pericardial knock and Kussmaul sign, and rarely produces marked pulsus paradoxus or electrical alternans.
whyNot.B: Pulmonary embolism can cause hypotension and raised JVP, but not muffled heart sounds, low voltage or electrical alternans.
whyNot.C: SVC obstruction causes facial and arm swelling with distended neck veins but does not cause hypotension or pulsus paradoxus.
whyNot.E: Cardiomyopathy causes systolic heart failure with pulmonary congestion and an S3, not pulsus paradoxus and electrical alternans.

items.objective: Recognize malignant pericardial tamponade.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had pericardiocentesis twice in the past 6 weeks for malignant pericardial effusion causing tamponade. Each time, cytology showed adenocarcinoma, and the effusion reaccumulated within 2 weeks. She now has a moderate recurrent effusion with early right atrial collapse. Her oncologist plans further systemic therapy, and her performance status is good. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to prevent recurrence?

options.label: D
options.html: Repeated needle pericardiocentesis whenever symptoms recur

items.explanationHtml:
Malignant pericardial effusions often recur after simple needle drainage. For recurrent effusion in a patient with reasonable life expectancy, a pericardial window (often subxiphoid or thoracoscopic) allows continuous drainage into the pleural or peritoneal space and lowers recurrence; extended catheter drainage or sclerosis are alternatives in selected patients, together with treatment of the cancer.

Takeaway: recurrent malignant effusion → definitive drainage (window or prolonged catheter), not repeated taps.

whyNot.A: Diuretics lower preload and can precipitate collapse in tamponade physiology; they do not stop effusion production.
whyNot.C: Colchicine prevents recurrence of inflammatory pericarditis, not malignant effusion.
