whyNot.D: Repeated taps expose her to repeated tamponade and procedural risk when a definitive option exists.
whyNot.E: Pericardiectomy is a major operation for constrictive pericarditis and is not needed when a window can provide drainage.

items.objective: Choose a pericardial window for recurrent malignant pericardial effusion.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of the right arm and difficulty finding words. Symptoms resolve over 4 hours. She has had 2 months of fatigue and night sweats. She is in sinus rhythm with a pulse of 78/min. She has no hypertension, diabetes or tobacco use. Brain MRI shows two small acute infarcts in different left-hemisphere arterial territories. Carotid duplex ultrasonography is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to identify the source?
items.explanationHtml:
Infarcts in more than one territory with normal carotids suggest a cardioembolic source. In a young patient in sinus rhythm with constitutional symptoms, echocardiography (transthoracic first, transesophageal if needed) is the key test, looking for a mass, vegetation, thrombus or shunt.

Takeaway: embolic stroke in a young patient → echocardiography.

whyNot.B: Coronary angiography assesses coronary stenosis; it does not look for a source of cerebral emboli.
whyNot.C: Lumbar puncture is for suspected infection or hemorrhage; the MRI already shows ischemic infarcts.
whyNot.D: Lipids are part of vascular risk assessment but would not identify an embolic source.
whyNot.E: EEG evaluates seizures; her deficits are explained by infarcts.

items.objective: Order echocardiography for a suspected cardioembolic stroke in a young patient.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) Transthoracic echocardiography in the same patient shows a 4.5-cm mobile, lobulated left atrial mass attached by a narrow stalk to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis; it prolapses into the mitral orifice in diastole. The left atrial appendage is clear and the valves are structurally normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A large, mobile, lobulated mass on a narrow stalk arising from the septum near the fossa ovalis and prolapsing through the mitral valve is the classic appearance of a left atrial myxoma. Her constitutional symptoms fit IL-6 production by the tumor.

Takeaway: septal stalk + left atrium + mobility = myxoma.

whyNot.A: Thrombus forms in the appendage in atrial fibrillation or mitral stenosis; she is in sinus rhythm, the appendage is clear, and thrombus rarely has a septal stalk.
whyNot.B: Vegetations attach to valve leaflets, usually with fever, bacteremia and regurgitation; her valves are normal.
whyNot.D: Fibroelastomas are small (usually under 2 cm) valve-based fronds, not a 4.5-cm septal mass.
whyNot.E: Angiosarcoma is usually right atrial, broad-based and invasive, often with a hemorrhagic effusion.

items.objective: Distinguish atrial myxoma from other left atrial masses on echocardiography.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) The mass is excised with its stalk and a cuff of atrial septum; pathology confirms a myxoma. She has no skin pigmentation, no endocrine disease and no family history of cardiac tumors. Her fatigue and night sweats resolve. Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up?

options.label: B
options.html: Periodic transthoracic echocardiography to detect recurrence

options.label: C
options.html: Adjuvant radiotherapy to the atrial septum

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrence after excision of a sporadic myxoma is uncommon but does occur, usually from incomplete removal or multifocal disease, so patients are followed with periodic echocardiography. Recurrence is more likely in familial disease, which this patient's history does not suggest.

Takeaway: after myxoma excision, follow with echocardiography; no adjuvant therapy is needed.

whyNot.A: The embolic source has been removed; anticoagulation adds bleeding risk without benefit.
whyNot.C: Myxoma is benign; radiotherapy has no role.
whyNot.D: Myxomas do not metastasize; PET-CT staging is unnecessary and exposes her to radiation.
whyNot.E: Because recurrence can occur, some echocardiographic surveillance is recommended.

items.objective: Plan echocardiographic surveillance after excision of a sporadic myxoma.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman undergoes resection of a left atrial mass attached by a short stalk to the interatrial septum. The mass is soft, lobulated and gelatinous. Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Sheets of large polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm and prominent vessels

options.label: B
options.html: Stellate and spindle cells scattered in an abundant mucopolysaccharide-rich matrix

options.label: D
options.html: Papillary fronds with dense elastic cores covered by endothelium

options.label: E
options.html: Enlarged vacuolated myocytes with cytoplasmic strands radiating from the nucleus

items.explanationHtml:
A pedunculated, gelatinous left atrial mass attached to the septum is a myxoma. Histology shows scattered stellate and spindle-shaped myxoma cells, often forming cords or rings around small vessels, in a loose myxoid (mucopolysaccharide) ground substance with hemorrhage and hemosiderin.

Takeaway: myxoma = myxoma cells in a myxoid matrix, most often on the left atrial side of the septum.

whyNot.A: Clear polygonal cells in a vascular network describe renal cell carcinoma, which can reach the right heart along the inferior vena cava, not a septal left atrial tumor.
whyNot.C: Mature fat is a lipoma, which is usually a firm, yellow mass, not gelatinous.
whyNot.D: Avascular papillary fronds with elastic cores are a papillary fibroelastoma, which arises on valve surfaces.
whyNot.E: Vacuolated 'spider cells' are a rhabdomyoma, the typical cardiac tumor of children with tuberous sclerosis, found in the ventricular walls.

items.objective: Identify the histology of a cardiac myxoma.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man has 4 months of low-grade fever, fatigue, arthralgia and a 5-kg weight loss. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL, ESR is 72 mm/h and serum protein electrophoresis shows a polyclonal increase in gamma globulins. Three sets of blood cultures are negative. Echocardiography shows a 5-cm mobile mass in the left atrium. After surgical excision of the mass, all symptoms resolve. Production of which of the following substances by the mass most likely explains his systemic symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Cardiac myxomas secrete interleukin-6. IL-6 acts on the hypothalamus (fever), the liver (acute-phase reactants, hepcidin, so anemia of inflammation and a high ESR) and B cells (polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia). The constitutional syndrome resolves after the tumor is removed.

Takeaway: fever, weight loss and inflammatory labs with a left atrial mass point to IL-6 from a myxoma.

whyNot.A: IL-2 is a T-cell growth factor made by activated T cells; it is not the cytokine linked to myxoma symptoms.
whyNot.B: Interferon-gamma activates macrophages and drives granuloma formation; it does not explain this tumor-related syndrome.
whyNot.C: Erythropoietin excess causes polycythemia, not anemia; it is associated with renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyNot.E: Atrial natriuretic peptide is made by atrial myocytes in response to stretch and causes natriuresis, not fever or weight loss.

items.objective: Link the constitutional symptoms of cardiac myxoma to tumor secretion of interleukin-6.

items.stemHtml: A 3-week-old girl is evaluated after a fetal ultrasound showed several echogenic masses in both ventricular walls. Her examination shows three hypopigmented macules on the trunk. The cardiac masses most likely result from loss of a protein whose normal function is to inhibit which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple ventricular masses in an infant with hypopigmented (ash-leaf) macules are rhabdomyomas in tuberous sclerosis complex. Hamartin (TSC1) and tuberin (TSC2) form a complex that inactivates Rheb and so restrains mTORC1; loss of either causes hamartomas in heart, brain, kidney and skin.

Takeaway: cardiac rhabdomyoma in an infant suggests tuberous sclerosis, a disorder of unchecked mTOR signalling.

whyNot.A: Loss of the PRKAR1A regulatory subunit releases protein kinase A in Carney complex, which causes myxomas, not rhabdomyomas.
whyNot.B: Neurofibromin (NF1) is a Ras GTPase-activating protein; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not cause cardiac rhabdomyomas.
whyNot.C: Loss of APC unleashes Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and causes colonic polyposis, not cardiac hamartomas.
whyNot.D: Loss of PTCH1 releases Hedgehog signalling in Gorlin syndrome, which is linked to cardiac fibroma, not multiple rhabdomyomas.

items.objective: Connect cardiac rhabdomyoma with tuberous sclerosis and loss of mTOR inhibition.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man has a left atrial mass removed. He had a second cardiac mass removed 4 years ago. He has many small brown macules on the lips, eyelids and conjunctivae. At age 19 he had ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome treated with bilateral adrenalectomy. His father died suddenly at age 40. A germline loss-of-function variant most likely affects a protein with which of the following functions?

options.label: A
options.html: Catalytic subunit of a receptor tyrosine kinase

options.label: C
options.html: Regulatory subunit that holds protein kinase A inactive

options.label: D
options.html: Transcription factor that drives cardiac septation

options.label: E
options.html: Ubiquitin ligase that targets hypoxia-inducible factor

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent cardiac myxomas, spotty mucocutaneous pigmentation and ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome (primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease) define Carney complex, an autosomal dominant disorder usually caused by inactivating variants of PRKAR1A. Its product is the type 1A regulatory subunit of protein kinase A; without it, the catalytic subunit is constitutively active and cAMP-dependent growth signals are unrestrained.

Takeaway: familial, multiple or recurrent myxomas with lentigines and endocrine tumors suggest Carney complex (PRKAR1A).

whyNot.A: Activating receptor tyrosine kinase variants (eg, RET) cause MEN2, which does not include myxomas or lentigines.
whyNot.B: Loss of the Ras GTPase-activating protein neurofibromin causes neurofibromatosis type 1 with café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not myxomas.
whyNot.D: Variants of septation transcription factors such as TBX5 or NKX2-5 cause structural defects (eg, Holt-Oram ASD), not tumors.
whyNot.E: Loss of the VHL ubiquitin ligase causes von Hippel-Lindau disease with hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

items.objective: Recognize Carney complex and its PRKAR1A protein kinase A defect.

items.stemHtml: At autopsy, a 71-year-old man who died of respiratory failure is found to have multiple firm white nodules within the myocardium and a 300-mL bloody pericardial effusion. Which of the following is the most likely nature of these cardiac lesions?
items.explanationHtml:
Tumors involving the heart in adults are much more often secondary than primary. Multiple myocardial nodules with a hemorrhagic pericardial effusion in an older adult who died of a respiratory illness most likely represent metastatic carcinoma, for example from the lung.

Takeaway: the most common tumor of the heart is a metastasis; the pericardium is the layer most often involved.

whyNot.A: Myxomas are usually single, intracavitary and attached to the atrial septum, not multiple intramyocardial nodules.
whyNot.B: Angiosarcoma is the most common primary malignant cardiac tumor but is rare overall; it typically forms a right atrial mass rather than scattered nodules.
whyNot.C: Rhabdomyomas occur in infants and children with tuberous sclerosis.
whyNot.E: Lipomas are rare, usually single, soft and yellow, and do not produce bloody effusions.

items.objective: Recognize that metastases are the most common tumors of the heart.

items.stemHtml: An investigator reviews autopsy records to determine which cancers most often spread to the heart. Relative to how often each cancer occurs, which of the following primary tumors shows the highest rate of cardiac metastasis?
items.explanationHtml:
Lung and breast carcinomas and hematologic cancers account for the largest number of cardiac metastases because they are common and lie near the heart. In proportion to the number of patients with each cancer, however, melanoma metastasizes to the heart most often, frequently to the myocardium.

Takeaway: melanoma has the highest propensity for cardiac metastasis; lung and breast cancer give the most cases in absolute terms.

whyNot.A: Prostate cancer spreads mainly to bone (osteoblastic lesions) and rarely to the heart.
whyNot.B: Colorectal cancer spreads mainly to the liver by the portal circulation; cardiac spread is rare.
whyNot.C: Papillary thyroid carcinoma spreads to cervical lymph nodes and rarely to the heart.
whyNot.E: Basal cell carcinoma is locally invasive and almost never metastasizes.

items.objective: Identify melanoma as the cancer with the highest rate of cardiac metastasis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness and shortness of breath that occur when she sits up from lying down and resolve when she lies back. She is in sinus rhythm. On auscultation in the upright position there is a low-pitched sound shortly after S2 followed by a soft diastolic rumble. Echocardiography shows a mobile left atrial mass on a stalk. Which of the following best explains her symptoms when upright?

options.label: A
options.html: Compression of the left atrium by pericardial fluid

options.label: B
options.html: Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract by the anterior mitral leaflet

options.label: C
options.html: Reduced venous return from loss of sympathetic vasoconstriction

options.label: D
options.html: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

options.label: E
options.html: Intermittent obstruction of left ventricular filling at the mitral orifice

items.explanationHtml:
A pedunculated left atrial myxoma falls into the mitral orifice during diastole, especially when the patient is upright, and acts as a ball valve. Left ventricular filling falls, so stroke volume and cardiac output drop (lightheadedness), and left atrial pressure rises (dyspnea). The sound after S2 is the tumor striking the ventricle.

Takeaway: positional symptoms of mitral obstruction in sinus rhythm suggest a mobile left atrial myxoma.

whyNot.A: Pericardial fluid compresses the chambers in tamponade; it does not produce an early diastolic sound or a stalked atrial mass.
whyNot.B: Systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet obstructs outflow in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it causes a systolic murmur, not a diastolic rumble.
whyNot.C: Autonomic failure causes orthostatic hypotension but would not explain a mobile atrial mass or a diastolic rumble.
whyNot.D: She is in sinus rhythm, and an arrhythmia would not reliably appear and disappear with posture.

items.objective: Explain the positional obstructive symptoms of a left atrial myxoma.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has a mobile 3-cm mass attached to the interatrial septum on the right atrial side. Fragments of this mass are most likely to lodge first in which of the following vascular beds?
items.explanationHtml:
Material leaving the right atrium passes through the tricuspid valve and right ventricle into the pulmonary arteries, where it lodges like a pulmonary embolus. Only a right-to-left shunt (for example a patent foramen ovale) would let it reach the systemic arteries.

Takeaway: right-sided tumors embolize to the lungs; left-sided tumors embolize to systemic organs such as the brain.

whyNot.A: The middle cerebral artery is reached by emboli from the left heart or by paradoxical embolism through a shunt, which is not described.
whyNot.C: The renal arteries receive emboli from the left heart and aorta.
whyNot.D: Splenic infarcts follow left-sided emboli, as in endocarditis of the mitral or aortic valve.
whyNot.E: Mesenteric embolism originates in the left heart, most often from atrial fibrillation.

items.objective: Predict the embolic destination of a right atrial tumor.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old woman has a transient episode of right arm weakness and aphasia. Echocardiography shows a 9-mm mobile mass on the aortic side of an aortic valve cusp; the valve is not regurgitant. Blood cultures are negative. The excised lesion floats in saline like a sea anemone; microscopy shows branching avascular papillae with a dense elastic and collagen core covered by a single layer of endothelium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A small, mobile, frond-like mass on a valve of an older adult with an embolic event, made of avascular papillae with an elastic core and endothelial covering, is a papillary fibroelastoma, the most common primary tumor of the cardiac valves (aortic most often).

Takeaway: papillary fibroelastoma is a valve tumor of older adults that can cause stroke.

whyNot.A: Lambl excrescences are tiny filamentous strands at valve closure lines; they are usually under a few millimetres and are not a 9-mm frond-like tumor.
whyNot.B: Nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations are small sterile platelet–fibrin thrombi, usually in cancer or hypercoagulable states, without an elastic papillary structure.
whyNot.D: Calcific nodules are immobile, cause stenosis and are made of calcium and fibrous tissue.
whyNot.E: Myxomas arise from the atrial septum, not the aortic valve, and are made of myxoma cells in a myxoid matrix.

items.objective: Recognize papillary fibroelastoma as an embolizing valve tumor.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man has 2 months of dyspnea and chest pain. Echocardiography shows a large pericardial effusion and a broad-based, infiltrating mass in the right atrium. Pericardiocentesis yields bloody fluid. Biopsy shows irregular anastomosing vascular channels lined by atypical, mitotically active cells that stain for CD31 and ERG. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Angiosarcoma is the most common primary malignant cardiac tumor in adults. It usually arises in the right atrium, infiltrates the wall and pericardium, bleeds into the pericardial space and metastasizes early. The malignant cells are endothelial, so they form vascular channels and express endothelial markers such as CD31 and ERG.

Takeaway: an invasive right atrial mass with hemorrhagic effusion and endothelial markers is angiosarcoma.

whyNot.A: Myxomas are benign, pedunculated and usually left atrial, with bland stellate cells in a myxoid matrix.
whyNot.C: Lymphoma cells express leukocyte markers such as CD45 and CD20, not endothelial markers, and do not form vascular channels.
whyNot.D: Rhabdomyomas are benign ventricular hamartomas of children.
whyNot.E: Renal cell carcinoma has clear cells and epithelial markers and reaches the right atrium along the inferior vena cava.

items.objective: Identify cardiac angiosarcoma by site, behavior and endothelial markers.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of intermittent palpitations for 2 weeks. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, treated with lisinopril and metformin. She has no history of stroke, heart failure or valvular disease. Pulse is 92/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg. Her rhythm strip is shown. Echocardiography shows normal valves and normal left ventricular function. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, and the complete blood count is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to reduce her stroke risk?
items.explanationHtml:
The strip shows atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 4: age 65–74 years (1), female sex (1), hypertension (1) and diabetes (1). Oral anticoagulation is clearly indicated. In AF without a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban is preferred over warfarin because it causes less intracranial hemorrhage and needs no INR monitoring.

Takeaway: Nonvalvular AF with a high CHA2DS2-VASc score: start a DOAC.

whyNot.A: Aspirin alone gives little stroke protection in AF and is not recommended for this purpose.
whyNot.B: Dual antiplatelet therapy is less effective than anticoagulation and carries a similar bleeding risk.
whyNot.D: With a score of 4, her annual stroke risk is well above the threshold at which anticoagulation is recommended.
whyNot.E: Appendage occlusion is reserved for patients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation; she has no contraindication.

items.objective: Choose a DOAC for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman who emigrated from Guatemala 10 years ago comes to the clinic because of exertional dyspnea and palpitations for 1 month. She had several episodes of joint pain and fever as a child. Pulse is 108/min and irregularly irregular. Auscultation shows a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Echocardiography shows rheumatic mitral stenosis with a valve area of 1.2 cm² and an enlarged left atrium; left ventricular function is normal. Rate control is started with metoprolol. Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
items.explanationHtml:
She has atrial fibrillation with moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (valve area 1.5 cm² or less). This combination carries a very high risk of left atrial thrombus and embolism, regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc score. Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist) is the anticoagulant of choice; in a randomized trial in rheumatic heart disease with AF, a factor Xa inhibitor was inferior to a vitamin K antagonist. The other setting in which DOACs should not be used is a mechanical heart valve.

Takeaway: AF with a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis requires warfarin, not a DOAC.

whyNot.A: Factor Xa inhibitors performed worse than warfarin in AF with rheumatic heart disease and are not recommended in moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
whyNot.B: Dabigatran was harmful in patients with mechanical valves and is not used in moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
whyNot.C: Rivaroxaban was inferior to vitamin K antagonists in rheumatic heart disease with AF.
whyNot.E: Long-term low-molecular-weight heparin is reserved for special situations (such as pregnancy) and is not standard here.

items.objective: Select warfarin for atrial fibrillation associated with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with a prior anterior myocardial infarction is brought to the emergency department because of palpitations and confusion for 1 hour. He is pale and diaphoretic and answers questions slowly. Pulse is 178/min and regular, blood pressure is 74/42 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. An ECG shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia with a QRS duration of 0.16 s. A palpable carotid pulse is present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
A wide-complex tachycardia in a patient with prior infarction is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise. He has a pulse but is unstable (hypotension and altered mental status), so the next step is immediate synchronized cardioversion, with procedural sedation if it does not delay treatment. Synchronizing the shock to the QRS avoids delivering it on the T wave, where it could induce ventricular fibrillation.

Takeaway: Any tachycardia with a pulse that causes instability is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

whyNot.A: Adenosine is for stable regular narrow (or likely aberrant, monomorphic) tachycardias; it delays definitive therapy in an unstable patient.
whyNot.B: Amiodarone is an option for stable VT; with hypotension and confusion, electricity comes first.
whyNot.C: A calcium channel blocker in VT can cause cardiovascular collapse and is contraindicated for undiagnosed wide-complex tachycardia.
whyNot.E: Unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless VT or VF; with a pulse, an unsynchronized shock risks inducing VF.

items.objective: Treat unstable tachycardia with a pulse by synchronized cardioversion.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a pounding heartbeat that began suddenly while she was climbing stairs 40 minutes ago. She has had two similar shorter episodes that stopped on their own. Pulse is 196/min and regular, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. She is alert and has no chest pain. An ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. A modified Valsalva maneuver does not change the rhythm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
A stable, regular narrow-complex tachycardia with abrupt onset in a young patient is most likely paroxysmal SVT (AV nodal re-entry or AV re-entry). After vagal maneuvers fail, IV adenosine given as a rapid push followed by a saline flush is the next step. It terminates most AV node–dependent re-entry and, if the rhythm is actually flutter or atrial tachycardia, the transient AV block unmasks the atrial activity.

Takeaway: Stable paroxysmal SVT: vagal maneuvers first, then IV adenosine.

whyNot.B: Amiodarone is not a first-line drug for paroxysmal SVT and has more adverse effects.
whyNot.C: Digoxin acts too slowly to terminate SVT and is not recommended for it.
whyNot.D: Oral flecainide is not used to terminate an acute episode; its role is in chronic suppression for selected patients without structural heart disease.
whyNot.E: Cardioversion is reserved for unstable patients or SVT that does not respond to drugs.

items.objective: Choose adenosine after failed vagal maneuvers for stable paroxysmal SVT.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man comes to the clinic because of two episodes of near-fainting over the past week. He takes atorvastatin and no other medications. Pulse is 52/min and blood pressure is 138/76 mm Hg. Serum electrolytes and thyroid-stimulating hormone are within the reference ranges. His rhythm strip is shown; a 12-lead ECG shows a QRS duration of 0.13 s with a right bundle branch block pattern. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat ECG after an exercise stress test

items.explanationHtml:
The strip shows second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II: a constant PR interval in conducted beats with intermittent nonconducted P waves. With a wide QRS, the block is below the AV node. Mobitz II is unpredictable and can progress suddenly to complete heart block or asystole. With no reversible cause (no AV nodal drugs, normal electrolytes and thyroid function), a permanent pacemaker is indicated; his presyncope makes the indication even stronger.

Takeaway: Mobitz II without a reversible cause is an indication for a permanent pacemaker.

whyNot.A: The rhythm already explains his symptoms and is itself an indication for pacing; further monitoring only delays treatment.
whyNot.B: Theophylline can help some bradycardias after transplantation or spinal injury but does not treat infranodal block.
whyNot.D: Mobitz II is not benign; waiting risks syncope or sudden death from complete heart block.
whyNot.E: Exercise testing may help localize 2:1 block, but here the diagnosis and indication are clear.

items.objective: Recognize Mobitz type II AV block and its indication for permanent pacing.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after fainting at home. She is now drowsy but arousable. Pulse is 38/min, blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg, and her skin is cool and clammy. Her rhythm strip is shown. Serum potassium is 4.4 mEq/L. Two doses of IV atropine have no effect on her heart rate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
The strip shows complete (third-degree) heart block: regular P waves at about 90/min, an independent wide-complex escape rhythm at about 38/min and no relationship between them. She has hypoperfusion (hypotension, altered mental status, cool skin). Atropine often fails when the escape rhythm is wide, because the block lies below the AV node. When atropine fails, the next step is transcutaneous pacing (or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion) as a bridge to transvenous and then permanent pacing.

Takeaway: Unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine: transcutaneous pacing, then transvenous pacing.

whyNot.A: Adenosine causes AV block and would worsen bradycardia.
whyNot.B: Amiodarone slows conduction and could suppress the escape rhythm.
whyNot.C: Metoprolol slows the heart further and lowers blood pressure.
whyNot.D: Cardioversion treats tachyarrhythmias; it has no role in bradycardia.

items.objective: Escalate from atropine to pacing in unstable complete heart block.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman is admitted with pneumonia and delirium. She receives IV azithromycin, IV ondansetron for nausea and IV haloperidol for agitation. On day 2, she has several brief spells of lightheadedness. Telemetry recordings during the spells are shown. Between spells, she is alert, pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 124/70 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 3.9 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
The recording shows sinus beats with a markedly prolonged QT followed by polymorphic VT whose amplitude waxes and wanes: torsades de pointes. Three QT-prolonging drugs (a macrolide, ondansetron and haloperidol) are the likely cause. With a pulse and self-terminating runs, the first-line treatment is IV magnesium sulfate, which suppresses the triggering early afterdepolarizations even when serum magnesium is normal. All offending drugs should be stopped and potassium kept in the upper normal range. If she becomes pulseless, defibrillate.

Takeaway: Torsades de pointes with a pulse: IV magnesium, stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes.

whyNot.A: Adenosine has no role in polymorphic VT.
whyNot.B: Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and can perpetuate torsades.
whyNot.C: Lidocaine is used for some monomorphic or ischemic VT but is not first-line for torsades.
whyNot.E: Procainamide prolongs the QT interval and can worsen torsades.

items.objective: Treat drug-induced torsades de pointes with IV magnesium.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of rapid palpitations for 2 hours. He is alert and has no chest pain. Pulse is about 230/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. An ECG shows an irregularly irregular tachycardia with wide QRS complexes that vary in shape and width from beat to beat; some RR intervals are as short as 0.20 s. A previous ECG showed a short PR interval and a delta wave. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
This is pre-excited atrial fibrillation in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome: very fast, irregular, wide complexes of varying shape because impulses reach the ventricle through the accessory pathway. He is stable, so pharmacologic conversion with IV procainamide (or ibutilide) is appropriate; if he becomes unstable, synchronized cardioversion. Agents that block only the AV node can increase conduction down the accessory pathway and precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Catheter ablation of the pathway is the definitive treatment afterwards.

Takeaway: Pre-excited AF: procainamide or cardioversion; never AV nodal blockers.

whyNot.A: Adenosine blocks the AV node and can increase conduction down the accessory pathway, risking VF.
whyNot.B: Diltiazem slows only the AV node and can accelerate the ventricular response through the pathway.
whyNot.C: Digoxin shortens the accessory pathway's refractory period and blocks the AV node; it is contraindicated.
whyNot.D: β-blockers act on the AV node and do not slow pathway conduction; they are avoided in pre-excited AF.

items.objective: Manage stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation without AV nodal blocking drugs.

items.stemHtml:
An 80-year-old man has had several episodes of lightheadedness and one syncopal episode over 2 months, as well as intermittent palpitations. He takes no medications. Thyroid function and electrolytes are normal. Echocardiography shows mild left atrial enlargement and normal ventricular function. A 14-day ambulatory monitor shows the following:

FindingResult
Underlying rhythmSinus rhythm, mean 54/min
Longest sinus pause5.1 s, at the end of an atrial fibrillation episode (patient-reported dizziness at the same time)
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation11 episodes, 2 min to 3 h, ventricular rate 120–150/min
AV conductionPR 0.18 s; no AV block

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
This is sick sinus syndrome in its tachy–brady form: paroxysmal AF alternating with sinus bradycardia, and a symptomatic pause when the AF stops (sinus node recovery is slow). The symptoms correlate with the pause, so a permanent pacemaker is indicated. Pacing comes first because the rate-controlling drugs he needs for the AF episodes would otherwise worsen the pauses. He should also be assessed for anticoagulation (his CHA2DS2-VASc score is at least 2 from age alone).

Takeaway: Tachy–brady syndrome with symptomatic pauses: pace first, then control the tachycardia.

whyNot.A: β-blockers would lengthen post-conversion pauses and worsen syncope unless a pacemaker is in place.
whyNot.B: Flecainide can suppress sinus node function and should not be used without pacing here.
whyNot.D: An electrophysiology study adds little when monitoring has already linked symptoms to a pause.
whyNot.E: Tilt-table testing evaluates reflex syncope; the cause has already been documented.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic tachy–brady syndrome with a permanent pacemaker before rate control.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman had a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted 9 days ago for complete heart block. She now has fatigue and lightheadedness. Pulse is 36/min. A rhythm strip shows regular pacing spikes at 60/min; about half of the ventricular pacing spikes are not followed by a QRS complex, and there are long pauses. Serum potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.label: B
options.html: Failure to capture from lead displacement

items.explanationHtml:
Pacing spikes that are not followed by a depolarization define failure to capture: the device fires, but the stimulus does not depolarize the myocardium. In the first weeks after implantation, the most common cause is lead dislodgement (other causes: lead fracture, raised capture threshold from inflammation or fibrosis, hyperkalemia, some drugs). A chest radiograph and device interrogation are the next steps, and the lead is usually repositioned.

Takeaway: Spikes without capture soon after implantation suggest lead dislodgement.

whyNot.A: A 9-day-old generator is not depleted, and battery depletion usually reduces the pacing rate or causes missing spikes.
whyNot.C: Oversensing inhibits output, so you would see pauses without spikes, not spikes without capture.
whyNot.D: Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia causes fast paced rhythms, not bradycardia.
whyNot.E: Undersensing causes extra spikes falling on or near intrinsic complexes; it does not explain spikes that fail to capture.

items.objective: Distinguish failure to capture from other pacemaker malfunctions.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man collapses in the hallway of a cardiology ward 2 days after admission for a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. A nurse finds him unresponsive with gasping respirations and no carotid pulse, and starts chest compressions. The defibrillator pads show coarse ventricular fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Ventricular fibrillation is a shockable rhythm, and the single most important intervention is early defibrillation. Deliver an unsynchronized shock as soon as the defibrillator is ready, then resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check. Each minute of delay lowers survival.

Takeaway: Witnessed VF: defibrillate immediately, then resume compressions.

whyNot.A: Amiodarone is given after the third shock for refractory VF, not before the first.
whyNot.B: In shockable rhythms, epinephrine is given after the second shock; it does not replace early defibrillation.
whyNot.C: Airway management should not delay defibrillation; bag-mask ventilation is adequate initially.
whyNot.D: A defibrillator cannot synchronize to the chaotic signal of VF, and attempting it delays the shock.

items.objective: Prioritize immediate defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation.

items.stemHtml: The man receives a shock, and CPR is resumed. At the 2-minute check he is still in ventricular fibrillation and receives a second shock; IV access is established and epinephrine is given during the next cycle. At the following check, VF persists and a third shock is delivered. CPR continues. Which drug should be given now?
items.explanationHtml:
VF persisting after three shocks (with epinephrine on board) is refractory VF. An antiarrhythmic is now indicated: amiodarone as an IV bolus (lidocaine is an alternative). Epinephrine continues every 3–5 minutes, and high-quality CPR and shocks continue at each check while reversible causes are sought.

Takeaway: Refractory VF/pulseless VT after the third shock: amiodarone (or lidocaine).

whyNot.A: Adenosine is for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia and has no role in VF.
whyNot.C: Atropine is not part of cardiac arrest algorithms and has no effect in VF.
whyNot.D: Calcium is given in arrest only for suspected hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity.
whyNot.E: Bicarbonate is reserved for specific causes, such as hyperkalemia or tricyclic overdose, not routine VF.

items.objective: Give amiodarone for refractory ventricular fibrillation after the third shock.

items.stemHtml: After a fourth shock, the man has return of spontaneous circulation. He remains comatose and is intubated. Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg on a low-dose norepinephrine infusion. A 12-lead ECG shows 3-mm ST elevation in leads V1–V4. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Electroencephalography and neurology consultation before any cardiac procedure

options.label: D
options.html: Transthoracic echocardiography and repeat ECG in 6 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Withdrawal of life support because of poor prognosis

items.explanationHtml:
After resuscitation from cardiac arrest, ST elevation on the ECG indicates an acute coronary occlusion as the likely cause. Emergent coronary angiography with percutaneous coronary intervention is recommended, even when the patient is comatose. Temperature control (prevention of fever) and hemodynamic support continue alongside. Neurologic prognosis cannot be judged this early.

Takeaway: ROSC with ST elevation: emergent coronary angiography, whether or not the patient is awake.

whyNot.B: CT angiography is for suspected pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection; the ECG points to an acute coronary occlusion.
whyNot.C: Neurologic evaluation does not take priority over reperfusion, and coma right after arrest does not preclude angiography.
whyNot.D: Delaying reperfusion for 6 hours would let the infarct complete itself.
whyNot.E: Prognosis should not be determined until at least 72 hours after return to normal temperature.

items.objective: Refer a resuscitated patient with ST elevation for emergent coronary angiography.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man who runs competitively is found to have an irregular pulse during a preparticipation examination. He has no symptoms. Blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. A rhythm strip is shown. Where is the conduction abnormality most likely located?
items.explanationHtml:
The strip shows regular P waves, a PR interval that lengthens with each beat and then a P wave that is not conducted: second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach). The progressive delay reflects the decremental conduction of the AV node, whose recovery time grows with each successive impulse. In a fit young athlete, high vagal tone is the usual cause and the rhythm is benign.

Takeaway: Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat localizes block to the AV node, which is usually benign.

whyNot.A: Sinoatrial exit block drops whole P–QRS–T complexes; the P waves here keep marching regularly.
whyNot.B: Atrial muscle disease causes atrial arrhythmias such as fibrillation, not progressive PR prolongation with dropped QRS complexes.
whyNot.D: Block in the His bundle usually produces Mobitz II, with a constant PR before the dropped beat.
whyNot.E: Disease of both bundle branches gives infranodal (often Mobitz II or complete) block with a wide QRS, not Wenckebach periodicity.

items.objective: Localize Mobitz type I second-degree AV block to the AV node from its rhythm strip.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman has had several brief episodes of sudden, regular palpitations. Between episodes she feels well. Her resting ECG is shown. Which of the following best explains the shape of the QRS complex on this tracing?

options.label: A
options.html: Early activation of part of the ventricle through tissue that bypasses the atrioventricular node

options.label: B
options.html: Delayed activation of the right ventricle because of block in the right bundle branch

options.label: C
options.html: Slowed conduction through the atrioventricular node with normal ventricular activation

options.label: D
options.html: Ventricular depolarization starting in an ectopic focus in the left ventricle

options.label: E
options.html: Prolonged repolarization caused by reduced potassium current in ventricular myocytes

items.explanationHtml:
The tracing shows a short PR interval, a slurred initial upstroke of the QRS (delta wave) and a mildly widened QRS: ventricular pre-excitation. An accessory pathway of ordinary myocardium conducts from atrium to ventricle without the AV node's delay, so part of the ventricle depolarizes early and slowly by cell-to-cell spread. The rest of the ventricle is then activated normally through the His–Purkinje system, producing a fusion complex. Her regular palpitations are most likely AV re-entrant tachycardia using that pathway.

Takeaway: Short PR + delta wave + slightly wide QRS = an accessory pathway pre-exciting the ventricle.

whyNot.B: Right bundle branch block widens the terminal part of the QRS (rsR′ in V1) and does not shorten the PR interval.
whyNot.C: Slower AV nodal conduction lengthens the PR interval; here it is short.
whyNot.D: A ventricular ectopic focus produces a wide complex not preceded by a related P wave at a short fixed interval.
whyNot.E: Prolonged repolarization lengthens the QT interval; it does not change the initial QRS upstroke or the PR interval.

items.objective: Explain the ECG triad of ventricular pre-excitation by an accessory pathway.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman with recurrent symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and a structurally normal heart on echocardiography is started on an antiarrhythmic drug. During a follow-up exercise stress test, her QRS duration widens from 0.09 s at rest to 0.13 s at peak heart rate, then returns to baseline in recovery. The QT interval at rest is unchanged from before treatment. Which drug was she most likely given?
items.explanationHtml:
Class IC drugs (flecainide, propafenone) bind sodium channels strongly and dissociate slowly. At faster heart rates there is less time between beats for the drug to unbind, so block accumulates and QRS duration widens: use dependence. They have little effect on action potential duration, so the QT barely changes apart from the QRS component. They are used for rhythm control in AF only when there is no structural or ischemic heart disease.

Takeaway: Rate-dependent QRS widening with little QT change is the hallmark of class IC sodium channel blockers.

whyNot.A: Amiodarone mainly prolongs repolarization and the QT interval; it does not cause prominent use-dependent QRS widening.
whyNot.C: Lidocaine dissociates from Na⁺ channels very quickly, so it hardly widens the QRS in normal tissue; it is also given IV for ventricular arrhythmias, not AF.
whyNot.D: Sotalol (β-blocker plus class III) prolongs the QT interval and slows the heart rate rather than widening the QRS with exercise.
whyNot.E: Verapamil slows AV nodal conduction and lengthens the PR interval; it does not affect QRS duration.

items.objective: Identify use-dependent Na⁺ channel blockade by class IC antiarrhythmics.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy with profound hearing loss since birth loses consciousness while swimming and is pulled from the pool. He recovers after a brief episode of CPR. His parents are healthy and are first cousins. An ECG shows sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 0.56 s. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Gain of function of the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of function of a slow delayed-rectifier potassium channel

options.label: C
options.html: Mutation of the cardiac ryanodine receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of function of the L-type calcium channel

items.explanationHtml:
Congenital deafness, a long QT interval, autosomal recessive inheritance (consanguineous unaffected parents) and an arrhythmic event during swimming point to Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome. It results from loss-of-function mutations in both copies of the genes for the slowly activating delayed-rectifier K⁺ current (IKs). Less outward K⁺ current in phase 3 prolongs repolarization and allows early afterdepolarizations that trigger torsades de pointes. The same channel is needed to secrete K⁺ into the endolymph, which explains the sensorineural deafness. Adrenergic stress, such as swimming, is a typical trigger when IKs is defective.

Takeaway: Long QT + congenital deafness = recessive loss of IKs potassium current (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen).

whyNot.A: A sodium channel gain of function causes long QT type 3, with events at rest or in sleep and no deafness.
whyNot.C: Ryanodine receptor mutations cause catecholaminergic polymorphic VT with a normal resting QT.
whyNot.D: An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave), not a long QT interval.
whyNot.E: Loss of L-type calcium current would shorten, not lengthen, the action potential plateau.

items.objective: Relate congenital long QT with deafness to loss of the slow delayed-rectifier potassium current.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. He takes the maximum tolerated dose of a β-blocker, along with sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. He is in sinus rhythm at 82/min. A drug is added that lowers his resting heart rate to 66/min without changing his blood pressure or myocardial contractility. Which of the following currents does this drug inhibit?

options.label: A
options.html: Acetylcholine-activated potassium current in atrial cells

options.label: B
options.html: Fast sodium current in Purkinje fibres

options.label: C
options.html: Hyperpolarization-activated mixed sodium–potassium current in the sinoatrial node

options.label: D
options.html: L-type calcium current in ventricular myocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current in ventricular myocytes

items.explanationHtml:
Ivabradine selectively blocks HCN channels, which carry the "funny" current (If) responsible for much of the spontaneous phase 4 depolarization in the sinoatrial node. Flattening phase 4 lowers the sinus rate. Because it does not act on β receptors or on calcium channels in working myocardium, contractility and blood pressure are unchanged. It is used in symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction when the sinus rate remains high despite maximal β-blockade.

Takeaway: Ivabradine slows the sinus rate by blocking If (HCN channels) without negative inotropy.

whyNot.A: Opening, not blocking, the acetylcholine-activated K⁺ current slows the heart; vagal stimulation and adenosine act this way.
whyNot.B: Blocking the fast Na⁺ current (class I drugs) slows conduction and widens the QRS rather than selectively lowering sinus rate.
whyNot.D: Blocking ventricular L-type Ca²⁺ current would reduce contractility and blood pressure.
whyNot.E: Blocking I<sub>Kr</sub> prolongs the QT interval (class III effect) rather than lowering sinus rate.

items.objective: Identify the funny current as the target of ivabradine and its effect on SA node automaticity.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation is admitted to begin dofetilide for rhythm control. Her serum potassium is 4.3 mEq/L and magnesium 2.0 mEq/L. Two hours after the first dose, her corrected QT interval has increased from 0.44 s to 0.50 s. Prolongation of which phase of the ventricular action potential best explains this change?
items.explanationHtml:
Dofetilide is a pure class III drug that blocks the rapid delayed-rectifier K⁺ current (IKr). This current drives repolarization in phase 3, so blocking it slows phase 3, lengthens the action potential and refractory period and prolongs the QT interval. Excess prolongation can cause early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes, which is why dofetilide is started in hospital with QT monitoring and renal dosing.

Takeaway: Class III drugs block K⁺ efflux in phase 3, prolonging repolarization and the QT interval.

whyNot.A: Phase 0 is the Na⁺-driven upstroke; slowing it widens the QRS (class I effect).
whyNot.B: Phase 1 is brief early repolarization through the transient outward current; it contributes little to the QT interval.
whyNot.C: The plateau is maintained by balanced Ca²⁺ entry and K⁺ exit; I<sub>Kr</sub> block mainly delays the final repolarization that follows it.
whyNot.E: Phase 4 is the resting potential of ventricular cells and is not part of the QT interval.

items.objective: Link I<sub>Kr</sub> blockade by class III antiarrhythmics to phase 3 prolongation and QT lengthening.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 30 minutes of regular palpitations. Pulse is 186/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. An ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves. Vagal maneuvers are unsuccessful. A rapid IV bolus of a drug is given, followed by a 6-second pause and then sinus rhythm at 84/min. She has transient flushing and chest tightness. This drug terminated the tachycardia by which of the following actions?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocking β<sub>1</sub>-adrenergic receptors in the sinoatrial node

options.label: B
options.html: Blocking L-type calcium channels throughout the myocardium

options.label: C
options.html: Increasing potassium conductance in atrioventricular nodal cells

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibiting the sodium–potassium ATPase in cardiac myocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Prolonging repolarization of atrial muscle by potassium channel block

items.explanationHtml:
Adenosine stimulates A1 receptors in the AV node. Through Gi signalling it opens adenosine/acetylcholine-sensitive K⁺ channels (hyperpolarizing the cells) and reduces L-type Ca²⁺ current, causing a transient AV block lasting seconds. This interrupts re-entrant circuits that include the AV node, such as AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, the most likely rhythm here. Its very short half-life explains the brief pause and short-lived flushing, chest tightness and dyspnea.

Takeaway: Adenosine causes seconds-long AV nodal block via A1-receptor-mediated K⁺ efflux, terminating AV node–dependent SVT.

whyNot.A: β-blockers slow the sinus rate and AV conduction over minutes; they do not produce a seconds-long pause with flushing.
whyNot.B: Verapamil and diltiazem block L-type channels mainly in nodal tissue and act over minutes, without flushing and a pause.
whyNot.D: Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; it acts slowly and is not used to terminate acute SVT.
whyNot.E: Atrial K⁺ channel blockers (e.g., ibutilide) convert atrial fibrillation or flutter; they do not act within seconds through the AV node.

items.objective: Explain how adenosine terminates paroxysmal SVT.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has had palpitations and exertional fatigue for 3 weeks. Pulse is 75/min and regular. His rhythm strip is shown. An electrophysiologist plans a catheter ablation to cure this rhythm. Ablation at which of the following sites is most likely to be curative?

options.label: B
options.html: Cavotricuspid isthmus of the right atrium

options.label: C
options.html: Slow pathway near the coronary sinus ostium

options.label: E
options.html: Crista terminalis near the sinoatrial node

items.explanationHtml:
The strip shows regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min with 4:1 conduction: typical atrial flutter. Typical flutter is a macro-re-entrant circuit that runs around the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium. The narrow band of tissue between the tricuspid annulus and the inferior vena cava, the cavotricuspid isthmus, is an obligatory part of the circuit. A line of ablation across it blocks the circuit and cures typical flutter in most patients.

Takeaway: Typical atrial flutter circles the tricuspid annulus; ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus cures it.

whyNot.A: Pulmonary vein isolation targets the triggers of atrial fibrillation, not the right atrial flutter circuit.
whyNot.C: Slow-pathway ablation cures AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, which has no flutter waves.
whyNot.D: The outflow tract is a common origin of idiopathic ventricular tachycardia and premature ventricular contractions, not of atrial flutter.
whyNot.E: Foci along the crista terminalis cause focal atrial tachycardia with discrete P waves, not sawtooth macro-re-entry.

items.objective: Locate the circuit and curative ablation target of typical atrial flutter.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old man has had three episodes of sudden lightheadedness and one fall while shaving or turning his head to reverse his car. During monitored gentle pressure over the right carotid bifurcation, his rhythm shows a sinus pause of 4.5 seconds and he reports the same lightheadedness. The afferent limb of the reflex responsible for this response travels in which nerve?
items.explanationHtml:
This is carotid sinus hypersensitivity, an exaggerated baroreceptor reflex. Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus send impulses through the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The efferent limb is increased vagal outflow (slowing the sinus node and AV node) and decreased sympathetic outflow (vasodilation). Recurrent syncope from the cardioinhibitory form is treated with a pacemaker.

Takeaway: Carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents run in CN IX; the efferent bradycardia runs in CN X.

whyNot.A: The facial nerve carries no baroreceptor fibres.
whyNot.C: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue.
whyNot.D: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm and carries no baroreceptor afferents.
whyNot.E: The vagus carries the efferent limb to the heart here, and the afferents from the aortic arch baroreceptors, but not those from the carotid sinus.

items.objective: Trace the afferent and efferent limbs of the carotid sinus reflex.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man comes for follow-up of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction caused by ischemic cardiomyopathy. Ejection fraction is 30%. He has dyspnea when climbing one flight of stairs. Medications are sacubitril–valsartan, metoprolol succinate, dapagliflozin, aspirin, atorvastatin and furosemide 20 mg daily. Pulse is 64/min and regular, and blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. He has no edema, and the lungs are clear. Serum potassium is 4.1 mEq/L, and estimated GFR is 62 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
items.explanationHtml:
His guideline-directed therapy lacks one of the four mortality-reducing classes: a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Potassium below 5.0 mEq/L and eGFR above 30 make spironolactone (or eplerenone) appropriate, with potassium and creatinine checked within about a week and again during titration.

Takeaway: HFrEF needs all four pillars (ARNI/ACEi/ARB, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) unless contraindicated.

whyNot.A: Digoxin reduces hospitalisation for symptoms but not mortality; it is added after the four core classes when symptoms persist.
whyNot.C: Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm with a resting heart rate of at least 70/min on a maximally tolerated beta-blocker; his rate is 64/min.
whyNot.D: Amlodipine is neutral in HFrEF and would only be used for uncontrolled hypertension or angina; his blood pressure is controlled.
whyNot.E: Hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate is reserved for self-identified Black patients with persistent NYHA III–IV symptoms on optimal therapy or for those who cannot take any renin–angiotensin blocker.

items.objective: Add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist to complete guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation is admitted with decompensated heart failure. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%, new since a normal study 3 years ago. After diuresis, she is euvolemic. Pulse is 92/min and irregularly irregular; blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Current medications are apixaban, atorvastatin, diltiazem, empagliflozin and sacubitril–valsartan, which were started or continued during this admission. Which of the following medications should be stopped?
items.explanationHtml:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are negatively inotropic and worsen outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Rate control in HFrEF should use an evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or bisoprolol), started at a low dose once she is euvolemic; digoxin or amiodarone are alternatives when needed.

Takeaway: in HFrEF, swap diltiazem or verapamil for an evidence-based beta-blocker.

whyNot.A: Apixaban prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation; her risk score is high (age, female sex, heart failure), so it should continue.
whyNot.B: A statin is appropriate cardiovascular prevention and is not harmful in heart failure.
whyNot.D: Empagliflozin is one of the four mortality-reducing drug classes in HFrEF.
whyNot.E: Sacubitril–valsartan reduces death and hospitalisation in HFrEF and should continue.

items.objective: Recognise non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as harmful in HFrEF.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe breathlessness that began 2 hours ago. He has hypertension and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. He is sitting upright, sweating and speaking in short phrases, but he is alert and answers questions appropriately. Pulse is 118/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 196/108 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 87% on a non-rebreather mask. Crackles are heard over both lung fields. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and left ventricular hypertrophy without ST elevation. Intravenous furosemide and high-dose nitroglycerin have been ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional immediate step?
items.explanationHtml:
This is hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. In an alert patient who can protect the airway, CPAP or BiPAP improves oxygenation, reduces the work of breathing, lowers preload and left ventricular afterload, and reduces the need for intubation. Together with high-dose nitroglycerin and an IV loop diuretic, most patients improve within an hour.

Takeaway: hypoxemic cardiogenic pulmonary edema in an awake patient → noninvasive ventilation plus nitrates and diuretic.

whyNot.A: Intravenous beta-blockade in acute pulmonary edema can precipitate cardiogenic shock; the tachycardia is a response to hypoxemia and catecholamines.
whyNot.B: A saline bolus adds volume to a patient who is already flooded.
whyNot.C: Intubation is for patients who are obtunded, cannot protect the airway or fail noninvasive ventilation; he is alert.
whyNot.E: Routine morphine is not recommended: it depresses breathing and causes vomiting, and observational data link it to more mechanical ventilation.

items.objective: Use noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation for hypoxemic acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema in an alert patient.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 20%) is admitted with 1 week of worsening fatigue, orthopnea and poor appetite. He is drowsy but oriented. Pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 92/68 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H2O, there are bibasilar crackles, and his hands and feet are cool and mottled. Urine output has been 15 mL/h over the past 4 hours. Serum creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.2 mg/dL), and venous lactate is 3.4 mmol/L. Troponin is unchanged from his chronic baseline. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
He is 'cold and wet': congested (high JVP, crackles) with poor perfusion (cool, mottled limbs, oliguria, rising creatinine and lactate) and low-normal blood pressure. This low-output state needs an inotrope such as dobutamine (or milrinone) to raise cardiac output and renal perfusion, alongside loop diuretics once perfusion improves. Norepinephrine is added if he becomes hypotensive. Hold or reduce his beta-blocker during low-output decompensation.

Takeaway: cold and wet heart failure with borderline blood pressure → inotropic support (dobutamine or milrinone).

whyNot.A: Nitroprusside unloads the ventricle in warm, hypertensive patients; with a blood pressure of 92/68 mm Hg and hypoperfusion it risks hypotension.
whyNot.B: Phenylephrine is a pure α1-agonist; raising afterload further lowers stroke volume in a failing ventricle.
whyNot.C: He is volume overloaded; fluids would worsen congestion without improving pump function.
whyNot.D: Beta-blocker doses are held or reduced, not increased, during low-output decompensation.

items.objective: Treat low-output ('cold and wet') decompensated heart failure with an inotrope.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 6 weeks of breathlessness on exertion and swollen ankles. She has lost 6 kg despite a good appetite, sweats more than usual and feels jittery. Pulse is 128/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 146/52 mm Hg. Her skin is warm and moist, there is a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, and the upper eyelids lag on downward gaze. Jugular venous pressure is raised, and there is pitting edema to the mid-shins. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her heart failure?

options.label: C
options.html: Hypertensive heart disease with preserved ejection fraction

items.explanationHtml:
Weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, lid lag, warm moist skin, atrial fibrillation and a wide pulse pressure point to hyperthyroidism. Thyroid hormone raises heart rate and contractility and lowers systemic vascular resistance, producing high-output heart failure; atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate adds a tachycardia-mediated component. Check TSH and free T4, control the rate with a beta-blocker, give anticoagulation according to stroke risk, and treat the thyroid disease.

Takeaway: new atrial fibrillation with high-output failure and wide pulse pressure in a young adult → check thyroid function.

whyNot.B: Ischemic cardiomyopathy causes low-output failure with cool extremities, and there is no history of coronary disease or angina.
whyNot.C: Hypertensive HFpEF occurs in older patients with long-standing hypertension; her diastolic pressure is low and the features of thyrotoxicosis dominate.
whyNot.D: Constrictive pericarditis causes right-sided congestion with a normal-sized heart but no weight loss, tremor or lid lag.
whyNot.E: There is no history of heavy alcohol use, and alcoholic cardiomyopathy does not explain tremor and lid lag.

items.objective: Recognise thyrotoxicosis as a cause of high-output heart failure.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy returns 4 months after diagnosis. Since then, he has taken target doses of sacubitril–valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone and empagliflozin. He has dyspnea walking two blocks. Repeat echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30%. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 66/min with a QRS duration of 98 ms. He has no other serious illnesses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his risk of death?
items.explanationHtml:
An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death is indicated when the ejection fraction remains ≤ 35% with NYHA class II–III symptoms after at least 3 months of optimised guideline-directed therapy, in a patient expected to live more than a year. His QRS is narrow, so resynchronisation would not help.

Takeaway: EF ≤ 35%, NYHA II–III, ≥ 3 months of GDMT → primary-prevention ICD; add CRT only for wide QRS (especially LBBB ≥ 150 ms).

whyNot.A: A wearable defibrillator bridges the waiting period early after a new diagnosis or myocardial infarction; he has completed optimisation and now qualifies for a permanent device.
whyNot.C: Resynchronisation requires a wide QRS, ideally left bundle branch block of at least 150 ms; his QRS is 98 ms.
whyNot.D: Prophylactic amiodarone does not reduce mortality in this setting and has substantial toxicity.
whyNot.E: Delaying a device leaves him exposed to sudden death; his EF has not improved despite optimal therapy.

items.objective: Apply the criteria for a primary-prevention ICD in HFrEF.

items.stemHtml:
A 69-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has a follow-up visit. Two weeks ago, spironolactone 25 mg daily was added to sacubitril–valsartan, bisoprolol and dapagliflozin. She feels well, with no edema. Results are shown.

SerumBefore spironolactoneToday
Sodium (mEq/L)138137
Potassium (mEq/L)4.65.9
Bicarbonate (mEq/L)2523
Creatinine (mg/dL)1.11.3

An ECG shows sinus rhythm with no peaked T waves or QRS widening. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue all medications and repeat electrolytes in 3 months

options.label: D
options.html: Stop spironolactone and recheck potassium within a few days

items.explanationHtml:
Potassium has risen above 5.5 mEq/L after an MRA was started on top of an ARNI. Without ECG changes this does not need emergency treatment, but the MRA should be stopped (or halved, depending on severity) and potassium rechecked within days. Once potassium is back below 5.0 mEq/L, a lower dose can be tried with close monitoring; review diet and other potassium-raising drugs (supplements, salt substitutes, NSAIDs, trimethoprim).

Takeaway: potassium above 5.5 mEq/L on an MRA → hold or reduce the MRA and recheck soon.

whyNot.A: Leaving potassium at 5.9 mEq/L without action and waiting 3 months risks dangerous hyperkalemia.
whyNot.B: Lisinopril raises potassium just as much and would lose the survival advantage of an ARNI.
whyNot.C: Dialysis is for severe or refractory hyperkalemia, usually with renal failure or ECG changes; neither is present.
whyNot.E: Adding a thiazide to force potassium loss while continuing the cause risks volume depletion and electrolyte problems; holding the MRA is the direct fix.

items.objective: Manage hyperkalemia after starting a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist in HFrEF.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man had 4 months of palpitations before seeing a physician. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 150/min, and echocardiography showed a mildly dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30% and no regional wall motion abnormality. Coronary angiography was normal. He was anticoagulated, started on guideline-directed heart failure therapy and underwent successful cardioversion; he remains in sinus rhythm at 68/min. Which of the following best describes the expected course of his ventricular function over the next 6 months?

options.label: B
options.html: No change, because myocyte loss is irreversible

options.label: D
options.html: Improvement only after implantable defibrillator placement

options.label: E
options.html: Improvement only if the cause proves to be genetic

items.explanationHtml:
Persistent tachycardia (here, atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate) can cause a dilated cardiomyopathy that usually recovers substantially, often fully, within weeks to months of rate or rhythm control. Reassess the EF after a few months of sinus rhythm before deciding on device therapy; recurrence of the tachycardia can cause a rapid relapse, so ongoing rhythm surveillance is important.

Takeaway: tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is largely reversible once the rate is controlled.

whyNot.A: Progressive decline is expected in untreated or ischemic disease, not when the driving tachyarrhythmia has been corrected.
whyNot.B: The hallmark of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is reversibility; there is little permanent myocyte loss.
whyNot.D: A defibrillator protects against sudden death but does not restore ventricular function.
whyNot.E: Recovery depends on removing the tachycardia, not on a genetic cause; genetic cardiomyopathies tend to recover less.

items.objective: Predict recovery of ventricular function in tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension and type 2 diabetes comes for follow-up of heart failure. She has dyspnea when walking one block. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, an ejection fraction of 62% and raised filling pressures. She takes furosemide, amlodipine, lisinopril and metformin. She has no edema, and her lungs are clear. Blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg. Estimated GFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which of the following added drugs is most likely to reduce her risk of hospitalisation for heart failure?
items.explanationHtml:
In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) reduce the combined risk of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation, driven mainly by fewer hospitalisations. Other priorities are diuretics for congestion, blood pressure control, weight loss and treating atrial fibrillation and sleep apnea.

Takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors are a first-line drug class across the whole ejection-fraction range.

whyNot.A: Digoxin has no proven benefit in HFpEF and is mainly used for rate control or symptoms in HFrEF.
whyNot.B: Long-acting nitrates did not improve activity or quality of life in HFpEF trials.
whyNot.C: Diltiazem can be used for rate control in HFpEF with atrial fibrillation, but she is not in atrial fibrillation and it does not reduce HF hospitalisation.
whyNot.D: Ivabradine is indicated only in HFrEF with sinus rhythm and a heart rate of at least 70/min.

items.objective: Choose an SGLT2 inhibitor to reduce hospitalisation in HFpEF.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 1 year ago. Echocardiography now shows a dilated, thin-walled left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Compared with his ventricular function before the infarction, which of the following best describes the change in his left ventricular pressure–volume relationships?

options.label: A
options.html: Lower end-diastolic volume and a steeper end-diastolic pressure–volume curve

options.label: B
options.html: Higher end-diastolic volume and a steeper end-systolic pressure–volume line

options.label: C
options.html: Higher end-systolic volume and a flatter end-systolic pressure–volume line

options.label: D
options.html: Lower end-systolic volume and a flatter end-diastolic pressure–volume curve

options.label: E
options.html: Unchanged end-systolic volume and a higher end-diastolic pressure

items.explanationHtml:
Loss of contracting myocardium reduces contractility, which on a pressure–volume diagram is a flatter end-systolic pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR). For any afterload, the ventricle empties less, so end-systolic volume rises. The ventricle dilates to preserve stroke volume (higher end-diastolic volume), and the loop shifts right and narrows: ejection fraction falls.

Takeaway: systolic dysfunction = flatter ESPVR, larger end-systolic volume, right-shifted loop.

whyNot.A: A smaller, stiffer ventricle with a steep diastolic curve describes diastolic dysfunction (for example, hypertensive hypertrophy), not a dilated post-infarct ventricle.
whyNot.B: A steeper ESPVR means stronger contraction (for example, with an inotrope); this ventricle has lost contractile muscle.
whyNot.D: End-systolic volume rises, not falls, when contractility is reduced.
whyNot.E: End-systolic volume cannot stay the same when contractility falls at a similar afterload.

items.objective: Describe how systolic dysfunction changes the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship and ventricular volumes.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 2 weeks of worsening shortness of breath and leg swelling. Crackles are heard at both lung bases, and jugular venous pressure is raised. A serum peptide measured to support the diagnosis is markedly increased. Which of the following is the main stimulus for secretion of this peptide?

options.label: B
options.html: Low sodium delivery to the macula densa

items.explanationHtml:
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and its inactive fragment NT-proBNP are released by ventricular myocytes in response to increased wall stretch from volume or pressure overload. BNP acts through particulate guanylyl cyclase to raise cGMP, causing natriuresis, diuresis and vasodilation, which partly offsets renin–angiotensin activation.

Takeaway: BNP is a stretch signal from the ventricle; a normal level argues against heart failure.

whyNot.B: Reduced sodium delivery to the macula densa triggers renin release, not natriuretic peptide release.
whyNot.C: Carotid body hypoxemia sensing drives ventilation, not BNP secretion.
whyNot.D: Rising osmolality releases antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary.
whyNot.E: Sympathetic (β1) stimulation of juxtaglomerular cells releases renin.

items.objective: Identify ventricular wall stretch as the stimulus for BNP secretion.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction takes lisinopril, carvedilol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. His physician plans to replace lisinopril with a fixed-dose combination of an angiotensin receptor blocker and a neprilysin inhibitor, and tells him to wait 36 hours after his last lisinopril dose before starting it. The delay is intended to reduce the risk of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Rebound hypertension from abrupt loss of angiotensin blockade

options.label: C
options.html: Acute kidney injury from efferent arteriolar dilation

options.label: D
options.html: First-dose hypotension from natriuretic peptide excess

items.explanationHtml:
Both ACE (kininase II) and neprilysin break down bradykinin. Taking an ACE inhibitor together with a neprilysin inhibitor lets bradykinin accumulate and greatly raises the risk of angioedema, so the combination is contraindicated and a 36-hour washout is required. Sacubitril is therefore paired with an ARB (valsartan), which does not affect bradykinin breakdown.

Takeaway: never combine a neprilysin inhibitor with an ACE inhibitor; stop the ACE inhibitor 36 hours before starting sacubitril–valsartan.

whyNot.A: Rebound hypertension is not a recognised problem when an ACE inhibitor is swapped for an ARB-containing drug; the washout is about bradykinin.
whyNot.B: Hyperkalemia is a concern with any renin–angiotensin blocker plus spironolactone, but a 36-hour gap does not address it; potassium monitoring does.
whyNot.C: Renin–angiotensin blockade dilates the efferent arteriole whichever drug is used; the delay does not change this.
whyNot.D: Hypotension can occur with sacubitril–valsartan, but the mandated washout specifically prevents angioedema.

items.objective: Explain why an ACE inhibitor must be stopped 36 hours before a neprilysin inhibitor is started.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has taken spironolactone for 8 months. He reports tender enlargement of both breasts. Examination shows bilateral subareolar tissue. Serum potassium is 4.6 mEq/L. His physician wants to keep the survival benefit of mineralocorticoid receptor blockade. Which of the following is the most appropriate replacement drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor but also antagonises the androgen receptor (and increases conversion to estrogen), causing gynecomastia, breast pain and reduced libido. Eplerenone is a more selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with far fewer antiandrogenic effects, and it also lowers mortality in HFrEF.

Takeaway: spironolactone-related gynecomastia → switch to eplerenone to keep the MRA benefit.

whyNot.A: Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel and spares potassium, but it is not a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and has no proven survival benefit in HFrEF.
whyNot.B: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide that can help congestion but does not block aldosterone or improve survival.
whyNot.C: Torsemide is a loop diuretic for congestion with no mortality benefit from aldosterone blockade.
whyNot.E: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase and has no role in replacing an MRA.

items.objective: Choose eplerenone when spironolactone causes antiandrogenic adverse effects in HFrEF.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with long-standing heavy alcohol use comes to the emergency department because of 3 weeks of breathlessness and leg swelling. His diet has consisted mostly of white rice and alcohol. Pulse is 112/min and bounding; blood pressure is 128/48 mm Hg. His hands and feet are warm. There is pitting edema to the knees, and ankle reflexes are absent. Echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Deficiency of a cofactor for which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
This is wet beriberi: high-output heart failure from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, with peripheral neuropathy (absent ankle reflexes). Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase. Impaired oxidative metabolism leads to peripheral vasodilation, low systemic vascular resistance and a compensatory rise in cardiac output that eventually fails.

Takeaway: warm, bounding high-output failure in a malnourished drinker = wet beriberi; give thiamine.

whyNot.A: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase uses NADP<sup>+</sup>, not a vitamin-derived cofactor whose deficiency causes heart failure.
