whyNot.C: Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin; biotin deficiency causes dermatitis and alopecia, not high-output failure.
whyNot.D: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires vitamin B12; deficiency causes anemia and neurologic disease.
whyNot.E: Lysyl hydroxylase requires vitamin C; deficiency (scurvy) causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

items.objective: Link wet beriberi (high-output heart failure) to thiamine-dependent enzymes.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has had increasing ankle swelling for 2 months. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 52 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is raised, the liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, and there is a left parasternal heave with a loud second heart sound at the upper left sternal border. Which of the following is the most important mechanism of her cardiac findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Left ventricular systolic failure transmitted backward to the right ventricle

options.label: B
options.html: Volume overload of the right ventricle from tricuspid regurgitation

options.label: C
options.html: Hypoxic constriction of pulmonary arterioles raising right ventricular afterload

options.label: D
options.html: Right ventricular myocardial ischemia from coronary atherosclerosis

items.explanationHtml:
Cor pulmonale is right ventricular hypertrophy and failure caused by lung disease. Alveolar hypoxia constricts the pulmonary arterioles (a reflex unique to the pulmonary circulation), and loss of capillary bed in emphysema adds to pulmonary vascular resistance. The pressure-loaded right ventricle hypertrophies (parasternal heave, loud P2) and then fails (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, edema).

Takeaway: chronic hypoxemic lung disease causes pulmonary hypertension through hypoxic vasoconstriction, leading to cor pulmonale; correcting hypoxemia with oxygen is the key therapy.

whyNot.A: Left heart failure is the commonest cause of right heart failure overall, but here there is severe hypoxemic COPD, which by definition makes this cor pulmonale.
whyNot.B: Tricuspid regurgitation can develop secondary to right ventricular dilation, but the primary load is pressure from pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot.D: Right ventricular ischemia occurs with right coronary occlusion and presents acutely, not as gradual right failure in severe COPD.
whyNot.E: Polycythemia raises viscosity and may add to pulmonary vascular resistance, but it does not produce a high-output state.

items.objective: Explain how chronic alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with known mitral valve prolapse suddenly becomes breathless while lifting a heavy box. In the emergency department, he is in respiratory distress with diffuse crackles. A short, soft apical systolic murmur is heard. A pulmonary artery catheter is placed. Which of the following findings on the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure tracing is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Prominent y descent with a square-root sign

options.label: C
options.html: Steep x descent with a small v wave

options.label: E
options.html: Large v waves during ventricular systole

items.explanationHtml:
Rupture of a chorda tendineae causes acute severe mitral regurgitation. The left atrium has not had time to dilate and is non-compliant, so the regurgitant volume during systole produces a giant v wave on the wedge (left atrial) tracing and an abrupt rise in pulmonary venous pressure, causing flash pulmonary edema. The murmur is often soft and short because atrial and ventricular pressures quickly equalise.

Takeaway: acute MR = small stiff left atrium, giant v waves, sudden pulmonary edema, and a deceptively soft murmur.

whyNot.A: Absent a waves indicate absent organised atrial contraction (atrial fibrillation), not acute regurgitation.
whyNot.B: A dip-and-plateau (square-root) pattern with a steep y descent is the signature of constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.C: A steep x descent with a small v wave is the normal or tamponade-like pattern; regurgitation blunts the x descent and enlarges the v wave.
whyNot.D: Irregular cannon a waves occur when the atrium contracts against a closed AV valve, as in complete heart block; they are seen in the jugular venous pulse.

items.objective: Recognise the giant v wave of acute mitral regurgitation from chordal rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man comes to a rural emergency department with crushing chest pain that began 2 hours ago. ECG shows 3-mm ST elevation in V1–V5. The nearest PCI-capable hospital can be reached in about 150 minutes, including the time to arrange transfer. He has no history of bleeding, stroke or recent surgery. Blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. He has received aspirin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Transfer for primary PCI without other reperfusion therapy

options.label: B
options.html: Fibrinolytic therapy, then transfer to the PCI-capable hospital

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous heparin and observation until troponin results are available

options.label: D
options.html: Exercise stress testing once the pain resolves

options.label: E
options.html: Fibrinolytic therapy and discharge if the pain resolves

items.explanationHtml:
Primary PCI is preferred only if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact when transfer is needed. With an expected delay of about 150 minutes, symptoms for less than 12 hours and no contraindications, he should receive a fibrinolytic (ideally within 30 minutes of arrival) and then be transferred to a PCI centre: immediately for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails, otherwise for angiography within about 2–24 hours (pharmacoinvasive strategy).

Takeaway: STEMI with expected PCI delay over 120 minutes → fibrinolysis within 30 minutes, then transfer.

whyNot.A: Transfer alone means about 150 minutes without reperfusion while myocardium is being lost; the 120-minute window cannot be met.
whyNot.C: STEMI is diagnosed from the ECG; waiting for troponin wastes the time in which reperfusion saves muscle.
whyNot.D: Stress testing is contraindicated in an acute STEMI.
whyNot.E: After fibrinolysis, patients need transfer for angiography; discharge would be unsafe.

items.objective: Choose fibrinolysis followed by transfer when primary PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes comes to the emergency department because of 3 hours of intermittent chest pressure at rest. She is pain-free on arrival. Pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg. Lungs are clear. ECG shows 1-mm horizontal ST depression in V4–V6. High-sensitivity troponin I is above the 99th percentile and rises further at 2 hours. She has received aspirin. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous alteplase followed by a heparin infusion

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge home with an outpatient exercise stress test next week

options.label: C
options.html: A P2Y12 inhibitor, heparin and coronary angiography within 24 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Emergency coronary artery bypass grafting this evening

options.label: E
options.html: Treadmill exercise test within the next hour for risk stratification

items.explanationHtml:
Rising troponin with ischemic ST depression is an NSTEMI. She should receive dual antiplatelet therapy and parenteral anticoagulation (for example, heparin or enoxaparin), along with a high-intensity statin and a beta-blocker if there is no contraindication, and coronary angiography within about 24 hours (early invasive strategy). Immediate angiography (within 2 hours) is reserved for refractory pain, instability, heart failure or arrhythmias.

Takeaway: stable NSTEMI → DAPT + anticoagulation + early (≤ 24 h) invasive strategy; no fibrinolysis.

whyNot.A: Fibrinolytics give no benefit and add bleeding in NSTE-ACS, where the artery is not completely occluded.
whyNot.B: Discharging a patient with a confirmed NSTEMI is unsafe; she needs inpatient treatment and angiography.
whyNot.D: Bypass surgery may be chosen after angiography defines the anatomy, but not as an immediate step without it.
whyNot.E: Exercise testing is contraindicated with an active NSTEMI and rising troponin.

items.objective: Manage a hemodynamically stable NSTEMI with antithrombotic therapy and an early invasive strategy.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 1 hour of chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF and 1-mm ST elevation in V4R. After a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet given by paramedics, his blood pressure fell from 110/70 to 78/50 mm Hg. Pulse is 58/min. Jugular venous pressure is raised, and the lungs are clear. The catheterisation laboratory has been activated. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?
items.explanationHtml:
Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R, hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs indicates right ventricular infarction. The ischemic right ventricle depends on preload to push blood through the lungs to the left heart; nitrates (and diuretics) drop preload and cause the sudden hypotension seen here. Give IV fluid to restore preload while arranging urgent reperfusion; add inotropes if hypotension persists.

Takeaway: right ventricular infarction is preload-dependent: give fluids, avoid nitrates and diuretics.

whyNot.B: Diuretics reduce preload and would worsen hypotension; the lungs are clear.
whyNot.C: Nitrates caused the drop in blood pressure and must be avoided in RV infarction.
whyNot.D: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in hypotension and bradycardia.
whyNot.E: Morphine is a venodilator that lowers preload and can deepen hypotension.

items.objective: Give fluids, not nitrates, for hypotension from right ventricular infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man comes to the clinic because of 2 months of chest tightness when he walks fast. He had a drug-eluting stent placed in the left anterior descending artery 3 years ago. His resting ECG shows sinus rhythm with complete left bundle branch block, unchanged from 2 years ago. He walks with a cane but can walk on a treadmill. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to evaluate for ischemia?
items.explanationHtml:
Left bundle branch block makes the ST segments uninterpretable for ischemia. With exercise, the delayed septal activation and the high heart rate cause reversible septal perfusion defects in the absence of coronary disease (false positives), so vasodilator stress perfusion imaging (regadenoson or adenosine) is preferred in LBBB and ventricular pacing.

Takeaway: LBBB or paced rhythm → vasodilator (not exercise) perfusion imaging.

whyNot.A: ST changes cannot be interpreted with LBBB.
whyNot.B: Exercise perfusion imaging in LBBB often shows false septal defects because of the high heart rate and abnormal septal activation.
whyNot.C: Ambulatory ECG looks for arrhythmias, not exertional ischemia, and ST analysis is uninterpretable with LBBB.
whyNot.E: Calcium scoring estimates atherosclerotic burden in patients without known disease; he already has a stent and needs functional testing.

items.objective: Select vasodilator stress perfusion imaging for suspected ischemia in a patient with LBBB.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 30 minutes of substernal chest pressure. He took sildenafil 6 hours ago. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. ECG shows 1-mm ST depression in V5–V6. He has received aspirin. Which of the following drugs should be withheld at this time?
items.explanationHtml:
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown, and nitrates increase cGMP production; together they can cause profound, refractory hypotension. Nitrates should be avoided for 24 hours after sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil. Pain can be managed with the other anti-ischemic therapies.

Takeaway: ask about PDE-5 inhibitors before giving any nitrate.

whyNot.A: High-intensity statin therapy is appropriate early in ACS and does not interact with sildenafil.
whyNot.B: Anticoagulation is appropriate for suspected NSTE-ACS.
whyNot.C: An oral beta-blocker is reasonable when there is no heart failure, hypotension or conduction block.
whyNot.D: A P2Y12 inhibitor is part of standard ACS treatment.

items.objective: Avoid nitrates after recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman comes for follow-up 3 months after an NSTEMI treated with a drug-eluting stent. She takes aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin 80 mg daily, and she reports no adverse effects. She attends cardiac rehabilitation. Fasting LDL cholesterol is 92 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in lipid management?

options.label: E
options.html: Continue the current regimen and recheck in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
After an acute coronary syndrome she is at very high risk. Her LDL cholesterol remains at or above 70 mg/dL despite a maximally tolerated high-intensity statin, so a non-statin agent should be added. Ezetimibe is the usual first addition; a PCSK9 inhibitor is added if LDL remains above goal. Many current recommendations aim even lower for very high-risk patients.

Takeaway: LDL still ≥ 70 mg/dL on maximal statin after ACS → add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor.

whyNot.A: Simvastatin 40 mg is a moderate-intensity statin, a step down from atorvastatin 80 mg.
whyNot.C: Niacin added to a statin did not reduce cardiovascular events and causes flushing and hyperglycemia.
whyNot.D: Fenofibrate targets triglycerides and has not shown outcome benefit on top of statins for LDL reduction.
whyNot.E: Her LDL is above the threshold for adding therapy; waiting a year leaves risk untreated.

items.objective: Intensify lipid-lowering therapy with ezetimibe when LDL remains high on a maximal statin after ACS.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department of a PCI-capable hospital 70 minutes after the onset of severe substernal pain radiating to the jaw. He is diaphoretic. Pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. Lungs are clear. ECG shows 4-mm ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF. He has received chewed aspirin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Activate the catheterisation laboratory for primary PCI

options.label: B
options.html: Give intravenous tenecteplase in the emergency department

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat the ECG and troponin in 3 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Arrange urgent CT angiography of the chest

options.label: E
options.html: Perform transthoracic echocardiography before deciding on reperfusion

items.explanationHtml:
This is an anterior STEMI presenting early to a hospital that can perform PCI. Primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact is the preferred reperfusion strategy; give a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation around the procedure. Nothing should delay reperfusion.

Takeaway: STEMI at a PCI-capable centre → primary PCI, door-to-device ≤ 90 minutes.

whyNot.B: Fibrinolysis is the alternative only when timely PCI is unavailable; PCI is superior when it can be done promptly.
whyNot.C: Repeating tests delays reperfusion in a clear STEMI.
whyNot.D: CT angiography is used when aortic dissection is suspected; nothing here suggests dissection (no tearing pain radiating to the back, no pulse or blood pressure differential, no neurologic deficit).
whyNot.E: Echocardiography should not delay reperfusion of a diagnostic STEMI.

items.objective: Choose primary PCI for STEMI presenting to a PCI-capable hospital.

items.stemHtml: The patient underwent primary PCI with a drug-eluting stent in the proximal left anterior descending artery 64 minutes after arrival. Before discharge on day 3, echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 50% with mild anterior hypokinesis. He has no history of stroke, bleeding or liver disease, and he is not taking an anticoagulant. Which of the following antiplatelet regimens is most appropriate after discharge?

options.label: D
options.html: Aspirin plus ticagrelor for 12 months, then aspirin alone

options.label: E
options.html: Aspirin plus ticagrelor for 1 month, then no antiplatelet therapy

items.explanationHtml:
After an acute coronary syndrome treated with a stent, the default is dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel) for 12 months, followed by long-term single antiplatelet therapy. In patients with high bleeding risk, the DAPT course can be shortened, usually by stopping aspirin and continuing the P2Y12 inhibitor.

Takeaway: ACS + stent → DAPT for 12 months by default, then lifelong single antiplatelet therapy.

whyNot.A: Aspirin alone soon after stenting for ACS leaves an unacceptable risk of stent thrombosis and recurrent infarction.
whyNot.B: Single P2Y12 monotherapy from the start is not the default; it is used after a short DAPT course in selected high-bleeding-risk patients.
whyNot.C: Warfarin is not indicated without atrial fibrillation, LV thrombus or another anticoagulation indication, and it raises bleeding.
whyNot.E: Stopping all antiplatelet therapy after an ACS is dangerous; lifelong single antiplatelet therapy is required.

items.objective: Prescribe 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS treated with a stent.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has had crushing chest pain for 50 minutes. Pulse is 54/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. His ECG is shown. Occlusion of which of the following arteries is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
The ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF (greater in III than in II) with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL: an inferior STEMI. Most inferior infarcts are caused by occlusion of the right coronary artery, which in right-dominant hearts gives the posterior descending artery and the AV nodal branch; that explains his bradycardia.

Takeaway: inferior leads (II, III, aVF) → usually the right coronary artery; look for bradycardia, AV block and right ventricular involvement.

whyNot.A: Left anterior descending occlusion causes ST elevation in V1–V4 (anterior and septal wall).
whyNot.B: The circumflex can cause an inferior infarct in left-dominant hearts, but it usually produces more elevation in II than III and often lateral changes; the right coronary artery is far more likely.
whyNot.C: Left main occlusion causes widespread ischemia, typically diffuse ST depression with ST elevation in aVR, and usually shock.
whyNot.E: A diagonal branch supplies the high lateral wall (I, aVL), where this ECG shows depression, not elevation.

items.objective: Localise an inferior STEMI on the ECG to the right coronary artery.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman is admitted with an anterior myocardial infarction. She is treated medically because she arrived 30 hours after symptom onset. On day 5, she suddenly becomes hypotensive and pulseless with organised electrical activity on the monitor, and resuscitation fails. Autopsy shows hemopericardium and a tear through the anterior left ventricular wall. Microscopic examination of the infarct margin is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Wavy myocytes with no inflammatory cells

options.label: B
options.html: Macrophages engulfing necrotic debris with early granulation tissue

options.label: C
options.html: Dense neutrophilic infiltrate with intact nuclei

options.label: D
options.html: Mature collagen scar with few cells

items.explanationHtml:
Around days 3–14 after infarction, macrophages remove necrotic myocytes and granulation tissue begins at the margins, but collagen has not yet been laid down. The wall is at its weakest, which is why free wall rupture (causing hemopericardium and tamponade with pulseless electrical activity) typically occurs in this window.

Takeaway: rupture of the free wall, septum or papillary muscle occurs while macrophages are clearing the infarct, roughly days 3–14.

whyNot.A: Wavy fibers without inflammation are seen in the first hours, before neutrophils arrive.
whyNot.C: Neutrophils predominate at about days 1–3; by day 5 macrophages are taking over.
whyNot.D: A mature collagen scar takes weeks to months to form; a scarred wall rarely ruptures.
whyNot.E: Contraction band necrosis follows reperfusion of lethally injured muscle; she was not reperfused.

items.objective: Relate the timing of free wall rupture to the macrophage phase of infarct healing.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with an acute anterior STEMI undergoes primary PCI of the proximal left anterior descending artery 5 hours after the onset of pain. He dies 2 days later of an unrelated stroke. Microscopic examination of the infarcted myocardium shows hypereosinophilic myocytes crossed by dense transverse bands. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the bands?

options.label: A
options.html: Neutrophil release of proteases into the sarcolemma

options.label: C
options.html: Hypercontraction caused by calcium influx when flow was restored

items.explanationHtml:
Contraction band necrosis is characteristic of reperfused infarcts. When blood returns to myocytes whose membranes are already damaged, calcium floods in, causing irreversible hypercontraction of sarcomeres, seen as dense eosinophilic transverse bands. Reperfusion also generates oxygen free radicals and can cause hemorrhage into the infarct.

Takeaway: contraction bands = calcium-driven hypercontraction of lethally injured myocytes after reperfusion.

whyNot.A: Neutrophil proteases digest necrotic tissue but do not produce transverse contraction bands.
whyNot.B: Amyloid appears as amorphous pink extracellular material with apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining, not bands within myocytes.
whyNot.D: Collagen deposition occurs weeks later during scar formation.
whyNot.E: Fatty change of myocytes occurs with hypoxia or toxins and is seen as vacuoles, not bands.

items.objective: Explain contraction band necrosis as a feature of reperfusion injury.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man gets substernal pressure after walking briskly uphill. The pain resolves within 2 minutes of placing a tablet under his tongue. Which of the following effects of the drug contributes most to relief of his pain?

options.label: A
options.html: Dilation of coronary arterioles distal to the stenosis

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased heart rate through direct sinoatrial node inhibition

items.explanationHtml:
Nitroglycerin releases nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP in vascular smooth muscle. At usual doses it mainly dilates veins, pooling blood in the periphery. Lower preload means a smaller end-diastolic volume, less wall tension (law of Laplace) and less myocardial oxygen demand, which is the main way it relieves exertional angina.

Takeaway: nitrates relieve stable angina mainly by venodilation → lower preload → lower wall stress and oxygen demand.

whyNot.A: Arterioles beyond a fixed stenosis are already maximally dilated during ischemia; nitrates dilate large epicardial vessels and veins more than resistance arterioles.
whyNot.B: Nitrates cause reflex tachycardia, not slowing; ivabradine and beta-blockers slow the sinus rate.
whyNot.C: Nitrates have no positive inotropic effect; greater contractility would raise oxygen demand.
whyNot.D: Inhibiting thromboxane synthesis is the action of aspirin, which does not relieve an angina attack.

items.objective: Explain how nitrates relieve exertional angina by reducing preload.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed in the right coronary artery for NSTEMI 3 weeks ago and has taken aspirin and clopidogrel as prescribed. He now presents with an inferior STEMI, and angiography shows thrombosis within the stent. Genetic testing shows two loss-of-function alleles of a hepatic enzyme. Which of the following best explains the failure of therapy?

options.label: A
options.html: Reduced conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite

options.label: D
options.html: Increased hepatic clearance of the active form of clopidogrel

items.explanationHtml:
Clopidogrel is a prodrug that must be activated, mainly by CYP2C19, to a metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 (ADP) receptor. Carriers of two loss-of-function CYP2C19 alleles (poor metabolisers) form little active drug, so platelet inhibition is weak and the risk of stent thrombosis rises. Prasugrel (also a prodrug, but less dependent on CYP2C19) or ticagrelor (active as given) are alternatives. Strong CYP2C19 inhibitors such as omeprazole can have a smaller, similar effect.

Takeaway: CYP2C19 poor metabolisers cannot activate clopidogrel well.

whyNot.B: Aspirin's action does not depend on the hepatic genotype tested; it irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1.
whyNot.C: Receptor up-regulation is not the mechanism of clopidogrel non-response.
whyNot.D: Loss-of-function alleles reduce activation; they do not speed clearance of the active metabolite.
whyNot.E: Absorption is not affected by CYP2C19 genotype.

items.objective: Explain clopidogrel resistance in CYP2C19 poor metabolisers.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman who smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily has had several episodes of chest tightness that wake her between 4 and 6 AM and last about 10 minutes. She has no pain with exercise. During an episode in hospital, the ECG shows ST elevation in V2–V5 that resolves completely after sublingual nitroglycerin. Coronary angiography shows no stenosis. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the most appropriate long-term drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of β1-adrenergic receptors in the sinoatrial node

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of the late inward sodium current

options.label: D
options.html: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Rest pain in the early morning with transient ST elevation and normal coronary arteries is vasospastic (variant) angina. Calcium channel blockers (for example, amlodipine or diltiazem) block L-type channels in coronary smooth muscle and are first-line prevention; long-acting nitrates can be added. Smoking cessation is essential.

Takeaway: vasospastic angina → calcium channel blocker (± nitrate); avoid non-selective beta-blockers.

whyNot.A: Beta-blockade does not prevent spasm and non-selective agents may worsen it by leaving α-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed.
whyNot.B: Ranolazine helps chronic stable angina but is not the treatment for coronary spasm.
whyNot.C: Aspirin prevents thrombosis but has no antispasm effect; high doses may even worsen spasm.
whyNot.E: Statins are not the main therapy for vasospasm in a patient without coronary atherosclerosis.

items.objective: Choose a calcium channel blocker for vasospastic angina based on its mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with exertional chest pain cannot exercise because of severe knee osteoarthritis. He undergoes myocardial perfusion imaging after intravenous regadenoson. Perfusion in the territory of a 90% left circumflex stenosis decreases relative to the rest of the myocardium. Which of the following best explains this finding?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased myocardial oxygen demand from tachycardia caused by the drug

options.label: B
options.html: Constriction of arterioles distal to the stenosis

options.label: C
options.html: Dilation of arterioles in normally supplied regions while distal arterioles are already maximally dilated

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced cardiac output from AV nodal blockade

options.label: E
options.html: Platelet aggregation at the stenosis triggered by the drug

items.explanationHtml:
Regadenoson is a selective adenosine A2A receptor agonist that dilates coronary resistance vessels. Beyond a severe stenosis, autoregulation has already dilated the arterioles to maintain resting flow, so they cannot dilate further. Flow rises several-fold in normal territories but little in the stenotic one, creating a relative perfusion defect ('coronary steal').

Takeaway: vasodilator stress reveals stenoses by heterogeneity of flow, not by raising oxygen demand.

whyNot.A: Vasodilator agents cause only a modest rise in heart rate; they work by uneven flow, which is why dobutamine (not regadenoson) is the demand-raising stress agent.
whyNot.B: A2A stimulation dilates, not constricts, coronary arterioles.
whyNot.D: A1 receptor stimulation can slow AV conduction, but a selective A2A agonist rarely does so, and reduced output would lower perfusion uniformly.
whyNot.E: Adenosine-pathway drugs do not trigger platelet aggregation.

items.objective: Explain coronary steal during vasodilator stress perfusion imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old woman was admitted 4 days ago with an NSTEMI and treated with PCI. Her cardiac enzymes had been falling. This morning she has a new episode of chest pain with new ST depression in V4–V6. Which of the following results most strongly supports a new (re)infarction?

options.label: A
options.html: A troponin level that is still above the reference range

options.label: C
options.html: A raised serum lactate dehydrogenase level

options.label: D
options.html: A raised serum myoglobin level that has been present since admission

items.explanationHtml:
Troponin stays raised for 7–10 days after an infarction, so an elevated value on day 4 is expected and does not by itself show new injury. CK-MB returns to normal within 2–3 days, so a fresh rise on day 4 indicates new myocardial necrosis. In current practice, a new rise of more than 20% in serial high-sensitivity troponin values also supports reinfarction.

Takeaway: CK-MB normalises in 2–3 days, so a new rise detects early reinfarction; a single raised troponin does not.

whyNot.A: An elevated troponin on day 4 is expected after the original infarct; only a new rise above the falling baseline would be informative.
whyNot.C: Lactate dehydrogenase is non-specific and rises late; it is no longer used for infarct diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Myoglobin is non-specific and an elevation present since admission says nothing about new injury.
whyNot.E: AST is found in liver and muscle and is not specific for myocardial injury.

items.objective: Use biomarker kinetics to recognise reinfarction a few days after a myocardial infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia dies suddenly. Autopsy shows an occlusive thrombus in the proximal left anterior descending artery overlying a disrupted atherosclerotic plaque. Which of the following plaque features most predisposed it to disruption?

options.label: A
options.html: Thin fibrous cap over a large lipid-rich core with many macrophages

options.label: B
options.html: Thick fibrous cap with abundant smooth muscle cells

options.label: C
options.html: Extensive calcification of the plaque base

options.label: D
options.html: Small lipid core with dense collagen

items.explanationHtml:
Vulnerable plaques have a thin fibrous cap, a large necrotic lipid core and many inflammatory cells. Macrophages secrete matrix metalloproteinases that degrade the collagen of the cap, and T-cell interferon-γ inhibits collagen synthesis by smooth muscle cells. When the cap ruptures, the thrombogenic core (tissue factor, collagen) is exposed and an occlusive thrombus forms. Many culprit plaques narrowed the lumen only moderately before rupture.

Takeaway: plaque vulnerability depends on cap thinness and inflammation more than on the degree of stenosis.

whyNot.B: A thick, smooth-muscle-rich cap is the stable plaque phenotype, typical of chronic stable angina.
whyNot.C: Dense calcification tends to make plaques stable, though it marks the overall burden of disease.
whyNot.D: A small lipid core under dense collagen is a stable, fibrous plaque.
whyNot.E: Concentric medial hyperplasia describes hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (malignant hypertension), not a rupture-prone atheroma.

items.objective: Identify the features of a rupture-prone (vulnerable) atherosclerotic plaque.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated after fainting while sprinting during a soccer match. He recovered within a minute. His uncle died suddenly at age 30. Examination shows a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases with Valsalva. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T-wave inversions. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 32 mm, a resting outflow gradient of 25 mm Hg and an ejection fraction of 70%. Ambulatory monitoring shows no arrhythmias. In addition to advice about exercise, which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his risk of death?
items.explanationHtml:
This adolescent has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with several major markers of sudden cardiac death risk: unexplained exertional syncope, sudden death in a relative and massive wall thickness (30 mm or more). The only proven way to prevent arrhythmic death is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Takeaway: in HCM, an ICD (not antiarrhythmic drugs) prevents sudden death in patients with high-risk features such as unexplained syncope, family history of sudden death or wall thickness ≥30 mm.

whyNot.A: Antiarrhythmic drugs such as amiodarone do not reliably prevent sudden death in HCM and have cumulative toxicity in a young patient.
whyNot.B: Septal reduction treats symptoms from significant outflow obstruction (gradient ≥50 mm Hg despite drugs); it does not substitute for an ICD and his gradient is modest.
whyNot.D: Diuretics shrink the ventricle and can worsen obstruction; they do not reduce arrhythmic risk.
whyNot.E: Digoxin increases contractility and can worsen outflow obstruction; it has no role in preventing sudden death.

items.objective: Select ICD placement for primary prevention of sudden death in high-risk hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman has had exertional dyspnea and chest tightness for 6 months. She has mild hypertension treated with diet alone. Blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min. A grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border increases on standing. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy (19 mm), systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, a resting outflow gradient of 64 mm Hg and an ejection fraction of 72%. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is treated first with a non-vasodilating β-blocker. Slowing the heart lengthens diastole, which increases ventricular filling, and reduced contractility lessens the dynamic outflow gradient. A non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem) is the alternative; disopyramide, a cardiac myosin inhibitor or septal reduction follow if symptoms persist.

Takeaway: obstructive HCM → β-blocker first; avoid vasodilators and diuretics that shrink the ventricle.

whyNot.B: Thiazides reduce preload and can worsen obstruction; diuretics are used cautiously only for congestion.
whyNot.C: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are arterial vasodilators; lower afterload increases the outflow gradient.
whyNot.D: ACE inhibitors are vasodilators and can worsen obstruction; they are not first-line in obstructive HCM.
whyNot.E: Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, shrinking the ventricle and sharply increasing the gradient, sometimes causing syncope.

items.objective: Choose first-line pharmacotherapy for symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman comes for follow-up 8 months after developing heart failure 3 weeks after the vaginal delivery of her second child. At diagnosis, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 25% and coronary angiography was normal. She has taken guideline-directed heart failure therapy since then and now has no symptoms. Echocardiography today shows an ejection fraction of 40%. She asks about having another child. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling?

options.label: A
options.html: Another pregnancy carries no added cardiac risk because her symptoms have resolved

options.label: B
options.html: Another pregnancy carries a high risk of recurrent heart failure and death and is discouraged

options.label: C
options.html: Another pregnancy is safe provided she takes lifelong anticoagulation

options.label: D
options.html: Another pregnancy is safe if delivered by planned cesarean section at 37 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: The disorder is inherited in an X-linked pattern, so only a male fetus is at risk

items.explanationHtml:
This is peripartum cardiomyopathy: new systolic heart failure near the end of pregnancy or within months of delivery with no other cause. Recovery of ejection fraction is the strongest predictor of outcome in a later pregnancy. When the ejection fraction has not normalised, a subsequent pregnancy carries a substantial risk of further deterioration and maternal death, so pregnancy is discouraged and effective contraception is recommended. Even with full recovery, relapse can occur, so any later pregnancy needs specialist planning.

Takeaway: peripartum cardiomyopathy with persistent LV dysfunction → advise against further pregnancy; relapse risk is highest when the EF has not recovered.

whyNot.A: Symptom resolution does not mean recovery; her ejection fraction remains reduced, which predicts a high relapse risk.
whyNot.C: Anticoagulation addresses thromboembolism, not the risk of recurrent cardiomyopathy and heart failure.
whyNot.D: The mode and timing of delivery do not remove the risk created by the extra hemodynamic load of pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is not an X-linked disorder; the risk concerns the mother's heart in a future pregnancy.

items.objective: Counsel a patient with peripartum cardiomyopathy and persistent LV dysfunction about future pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had worsening dyspnea and leg edema for 3 months. He has drunk about 12 beers daily for 20 years. He has no chest pain. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is raised, an S3 is heard, and there is pitting edema to the knees. Echocardiography shows four-chamber dilation and an ejection fraction of 25%. Coronary CT angiography shows no coronary disease. Guideline-directed heart failure therapy is started. Which of the following interventions offers the best chance of substantial recovery of his ventricular function?
items.explanationHtml:
This man has alcohol-related dilated cardiomyopathy after excluding coronary disease. Alcohol is directly toxic to myocytes, and complete abstinence, together with guideline-directed therapy, can lead to marked improvement or normalisation of the ejection fraction. Support for alcohol use disorder (counselling and pharmacotherapy) is part of the treatment.

Takeaway: in alcoholic cardiomyopathy, total abstinence plus standard HFrEF therapy is the intervention most likely to restore function.

whyNot.A: A primary-prevention ICD is considered only if the ejection fraction stays ≤35% after at least about 3 months of optimised therapy (and abstinence); recovery is likely.
whyNot.B: Thiamine is reasonable in heavy drinkers, but thiamine deficiency gives a high-output state; supplementation alone will not reverse direct alcohol toxicity.
whyNot.C: Digoxin may reduce hospitalisation in selected patients but does not reverse the cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.D: Transplant is reserved for advanced heart failure refractory to therapy; active alcohol use is a contraindication.

items.objective: Identify abstinence as the key disease-modifying step in alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man is admitted with an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction that began 20 hours before arrival; he underwent PCI of the right coronary artery on day 1. On day 3, he suddenly becomes short of breath. Blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Crackles are heard throughout both lungs. A new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Abrupt pulmonary edema and hypotension with a new murmur days after infarction means a mechanical complication until proven otherwise (papillary muscle rupture, septal rupture or, less often, free wall rupture). Bedside transthoracic echocardiography is fast, available and distinguishes these.

Takeaway: new murmur + sudden deterioration after MI → urgent echocardiography.

whyNot.B: Repeat angiography looks for reocclusion but cannot show a ruptured papillary muscle or septum; echocardiography comes first.
whyNot.C: CT pulmonary angiography is for suspected pulmonary embolism; a new holosystolic murmur with pulmonary edema points to a cardiac mechanical cause.
whyNot.D: MRI is too slow and impractical in an unstable patient.
whyNot.E: Stress testing is contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure after infarction.

items.objective: Use urgent echocardiography to evaluate a new murmur with deterioration after myocardial infarction.

items.stemHtml: Echocardiography in the patient from the previous item shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet with an attached mobile mass consistent with a ruptured posteromedial papillary muscle head, and severe mitral regurgitation. The ventricular septum is intact. Despite intravenous furosemide, his blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg and he requires high-flow oxygen. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous metoprolol with close observation in the CCU

options.label: B
options.html: Medical therapy now, elective mitral valve surgery in 6 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Mechanical support as a bridge to emergency mitral valve surgery

options.label: D
options.html: Systemic fibrinolytic therapy and repeat angiography tomorrow

options.label: E
options.html: Diuresis and discharge with outpatient echocardiography in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Papillary muscle rupture with cardiogenic shock is a surgical emergency. Mortality with medical therapy alone is very high. The patient is stabilised with afterload reduction where blood pressure allows and with temporary mechanical support (such as an intra-aortic balloon pump, which lowers afterload and augments coronary perfusion) as a bridge to emergency mitral valve repair or replacement.

Takeaway: acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture → mechanical support as a bridge to emergency surgery.

whyNot.A: β-Blockers reduce contractility and would worsen cardiogenic shock.
whyNot.B: Delaying surgery for weeks is not survivable for most patients in shock from acute severe MR.
whyNot.D: Fibrinolysis treats thrombotic occlusion; it does nothing for a mechanical rupture and adds bleeding risk before surgery.
whyNot.E: He is in cardiogenic shock; discharge is unsafe and the lesion will not heal with diuresis.

items.objective: Manage post-infarction papillary muscle rupture with emergency surgery and bridging support.

items.stemHtml:
A 68-year-old woman is admitted 5 days after the onset of chest pain from an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction for which she did not seek care. Today she has worsening dyspnea and hypotension. A harsh grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur with a palpable thrill is heard at the left lower sternal border. A pulmonary artery catheter is placed. Oxygen saturation results are shown.

SiteOxygen saturation
Superior vena cava62%
Right atrium63%
Right ventricle81%
Pulmonary artery82%
Systemic artery94%

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A harsh holosystolic murmur with a thrill at the left lower sternal border days after an anterior infarction, plus an oxygen saturation step-up between the right atrium and the right ventricle, shows left-to-right shunting into the right ventricle: ventricular septal rupture. Oxygenated left ventricular blood enters the right ventricle, so its saturation exceeds that of the right atrium.

Takeaway: post-MI septal rupture = harsh LLSB murmur with thrill + O2 step-up in the RV; confirm with echocardiography and arrange closure.

whyNot.A: Papillary muscle rupture produces acute mitral regurgitation with tall v waves in the wedge tracing but no oxygen step-up in the right heart.
whyNot.B: Right ventricular infarction follows inferior, not anterior, infarction and causes hypotension with clear lungs and no shunt.
whyNot.C: Free wall rupture causes hemopericardium and tamponade, usually without a new murmur or a right-heart oxygen step-up.
whyNot.E: An aneurysm develops over weeks and causes heart failure or arrhythmias, not an intracardiac shunt.

items.objective: Interpret a right-heart oxygen step-up to diagnose post-infarction ventricular septal rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is in the emergency department with an acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He was given sublingual nitroglycerin by paramedics, after which his blood pressure fell from 112/70 to 78/50 mm Hg. Pulse is 54/min. Jugular venous pressure is raised to the angle of the jaw. The lungs are clear. A right-sided ECG shows 1.5-mm ST elevation in lead V4R. Transfer to the catheterization laboratory is under way. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for his hypotension?
items.explanationHtml:
Inferior infarction with hypotension, a raised jugular venous pressure, clear lungs, ST elevation in V4R and collapse after a nitrate means right ventricular infarction. The ischemic right ventricle depends on preload to push blood to the left heart, so a fluid bolus is the first treatment while reperfusion is arranged. Inotropes are added if fluids do not restore output.

Takeaway: RV infarction is preload-dependent: give IV fluids and avoid nitrates, diuretics and morphine.

whyNot.A: Diuretics reduce preload and would worsen hypotension in a preload-dependent right ventricle.
whyNot.C: Morphine causes venodilation and lowers preload, deepening hypotension.
whyNot.D: β-Blockers worsen hypotension and bradycardia; they are contraindicated in shock and heart block.
whyNot.E: Further nitrate would repeat the venodilation that caused the drop in pressure.

items.objective: Treat hypotension in right ventricular infarction with volume rather than preload-lowering drugs.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man comes for review 6 weeks after a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with delayed PCI of the left anterior descending artery. He takes aspirin, ticagrelor, a high-intensity statin, metoprolol and sacubitril–valsartan. ECG shows persistent ST elevation with Q waves in V1–V4. Echocardiography shows a thin, dyskinetic apex with a wide neck, an ejection fraction of 35% and a 1.6-cm laminated echodensity attached to the apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent ST elevation weeks after infarction with a thin, dyskinetic, wide-necked apical segment describes a true left ventricular aneurysm. The stagnant blood in the aneurysm has produced a left ventricular thrombus, which carries a risk of stroke and systemic embolism. Oral anticoagulation is added (typically for at least about 3 months, then reassessed with imaging), with careful review of the antiplatelet regimen to limit bleeding.

Takeaway: post-MI LV thrombus → oral anticoagulation; persistent ST elevation weeks after MI suggests an aneurysm.

whyNot.B: Higher-dose aspirin does not treat an established ventricular thrombus and raises bleeding risk.
whyNot.C: Fibrinolysis can fragment the thrombus and cause embolism and bleeding; it is not used for LV thrombus.
whyNot.D: Resection of a true aneurysm is reserved for refractory heart failure or ventricular arrhythmia, not as an emergency for thrombus.
whyNot.E: A short course of heparin does not provide the months of anticoagulation needed for thrombus resolution.

items.objective: Manage left ventricular thrombus in a post-infarction aneurysm with oral anticoagulation.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college soccer player was hospitalised 3 weeks ago with chest pain, troponin elevation and a cardiac MRI diagnosis of acute myocarditis after a viral illness. His ejection fraction was 50% and recovered to 60% before discharge. He has no symptoms and wants to return to competitive training next week. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Return to full competition now, as his ejection fraction is normal

options.label: B
options.html: Return once a repeat troponin is normal, without further testing

options.label: C
options.html: No competitive sport for 3–6 months, then reassessment before return

options.label: D
options.html: Permanent disqualification from all competitive sports

options.label: E
options.html: Defibrillator implantation before any return to competitive sport

items.explanationHtml:
After acute myocarditis, athletes should refrain from competitive sports and strenuous exercise for about 3–6 months. Return is allowed when ventricular function and biomarkers have normalised and there are no clinically relevant arrhythmias on ambulatory monitoring and exercise testing. Persistent inflammation increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death during exertion.

Takeaway: myocarditis → no competitive sport for 3–6 months, then return only after normal reassessment.

whyNot.A: A normal ejection fraction does not exclude ongoing inflammation and arrhythmic risk in the first months.
whyNot.B: A single normal troponin is not enough; rhythm monitoring and exercise testing are needed after a period of rest.
whyNot.D: Most athletes can return after recovery; permanent restriction is not indicated with complete recovery.
whyNot.E: An ICD is not indicated in recovered myocarditis without sustained ventricular arrhythmia or other high-risk features.

items.objective: Advise on return to competitive sport after acute myocarditis.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old man has heart failure with an ejection fraction of 50%, a left ventricular wall thickness of 18 mm and low-voltage QRS complexes on ECG. Serum free light chain ratio is normal, and serum and urine immunofixation show no monoclonal protein. Technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy shows intense myocardial uptake (grade 3). Genetic testing shows no variant in the transthyretin gene. His congestion is controlled with furosemide. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Strong bone-tracer uptake in the absence of a monoclonal protein establishes wild-type transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy without biopsy. A transthyretin stabiliser such as tafamidis binds the transthyretin tetramer, prevents its dissociation into amyloidogenic monomers, and reduces mortality and heart failure hospitalisations. Diuretics manage congestion.

Takeaway: ATTR cardiomyopathy (positive bone scan, no monoclonal protein) → transthyretin stabiliser plus diuretics.

whyNot.A: Plasma-cell–directed chemotherapy treats AL amyloidosis, which has been excluded.
whyNot.B: Digoxin binds amyloid fibrils and can cause toxicity; it does not slow disease progression.
whyNot.C: Mavacamten reduces contractility in obstructive HCM and would be harmful in amyloid cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.E: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers bind amyloid fibrils and can cause heart block and profound hypotension.

items.objective: Select disease-modifying therapy for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy collapses and dies while playing basketball. He had no known illness. His father died suddenly at age 38. At autopsy, the heart weighs 520 g (normal for age and size, about 300 g). The interventricular septum is 28 mm thick, and the left ventricular cavity is small. Microscopy of the septum shows disorganized, branching myocytes with interstitial fibrosis. A pathogenic variant in the gene for which of the following proteins is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with myocyte disarray, sudden exertional death in a young athlete and an autosomal dominant family history define hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It is a disease of the sarcomere; the most commonly affected genes encode β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) and cardiac myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3).

Takeaway: HCM = autosomal dominant sarcomere gene variant → myocyte disarray, asymmetric septal hypertrophy and risk of exertional sudden death.

whyNot.A: Dystrophin defects (Duchenne, Becker) cause a dilated, not hypertrophic, cardiomyopathy along with skeletal muscle weakness.
whyNot.C: Fibrillin-1 variants cause Marfan syndrome: aortic root dilation and mitral valve prolapse, not septal hypertrophy with disarray.
whyNot.D: Lamin A/C variants cause dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disease.
whyNot.E: Transthyretin causes amyloid cardiomyopathy in older adults; the walls are thick from extracellular amyloid, not myocyte disarray.

items.objective: Identify the sarcomere protein defect underlying hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for exertional lightheadedness. A grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border without radiation to the carotids. The murmur becomes louder when he stands up from a squatting position. Echocardiography shows a 21-mm-thick interventricular septum and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Which of the following manoeuvres is most likely to decrease the intensity of his murmur?

options.label: B
options.html: Strain phase of the Valsalva manoeuvre

items.explanationHtml:
In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, outflow obstruction is dynamic: it worsens when the left ventricle is smaller. Sustained handgrip raises systemic vascular resistance (afterload); the ventricle empties less completely and stays larger, so the septum and mitral leaflet are held further apart and the murmur softens.

Takeaway: anything that enlarges the LV (handgrip, squatting, leg raise) softens the HCM murmur; anything that shrinks it (Valsalva, standing, vasodilators) makes it louder.

whyNot.B: Valsalva strain reduces venous return and left ventricular volume, which worsens obstruction and makes the murmur louder.
whyNot.C: Amyl nitrite is a vasodilator that lowers afterload and preload, shrinking the ventricle and increasing the murmur.
whyNot.D: Nitroglycerin reduces preload (venodilation), so the ventricle is smaller and the outflow gradient rises.
whyNot.E: Abrupt standing pools blood in the legs, reducing preload and increasing the murmur, as in this patient's history.

items.objective: Predict how manoeuvres that change ventricular volume alter the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old woman develops crushing chest pain 2 hours after learning that her son has died in a car crash. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V2–V5. Serum troponin is raised. Emergency coronary angiography shows no stenosis greater than 30%. Left ventriculography shows akinesis and ballooning of the apex with hyperdynamic contraction of the basal segments. Six weeks later, echocardiography is normal. Which of the following best explains her ventricular dysfunction?

options.label: A
options.html: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with spontaneous thrombolysis

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden emotional stress, an ACS-like presentation, nonobstructed coronaries, apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis and full recovery within weeks describe takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy. A surge of catecholamines produces reversible myocardial stunning; the apex, with its high density of β-adrenergic receptors, is most affected.

Takeaway: takotsubo = stress-triggered catecholamine surge → transient apical ballooning with normal coronaries; recovery in weeks.

whyNot.A: Plaque rupture would leave a culprit lesion and a wall-motion defect matching one coronary territory, not apical ballooning that extends beyond a single territory with normal arteries.
whyNot.C: Lymphocytic myocarditis usually follows a viral illness and does not produce this regional apical pattern triggered by emotional stress.
whyNot.D: Spontaneous coronary dissection is visible on angiography as an intimal flap or long smooth narrowing; the arteries here were essentially normal.
whyNot.E: Amyloid deposition causes progressive restrictive disease, not an abrupt, fully reversible apical wall-motion abnormality.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism and course of takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man who grew up in a rural village in Bolivia comes to the clinic because of progressive dyspnea and leg swelling for 6 months. He also reports difficulty swallowing solid food for several years. ECG shows right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30% and a thin-walled apical aneurysm. Coronary angiography is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his heart disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi transmitted by triatomine (reduviid) bugs in rural Latin America, can appear decades after infection. Its cardiomyopathy classically causes conduction disease (right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block), dilated cardiomyopathy and an apical aneurysm. Destruction of enteric neurons explains megaesophagus (dysphagia) and megacolon.

Takeaway: heart failure + RBBB + apical aneurysm + dysphagia in someone from rural Latin America = chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy.

whyNot.A: Coxsackie B causes acute viral myocarditis that can progress to DCM, but not the combination of apical aneurysm, fascicular block and megaesophagus.
whyNot.B: Lyme carditis mainly causes fluctuating AV block, is usually acute and reversible, and is acquired in North America and Europe.
whyNot.C: Toxoplasma myocarditis is rare and mainly seen in severely immunocompromised patients; it does not cause megaesophagus.
whyNot.D: Trypanosoma brucei causes African sleeping sickness, a neurologic illness transmitted by the tsetse fly.

items.objective: Recognise chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy and its causative organism.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man has worsening exertional dyspnea and ankle swelling. He had carpal tunnel release in both wrists 8 years ago. Blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is raised. ECG shows low QRS voltage in the limb leads. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular wall thickening to 17 mm, biatrial enlargement and an ejection fraction of 55%. Serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chains are normal. An endomyocardial biopsy shows extracellular material with apple-green birefringence after Congo red staining. This material is most likely derived from which of the following proteins?
items.explanationHtml:
An older man with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, thick walls but low ECG voltage, a history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and no monoclonal protein most likely has wild-type transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid cardiomyopathy. Misfolded transthyretin, a liver-made transport protein for thyroxine and retinol, deposits as amyloid fibrils in the myocardium and in the carpal ligaments.

Takeaway: thick walls + low voltage + carpal tunnel history in an older man with no monoclonal protein = ATTR amyloid cardiomyopathy.

whyNot.A: AL amyloid comes from a plasma-cell clone; normal free light chains and immunofixation make it unlikely.
whyNot.B: Serum amyloid A deposits (AA amyloidosis) follow chronic inflammation and mainly affect the kidneys.
whyNot.C: β<sub>2</sub>-Microglobulin amyloid occurs with long-term dialysis and involves joints and carpal tunnels, not usually the heart.
whyNot.E: Isolated atrial amyloid from atrial natriuretic peptide is confined to the atria and does not thicken the ventricular walls.

items.objective: Identify the precursor protein in senile (wild-type transthyretin) cardiac amyloidosis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man is admitted with an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction that began 14 hours earlier. On day 4, he suddenly becomes dyspneic. Blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over both lungs, and a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Rupture of a structure supplied by which of the following arteries most likely caused this deterioration?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden pulmonary edema with a new apical holosystolic murmur several days after infarction indicates papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation. The posteromedial papillary muscle is affected far more often because it usually depends on a single artery, the posterior descending artery (from the right coronary artery in right-dominant hearts), the vessel involved in inferior infarction. The anterolateral muscle has a dual supply from the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries.

Takeaway: inferior MI → posteromedial papillary muscle (single supply from the PDA) → rupture with acute MR at days 2–7.

whyNot.A: The LAD supplies the anterior wall and septum and contributes to the anterolateral papillary muscle, which has a dual supply and rarely ruptures.
whyNot.B: The circumflex contributes to the anterolateral muscle; dual supply protects it.
whyNot.C: The sinoatrial nodal artery supplies the SA node and nearby atrium; its loss causes sinus node dysfunction, not mitral regurgitation.
whyNot.D: The acute marginal artery supplies the right ventricular free wall, not a mitral papillary muscle.

items.objective: Relate post-infarction papillary muscle rupture to coronary anatomy.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman is found unresponsive at home 6 days after being discharged following a large anterior myocardial infarction for which she presented late. Resuscitation fails. Autopsy shows a large hemopericardium and a tear through the anterior left ventricular wall. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely at the edge of the infarct?
items.explanationHtml:
About 3–7 days after infarction, macrophages phagocytose dead myocytes, and granulation tissue is only beginning at the margins. The wall is at its weakest, so free wall rupture with hemopericardium and tamponade typically happens in this period, especially in older women with a first, large, late-reperfused infarct.

Takeaway: rupture peaks when macrophages have cleared necrotic muscle but collagen has not yet formed (roughly days 3–14).

whyNot.A: Wavy fibres without inflammation are seen in the first hours (up to about a day).
whyNot.B: A neutrophil-dominated infiltrate is typical of days 1–3.
whyNot.C: A dense collagen scar takes about 2 months or more to form.
whyNot.E: Granulation tissue fills the infarct at about 1–2 weeks and beyond; at day 6 it is only beginning at the edges.

items.objective: Match the histology of a healing infarct to the timing of free wall rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has had progressive dyspnea, palpitations and chest discomfort for 5 days. Two weeks ago he had fever, sore throat and diarrhea that resolved. Serum troponin is markedly raised. Coronary angiography is normal. Cardiac MRI shows patchy subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the lateral wall. An endomyocardial biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Lymphocytic infiltrate with adjacent myocyte necrosis

options.label: C
options.html: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophils and extensive necrosis

items.explanationHtml:
Chest pain and heart failure symptoms after a viral illness, high troponin with normal coronaries, and a non-coronary pattern of late gadolinium enhancement point to viral myocarditis. Biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis next to the inflammatory cells.

Takeaway: viral myocarditis = lymphocytes plus myocyte necrosis; MRI enhancement is subepicardial or mid-wall rather than subendocardial.

whyNot.B: Noncaseating granulomas suggest cardiac sarcoidosis, which typically presents with heart block or ventricular tachycardia rather than a post-viral illness.
whyNot.C: Giant cell myocarditis is rare, fulminant and associated with autoimmune disease; the giant cells and eosinophils distinguish it from the usual lymphocytic form.
whyNot.D: Myocyte disarray is the hallmark of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an inherited condition, not an acute inflammatory one.
whyNot.E: Aschoff bodies are the lesion of acute rheumatic carditis after streptococcal pharyngitis, typically in children with arthritis and chorea.

items.objective: Recognise the histologic hallmark of viral myocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension for 25 years has exertional dyspnea. Blood pressure is 172/96 mm Hg. Palpation shows a sustained apical impulse that is not displaced. An S4 is heard. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular wall thickness of 14 mm, a normal cavity size and an ejection fraction of 65%. Which of the following changes in her ventricular myocytes best explains these findings?

options.label: D
options.html: Replacement of myocytes by fibrofatty tissue

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic pressure overload from hypertension raises wall stress during systole. Myocytes respond by adding new sarcomeres in parallel, thickening each cell and the wall: concentric hypertrophy. The thick wall normalises systolic wall stress but relaxes poorly, so filling depends on atrial contraction (S4) and diastolic dysfunction follows.

Takeaway: pressure overload → sarcomeres in parallel → concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction; volume overload → sarcomeres in series → eccentric hypertrophy.

whyNot.A: Adult cardiac myocytes are essentially terminally differentiated; the heart grows by hypertrophy, not hyperplasia.
whyNot.B: Sarcomeres added in series lengthen myocytes and dilate the chamber (eccentric hypertrophy), the response to volume overload.
whyNot.D: Fibrofatty replacement, mainly of the right ventricle, defines arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.E: Glycogen accumulation in myocytes occurs in Pompe disease and some PRKAG2 disorders, not hypertensive heart disease.

items.objective: Explain concentric hypertrophy as the myocyte response to pressure overload.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has had sharp, positional chest pain for 3 days that improves when he leans forward. He had an upper respiratory infection 10 days ago. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. A friction rub is heard. ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression. Troponin is within the reference range. C-reactive protein is raised. Echocardiography shows a trace pericardial effusion and normal ventricular function. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Ibuprofen plus colchicine, as an outpatient

items.explanationHtml:
This is uncomplicated acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis with no high-risk features (no high fever, no large effusion or tamponade, normal troponin, immunocompetent, not anticoagulated). First-line treatment is a high-dose NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine for about 3 months, managed as an outpatient. Colchicine speeds resolution and reduces recurrence.

Takeaway: uncomplicated acute pericarditis → NSAID + colchicine at home; reserve steroids for second line.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids are second line; used first in viral pericarditis they increase the risk of recurrence.
whyNot.C: There is no evidence of bacterial (purulent) pericarditis; he is not toxic and the effusion is trivial.
whyNot.D: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, positional pain and a normal troponin indicate pericarditis, not an acute coronary occlusion.
whyNot.E: Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade or suspected purulent, tuberculous or malignant effusion, not a trace effusion.

items.objective: Treat uncomplicated acute pericarditis with an NSAID plus colchicine as an outpatient.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man is recovering in hospital from a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with PCI 2 days ago. He now has new sharp chest pain that is worse with deep breathing and when lying flat. A friction rub is heard. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Echocardiography shows anterior akinesis, a small pericardial effusion, no new wall-motion change and no valve dysfunction. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his pain?
items.explanationHtml:
Pleuritic, positional pain with a rub 1–3 days after a transmural infarct is early peri-infarction pericarditis. The preferred anti-inflammatory is aspirin, which he already needs for secondary prevention. Other NSAIDs and glucocorticoids are avoided early after infarction because they may impair scar formation and increase the risk of ventricular rupture.

Takeaway: pericarditis after MI → aspirin, not other NSAIDs or steroids.

whyNot.B: Non-aspirin NSAIDs such as indomethacin impair infarct healing and are associated with rupture and more cardiovascular events after MI.
whyNot.C: Steroids early after MI may impair healing and thin the infarcted wall.
whyNot.D: Additional anticoagulation increases the risk of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and does not treat the inflammation.
whyNot.E: The echocardiogram shows no new ischemia and the pain is typical of pericarditis; repeat angiography is not needed.

items.objective: Choose aspirin for pericarditis early after myocardial infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma comes to the emergency department because of worsening dyspnea for 3 days. Pulse is 124/min, blood pressure is 86/64 mm Hg, and respirations are 26/min. The systolic pressure falls by 18 mm Hg on inspiration. Jugular venous pressure is 15 cm H2O. Heart sounds are distant. The lungs are clear. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension, tachycardia, a raised jugular venous pressure, distant heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus in a patient with cancer suggest cardiac tamponade. Bedside echocardiography confirms the effusion and shows chamber collapse within minutes, and it guides pericardiocentesis.

Takeaway: suspected tamponade → immediate bedside echocardiography.

whyNot.A: CT takes the unstable patient away from the resuscitation area and adds contrast; echocardiography answers the question faster.
whyNot.B: Right heart catheterisation shows equalised pressures but is invasive, slow and unnecessary for diagnosis.
whyNot.C: BNP does not distinguish tamponade from other causes of dyspnea and does not guide drainage.
whyNot.D: A chest radiograph may show an enlarged silhouette but cannot assess hemodynamic effect.

items.objective: Use bedside echocardiography to confirm suspected cardiac tamponade.

items.stemHtml: Echocardiography in the patient from the previous item shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse and a dilated inferior vena cava that does not collapse with inspiration. Blood pressure is now 80/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Echocardiographic chamber collapse with hypotension confirms cardiac tamponade. The treatment is urgent drainage by pericardiocentesis, usually echocardiography-guided with a catheter left in place. A fluid bolus may support pressure while drainage is arranged.

Takeaway: tamponade → drain the pericardium now; avoid diuretics, vasodilators and, when possible, positive-pressure ventilation before drainage.

whyNot.A: Diuretics lower the filling pressure that keeps the compressed heart filling and can precipitate collapse.
whyNot.B: Positive-pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, further reducing venous return; it can cause arrest in tamponade.
whyNot.D: Anti-inflammatory drugs treat pericarditis but act far too slowly to relieve hemodynamic compression.
whyNot.E: Venodilation reduces preload and would worsen hypotension.

items.objective: Treat cardiac tamponade with urgent pericardiocentesis.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous items improves after removal of 900 mL of bloody fluid. Cytology shows adenocarcinoma cells. Two weeks later, the effusion has reaccumulated to a large size with early right atrial collapse, although she is hemodynamically stable. She wishes to continue systemic cancer therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the effusion?

options.label: E
options.html: Observation with repeat echocardiography in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
A recurrent malignant pericardial effusion needs a lasting drainage route. A pericardial window (surgical, or percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy) lets fluid drain into the pleural or peritoneal space and prevents recurrent tamponade, alongside treatment of the cancer. Extended catheter drainage or intrapericardial therapy are alternatives in selected patients.

Takeaway: recurrent malignant effusion → pericardial window (or extended drainage), not repeated taps.

whyNot.A: Repeated needle drainage exposes her to repeated tamponade and procedural risk without preventing reaccumulation.
whyNot.B: Pericardiectomy is the operation for chronic constrictive pericarditis; it is too extensive for palliation of a malignant effusion.
whyNot.C: Colchicine reduces recurrence of inflammatory pericarditis but does not prevent malignant fluid accumulation.
whyNot.E: Early right atrial collapse with rapid reaccumulation means tamponade is likely to recur soon.

items.objective: Manage a recurrent malignant pericardial effusion with a pericardial window.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has had progressive edema, abdominal distension and fatigue for a year despite increasing doses of furosemide. She received chest radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 24. Jugular venous pressure is raised and rises on inspiration. An early diastolic sound follows S2. There is hepatomegaly and ascites. CT shows a diffusely thickened, calcified pericardium. Echocardiography shows normal ventricular wall thickness, normal ejection fraction and a septal bounce. Cardiac catheterisation confirms constrictive physiology. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic constrictive pericarditis with a calcified pericardium and refractory congestion is treated definitively by surgical pericardiectomy, which removes the rigid shell. Diuretics only relieve symptoms. Outcomes are poorer after radiation-induced constriction because the myocardium may also be damaged, but surgery remains the only curative option.

Takeaway: chronic calcific constriction with symptoms despite diuretics → pericardiectomy.

whyNot.B: Transplant is not needed when ventricular function is normal; removing the constricting pericardium addresses the problem.
whyNot.C: There is no significant effusion to drain; constriction is due to thickened tissue, not fluid.
whyNot.D: Radiation can damage valves, but nothing here indicates aortic valve disease.
whyNot.E: Anti-inflammatory therapy may help transient inflammatory constriction after recent pericarditis, not chronic calcific disease from radiation years ago.

items.objective: Select pericardiectomy for chronic symptomatic constrictive pericarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis has had pleuritic chest pain for 3 days. He has missed several sessions. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg without inspiratory fall. A friction rub is heard. Serum urea nitrogen is 132 mg/dL. ECG shows no ST changes. Echocardiography shows a moderate pericardial effusion without chamber collapse. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Uremic pericarditis (and dialysis-associated pericarditis from inadequate dialysis) responds to starting or intensifying dialysis. The ECG usually lacks the typical ST elevation because the myocardium is not inflamed. Heparin use during dialysis should be minimised because of the risk of hemopericardium. Drainage is reserved for tamponade or failure to improve.

Takeaway: uremic pericarditis without tamponade → more dialysis.

whyNot.A: There is no tamponade (no hypotension, no pulsus paradoxus, no chamber collapse), so emergency drainage is not indicated.
whyNot.C: Steroids do not address the underlying uremia and are not first line.
whyNot.D: A window is reserved for recurrent or refractory effusions despite adequate dialysis.
whyNot.E: Nothing suggests bacterial pericarditis; he is not septic, and the cause is uremia.

items.objective: Treat uremic pericarditis by intensifying dialysis.

items.stemHtml:
A 70-year-old woman has had fatigue, weight gain and constipation for 6 months. A chest radiograph done for a cough shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. She has no chest pain or dyspnea. Pulse is 54/min and blood pressure is 132/88 mm Hg without inspiratory fall. Echocardiography shows a moderate pericardial effusion without chamber collapse. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with low QRS voltage. Laboratory results are shown.

TestResultReference range
Thyroid-stimulating hormone62 μU/mL0.4–4.0 μU/mL
Free thyroxine0.3 ng/dL0.9–1.7 ng/dL
Sodium133 mEq/L136–145 mEq/L
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL0.6–1.2 mg/dL
C-reactive proteinWithin reference range

Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the effusion?
items.explanationHtml:
Fatigue, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, mild hyponatremia, a very high TSH and a low free T4 indicate primary hypothyroidism, a recognised cause of a slowly accumulating, often large but well-tolerated pericardial effusion with low inflammation (normal CRP, no pain). Without tamponade, the effusion resolves gradually with levothyroxine (started at a lower dose in older patients with possible coronary disease).

Takeaway: hypothyroid pericardial effusion without tamponade → treat the hypothyroidism, not the fluid.

whyNot.A: Drainage is for tamponade or diagnostic uncertainty about infection or malignancy; the cause is clear and she is stable.
whyNot.B: There is no inflammation (no pain, normal CRP), so NSAIDs and colchicine are not indicated.
whyNot.C: Diuretics do not remove pericardial fluid and could lower preload.
whyNot.D: Steroids have no role in hypothyroid effusion.

items.objective: Treat a hypothyroid pericardial effusion with thyroid hormone replacement.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has had sharp chest pain for 2 days. The pain worsens when he lies down and takes a deep breath and eases when he sits forward. He had a runny nose and myalgias a week ago. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100 °F). A high-pitched scratching sound is heard at the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward. Selected ECG leads are shown. Serum troponin is within the reference range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
