Pleuritic, positional chest pain after a viral illness, a friction rub and an ECG with concave ST elevation with PR depression in leads II and V5, and the mirror image (PR elevation, ST depression) in aVR, indicate acute pericarditis. The changes are diffuse rather than confined to one coronary territory.

Takeaway: diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression (with PR elevation in aVR) + pleuritic positional pain + rub = acute pericarditis.

whyNot.A: An anterior STEMI gives territorial ST elevation with reciprocal depression in the inferior leads, pressure-like pain that is not positional and a troponin rise.
whyNot.B: Early repolarization causes ST elevation (often with a notched J point) in healthy young people but no PR depression, no rub and no pleuritic pain.
whyNot.D: Brugada syndrome shows coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a right bundle branch block–like pattern and presents with syncope or arrest, not pleuritic pain.
whyNot.E: Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves, then PR prolongation and QRS widening, not PR depression with concave ST elevation.

items.objective: Recognise the ECG pattern of acute pericarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman with acute viral pericarditis reports sharp chest pain that radiates to the top of her left shoulder along the upper border of the trapezius muscle. Irritation of afferent fibres carried in which of the following nerves best explains the radiation of her pain?
items.explanationHtml:
The fibrous and parietal pericardium receive sensory fibres from the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). Pain from these fibres is referred to the skin of the same spinal segments, over the trapezius ridge and shoulder. The visceral pericardium is insensitive to pain.

Takeaway: pericardial (and diaphragmatic) pain refers to the trapezius ridge via the phrenic nerve, C3–C5.

whyNot.A: Greater splanchnic nerves carry visceral pain from foregut organs, referred to the epigastrium.
whyNot.B: The intercostobrachial nerve supplies skin of the medial upper arm and axilla, the territory of the arm pain of myocardial ischemia rather than pericardial pain.
whyNot.C: The vagus nerve carries visceral afferents for reflexes, not the somatic-type pain of the parietal pericardium.
whyNot.E: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the larynx; it can be compressed by an enlarged left atrium but does not carry pericardial pain.

items.objective: Explain referred pericardial pain through phrenic nerve innervation.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has progressive dyspnea. Blood pressure is 96/70 mm Hg during expiration and 80/62 mm Hg during inspiration. Jugular venous pressure is raised, and heart sounds are muffled. Echocardiography shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion. Which of the following best explains the inspiratory fall in her systolic blood pressure?

options.label: A
options.html: Bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle as right ventricular filling increases

options.label: B
options.html: Greater left ventricular afterload from more negative intrathoracic pressure, with no change in filling

options.label: C
options.html: Inspiratory pooling of blood in the hepatic veins that reduces right ventricular filling

options.label: D
options.html: Reflex vagal slowing of the heart rate during inspiration

options.label: E
options.html: Inspiratory compression of the aorta by the expanding lungs

items.explanationHtml:
This is pulsus paradoxus in cardiac tamponade. The pericardium contains a fixed total volume. Inspiration increases venous return to the right ventricle; because the free walls cannot expand outward, the septum shifts into the left ventricle (ventricular interdependence). Left ventricular filling and stroke volume fall, and systolic pressure drops by more than 10 mm Hg.

Takeaway: pulsus paradoxus in tamponade comes from inspiratory septal shift that steals left ventricular filling.

whyNot.B: Afterload effects from intrathoracic pressure are small and are not the main reason for the exaggerated fall; the key change is reduced left ventricular filling.
whyNot.C: Inspiration increases, not decreases, venous return to the right heart.
whyNot.D: Inspiration normally speeds the heart rate (respiratory sinus arrhythmia); slowing would not explain a fall in systolic pressure.
whyNot.E: The lungs do not compress the aorta during inspiration.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in cardiac tamponade.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man develops hypotension and a raised jugular venous pressure 6 hours after cardiac surgery. A pulmonary artery catheter shows right atrial pressure 19 mm Hg, right ventricular diastolic pressure 19 mm Hg, pulmonary artery diastolic pressure 20 mm Hg and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 20 mm Hg. Which of the following findings in the jugular venous pulse is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Equal diastolic pressures in all chambers after cardiac surgery suggest cardiac tamponade (for example from postoperative bleeding). Because pericardial pressure restricts filling throughout diastole, blood cannot rush into the right ventricle when the tricuspid valve opens, so the y descent is blunted or absent. The x descent (atrial relaxation during ventricular systole, when cardiac volume falls) is preserved.

Takeaway: tamponade = equalised diastolic pressures + lost y descent; constriction = prominent y descent.

whyNot.A: Giant v waves are typical of severe tricuspid regurgitation (or mitral regurgitation in the wedge tracing).
whyNot.C: Cannon a waves occur when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block or ventricular tachycardia.
whyNot.D: A prominent y descent reflects rapid early diastolic filling that then stops, as in constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.E: Absent a waves occur in atrial fibrillation because there is no organised atrial contraction.

items.objective: Relate the jugular venous waveform to the hemodynamics of cardiac tamponade.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man has had increasing abdominal girth and leg swelling for 8 months. He received mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma 20 years ago. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H2O and rises further with inspiration. The liver is enlarged, and shifting dullness is present. An early diastolic sound is heard shortly after S2 at the left sternal border. A chest radiograph shows a rim of calcification around the heart. Which of the following best explains the extra heart sound?

options.label: A
options.html: Sudden halt of early diastolic ventricular filling by a rigid pericardium

options.label: B
options.html: Opening of a thickened, stenotic mitral valve

options.label: C
options.html: Atrial contraction into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle

options.label: D
options.html: Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve

options.label: E
options.html: Rubbing of inflamed parietal and visceral pericardium

items.explanationHtml:
Prior mediastinal radiation, right-sided congestion with ascites, a Kussmaul sign and a calcified pericardial rim indicate constrictive pericarditis. The ventricles fill rapidly in early diastole until they reach the limit set by the rigid pericardium, where filling stops abruptly and produces the pericardial knock, an early diastolic sound that occurs earlier and is higher-pitched than an S3.

Takeaway: constrictive pericarditis = Kussmaul sign + pericardial knock + calcified pericardium; radiation and cardiac surgery are common causes in high-income countries.

whyNot.B: An opening snap of mitral stenosis is also early diastolic, but this patient has no diastolic rumble and has calcification of the pericardium, not the valve.
whyNot.C: An S4 from atrial contraction occurs late in diastole, just before S1.
whyNot.D: Delayed pulmonic closure produces a split S2 rather than a separate early diastolic sound.
whyNot.E: A friction rub is a scratchy, multi-component sound of acute inflammation, not a single diastolic sound in chronic constriction.

items.objective: Explain the pericardial knock of constrictive pericarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease has missed three dialysis sessions. He has sharp chest pain that is worse when lying flat. Serum urea nitrogen is 148 mg/dL. A loud friction rub is heard. He dies 2 days later of hyperkalemia. At autopsy, the pericardial surfaces are covered with a rough, shaggy, adherent layer. Which of the following types of inflammation is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Uremia irritates the serosal surfaces and increases vascular permeability, so fibrinogen leaks into the pericardial space and polymerises into a rough fibrin coat ("bread-and-butter" appearance) that rubs during each heartbeat. Fibrinous pericarditis is typical of uremia, transmural infarction, rheumatic fever and post-surgical pericarditis.

Takeaway: uremic and post-infarction pericarditis are fibrinous; the rough fibrin surfaces produce the friction rub.

whyNot.A: Caseous necrosis in the pericardium points to tuberculosis.
whyNot.B: Granulomatous pericarditis suggests tuberculosis, fungal infection or sarcoidosis, not uremia.
whyNot.C: Purulent pericarditis comes from bacterial infection, with neutrophil-rich pus.
whyNot.D: Serous pericarditis has thin, protein-poor fluid without a rough adherent coat; it is typical of viral and autoimmune disease.

items.objective: Identify fibrinous pericarditis as the typical lesion of uremia.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man develops fever, pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial rub 3 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction. Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion and no new wall-motion abnormality. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 78 mm/h. Which of the following best explains this complication?

options.label: A
options.html: Extension of transmural necrosis to the overlying pericardium

options.label: B
options.html: Immune response to myocardial antigens exposed by the infarction

options.label: C
options.html: Bacterial seeding of the pericardium from the catheterization site

options.label: D
options.html: Leakage of blood from a ventricular pseudoaneurysm

options.label: E
options.html: Reactivation of a latent viral infection in the pericardium

items.explanationHtml:
Pericarditis with fever, effusion and high inflammatory markers weeks after infarction is post-cardiac injury (Dressler) syndrome. Necrosis exposes myocardial and pericardial antigens that provoke an autoimmune reaction, producing a sterile serositis that can also involve the pleura.

Takeaway: pericarditis 1–3 days after MI = local inflammation over the infarct; weeks after MI = autoimmune post-cardiac injury syndrome.

whyNot.A: Direct inflammation over a transmural infarct causes pericarditis in the first few days, not 3 weeks later.
whyNot.C: Purulent pericarditis would cause a toxic illness with bacteremia; catheterisation sites rarely seed the pericardium.
whyNot.D: A leaking pseudoaneurysm causes hemopericardium and hemodynamic compromise, and echocardiography would show the defect.
whyNot.E: There is no evidence of a latent virus; the timing after myocardial injury points to an immune mechanism.

items.objective: Explain the immune mechanism of post-infarction (Dressler) pericarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with lung adenocarcinoma has dyspnea and lightheadedness. Pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 92/68 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is raised. Her ECG rhythm strip is shown. Which of the following best explains the beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude?

options.label: A
options.html: Alternating block in the left anterior fascicle

options.label: B
options.html: Alternating strength of left ventricular contraction

options.label: C
options.html: Premature ventricular beats in a bigeminal pattern

options.label: D
options.html: Swinging of the heart within a large pericardial effusion

options.label: E
options.html: Respiratory variation in the position of the diaphragm

items.explanationHtml:
Sinus tachycardia with low voltage and QRS complexes that alternate in amplitude every other beat is electrical alternans. In a large pericardial effusion the heart swings back and forth within the fluid, so its electrical axis relative to the electrodes changes with each beat. With hypotension and a raised jugular venous pressure in a patient with cancer, this points to malignant effusion with tamponade.

Takeaway: electrical alternans + low voltage + tachycardia = large effusion, often with tamponade.

whyNot.A: Fascicular block changes the axis consistently; it does not alternate with each beat in this pattern.
whyNot.B: Alternating contraction strength is pulsus alternans, a sign of severe left ventricular dysfunction detected in the pulse, not in QRS amplitude.
whyNot.C: Bigeminy would show premature, wide QRS complexes with compensatory pauses; here every complex is narrow and evenly spaced.
whyNot.E: Respiratory variation changes amplitude gradually over several beats with each breath, not on alternate beats.

items.objective: Interpret electrical alternans as a sign of a large pericardial effusion.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man has had pleuritic chest pain and joint aches for 3 weeks. Five months ago he started a new antihypertensive drug that acts by directly relaxing arteriolar smooth muscle. He has a friction rub. Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion. Antinuclear antibodies are positive at a high titre. Antibodies against double-stranded DNA are negative. Antibodies against which of the following are most likely to be present?
items.explanationHtml:
Hydralazine, a direct arteriolar vasodilator, can cause drug-induced lupus, especially in slow acetylators. Serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis), arthralgia and fever are typical, while kidney and central nervous system disease are rare. Anti-histone antibodies are present in most cases; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are usually absent. Symptoms resolve after the drug is stopped.

Takeaway: pericarditis in a patient on hydralazine, procainamide or isoniazid with positive ANA and anti-histone antibodies = drug-induced lupus.

whyNot.A: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
whyNot.B: Anti-CCP antibodies are specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
whyNot.D: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies occur in inflammatory myopathy with interstitial lung disease.
whyNot.E: Anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific for idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus and are not typical of the drug-induced form.

items.objective: Recognise drug-induced lupus pericarditis and its antibody marker.

items.stemHtml: An 85-year-old woman has had exertional dyspnea and two episodes of near-syncope over 4 months. She has chronic kidney disease stage 3, COPD and frailty but lives independently. A grade 3/6 late-peaking systolic murmur radiates to the carotids. Echocardiography shows a calcified trileaflet aortic valve with a peak velocity of 4.6 m/s, mean gradient of 52 mm Hg, valve area of 0.7 cm2 and ejection fraction of 60%. CT angiography shows iliofemoral arteries suitable for catheter access. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Medical therapy with repeat echocardiography in 1 year

options.label: C
options.html: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Surgical aortic valve replacement through a sternotomy

items.explanationHtml:
She has symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, which needs valve replacement because survival without it is poor. At 85 years with frailty, lung and kidney disease, and suitable femoral access, transcatheter aortic valve replacement is preferred over surgery after heart team review.

Takeaway: symptomatic severe AS → valve replacement; older or higher-risk patients with suitable anatomy → TAVR.

whyNot.A: Watchful waiting is inappropriate once severe stenosis causes symptoms; mortality rises sharply.
whyNot.C: Balloon valvuloplasty gives only short-lived benefit and is a bridge, not definitive therapy.
whyNot.D: Surgical replacement is favoured in younger, lower-risk patients; her age and comorbidities make TAVR the better choice.
whyNot.E: No drug relieves fixed outflow obstruction; nitrates can cause dangerous hypotension in severe AS.

items.objective: Choose TAVR for an older, higher-risk patient with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man comes for a pre-employment physical examination. He feels well and exercises regularly. Blood pressure is 132/62 mm Hg. A soft, grade 2/6, high-pitched decrescendo murmur is heard in early diastole at the left sternal border with the patient sitting forward. The rest of the examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassurance that the murmur is functional

items.explanationHtml:
A diastolic murmur is never innocent. An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border suggests aortic regurgitation (for example from a bicuspid valve or root dilation). Transthoracic echocardiography defines the cause, severity, ventricular size and function, and aortic dimensions.

Takeaway: any diastolic murmur → echocardiography, even without symptoms.

whyNot.A: Functional murmurs are soft and systolic; diastolic murmurs always need evaluation.
whyNot.B: Exercise testing can help assess symptoms but does not show valve anatomy or severity.
whyNot.C: Catheterisation is invasive and reserved for discordant noninvasive data or coronary assessment before surgery.
whyNot.E: Delaying evaluation risks missing progressive ventricular dilation or an aortopathy.

items.objective: Evaluate a diastolic murmur with echocardiography.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl is brought for a well-child visit. Her parents have no concerns, and she keeps up with her friends. Growth is normal. A grade 2/6, low-pitched, vibratory, musical mid-systolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. It is louder when she lies supine and softer when she stands. S1 and S2 are normal, with physiologic splitting of S2. Femoral pulses are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A soft, vibratory, musical mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border in a well young child, louder supine and softer standing, with normal heart sounds and pulses, is a classic innocent (Still) murmur. No investigation is needed; explain to the family that the heart is normal.

Takeaway: soft, musical, position-dependent systolic murmur with normal S2 and pulses in a well child → innocent murmur, reassure.

whyNot.B: An ECG adds nothing when the history and examination fit an innocent murmur.
whyNot.C: A chest radiograph is not needed and exposes the child to radiation unnecessarily.
whyNot.D: Echocardiography is for murmurs with concerning features (diastolic, harsh, loud, fixed split S2, symptoms, abnormal pulses).
whyNot.E: Referral is not needed for a clearly innocent murmur.

items.objective: Recognise an innocent Still murmur and reassure.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man had his aortic valve replaced with a bileaflet mechanical prosthesis 3 years ago for a stenotic bicuspid valve. He takes warfarin, and his INR has been in range at monthly checks. He asks whether he can switch to apixaban because his friend with atrial fibrillation takes it without blood tests. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
items.explanationHtml:
Patients with mechanical heart valves require lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist. Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated: in a randomised trial of dabigatran in mechanical valves, both valve thrombosis and bleeding increased, and other DOACs have not been shown to be safe. Home INR testing can make warfarin more convenient.

Takeaway: mechanical valve → warfarin for life; never a DOAC.

whyNot.A: Apixaban has not been shown to prevent valve thrombosis with mechanical valves and is contraindicated.
whyNot.B: Dabigatran caused more valve thrombosis and bleeding than warfarin in patients with mechanical valves, despite having a reversal agent.
whyNot.C: Aspirin alone does not prevent mechanical valve thrombosis.
whyNot.D: Rivaroxaban, like other factor Xa inhibitors, is not an accepted anticoagulant for mechanical valves.

items.objective: Maintain warfarin, not a DOAC, for anticoagulation of a mechanical heart valve.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 28 weeks' gestation has had worsening shortness of breath for 2 weeks and now cannot lie flat. She had rheumatic fever as a child in Pakistan. Pulse is 116/min and regular, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. An opening snap and a diastolic rumble are heard at the apex. Echocardiography shows severe mitral stenosis with a valve area of 1.0 cm2 and a mean gradient of 14 mm Hg at this heart rate. In addition to a low-dose diuretic, which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Pregnancy raises blood volume and heart rate. In mitral stenosis, tachycardia shortens diastole, raising the gradient and left atrial pressure and causing pulmonary edema. A β1-selective blocker such as metoprolol slows the heart, lengthens diastolic filling time and lowers left atrial pressure; cautious diuresis relieves congestion. Balloon commissurotomy is considered if symptoms persist despite medical therapy.

Takeaway: symptomatic MS in pregnancy → β1-selective blocker + careful diuretic; slow the heart to lengthen diastole.

whyNot.A: Digoxin controls rate in atrial fibrillation but is weak at slowing sinus tachycardia driven by exertion and pregnancy.
whyNot.B: Hydralazine lowers afterload, which does not relieve the fixed obstruction at the mitral valve and can cause reflex tachycardia.
whyNot.D: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic in the second and third trimesters and do not address the problem.
whyNot.E: Nifedipine is a vasodilator that can cause reflex tachycardia, worsening the gradient.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy with a β1-selective blocker.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated in hospital for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of the aortic valve. On day 3, he suddenly becomes severely dyspneic. Blood pressure is 92/40 mm Hg and pulse is 128/min. A short, soft diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, and crackles are heard over both lungs. Echocardiography shows a perforated aortic leaflet with severe aortic regurgitation and normal left ventricular size. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Six weeks of intravenous antibiotics, then elective surgery

items.explanationHtml:
Acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis causes pulmonary edema and shock because the normal-sized ventricle cannot accommodate the sudden regurgitant volume. Heart failure from valve destruction is the strongest indication for urgent surgery in endocarditis; antibiotics continue after the operation.

Takeaway: acute severe AR with heart failure → urgent valve surgery; no balloon pump, no β-blockade.

whyNot.A: Balloon inflation in diastole increases regurgitation; an intra-aortic balloon pump is contraindicated in significant aortic regurgitation.
whyNot.C: Delaying surgery in a patient with heart failure from acute regurgitation carries very high mortality.
whyNot.D: Tachycardia limits diastolic time and regurgitant volume; β-blockade can worsen hemodynamics.
whyNot.E: TAVR is not used in active endocarditis and does not allow debridement of infected tissue.

items.objective: Manage acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis with urgent surgery.

items.stemHtml:
A 71-year-old man with known aortic stenosis has yearly echocardiography. He walks 3 km daily and has no chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness or syncope. Results are shown.

Measure2 years ago1 year agoToday
Peak aortic velocity (m/s)3.74.14.4
Mean gradient (mm Hg)334247
Aortic valve area (cm2)1.10.90.8
LV ejection fraction (%)625845

Coronary angiography shows no significant stenosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Start lisinopril and repeat echocardiography in 6 months

options.label: E
options.html: Cardiac MRI to measure myocardial fibrosis before deciding

items.explanationHtml:
He has severe aortic stenosis (velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, area ≤1.0 cm2). Although asymptomatic, his ejection fraction has fallen below 50%, a sign that the ventricle is failing against the fixed obstruction. This is an indication for aortic valve replacement (the approach chosen by the heart team).

Takeaway: asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF <50% → valve replacement.

whyNot.A: Continued surveillance is appropriate only for asymptomatic severe AS with a preserved ejection fraction.
whyNot.B: No drug slows aortic stenosis or reverses the LV dysfunction it causes.
whyNot.C: Balloon valvuloplasty gives only temporary relief and is a bridge in unstable patients.
whyNot.E: MRI may add risk information in borderline cases, but an EF below 50% is already a clear indication.

items.objective: Recommend valve replacement for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis with reduced ejection fraction.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with known mitral valve prolapse has no symptoms and exercises regularly. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Echocardiography shows prolapse of the posterior leaflet with a flail segment, severe mitral regurgitation, an ejection fraction of 55% and a left ventricular end-systolic diameter of 44 mm. Pulmonary artery systolic pressure is normal. He is in sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Clinical review and echocardiography in 12 months

options.label: C
options.html: Start an ACE inhibitor and observe

options.label: E
options.html: Mitral valve replacement with a mechanical prosthesis

items.explanationHtml:
Severe primary mitral regurgitation from a flail posterior leaflet causes chronic volume overload that silently damages the ventricle. The ventricle is already showing strain (ejection fraction ≤60% and end-systolic diameter ≥40 mm), so surgery is indicated even without symptoms. Repair is preferred over replacement, especially for posterior leaflet prolapse, because it preserves the subvalvular apparatus and avoids lifelong anticoagulation.

Takeaway: asymptomatic severe primary MR with LVEF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm → surgery; repair over replacement.

whyNot.B: Watchful waiting is reasonable only while the LV remains normal (EF >60% and end-systolic diameter <40 mm).
whyNot.C: Vasodilators do not delay surgery in chronic primary MR with normal blood pressure.
whyNot.D: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is reserved for patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk.
whyNot.E: Replacement is inferior to repair when repair is feasible, and a mechanical valve commits him to lifelong warfarin.

items.objective: Refer asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation with early LV dysfunction for mitral valve repair.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous item undergoes successful surgical mitral valve repair with leaflet resection and placement of an annuloplasty ring. Six months later, he is scheduled for a dental scaling procedure that will cause gingival bleeding. He has no penicillin allergy. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding endocarditis prophylaxis?

options.label: A
options.html: No prophylaxis, because his native valve was repaired, not replaced

options.label: B
options.html: Prophylaxis only for gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures

options.label: D
options.html: Doxycycline for 5 days after the procedure

options.label: E
options.html: A single dose of amoxicillin before the procedure

items.explanationHtml:
Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue is recommended for the highest-risk patients, including those with prosthetic material used for valve repair, such as annuloplasty rings (as well as prosthetic valves and prior endocarditis). The standard regimen is a single dose of oral amoxicillin 30–60 minutes before the procedure.

Takeaway: annuloplasty rings, prosthetic valves and prior endocarditis → amoxicillin before gingival dental procedures.

whyNot.A: Prosthetic material used in valve repair, such as an annuloplasty ring, places him in the high-risk group.
whyNot.B: Prophylaxis is no longer recommended solely for gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures; dental procedures are the indication.
whyNot.C: Lifelong daily penicillin is used to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever, not endocarditis after valve repair.
whyNot.D: Prophylaxis is a single pre-procedure dose; a post-procedure course of doxycycline is not the recommended regimen.

items.objective: Apply endocarditis prophylaxis rules to a patient with an annuloplasty ring.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has had palpitations for 3 days. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 118/min. Echocardiography shows moderate mitral stenosis (valve area 1.3 cm2) and a dilated left atrium with no thrombus. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg, creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, and she has no other medical conditions. Metoprolol is started for rate control. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic therapy?

options.label: E
options.html: No antithrombotic therapy because of her low CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score

items.explanationHtml:
Atrial fibrillation with moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis carries a very high stroke risk regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc score. Anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) is indicated; a randomised trial in rheumatic heart disease with atrial fibrillation found a DOAC (rivaroxaban) inferior to warfarin, and DOAC trials in atrial fibrillation excluded moderate–severe mitral stenosis.

Takeaway: AF + moderate/severe rheumatic MS → warfarin, regardless of risk score.

whyNot.A: DOACs are not recommended in moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.
whyNot.B: Aspirin does not adequately prevent stroke in atrial fibrillation.
whyNot.D: Dual antiplatelet therapy is less effective than anticoagulation for AF-related stroke and adds bleeding risk.
whyNot.E: The CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score does not apply to AF with moderate–severe mitral stenosis, which is high-risk by itself.

items.objective: Choose warfarin for atrial fibrillation in rheumatic mitral stenosis.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old man has had exertional chest pressure and two episodes of lightheadedness while climbing stairs. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. A grade 3/6 late-peaking systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border, radiating to both carotid arteries. The carotid upstroke is delayed and weak. S2 is soft. Serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes the most likely process affecting his valve?

options.label: A
options.html: Dystrophic calcification of a trileaflet valve

options.label: B
options.html: Commissural fusion after recurrent rheumatic carditis

items.explanationHtml:
A late-peaking ejection murmur radiating to the carotids with a weak, delayed carotid upstroke and a soft S2 indicates severe aortic stenosis. In an older adult with atherosclerotic risk factors, the usual cause is age-related calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve. Calcium deposits in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium: dystrophic calcification.

Takeaway: calcific AS in older adults = dystrophic calcification (normal serum calcium) driven by the same risk factors as atherosclerosis.

whyNot.B: Rheumatic aortic stenosis is uncommon in isolation; it almost always accompanies rheumatic mitral disease and presents earlier in life.
whyNot.C: Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, not aortic stenosis.
whyNot.D: Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissue when serum calcium or phosphate is high; his calcium is normal.
whyNot.E: Endocarditis destroys leaflets and causes regurgitation, with fever and positive blood cultures.

items.objective: Identify dystrophic calcification as the mechanism of age-related aortic stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. She is 142 cm (4 ft 8 in) tall and has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples and a low posterior hairline. Blood pressure in the right arm is 148/86 mm Hg; femoral pulses are weak and delayed. An early systolic ejection click is heard at the apex. Karyotype is 45,X. Which of the following valve abnormalities is she most likely to have?

options.label: B
options.html: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve

items.explanationHtml:
Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with left-sided obstructive lesions: bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta (upper-limb hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses). A bicuspid valve produces an early systolic ejection click as the doming leaflets open and calcifies to stenosis decades earlier than a trileaflet valve.

Takeaway: Turner syndrome → bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation; an ejection click suggests a mobile bicuspid valve.

whyNot.A: Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click and is linked with connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome.
whyNot.B: Ebstein anomaly is associated with maternal lithium exposure, not Turner syndrome.
whyNot.D: Pulmonic stenosis is typical of Noonan syndrome, which can resemble Turner syndrome physically but has a normal karyotype.
whyNot.E: Tricuspid atresia is a cyanotic lesion presenting in infancy.

items.objective: Associate Turner syndrome with bicuspid aortic valve.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has occasional palpitations. While supine, a mid-systolic click followed by a short late systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Echocardiography shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets that bulge into the left atrium in systole. Which of the following manoeuvres will most likely make the click occur earlier in systole?

options.label: E
options.html: Standing up from a squatting position

items.explanationHtml:
In mitral valve prolapse, the leaflets prolapse when the shrinking ventricle no longer keeps the chordae taut. A smaller left ventricle reaches that point sooner, so the click occurs earlier and the murmur lasts longer. Standing up reduces venous return and left ventricular volume.

Takeaway: less LV volume (standing, Valsalva) → earlier click and longer murmur in MVP; more volume (squatting, handgrip, leg raise) → later click.

whyNot.A: Squatting increases venous return and afterload, enlarging the ventricle and delaying the click.
whyNot.B: Leg raise increases venous return and ventricular size, delaying the click.
whyNot.C: Handgrip raises afterload; the ventricle stays larger, delaying the click (although the regurgitant murmur may be louder).
whyNot.D: Phenylephrine raises afterload by vasoconstriction, enlarging the ventricle and delaying prolapse.

items.objective: Predict the effect of ventricular volume on the click of mitral valve prolapse.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman who emigrated from Nepal has had worsening dyspnea for 2 years. She had several episodes of migratory joint pain and fever as a child. An opening snap is heard after S2, followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Two years ago, the interval between S2 and the opening snap was 0.10 s; today it is 0.06 s. Which of the following best explains the change in this interval?

options.label: A
options.html: Improving compliance of the left ventricular wall

options.label: B
options.html: Rising left atrial pressure as the orifice narrows

options.label: C
options.html: Slowing of the resting heart rate over time

options.label: E
options.html: Falling pulmonary artery pressure with treatment

items.explanationHtml:
In mitral stenosis, the valve opens when left ventricular pressure falls below left atrial pressure during isovolumetric relaxation. As the orifice narrows, left atrial pressure rises, so the crossover point is reached sooner after aortic valve closure. A shortening S2–opening snap interval therefore indicates progressing stenosis.

Takeaway: in MS, a shorter S2–OS interval = higher left atrial pressure = more severe stenosis.

whyNot.A: Ventricular compliance does not explain the timing; the left ventricle is not the problem in mitral stenosis.
whyNot.C: A slower heart rate lengthens diastole but does not determine when the mitral valve opens after S2.
whyNot.D: Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic murmur and can produce an Austin Flint rumble, but it does not shorten the S2–OS interval.
whyNot.E: Progressive mitral stenosis raises, rather than lowers, pulmonary artery pressure.

items.objective: Explain why a shorter S2–opening snap interval indicates more severe mitral stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had progressive exertional dyspnea for a year. Blood pressure is 168/48 mm Hg. Pulses are bounding and collapse quickly, and his head bobs with each heartbeat. A high-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. The apical impulse is displaced laterally. Which of the following best explains his wide pulse pressure?

options.label: A
options.html: Reduced arterial compliance from age-related stiffening of the aorta

options.label: B
options.html: Systemic vasodilation from excess thyroid hormone

options.label: C
options.html: Fixed obstruction to left ventricular outflow

options.label: D
options.html: Large stroke volume combined with diastolic backflow into the left ventricle

options.label: E
options.html: Shunting of blood through an arteriovenous fistula

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic aortic regurgitation lets part of each stroke volume flow back into the left ventricle during diastole, so diastolic aortic pressure falls. The dilated ventricle then ejects both the forward and the regurgitant volume as a very large stroke volume, which raises systolic pressure. A high systolic and low diastolic pressure produce the wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses and head bobbing.

Takeaway: chronic AR = big stroke volume + diastolic runoff into the LV → wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses.

whyNot.A: Aortic stiffening widens pulse pressure in older adults (isolated systolic hypertension) but does not cause a diastolic murmur or bounding, collapsing pulses.
whyNot.B: Thyrotoxicosis can widen pulse pressure through high output, but it does not cause a decrescendo diastolic murmur or a displaced apex.
whyNot.C: Fixed outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis) narrows the pulse pressure and gives a slow-rising pulse.
whyNot.E: An arteriovenous fistula causes a continuous bruit and high output, not a diastolic decrescendo murmur.

items.objective: Explain the wide pulse pressure of chronic aortic regurgitation.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy in Ethiopia has fever, painful swelling that moves from his knees to his elbows over a week, and a new soft apical holosystolic murmur. Three weeks ago he had a severe sore throat that was not treated. Antistreptolysin O titre is raised. Which of the following best explains his cardiac injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibodies against streptococcal antigens that cross-react with cardiac proteins

options.label: B
options.html: Direct invasion of the endocardium by streptococci

options.label: C
options.html: Deposition of circulating immune complexes in the valve leaflets

options.label: D
options.html: A streptococcal exotoxin acting as a superantigen on T cells

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, migratory polyarthritis and carditis weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis define acute rheumatic fever. Antibodies (and T cells) directed against streptococcal antigens, especially the M protein, cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve tissue: molecular mimicry, a type II hypersensitivity reaction. Acute carditis usually causes mitral regurgitation; years of repeated injury lead to mitral stenosis.

Takeaway: rheumatic heart disease = molecular mimicry (type II) after group A strep pharyngitis; the mitral valve is affected most.

whyNot.B: The heart is not infected in rheumatic fever; blood cultures are negative and the injury is immune-mediated.
whyNot.C: Immune complex (type III) injury explains post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not rheumatic carditis.
whyNot.D: Superantigen exotoxins cause streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, not rheumatic carditis.
whyNot.E: Septic emboli would cause infective endocarditis or abscesses with bacteremia, not this delayed sterile illness.

items.objective: Explain molecular mimicry in rheumatic heart disease.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman has episodes of facial flushing and watery diarrhea. CT shows multiple liver masses. Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid excretion is markedly increased. She has a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Echocardiography shows thickened, retracted tricuspid and pulmonic valve leaflets; the mitral and aortic valves are normal. Which of the following best explains why her left-sided valves are spared?

options.label: A
options.html: The left heart receives blood that has bypassed the liver

options.label: C
options.html: The lungs inactivate serotonin by monoamine oxidase

options.label: D
options.html: High left-sided pressures prevent plaque formation

options.label: E
options.html: Aortic and mitral leaflets have no fibroblasts

items.explanationHtml:
In carcinoid heart disease, vasoactive substances (especially serotonin) from hepatic metastases of a neuroendocrine tumour enter the hepatic veins and reach the right heart, where they stimulate fibrous plaques on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. Lung monoamine oxidase inactivates serotonin before blood reaches the left heart, which is therefore usually spared (unless there is a right-to-left shunt or a bronchial carcinoid).

Takeaway: carcinoid heart disease affects right-sided valves because the lungs inactivate serotonin.

whyNot.A: The left heart receives blood from the lungs, which is downstream of the liver; it has not bypassed metabolism but has passed through the lungs.
whyNot.B: Valvular interstitial cells on both sides express serotonin receptors; drugs acting on these receptors can injure left-sided valves.
whyNot.D: Pressure does not protect valves from serotonin-driven fibrosis; the protective factor is pulmonary metabolism.
whyNot.E: All heart valves contain interstitial cells with fibroblast-like properties.

items.objective: Explain right-sided valve involvement in carcinoid heart disease.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man had his aortic valve replaced with a mechanical prosthesis 4 years ago. He has fatigue and dark urine. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, reticulocytes 4.5%, lactate dehydrogenase markedly raised and haptoglobin undetectable. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. Echocardiography shows a paravalvular leak. Which of the following is most likely seen on a peripheral blood smear?
items.explanationHtml:
High-velocity, turbulent flow through a paravalvular leak or across a mechanical valve physically fragments red cells. This mechanical intravascular hemolysis gives anemia, reticulocytosis, high LDH, low haptoglobin, hemoglobinuria (dark urine) and fragmented red cells, schistocytes, on the smear. The Coombs test is negative.

Takeaway: anemia with schistocytes and a negative Coombs test after valve surgery → mechanical hemolysis from a leak or prosthesis.

whyNot.A: Spherocytes are typical of hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolysis, which would usually give a positive Coombs test.
whyNot.B: Bite cells result from oxidative injury in G6PD deficiency.
whyNot.C: Target cells are seen in thalassemia, liver disease and hemoglobin C disease.
whyNot.D: Sickle cells are seen in sickle cell disease.

items.objective: Recognise mechanical hemolysis with schistocytes as a prosthetic valve complication.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman with severe calcific aortic stenosis has recurrent melena. Colonoscopy and capsule endoscopy show several bleeding angiodysplasias of the small bowel. Platelet count and prothrombin time are within the reference ranges. Analysis of her plasma most likely shows which of the following?

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand factor multimers

options.label: E
options.html: Prolonged prothrombin time from vitamin K deficiency

items.explanationHtml:
The combination of severe aortic stenosis and bleeding from gastrointestinal angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome) involves an acquired von Willebrand syndrome. High shear stress across the stenotic valve unfolds von Willebrand factor and exposes its cleavage site to ADAMTS13, which breaks down the largest multimers that are most active in platelet adhesion. Valve replacement usually corrects the defect and reduces bleeding.

Takeaway: AS + GI angiodysplasia bleeding → shear-induced loss of large vWF multimers; valve replacement helps.

whyNot.A: Acquired factor VIII inhibitors cause soft-tissue and muscle bleeding with a prolonged aPTT, unrelated to aortic stenosis.
whyNot.B: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, with thrombocytopenia and schistocytes; her platelets are normal and ADAMTS13 is active.
whyNot.C: Factor IX deficiency (hemophilia B) is inherited and causes joint and muscle bleeding beginning early in life.
whyNot.E: Her prothrombin time is normal, which excludes clinically important vitamin K deficiency.

items.objective: Explain acquired von Willebrand syndrome in severe aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome).

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man is brought for evaluation after two falls at home in the past month, both shortly after getting out of bed. He has hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Medications are amlodipine, which he has taken for 6 years, and doxazosin, started 5 weeks ago. Blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg after 5 minutes supine and 116/76 mm Hg after 3 minutes standing; heart rate is 70/min supine and 82/min standing. Neurologic examination is normal. ECG shows sinus rhythm with no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
His falls follow standing and began after doxazosin was started; standing pressure falls 26 mm Hg systolic with an appropriate heart-rate rise. This is drug-induced orthostatic hypotension. The first step is to remove or replace the culprit (a uroselective agent such as tamsulosin, or a 5α-reductase inhibitor, can be considered for his prostate symptoms), then recheck orthostatic vitals.

Takeaway: in an older adult with new orthostatic hypotension, stop the offending drug before adding treatment.

whyNot.A: Pressor drugs are for symptoms that persist after reversible causes are removed.
whyNot.B: Fludrocortisone adds volume but is unnecessary when a culprit drug is present, and it causes hypokalemia and supine hypertension.
whyNot.C: Postural falls with a normal ECG and a clear drug cause do not need prolonged rhythm monitoring.
whyNot.E: Orthostatic hypotension is already shown at the bedside; tilt testing is for unclear or delayed cases.

items.objective: Manage drug-induced orthostatic hypotension in an older adult by deprescribing.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man reports 6 months of dizziness when standing, worse in the morning. He has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for 22 years, with numbness of both feet, early satiety and erectile dysfunction. He takes metformin and insulin glargine. Blood pressure is 146/86 mm Hg supine and 112/70 mm Hg after 3 minutes standing; heart rate is 84/min supine and 86/min standing. Hemoglobin A1c is 8.4%. Serum electrolytes, creatinine and hemoglobin are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A 34 mm Hg systolic fall with a heart-rate rise of only 2/min (ratio far below 0.5 beats/min per mm Hg) indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. In a patient with long-standing diabetes, sensory neuropathy, gastroparesis and erectile dysfunction, the cause is diabetic cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. Morning symptoms reflect nocturnal pressure diuresis from supine hypertension.

Takeaway: a large standing pressure fall with little heart-rate rise points to neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

whyNot.B: Volume depletion would produce a brisk heart-rate rise and usually abnormal BUN or creatinine.
whyNot.C: Reflex syncope needs a trigger and prodrome and does not produce a reproducible fall on standing.
whyNot.D: Sick sinus syndrome causes bradycardia or pauses, not a reproducible postural pressure fall.
whyNot.E: Aortic stenosis causes exertional symptoms and a systolic ejection murmur.

items.objective: Diagnose neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from the heart-rate response.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with Parkinson disease has lightheadedness when she stands, most noticeable after breakfast. Her medications are carbidopa-levodopa only; she stopped an antihypertensive 2 months ago on her physician's advice. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg supine and 100/66 mm Hg after 3 minutes standing; heart rate is 72/min and 75/min. She drinks about 1 L of fluid daily. Serum electrolytes and creatinine are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin fludrocortisone each morning with potassium checks

options.label: C
options.html: Advise more fluid and salt, staged rising and compression garments

options.label: D
options.html: Begin midodrine three times daily during waking hours

options.label: E
options.html: Stop carbidopa-levodopa to remove a vasodilating drug

items.explanationHtml:
She has neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from Parkinson disease, and no culprit antihypertensive remains. Non-drug measures come first for everyone: about 2–3 L of fluid daily and liberal salt (no heart or kidney contraindication here), staged rising, compression of the legs and abdomen, counter-manoeuvres, head-of-bed elevation and small meals. Drugs are added if symptoms persist.

Takeaway: non-drug measures are the first treatment of symptomatic orthostatic hypotension once culprit drugs are removed.

whyNot.A: Fludrocortisone is a second-step option with hypokalemia and supine hypertension risks.
whyNot.B: Pyridostigmine has a modest effect and is not the first step.
whyNot.D: Midodrine is reasonable if symptoms persist despite non-drug measures.
whyNot.E: Stopping levodopa would worsen her parkinsonism; dose timing can be adjusted instead.

items.objective: Begin non-pharmacologic management of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with pure autonomic failure has orthostatic dizziness that limits her to the house despite 3 months of adequate fluid and salt intake, compression garments, staged rising and head-of-bed elevation. She takes no other medications. Supine blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg and standing pressure after 1 minute is 88/56 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
When non-drug measures fail, a pressor is added. Midodrine (peripheral α1 agonist) raises standing pressure and is taken during the upright hours of the day. Droxidopa and fludrocortisone are alternatives. Supine pressure should be monitored because supine hypertension is the main adverse effect.

Takeaway: midodrine is a standard pressor for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension refractory to non-drug measures.

whyNot.A: Diuretics reduce intravascular volume and worsen orthostatic hypotension.
whyNot.B: Prazosin is an α<sub>1</sub> antagonist and is a classic cause of orthostatic hypotension.
whyNot.C: Clonidine reduces central sympathetic outflow and lowers pressure.
whyNot.D: β blockers lower heart rate and cardiac output and would worsen orthostatic hypotension.

items.objective: Select pharmacotherapy for orthostatic hypotension refractory to non-drug measures.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with multiple system atrophy takes midodrine at 8 AM, 1 PM and 9 PM for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; his standing symptoms have improved. Home readings show daytime standing pressures of 110–120/70 mm Hg and pressures of 180–190/100 mm Hg when he lies in bed at night. He wakes twice nightly to urinate. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Double the evening midodrine dose and add pyridostigmine at night

options.label: B
options.html: Move the last midodrine dose to late afternoon and raise the head of the bed at night

options.label: C
options.html: Add long-acting amlodipine each morning and continue the current midodrine schedule

options.label: D
options.html: Stop midodrine and begin a daily thiazide diuretic for the hypertension

options.label: E
options.html: Add fludrocortisone and continue the current midodrine schedule

items.explanationHtml:
He has supine hypertension, made worse by a bedtime pressor dose; high nocturnal pressure also drives pressure natriuresis (nocturia) and worse morning orthostasis. The last midodrine dose should be taken at least about 4 hours before lying down, and the head of the bed raised by about 10–20°. If supine pressure stays very high, a short-acting antihypertensive at bedtime only can be added.

Takeaway: manage supine hypertension by avoiding late pressor doses and lying flat, not with daytime long-acting antihypertensives.

whyNot.A: A larger evening dose would raise nocturnal supine pressure further.
whyNot.C: A long-acting daytime antihypertensive would lower standing pressure during the day and cause falls.
whyNot.D: Stopping midodrine and adding a diuretic would make his daytime orthostatic hypotension much worse.
whyNot.E: Fludrocortisone expands volume and worsens supine hypertension.

items.objective: Manage supine hypertension in a patient treated for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman briefly lost consciousness while standing up from the dinner table. Her daughter says she became pale, slumped to the floor and woke within 20 seconds, fully oriented. There was no tongue biting, incontinence or confusion. She has hypertension treated with lisinopril and recently began hydrochlorothiazide. She has no chest pain, palpitations or exertional symptoms. Cardiac and neurologic examinations are normal. In addition to a detailed history and physical examination, which of the following is the most appropriate initial evaluation?

options.label: B
options.html: Orthostatic vital signs and a 12-lead ECG

items.explanationHtml:
Every patient with syncope needs a history (including a witness account), a physical examination with orthostatic vital signs, and a 12-lead ECG. These identify orthostatic syncope (likely here, after a new thiazide and on standing) and flag cardiac causes. Further tests are chosen from these findings.

Takeaway: start syncope evaluation with history, examination including orthostatic vital signs, and a 12-lead ECG.

whyNot.A: Carotid disease does not cause syncope without focal symptoms.
whyNot.C: Head imaging is low yield in syncope without head injury or focal neurologic deficits.
whyNot.D: Troponin testing is reserved for suspected acute coronary syndrome.
whyNot.E: EEG is used when seizure is suspected; brief loss of consciousness with quick full recovery argues against seizure.

items.objective: Order the initial evaluation for a patient with syncope.

items.stemHtml:
An 81-year-old woman in assisted living reports lightheadedness on standing for 4 days during a heat wave. She takes hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril for hypertension. Her mucous membranes are dry. Results are shown:

MeasurementSupine (5 min)Standing 1 minStanding 3 min
Blood pressure (mm Hg)134/78108/68104/66
Heart rate (/min)80104108
Serum testResult
Sodium137 mEq/L
Potassium3.7 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen (BUN)38 mg/dL
Creatinine1.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
Glucose104 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most likely cause of her orthostatic hypotension?
items.explanationHtml:
Standing pressure falls 30 mm Hg systolic with a heart-rate rise of 28/min, an intact baroreflex response. Dry mucous membranes, a BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20 and a creatinine rise from baseline (prerenal injury) during a heat wave on a thiazide and an ACE inhibitor indicate volume depletion. Treatment is fluid replacement and holding the diuretic and ACE inhibitor until she is euvolemic.

Takeaway: orthostatic hypotension with a brisk heart-rate rise and prerenal laboratory findings indicates volume depletion.

whyNot.A: POTS is defined by tachycardia without a fall in blood pressure, usually in younger patients.
whyNot.B: Autonomic failure produces little or no heart-rate rise on standing.
whyNot.C: Primary adrenal insufficiency usually causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, which are absent.
whyNot.E: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity causes syncope with neck pressure or head turning, not a reproducible postural fall.

items.objective: Interpret orthostatic vital signs and laboratory results to identify hypovolemic orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: An 83-year-old man is found to have orthostatic hypotension during a routine visit; his systolic pressure falls 24 mm Hg after 3 minutes standing. He has mild cognitive impairment and takes several medications for hypertension and insomnia. If his orthostatic hypotension is not addressed, which of the following outcomes is he at most increased risk of?
items.explanationHtml:
Orthostatic hypotension in older adults is associated with falls and fall-related injury (including hip fracture), syncope, stroke, faster cognitive decline and higher mortality. This is why every older patient who falls needs orthostatic vital signs and a medication review, and why antihypertensive and sedative regimens are simplified when OH is found.

Takeaway: orthostatic hypotension in older adults predicts falls and fractures.

whyNot.B: Kidney stones have no link to postural blood pressure changes.
whyNot.C: Peptic ulcer disease is unrelated to orthostatic hypotension.
whyNot.D: Hypothyroidism is not caused by orthostatic hypotension.
whyNot.E: Glaucoma is not a consequence of orthostatic hypotension.

items.objective: Identify the clinical consequences of orthostatic hypotension in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has 18 months of dizziness on standing, urinary urgency and loud snoring with stridor during sleep noted by his wife. Over 6 months he has developed slurred speech, a wide-based unsteady gait and slowed movements. Carbidopa-levodopa produced no benefit. Blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg supine and 98/62 mm Hg after 3 minutes standing; heart rate 74/min and 76/min. Examination shows rigidity, dysmetria and an intention tremor. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Early prominent autonomic failure (neurogenic OH, urinary symptoms, nocturnal stridor) together with cerebellar signs and parkinsonism that does not respond to levodopa is characteristic of multiple system atrophy. It progresses faster than Parkinson disease.

Takeaway: neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with cerebellar signs and levodopa-unresponsive parkinsonism suggests multiple system atrophy.

whyNot.A: Pure autonomic failure has no motor or cerebellar signs.
whyNot.B: Parkinson disease typically responds well to levodopa and lacks cerebellar signs; autonomic failure appears later.
whyNot.C: Progressive supranuclear palsy features vertical gaze palsy and early falls rather than early autonomic failure.
whyNot.D: Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, without neurogenic OH.

items.objective: Diagnose multiple system atrophy as a cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: The patient is diagnosed with multiple system atrophy. Three months later he reports that his worst dizziness occurs within an hour after lunch and dinner; home readings show standing systolic pressures in the 80s at those times. His usual meals are large and rich in bread, rice and sweets, with a glass of wine at dinner. Which of the following dietary recommendations is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Eat two large meals a day so that symptoms are limited to two periods

options.label: B
options.html: Switch from wine to beer to lower the alcohol content of each drink

options.label: C
options.html: Eat smaller, more frequent meals with less refined carbohydrate and avoid alcohol

options.label: D
options.html: Restrict dietary sodium to less than 1.5 g/day

options.label: E
options.html: Increase refined carbohydrate to prevent post-meal hypoglycemia

items.explanationHtml:
He has postprandial hypotension: splanchnic vasodilation after a meal, especially a large carbohydrate-rich one, pools blood that a failing baroreflex cannot compensate for. Smaller, more frequent meals lower in refined carbohydrate, avoiding alcohol, drinking water before meals and staying seated or reclining briefly after eating reduce the fall.

Takeaway: postprandial hypotension is managed with small, low-refined-carbohydrate meals and avoiding alcohol.

whyNot.A: Large meals cause greater splanchnic pooling and deeper falls in pressure.
whyNot.B: Any alcohol is a vasodilator; beer also adds carbohydrate and volume of alcohol.
whyNot.D: Salt restriction lowers plasma volume and worsens orthostatic hypotension; liberal salt is advised.
whyNot.E: Refined carbohydrate is the strongest dietary trigger of postprandial hypotension.

items.objective: Recommend dietary measures for postprandial hypotension in autonomic failure.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man stands up quickly after lying on a couch. Within the first few seconds his arterial pressure dips, then returns to baseline. Which of the following changes is most directly responsible for initiating the correction of his blood pressure?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased vagal efferent activity to the sinoatrial node

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased sympathetic activity to skeletal-muscle arterioles

options.label: C
options.html: Increased firing of carotid sinus afferent fibers in the glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: D
options.html: Decreased firing of carotid sinus afferent fibers in the glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Increased release of atrial natriuretic peptide

items.explanationHtml:
Standing pools blood in dependent veins, so stroke volume and arterial pressure fall. Less stretch of the carotid sinus reduces afferent firing in the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The medulla responds by withdrawing vagal tone and raising sympathetic outflow, which increases heart rate, contractility and vascular resistance.

Takeaway: a fall in arterial pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which triggers sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal.

whyNot.A: Vagal outflow falls on standing so that heart rate can rise.
whyNot.B: Sympathetic activity to resistance vessels increases to raise peripheral resistance.
whyNot.C: Afferent firing increases when arterial pressure rises (for example, carotid massage), which slows the heart.
whyNot.E: Atrial stretch falls on standing, so ANP release decreases rather than increases.

items.objective: Describe the baroreceptor reflex response to standing.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has had 2 years of lightheadedness on standing, urinary urgency with incontinence and erectile dysfunction. Over the past year he has developed slowness, rigidity and an unsteady wide-based gait. A trial of carbidopa-levodopa gave little benefit. Supine blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg and standing blood pressure after 3 minutes is 104/70 mm Hg, with a heart rate of 70/min supine and 72/min standing. Which of the following findings is most likely on microscopic examination of his brain after death?

options.label: A
options.html: α-Synuclein inclusions in pigmented neurons of the substantia nigra only

options.label: B
options.html: Extracellular β-amyloid plaques in the cerebral cortex

options.label: C
options.html: Tau-positive neurofibrillary tangles in the midbrain and globus pallidus

options.label: D
options.html: Spongiform vacuolation of the cortical gray matter

options.label: E
options.html: α-Synuclein inclusions in the cytoplasm of oligodendrocytes

items.explanationHtml:
Early, severe autonomic failure (neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with a flat heart-rate response, urinary and erectile dysfunction) combined with poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism and cerebellar signs indicates multiple system atrophy. Its hallmark is α-synuclein-containing glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes, with neuron loss in the striatum, substantia nigra, pons, cerebellum and the intermediolateral cell columns.

Takeaway: multiple system atrophy is an oligodendroglial α-synucleinopathy with early autonomic failure and poor levodopa response.

whyNot.A: Neuronal Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra characterize Parkinson disease, which usually responds well to levodopa and develops autonomic failure later.
whyNot.B: Amyloid plaques define Alzheimer disease, a memory-first dementia without this motor-autonomic picture.
whyNot.C: Midbrain tau pathology suggests progressive supranuclear palsy, with vertical gaze palsy and early falls rather than prominent autonomic failure.
whyNot.D: Spongiform change suggests prion disease, which progresses over months with myoclonus and dementia.

items.objective: Recognize multiple system atrophy as a cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and identify its histopathology.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia takes his first dose of a newly prescribed drug at breakfast. An hour later he feels faint when he gets up from his chair, and his standing blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Which of the following actions of the drug most likely explains his symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of muscarinic receptors on detrusor muscle

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of α<sub>1</sub>-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.html: Stimulation of α<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors in the brainstem

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of 5α-reductase in prostatic stromal cells

options.label: E
options.html: Blockade of β<sub>1</sub>-adrenergic receptors on cardiac myocytes

items.explanationHtml:
α1 blockers such as terazosin and doxazosin relax prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle, but they also dilate arterioles and veins. Venodilation reduces venous return on standing, and the effect is greatest with the first dose or a dose increase. Starting at a low dose at bedtime reduces the risk.

Takeaway: α1 antagonists cause first-dose orthostatic hypotension through venous and arteriolar dilation.

whyNot.A: Antimuscarinics treat overactive bladder and cause dry mouth and urinary retention, not first-dose hypotension.
whyNot.C: Central α<sub>2</sub> agonists (clonidine) lower pressure but are not prostatic hyperplasia drugs.
whyNot.D: 5α-reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate over months and cause little hypotension.
whyNot.E: β<sub>1</sub> blockade slows the heart, but β blockers are not used for prostatic hyperplasia.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of orthostatic hypotension caused by α<sub>1</sub> antagonists.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus for 35 years reports dizziness whenever she stands. She has burning pain in both feet and early satiety with vomiting of undigested food. Blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg supine and 98/64 mm Hg after 3 minutes standing; heart rate is 96/min supine and 98/min standing. Serum electrolytes and hemoglobin are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her orthostatic symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Failure of sympathetic efferent nerves to release norepinephrine on standing

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of circulating volume from glucose-driven osmotic diuresis

options.label: D
options.html: Excess vagal efferent discharge to the sinoatrial node

options.label: E
options.html: Obstruction of left ventricular outflow by a calcified valve

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing diabetes with distal painful neuropathy and gastroparesis points to diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Damage to small autonomic fibers impairs sympathetic efferent release of norepinephrine, so vascular resistance and heart rate do not rise when she stands. A high, fixed resting heart rate reflects early vagal denervation.

Takeaway: orthostatic hypotension with almost no heart-rate rise in long-standing diabetes indicates autonomic neuropathy.

whyNot.B: Volume depletion would produce a brisk compensatory heart-rate rise on standing.
whyNot.C: Aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalemia and hyponatremia, which are absent here.
whyNot.D: Vagal denervation, not excess vagal discharge, explains her resting tachycardia.
whyNot.E: Aortic stenosis causes exertional syncope and a systolic murmur, not purely postural symptoms.

items.objective: Relate the flat heart-rate response in orthostatic hypotension to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension due to Parkinson disease is started on a prodrug whose active metabolite stimulates α1-adrenergic receptors on arterioles and veins. Which of the following adverse effects is this drug most likely to cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Midodrine is converted to desglymidodrine, a peripheral α1 agonist that raises vascular resistance and venous tone. Its main hazard is supine hypertension; patients take it during upright daytime hours and avoid lying flat for several hours after a dose. Piloerection, scalp itching and urinary retention (α1 receptors at the bladder neck) also occur.

Takeaway: midodrine is a peripheral α1 agonist whose dose-limiting effect is supine hypertension.

whyNot.A: Hyperkalemia follows drugs that block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system or potassium-sparing diuretics.
whyNot.B: Gingival overgrowth occurs with phenytoin, cyclosporine and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
whyNot.D: α<sub>1</sub> agonism does not lower blood glucose.
whyNot.E: Cough results from bradykinin accumulation with ACE inhibitors.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism and principal adverse effect of midodrine.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman with pure autonomic failure is treated with a synthetic corticosteroid that has strong mineralocorticoid activity to expand her plasma volume. Three weeks later she reports muscle cramps and weakness. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Fludrocortisone acts on mineralocorticoid receptors in the principal cells of the collecting duct. More epithelial sodium channels and Na+/K+-ATPase activity increase sodium reabsorption (expanding volume) and drive potassium and hydrogen-ion secretion. The result is hypokalemia and a tendency to metabolic alkalosis, plus edema and supine hypertension.

Takeaway: fludrocortisone expands volume through mineralocorticoid action and causes hypokalemia.

whyNot.A: Mineralocorticoid excess retains sodium; serum sodium stays normal or rises slightly.
whyNot.B: Mineralocorticoids do not raise serum calcium.
whyNot.D: Increased distal hydrogen-ion secretion favors metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.
whyNot.E: Hyperkalemia results from aldosterone deficiency or blockade, the opposite of this drug's action.

items.objective: Predict the electrolyte effect of fludrocortisone from its mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from Parkinson disease is given an oral synthetic amino acid that acts as a direct precursor of norepinephrine. Which of the following enzymes converts this drug into its active form?
items.explanationHtml:
Droxidopa (L-threo-dihydroxyphenylserine) already carries the β-hydroxyl group of norepinephrine. Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase removes its carboxyl group and yields norepinephrine directly, bypassing tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine β-hydroxylase. Carbidopa, a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor taken with levodopa, can blunt this conversion at high doses.

Takeaway: droxidopa is decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to norepinephrine.

whyNot.A: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step from tyrosine to L-DOPA and is bypassed.
whyNot.B: COMT degrades catecholamines rather than activating them.
whyNot.C: PNMT converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla.
whyNot.D: Dopamine β-hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine; droxidopa does not pass through dopamine.

items.objective: Describe how droxidopa is converted to norepinephrine.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue, weight loss, salt craving and dizziness on standing. Her skin is diffusely darker, including the palmar creases and gums. Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg supine and 82/54 mm Hg standing, with heart rate rising from 88/min to 116/min. Serum sodium is 129 mEq/L and potassium 5.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex

options.label: B
options.html: Ectopic vasopressin secretion by a lung tumor

items.explanationHtml:
Hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and orthostatic hypotension indicate primary adrenal insufficiency, most often autoimmune adrenalitis in high-income countries. Loss of aldosterone causes renal sodium wasting and volume depletion (hence a brisk heart-rate rise), and loss of cortisol removes negative feedback so ACTH and pro-opiomelanocortin-derived melanocyte-stimulating activity rise, darkening the skin.

Takeaway: primary adrenal insufficiency causes non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation.

whyNot.B: SIADH causes euvolemic hyponatremia without hyperkalemia or orthostatic hypotension.
whyNot.C: Pituitary (secondary) insufficiency spares aldosterone and lowers ACTH, so there is no hyperkalemia or hyperpigmentation.
whyNot.D: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppression is a secondary insufficiency, so aldosterone and potassium are preserved.
whyNot.E: Pheochromocytoma usually causes paroxysmal hypertension, not hyperkalemia or pigmentation.

items.objective: Recognize primary adrenal insufficiency as a cause of orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman has 3 days of watery diarrhea and poor oral intake. She feels lightheaded on standing. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg supine and 102/66 mm Hg standing; heart rate rises from 84/min to 112/min. Compared with her usual healthy state, which of the following is most likely increased now?
items.explanationHtml:
Volume depletion lowers renal perfusion pressure and raises renal sympathetic activity, both of which stimulate juxtaglomerular cells to release renin. Angiotensin II and aldosterone then increase vascular tone and sodium retention. The brisk heart-rate rise shows that her baroreflex is intact, so this is non-neurogenic OH.

Takeaway: hypovolemic orthostatic hypotension activates renin with a brisk compensatory tachycardia.

whyNot.A: Reduced venous return lowers end-diastolic volume and stroke volume.
whyNot.C: Aldosterone and reduced filtration make the kidney retain sodium, so urine sodium falls (often below 20 mEq/L).
whyNot.D: ANP is released in response to atrial stretch, which falls with volume depletion.
whyNot.E: Central venous pressure falls when intravascular volume is lost.

items.objective: Predict neurohormonal changes in hypovolemic orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman develops orthostatic hypotension after a low-dose thiazide diuretic is added to her regimen, although a younger patient given the same drug had no symptoms. Which of the following age-related changes most contributes to her greater susceptibility?

options.label: A
options.html: Greater early diastolic filling of the left ventricle

options.label: B
options.html: Enhanced cardiac responsiveness to β-adrenergic stimulation

options.label: C
options.html: A heightened thirst response to rising plasma osmolality

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced sensitivity of the arterial baroreflex

options.label: E
options.html: Increased secretion of renin in response to volume loss

items.explanationHtml:
With age, stiffer arterial walls stretch less for a given pressure change, and central baroreflex processing weakens, so heart rate and vascular resistance rise less on standing. Aging also blunts β-adrenergic responsiveness, renin-aldosterone release and thirst, and the stiffer ventricle depends more on preload, so modest volume loss lowers stroke volume more.

Takeaway: older adults are prone to orthostatic hypotension because baroreflex sensitivity and other compensations decline with age.

whyNot.A: Early diastolic filling falls with age as the ventricle stiffens; atrial contraction contributes more.
whyNot.B: Cardiac β-adrenergic responsiveness declines with age.
whyNot.C: Thirst is reduced in older adults, which favors dehydration.
whyNot.E: Renin and aldosterone responses are blunted in older adults.

items.objective: Explain why aging increases susceptibility to orthostatic hypotension.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. Average seated blood pressure, measured correctly, is 134/86 mm Hg; it was 136/84 mm Hg 1 month ago, and home readings over 1 week average 133/85 mm Hg. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or kidney disease. BMI is 29 kg/m2. Serum creatinine, potassium, lipids, glucose and urinalysis are normal, and his estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk is 3%. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: No intervention until blood pressure reaches 140/90 mm Hg

options.label: C
options.html: Lifestyle modification and reassessment in 3 to 6 months

options.label: D
options.html: Lifestyle modification plus amlodipine and chlorthalidone

items.explanationHtml:
He has confirmed stage 1 hypertension (130–139/80–89 mm Hg) without cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD or high estimated risk. The first step is lifestyle change (weight loss, DASH-style diet, less sodium, more potassium, exercise, limiting alcohol), with drug treatment if pressure stays at or above 130/80 mm Hg after 3–6 months.

Takeaway: low-risk stage 1 hypertension starts with lifestyle modification and reassessment in 3–6 months.

whyNot.A: Immediate drug therapy for stage 1 is for patients with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD or high risk.
whyNot.B: Stage 1 hypertension starts at 130/80 mm Hg and needs intervention now, at least with lifestyle change.
whyNot.D: Two-drug initial therapy is used for stage 2 hypertension.
whyNot.E: Home readings already confirm the office values, so ambulatory monitoring adds little.

items.objective: Manage low-risk stage 1 hypertension.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has office blood pressures of 148/94 mm Hg and 150/92 mm Hg at two visits 1 month apart, measured with correct technique.
