She feels well and has no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or kidney disease. Her examination, ECG, urinalysis and basic metabolic panel are normal. She says her pressure is “always fine” at the pharmacy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Home or 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring

options.label: B
options.html: Begin amlodipine with lisinopril as a single pill

options.label: C
options.html: Plasma aldosterone concentration and renin activity

options.label: E
options.html: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess for LVH

items.explanationHtml:
Out-of-office readings should confirm a diagnosis of hypertension before lifelong treatment begins. Here they are especially important because she suggests white-coat hypertension (high office readings with normal readings elsewhere). If home or ambulatory averages are normal, she needs lifestyle advice and periodic monitoring rather than drugs.

Takeaway: confirm office hypertension with home or ambulatory readings, which also detect white-coat hypertension.

whyNot.B: Combination therapy would be appropriate for confirmed stage 2 hypertension.
whyNot.C: Primary aldosteronism screening is for resistant hypertension, hypokalemia or other specific clues.
whyNot.D: Starting a drug before confirming the diagnosis risks treating white-coat hypertension.
whyNot.E: Echocardiography is not part of the routine initial evaluation.

items.objective: Confirm the diagnosis of hypertension with out-of-office blood pressure measurement.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus has an average blood pressure of 146/90 mm Hg on repeated office and home readings. He takes metformin. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL, potassium 4.4 mEq/L, and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 290 mg/g (reference < 30 mg/g) on two samples. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to include in his antihypertensive regimen?
items.explanationHtml:
In hypertension with diabetes or CKD and albuminuria, an ACE inhibitor or ARB lowers pressure and reduces intraglomerular pressure (efferent arteriolar dilation), slowing albuminuria and kidney decline. With stage 2 pressure, it is usually started together with a second agent (a CCB or thiazide-type diuretic). Check creatinine and potassium within a few weeks. SGLT2 inhibitors add kidney protection in this setting.

Takeaway: use an ACE inhibitor or ARB in hypertension with albuminuria.

whyNot.A: Hydralazine is a later-line vasodilator with reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
whyNot.C: α blockers are add-on agents (useful in prostatic hyperplasia), not first-line, and do not reduce albuminuria.
whyNot.D: Clonidine is reserved for resistant cases and causes sedation and rebound hypertension.
whyNot.E: β blockers are not first-line for hypertension without a cardiac indication.

items.objective: Choose an ACE inhibitor or ARB for hypertension with diabetic albuminuria.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old Black woman has confirmed stage 1 hypertension with an average of 138/86 mm Hg after 6 months of lifestyle change. She has no diabetes, CKD or heart failure; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is normal, and her estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk is high. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial antihypertensive drug?
items.explanationHtml:
In Black adults without CKD or heart failure, thiazide-type diuretics and calcium channel blockers lower pressure and prevent stroke and heart failure more effectively than ACE inhibitors as single initial agents. Chlorthalidone is a long-acting thiazide-like diuretic. Many patients will eventually need a combination, and an ACE inhibitor or ARB can then be added.

Takeaway: for Black adults without CKD or heart failure, start with a thiazide-type diuretic or a calcium channel blocker.

whyNot.A: ACE inhibitor monotherapy is less effective initially in this group without a compelling indication such as albuminuric CKD.
whyNot.B: Spironolactone is a fourth-line drug for resistant hypertension or for primary aldosteronism.
whyNot.D: α blockers increase heart failure risk as first-line agents.
whyNot.E: Atenolol is not a first-line antihypertensive and is inferior for stroke prevention.

items.objective: Select an initial antihypertensive for a Black adult without compelling indications.

items.stemHtml:
A 49-year-old man has had poorly controlled hypertension for 3 years despite good adherence (confirmed by pill counts) and correct home measurement technique. He uses no NSAIDs, decongestants or stimulants. Findings are shown:

Current medications (daily)
Amlodipine 10 mg
Lisinopril 40 mg
Chlorthalidone 25 mg
FindingResult
Home blood pressure average154/96 mm Hg
Serum sodium143 mEq/L
Serum potassium3.1 mEq/L
Serum bicarbonate31 mEq/L
Serum creatinine0.9 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: D
options.html: Morning plasma aldosterone concentration and renin activity

items.explanationHtml:
He has true resistant hypertension (above goal on three drugs of different classes, including a diuretic, at full doses with confirmed adherence) plus hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Primary aldosteronism is the most common treatable secondary cause and should be screened for with a plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio. The ACE inhibitor raises renin, so a suppressed renin despite it is especially telling; a high ratio is confirmed with salt-loading testing.

Takeaway: resistant hypertension, especially with hypokalemia, calls for an aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

whyNot.A: Renal artery imaging fits an older patient with atherosclerotic disease or a creatinine rise on RAAS blockade, not hypokalemia with alkalosis here.
whyNot.B: Cushing syndrome testing is for clinical features of cortisol excess.
whyNot.C: Pheochromocytoma screening is for paroxysmal symptoms or an adrenal mass with suggestive features.
whyNot.E: Thyroid disease rarely causes this picture of resistant hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis.

items.objective: Screen for primary aldosteronism in resistant hypertension with hypokalemia.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe headache, vomiting and confusion for 6 hours. He ran out of his antihypertensive medications a month ago. Blood pressure is 232/138 mm Hg in both arms and pulse 96/min. He is oriented to person only. Funduscopy shows bilateral papilledema. There are no focal neurologic deficits, and noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage or infarct. Serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: IV nicardipine infusion to lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour

options.label: B
options.html: Oral clonidine and amlodipine with discharge home

options.label: C
options.html: No antihypertensive treatment until MRI of the brain is done

options.label: D
options.html: IV nitroprusside infusion to reach 120/80 mm Hg within the first hour

options.label: E
options.html: Sublingual nifedipine and observation for 2 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Confusion, papilledema and acute kidney injury with severe hypertension indicate a hypertensive emergency (hypertensive encephalopathy). He needs ICU admission and a titratable IV drug such as nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol. Lower pressure by no more than about 25% in the first hour, then to about 160/100–110 mm Hg over the next 2–6 hours, then gradually toward normal over 24–48 hours, because autoregulation is shifted upward.

Takeaway: hypertensive emergency: titratable IV drug, reduce mean pressure by ≤ 25% in the first hour.

whyNot.B: Oral therapy and discharge are for severe hypertension without acute organ damage.
whyNot.C: Treatment should not wait; CT has excluded hemorrhage, and encephalopathy improves as pressure is lowered.
whyNot.D: Normalising pressure within an hour risks cerebral, coronary and renal ischemia (aortic dissection is the exception).
whyNot.E: Sublingual nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous falls and is contraindicated.

items.objective: Manage hypertensive emergency with controlled IV pressure reduction.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a prescription refill. She stopped lisinopril and amlodipine 5 days ago when she ran out. She feels well and has no headache, chest pain, dyspnea, visual changes or neurologic symptoms. Blood pressure is 188/112 mm Hg on repeat measurement after rest. Cardiac, pulmonary, funduscopic and neurologic examinations are normal. ECG is unchanged from last year, and serum creatinine and urinalysis are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Transfer to the emergency department for head CT

options.label: B
options.html: Give sublingual nifedipine and observe for 1 hour

options.label: C
options.html: Give IV hydralazine in the clinic and recheck in 30 minutes

options.label: D
options.html: Admit to the intensive care unit for IV labetalol

options.label: E
options.html: Restart her oral medications and arrange follow-up within a few days

items.explanationHtml:
Severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage (often called hypertensive urgency) does not need rapid lowering. The cause here is stopping her medications. Restarting or intensifying oral therapy, reinforcing adherence and follow-up within days are appropriate; IV drugs and rapid reduction can cause ischemia.

Takeaway: severe hypertension without acute organ damage is treated with oral therapy and close follow-up, not rapid IV lowering.

whyNot.A: She has no neurologic symptoms or signs, so imaging is not indicated.
whyNot.B: Sublingual nifedipine is dangerous and has no role.
whyNot.C: IV hydralazine produces unpredictable falls and is not indicated without organ damage.
whyNot.D: ICU admission and IV agents are for hypertensive emergencies with acute organ damage.

items.objective: Manage severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, approximately how many patients need to be treated to the intensive target for 3.5 years to prevent one primary outcome event?
items.explanationHtml:
Absolute risk reduction = 8.5% − 6.0% = 2.5% = 0.025. Number needed to treat = 1 / 0.025 = 40.

Takeaway: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction.

whyNot.A: 12 would need an absolute reduction of about 8 percentage points.
whyNot.B: 25 would need an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points.
whyNot.D: 63 corresponds to the harm from acute kidney injury (1 / 0.016), not the benefit.
whyNot.E: 120 does not follow from either event rate.

items.objective: Calculate the number needed to treat from a trial's event rates.

items.stemHtml: A physician wants to apply the results of this study to a 66-year-old patient with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and a prior ischemic stroke. Which of the following is the main limitation of the study for this decision?

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of statistical power from a small sample

items.explanationHtml:
Patients with diabetes and prior stroke were excluded, so the trial cannot show whether the benefit-to-harm balance of the intensive target holds for them. This is a limit of external validity: the results are internally valid for the enrolled population but may not generalize to groups who were not studied.

Takeaway: exclusion criteria limit the generalizability (external validity) of trial results.

whyNot.B: With 8,000 patients and a narrow confidence interval, the study was not underpowered for its primary outcome.
whyNot.C: Recall bias affects retrospective studies that rely on participants' memory.
whyNot.D: Randomization prevents confounding by indication in the comparison of the two targets.
whyNot.E: Lead-time bias concerns screening programs that diagnose disease earlier, not treatment targets.

items.objective: Identify limits of external validity in a randomized trial.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on a new drug. Six weeks later she reports a persistent, nonproductive cough that keeps her awake. Her lungs are clear, and chest radiography is normal. Accumulation of which of the following substances most likely explains her symptom?
items.explanationHtml:
ACE (kininase II) both converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin. ACE inhibitors therefore raise bradykinin and substance P in the airway, causing a dry cough in a minority of patients and, rarely, angioedema. Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker, which leaves bradykinin metabolism intact, usually resolves the cough.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema come from bradykinin accumulation.

whyNot.A: Histamine release is not the mechanism of ACE inhibitor cough.
whyNot.B: Angiotensin II formation falls with ACE inhibition.
whyNot.C: Leukotrienes mediate aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, not ACE inhibitor cough.
whyNot.D: Aldosterone falls with ACE inhibition, which is why potassium rises.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of ACE inhibitor-induced cough.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with hypertension has been treated with hydrochlorothiazide for 1 year. Which of the following laboratory changes is most likely to have developed as a result of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Thiazides block the Na+–Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Lower intracellular sodium enhances basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange and calcium reabsorption, and mild volume contraction increases proximal calcium reabsorption, so urinary calcium falls and serum calcium can rise. Other effects are hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia and higher lipids.

Takeaway: thiazides lower urinary calcium and can raise serum calcium, a useful effect in calcium stone formers.

whyNot.B: Thiazides compete with urate for proximal secretion and cause hyperuricemia.
whyNot.C: More sodium delivered to the collecting duct increases potassium secretion, causing hypokalemia.
whyNot.D: Thiazides tend to raise glucose (hypokalemia impairs insulin release).
whyNot.E: Volume contraction and distal H<sup>+</sup> secretion cause metabolic alkalosis, raising bicarbonate.

items.objective: Predict electrolyte and metabolic effects of thiazide diuretics.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has hypertension that remains at 162/98 mm Hg despite three medications. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. CT of the abdomen shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal mass. Which of the following sets of plasma findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: High aldosterone and high renin activity

options.label: B
options.html: High aldosterone and low renin activity

options.label: C
options.html: Low aldosterone and low renin activity

options.label: E
options.html: Low aldosterone and high renin activity

items.explanationHtml:
An aldosterone-producing adenoma secretes aldosterone autonomously. Sodium retention expands volume and raises pressure, which suppresses renin release from juxtaglomerular cells. Aldosterone-driven potassium and hydrogen-ion secretion explains the hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. A raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the screening test.

Takeaway: primary aldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin.

whyNot.A: High aldosterone with high renin is secondary aldosteronism (renovascular disease, diuretics, renin-secreting tumor).
whyNot.C: Low aldosterone and low renin suggest another mineralocorticoid (for example, licorice, deoxycorticosterone excess or Liddle syndrome).
whyNot.D: Cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome) can cause hypertension but would not match an isolated aldosterone-type picture with this mass.
whyNot.E: Low aldosterone with high renin occurs in primary adrenal insufficiency.

items.objective: Distinguish primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism using renin and aldosterone.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with headache and blurred vision. He stopped his antihypertensive medications 2 months ago. Blood pressure is 238/136 mm Hg. Funduscopy shows bilateral papilledema and flame hemorrhages. Serum creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL (it was 1.0 mg/dL last year). A kidney biopsy specimen would most likely show which of the following changes in the arterioles?

options.label: A
options.html: Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of the wall alone

options.label: B
options.html: Ring-like medial calcification without luminal narrowing

options.label: D
options.html: Concentric laminated thickening of the wall with fibrinoid necrosis

items.explanationHtml:
Severe hypertension with papilledema and acute kidney injury is malignant hypertension (a hypertensive emergency). Its arteriolar lesion is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis: concentric “onion-skin” layers of smooth-muscle cells and reduplicated basement membrane, often with fibrinoid necrosis (necrotizing arteriolitis). Petechial cortical hemorrhages give a “flea-bitten” kidney.

Takeaway: malignant hypertension produces hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis.

whyNot.A: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the slow lesion of benign hypertension and diabetes.
whyNot.B: Medial calcification (Mönckeberg) affects medium-sized muscular arteries and does not narrow the lumen.
whyNot.C: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis involves small vessels in hypersensitivity vasculitis, not malignant hypertension.
whyNot.E: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is seen in giant cell and Takayasu arteritis of larger arteries.

items.objective: Identify the arteriolar pathology of malignant hypertension.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has new hypertension of 168/104 mm Hg. She does not smoke, has a normal body mass index and takes no medications. An epigastric bruit is heard. Serum potassium is 3.3 mEq/L. CT angiography shows alternating stenoses and dilations of the middle and distal right renal artery. Which of the following best describes the most likely underlying arterial lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Cystic degeneration of the media with loss of elastic fibers

options.label: B
options.html: Organized thrombus from a cardiac embolus

options.label: C
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic branches

options.label: D
options.html: Atherosclerotic plaque at the origin of the renal artery

options.label: E
options.html: Noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic fibroplasia of the arterial media

items.explanationHtml:
A young woman with renovascular hypertension and a “string of beads” in the mid-to-distal renal artery has fibromuscular dysplasia, most often medial fibroplasia. Reduced renal perfusion activates renin (secondary aldosteronism, hence mild hypokalemia). Balloon angioplasty is usually curative or markedly improves pressure.

Takeaway: fibromuscular dysplasia is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic arteriopathy that causes renovascular hypertension in young women.

whyNot.A: Cystic medial degeneration underlies aortic dissection in Marfan syndrome, not beaded renal arteries.
whyNot.B: An embolus causes sudden flank pain and infarction, not chronic beaded stenoses.
whyNot.C: Takayasu arteritis is granulomatous, affects the aorta and its proximal branches, and has systemic symptoms and elevated inflammatory markers.
whyNot.D: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis affects the ostium or proximal artery in older patients with vascular risk factors.

items.objective: Recognize fibromuscular dysplasia as a cause of renovascular hypertension.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly elevated, and imaging shows a 4-cm right adrenal mass. Before surgery, a β blocker is not given as the first drug. Which of the following best explains why starting with a β blocker alone is dangerous?

options.label: A
options.html: It prevents reuptake of norepinephrine into nerve terminals

options.label: B
options.html: It leaves catecholamine stimulation of vascular α<sub>1</sub> receptors unopposed

options.label: C
options.html: It blocks the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine

options.label: D
options.html: It increases catecholamine release from the tumor

options.label: E
options.html: It stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular cells

items.explanationHtml:
Catecholamines from a pheochromocytoma act on both α and β receptors. β2-mediated vasodilation in skeletal-muscle arterioles partly offsets α1-mediated vasoconstriction. Blocking β receptors first removes this offset, so α1 vasoconstriction is unopposed and pressure can rise sharply. α blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) is given first, then a β blocker for tachycardia.

Takeaway: in pheochromocytoma, give α blockade before β blockade to avoid unopposed α1 vasoconstriction.

whyNot.A: Reuptake inhibition is caused by cocaine and tricyclic antidepressants.
whyNot.C: PNMT converts norepinephrine to epinephrine; β blockers do not inhibit it.
whyNot.D: β blockers do not stimulate catecholamine secretion from the tumor.
whyNot.E: β<sub>1</sub> blockade reduces renin release.

items.objective: Explain why α blockade must precede β blockade in pheochromocytoma.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with hypertension develops bilateral ankle swelling 4 weeks after amlodipine is added to his regimen. Serum albumin, creatinine and urinalysis are normal, and he has no dyspnea. Which of the following best explains the edema?

options.label: A
options.html: Reduced left ventricular contractility that raises systemic venous pressure

options.label: B
options.html: Renal sodium and water retention caused by increased aldosterone release

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure from urinary loss of albumin

options.label: D
options.html: Greater dilation of precapillary arterioles than of venules, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure

options.label: E
options.html: Obstruction of lymphatic drainage by drug-induced interstitial fibrosis

items.explanationHtml:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles much more than venules. More pressure is transmitted into the capillary bed while venous outflow resistance is unchanged, so capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration rise. The edema is not from salt retention, so diuretics help little. Adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB, which dilates venules too, or lowering the dose reduces it.

Takeaway: dihydropyridine CCB edema results from arteriolar-dominant dilation raising capillary hydrostatic pressure.

whyNot.A: Amlodipine has little negative inotropic effect at usual doses, and there are no signs of heart failure.
whyNot.B: Dihydropyridines cause little renal sodium retention; that is why diuretics barely help this edema.
whyNot.C: Albumin and urinalysis are normal, so oncotic pressure is not the cause.
whyNot.E: Calcium channel blockers do not obstruct lymphatics.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker-induced edema.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man is ready for discharge 4 days after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting coronary stent. Before admission he took no medications. Fasting LDL cholesterol is 134 mg/dL. Liver enzymes are normal. In addition to dual antiplatelet therapy and a β blocker, which of the following lipid therapies is most appropriate?
items.explanationHtml:
Every patient with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease should take a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg), started in hospital after an acute coronary syndrome. If LDL remains above goal on the maximum tolerated statin, ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor are added.

Takeaway: after acute coronary syndrome, start a high-intensity statin.

whyNot.B: Fibrates have not reduced cardiovascular events added to or in place of statins in this setting.
whyNot.C: Over-the-counter fish oil has not shown cardiovascular benefit.
whyNot.D: Ezetimibe is an add-on to a statin, not a replacement for one.
whyNot.E: Pravastatin 20 mg is low intensity and insufficient after MI.

items.objective: Prescribe high-intensity statin therapy after an acute coronary syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman is found to have an LDL cholesterol of 232 mg/dL on two measurements. Triglyceride, TSH, liver tests and urinalysis are normal. She has xanthelasma, and her brother had a myocardial infarction at 44. A high-intensity statin is started, and she is counseled to avoid pregnancy while taking it. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional step?

options.label: B
options.html: Lipid testing of her first-degree relatives, including children

options.label: D
options.html: CT coronary artery calcium scoring before continuing the statin

items.explanationHtml:
LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL with premature coronary disease in a sibling makes familial hypercholesterolemia likely. Because it is autosomal dominant, about half of her first-degree relatives are affected, so cascade screening (lipid testing, and genetic testing if a variant is found) identifies relatives, including children, who benefit from early treatment.

Takeaway: suspected familial hypercholesterolemia calls for cascade testing of first-degree relatives.

whyNot.A: Angiography is for symptoms or abnormal stress testing, not screening.
whyNot.C: She needs a lipid panel 4–12 weeks after starting therapy to check response, not in 5 years.
whyNot.D: LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL warrants a high-intensity statin regardless of calcium score; a zero score in a young person would not change that.
whyNot.E: Carotid ultrasound does not change management here.

items.objective: Recommend cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 3 years comes for routine care. She does not smoke, has no known cardiovascular disease, and her blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.8%. Fasting LDL cholesterol is 118 mg/dL, HDL 52 mg/dL and triglyceride 140 mg/dL. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate lipid management?

options.label: D
options.html: No drug therapy unless LDL exceeds 160 mg/dL

items.explanationHtml:
Adults aged 40–75 with diabetes benefit from at least a moderate-intensity statin regardless of baseline LDL. High intensity is preferred when there are multiple additional risk factors, target-organ damage or a high estimated risk, which she does not have.

Takeaway: adults aged 40–75 with diabetes should take at least a moderate-intensity statin.

whyNot.A: Ezetimibe is an add-on agent, not first-line.
whyNot.B: Fibrates are for severe hypertriglyceridemia and do not replace statins.
whyNot.D: Statin benefit in diabetes does not depend on an LDL threshold.
whyNot.E: Niacin worsens glycemic control and provides no outcome benefit.

items.objective: Apply statin therapy to adults aged 40–75 with diabetes.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman began atorvastatin 40 mg daily 2 months ago after a transient ischemic attack. She now reports symmetric aching of the thighs and shoulders without weakness. Strength is normal. Serum creatine kinase and TSH are normal, and she takes no other medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue atorvastatin and add coenzyme Q10 supplements

options.label: B
options.html: Stop atorvastatin permanently and begin niacin instead

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain a quadriceps muscle biopsy before any change

options.label: D
options.html: Switch atorvastatin to fenofibrate at a standard dose

options.label: E
options.html: Pause atorvastatin, then rechallenge at a lower dose or another statin

items.explanationHtml:
She has statin-associated muscle symptoms with a normal CK and no weakness. She needs ongoing LDL lowering after a TIA, so the statin is paused until symptoms resolve and then reintroduced at a lower dose, as a different statin, or on alternate days. Most patients tolerate a rechallenge; ezetimibe, bempedoic acid or a PCSK9 inhibitor are used if they do not.

Takeaway: for mild statin muscle symptoms with normal CK, pause and rechallenge rather than abandon statin therapy.

whyNot.A: Coenzyme Q10 has not been shown to relieve statin muscle symptoms.
whyNot.B: Niacin has no outcome benefit and many adverse effects; most patients tolerate another statin regimen.
whyNot.C: Biopsy is for persistent weakness or high CK after stopping, as in immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.
whyNot.D: Fenofibrate does not provide statin-level LDL lowering or event reduction.

items.objective: Manage statin-associated muscle symptoms with a normal creatine kinase.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has a fasting serum triglyceride of 1,320 mg/dL on routine testing. He drinks 6–8 beers daily and has type 2 diabetes mellitus with a hemoglobin A1c of 10.2%. He has no abdominal pain. LDL cannot be calculated. TSH and serum creatinine are normal. He is counseled to stop drinking and his diabetes therapy is intensified. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to add now?
items.explanationHtml:
Triglyceride above about 1,000 mg/dL carries a high risk of acute pancreatitis. Alongside removing secondary causes (alcohol, hyperglycemia), a fibrate is started to lower triglyceride quickly; prescription omega-3 fatty acids can be added. A statin is considered for cardiovascular risk once triglyceride falls.

Takeaway: severe hypertriglyceridemia (about ≥ 1,000 mg/dL) is treated with a fibrate plus removal of secondary causes to prevent pancreatitis.

whyNot.B: Bile acid sequestrants raise triglyceride and are contraindicated with severe hypertriglyceridemia.
whyNot.C: Ezetimibe lowers LDL with little effect on triglyceride.
whyNot.D: PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL and have little effect on triglyceride.
whyNot.E: Cholestyramine, like colesevelam, increases triglyceride.

items.objective: Treat severe hypertriglyceridemia to prevent pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has a total cholesterol of 312 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol of 214 mg/dL; her values were normal 3 years ago. She reports fatigue, weight gain of 6 kg, constipation and feeling cold. Pulse is 58/min. Her skin is dry, and ankle reflexes show delayed relaxation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Genetic testing for LDL receptor mutations

items.explanationHtml:
A recent sharp rise in LDL with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia and delayed reflex relaxation suggests hypothyroidism, a common secondary cause of hypercholesterolemia (fewer hepatic LDL receptors). Measure TSH; treating hypothyroidism often normalises LDL, and untreated hypothyroidism raises the risk of statin myopathy.

Takeaway: exclude hypothyroidism (TSH) in new hypercholesterolemia.

whyNot.A: Familial hypercholesterolemia is lifelong, and her LDL was normal 3 years ago.
whyNot.C: Nephrotic syndrome raises LDL, but there is no edema or proteinuria history, and her symptoms point to the thyroid.
whyNot.D: CK may be raised in hypothyroidism but does not establish the diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Lp(a) is genetically fixed and would not explain a recent rise.

items.objective: Identify hypothyroidism as a secondary cause of hypercholesterolemia.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man had an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction 4 months ago. He takes aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, lisinopril and atorvastatin 80 mg daily, with good adherence confirmed by pharmacy records. He has no muscle symptoms. Fasting LDL cholesterol is 104 mg/dL, which is well above his treatment goal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in lipid management?
items.explanationHtml:
He is at very high risk and his LDL is above goal on a maximum-dose high-intensity statin. The next step is ezetimibe, which lowers LDL about another 20% and reduced events when added to a statin after acute coronary syndrome.

Takeaway: add ezetimibe when LDL is above goal on a maximally tolerated statin.

whyNot.A: Bile acid sequestrants lower LDL modestly, are poorly tolerated and lack the outcome data of ezetimibe.
whyNot.B: Rosuvastatin 5 mg is moderate intensity, a step down from atorvastatin 80 mg.
whyNot.C: Fibrates mainly lower triglyceride and have not reduced events on top of statins.
whyNot.E: Niacin added to statins has not reduced events and causes adverse effects.

items.objective: Add ezetimibe for LDL above goal on maximal statin therapy.

items.stemHtml: Ezetimibe was added. Three months later, with good adherence to atorvastatin 80 mg and ezetimibe, his fasting LDL cholesterol is 92 mg/dL, still well above goal. Liver enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: Continue the current regimen and recheck in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
For a very-high-risk patient whose LDL stays above goal on a maximal statin plus ezetimibe, a PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab or alirocumab; inclisiran is an alternative) lowers LDL by roughly a further 50–60% and reduces major cardiovascular events.

Takeaway: add a PCSK9 inhibitor when LDL remains above goal on statin plus ezetimibe in very-high-risk ASCVD.

whyNot.A: Cholestyramine is less effective and poorly tolerated; swapping does not add LDL lowering.
whyNot.B: Niacin has no event benefit added to statins and worsens glucose and urate.
whyNot.D: Fenofibrate does not lower LDL meaningfully or reduce events on top of statins.
whyNot.E: Leaving LDL above goal for a year forgoes event reduction in a very-high-risk patient.

items.objective: Escalate to a PCSK9 inhibitor for persistent LDL elevation after MI.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has had three episodes of acute pancreatitis. Plasma from a fasting sample is milky, and serum triglyceride is 2,850 mg/dL. Lipoprotein lipase activity measured after heparin injection is absent. He does not respond to a 3-month trial of fenofibrate. In addition to avoiding alcohol later in life, which of the following dietary plans is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Low-sodium DASH-style diet with plenty of nuts and seeds

options.label: B
options.html: High-protein diet with daily fish oil capsule supplements

options.label: C
options.html: Low-carbohydrate, high-fat ketogenic diet with added olive oil

options.label: D
options.html: Very low total fat (10–15% of calories) with medium-chain triglycerides

options.label: E
options.html: Low dietary cholesterol with otherwise normal total fat intake

items.explanationHtml:
In familial chylomicronemia, dietary long-chain fat cannot be cleared because LPL is absent, so chylomicrons accumulate and cause pancreatitis. Fibrates work poorly. The mainstay is a very-low-fat diet (about 10–15% of calories from fat, often < 20 g/day), with essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins supplied. Medium-chain triglycerides are absorbed directly into portal blood without forming chylomicrons, so they provide calories safely.

Takeaway: familial chylomicronemia is managed with a very-low-fat diet, using medium-chain triglycerides for calories.

whyNot.A: Sodium restriction does not affect chylomicron levels.
whyNot.B: Fish oil is long-chain fat that still forms chylomicrons, and high protein does not address the defect.
whyNot.C: A high-fat diet would increase chylomicron production and pancreatitis risk.
whyNot.E: The problem is triglyceride-rich chylomicrons from total fat, not dietary cholesterol.

items.objective: Choose dietary management for familial chylomicronemia syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man begins atorvastatin for hypercholesterolemia. Three months later his serum LDL cholesterol has fallen by 50%. Which of the following changes in hepatocytes is mainly responsible for this decrease?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased synthesis of bile acids from cholesterol

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased secretion of PCSK9 into plasma

options.label: D
options.html: Decreased uptake of cholesterol by the NPC1L1 transporter

options.label: E
options.html: Increased number of LDL receptors on the cell surface

items.explanationHtml:
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis. The fall in intracellular cholesterol activates the SREBP-2 transcription factor, which increases expression of LDL receptors. More receptors clear more LDL from plasma, which accounts for most of the drop in LDL.

Takeaway: statins lower plasma LDL mainly by up-regulating hepatic LDL receptors.

whyNot.A: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; compensatory enzyme up-regulation does not overcome the drug.
whyNot.B: Increased bile acid synthesis is the mechanism of bile acid sequestrants.
whyNot.C: SREBP-2 activation actually increases PCSK9 expression somewhat, which slightly blunts the statin effect.
whyNot.D: NPC1L1 in the intestine is the target of ezetimibe.

items.objective: Explain how statins lower plasma LDL cholesterol.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy has firm nodules on both Achilles tendons and the extensor tendons of his hands. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 42. Fasting serum LDL cholesterol is 286 mg/dL, HDL 48 mg/dL and triglyceride 110 mg/dL. A mutation in the gene for which of the following proteins is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Very high LDL with normal triglyceride, tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease in a parent indicate heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an autosomal dominant disorder usually caused by mutations in the LDL receptor gene (less often apoB-100 or gain-of-function PCSK9). Impaired hepatic clearance raises LDL from birth.

Takeaway: familial hypercholesterolemia: autosomal dominant LDL-receptor defect with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease.

whyNot.A: ApoC-II deficiency mimics LPL deficiency with severe hypertriglyceridemia.
whyNot.C: LPL deficiency raises chylomicrons and triglyceride, causing pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.
whyNot.D: ApoE2 homozygosity raises remnant lipoproteins, increasing both cholesterol and triglyceride, with palmar xanthomas.
whyNot.E: MTP deficiency causes abetalipoproteinemia with very low lipids.

items.objective: Identify the genetic defect in familial hypercholesterolemia.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated after her second episode of acute pancreatitis. She has crops of small yellow papules with red halos on her buttocks and elbows, and funduscopy shows pale, creamy retinal vessels. A blood sample left in the refrigerator overnight forms a thick creamy layer above clear plasma. Serum triglyceride is 2,400 mg/dL. Deficient activity of which of the following is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Childhood pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis and a creamy supernatant (chylomicrons float) with very high triglyceride indicate familial chylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or its activator apoC-II. Without LPL, chylomicron triglyceride cannot be hydrolysed in capillaries.

Takeaway: LPL (or apoC-II) deficiency causes chylomicronemia with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.

whyNot.A: LCAT deficiency causes low HDL, corneal opacities, anemia and kidney disease.
whyNot.B: CETP deficiency raises HDL and is clinically mild.
whyNot.D: LDL receptor defects raise LDL, not chylomicrons, and cause tendon xanthomas.
whyNot.E: Hepatic lipase deficiency causes modest elevations of remnant and HDL particles, not this degree of chylomicronemia.

items.objective: Recognize familial chylomicronemia from lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus has yellow-orange discoloration in the creases of his palms and raised yellow nodules over his elbows. Total cholesterol is 380 mg/dL and triglyceride 420 mg/dL, both rising in parallel. Lipoprotein electrophoresis shows a broad β band. Genetic testing would most likely show homozygosity for an allele of which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Palmar crease xanthomas, tuberoeruptive xanthomas, and roughly equal rises in cholesterol and triglyceride from remnant accumulation (broad β band) indicate dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III). It requires apoE2/E2 homozygosity, which binds remnant receptors poorly, plus a second metabolic hit such as diabetes, obesity or hypothyroidism. Patients develop premature coronary and peripheral arterial disease.

Takeaway: dysbetalipoproteinemia: apoE2/E2 plus a second hit, remnant accumulation and palmar xanthomas.

whyNot.A: ApoC-II deficiency causes chylomicronemia with triglyceride far higher than cholesterol.
whyNot.B: ApoA-I deficiency causes very low HDL.
whyNot.C: ApoB-100 defects cause familial defective apoB with isolated high LDL and tendon xanthomas.
whyNot.E: Gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations cause an FH phenotype with isolated high LDL.

items.objective: Identify dysbetalipoproteinemia and its apolipoprotein E genotype.

items.stemHtml: A 10-month-old boy has failure to thrive and frequent pale, bulky, foul-smelling stools since starting solid foods. A blood smear shows red cells with irregular spiny projections. Serum total cholesterol is 38 mg/dL and triglyceride 9 mg/dL; apoB is undetectable. Without treatment, deficiency of which of the following vitamins is most likely to cause neurologic disease in this child?
items.explanationHtml:
Absent apoB lipoproteins, fat malabsorption and acanthocytes indicate abetalipoproteinemia, caused by deficiency of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, which loads lipid onto apoB-48 and apoB-100. Fat-soluble vitamins cannot be exported from enterocytes; vitamin E deficiency causes spinocerebellar degeneration, ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy. Treatment is a low-fat diet with large doses of vitamin E and the other fat-soluble vitamins.

Takeaway: abetalipoproteinemia (MTP deficiency) causes fat malabsorption, acanthocytes and vitamin E-deficiency neurologic disease.

whyNot.B: Thiamine is water-soluble and unaffected by chylomicron failure.
whyNot.C: B<sub>12</sub> is water-soluble and absorbed in the ileum with intrinsic factor, independent of lipoprotein assembly.
whyNot.D: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not spinocerebellar degeneration.
whyNot.E: Pyridoxine is water-soluble and absorbed normally.

items.objective: Link abetalipoproteinemia to fat-soluble vitamin E deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man takes simvastatin for coronary artery disease. He is treated for community-acquired pneumonia with clarithromycin. Five days later he has diffuse muscle pain, weakness and dark urine. Serum creatine kinase is 18,500 U/L. Which of the following best explains this adverse reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Induction of the hepatic enzyme that activates simvastatin

options.label: B
options.html: Antibody-mediated destruction of skeletal muscle by clarithromycin

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of the hepatic enzyme that metabolizes simvastatin

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of renal tubular secretion of simvastatin

options.label: E
options.html: Displacement of simvastatin from plasma albumin

items.explanationHtml:
Simvastatin (like lovastatin and, to a lesser degree, atorvastatin) is metabolised by CYP3A4. Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, so statin levels rise and muscle toxicity follows, here rhabdomyolysis. Other CYP3A4 inhibitors include azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone and grapefruit juice. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are not mainly CYP3A4-dependent.

Takeaway: CYP3A4 inhibitors raise simvastatin levels and can precipitate rhabdomyolysis.

whyNot.A: Clarithromycin inhibits, not induces, CYP3A4; induction would lower statin levels.
whyNot.B: Macrolides do not cause immune destruction of muscle.
whyNot.D: Simvastatin is cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism, not renal secretion.
whyNot.E: Protein-binding displacement causes only transient changes in free drug and rarely clinical toxicity.

items.objective: Explain the CYP3A4 interaction that causes statin-induced rhabdomyolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old woman with low HDL cholesterol starts extended-release niacin. Within 30 minutes of each dose she develops warmth, redness and itching of her face and upper trunk. Taking aspirin 30 minutes before the dose prevents the reaction. Which of the following mediators is mainly responsible for her symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Niacin activates the GPR109A receptor on epidermal Langerhans cells and keratinocytes, which release vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGD2 and PGE2). This causes cutaneous flushing. Aspirin and other NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase and reduce it. Tolerance develops with continued use.

Takeaway: niacin flushing is prostaglandin-mediated and is reduced by aspirin.

whyNot.A: Histamine causes urticaria and flushing in anaphylaxis or with vancomycin, which aspirin would not prevent.
whyNot.B: Leukotrienes cause bronchoconstriction, not niacin flushing, and are increased rather than blocked by aspirin.
whyNot.C: Serotonin causes flushing in carcinoid syndrome.
whyNot.D: Bradykinin accumulation causes ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema.

items.objective: Identify the mediator of niacin-induced flushing.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with familial hypercholesterolemia and prior myocardial infarction is given a subcutaneous monoclonal antibody every 2 weeks in addition to a statin and ezetimibe. His LDL cholesterol falls by a further 58%. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the new drug?

options.label: A
options.html: It activates PPAR-α to increase lipoprotein lipase

options.label: B
options.html: It binds bile acids in the intestinal lumen

options.label: C
options.html: It inhibits the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis

options.label: D
options.html: It prevents LDL receptors from being targeted for lysosomal degradation

options.label: E
options.html: It blocks the intestinal sterol transporter NPC1L1

items.explanationHtml:
Evolocumab and alirocumab bind circulating PCSK9. Normally PCSK9 attaches to the LDL receptor and directs it to the lysosome after endocytosis. Blocking it lets receptors recycle to the cell surface, so hepatic LDL clearance rises sharply. These drugs reduce cardiovascular events on top of statins.

Takeaway: PCSK9 antibodies increase LDL-receptor recycling.

whyNot.A: PPAR-α agonism is the mechanism of fibrates, which mainly lower triglyceride.
whyNot.B: Bile acid binding is the mechanism of cholestyramine and colesevelam.
whyNot.C: HMG-CoA reductase is inhibited by statins.
whyNot.E: NPC1L1 is blocked by ezetimibe.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of PCSK9 inhibitors.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man comes to the emergency department 1 hour after the abrupt onset of severe, tearing pain between his shoulder blades. He has hypertension treated irregularly. Blood pressure is 184/104 mm Hg in the right arm and 152/90 mm Hg in the left arm; pulse is 104/min. He is alert and oriented; lungs are clear and there is no murmur. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy without ST-segment changes. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Abrupt tearing interscapular pain with an inter-arm pressure difference of more than 20 mm Hg in a hypertensive patient is an acute aortic dissection until proven otherwise. He is hemodynamically stable with normal renal function, so CT angiography is the best confirmatory test: it is fast, defines whether the ascending aorta is involved and shows branch-vessel malperfusion.

Takeaway: Stable patient with suspected dissection → CT angiography; unstable patient → transesophageal echo at the bedside.

whyNot.A: Coronary angiography is for acute coronary syndromes; catheter manipulation in a dissected aorta is hazardous and it does not image the aorta well.
whyNot.C: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific; with this high pretest probability it cannot replace imaging.
whyNot.D: Transthoracic echo can show root involvement, effusion or regurgitation, but it cannot see most of the descending aorta and cannot exclude dissection.
whyNot.E: A V/Q scan evaluates pulmonary embolism, which does not fit tearing back pain with an arm pressure gap.

items.objective: Choose CT angiography to confirm suspected aortic dissection in a hemodynamically stable patient.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) CT angiography in the same 61-year-old man shows an intimal flap that begins just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery and extends to the renal arteries. The ascending aorta and arch are normal, and all visceral and renal branches fill normally. He has received intravenous morphine. Blood pressure is now 178/100 mm Hg and pulse 102/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Emergency open surgical repair of the descending aorta

items.explanationHtml:
This is an uncomplicated Stanford type B dissection: the ascending aorta is spared and there is no malperfusion or rupture. Treatment is medical. The first drug is an intravenous beta-blocker (esmolol, labetalol or metoprolol) to bring heart rate to about 60/min and reduce the force and rate of rise of aortic pressure, which reduces shear on the flap. If systolic pressure then remains above about 120 mm Hg, a vasodilator is added.

Takeaway: In aortic dissection, give an intravenous beta-blocker first for rate control, then a vasodilator if pressure stays high.

whyNot.A: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically; surgery or endovascular repair is reserved for malperfusion, rupture, expansion or refractory pain or hypertension.
whyNot.C: Anticoagulation can enlarge the false lumen and cause bleeding; it has no role in acute dissection.
whyNot.D: Nitroprusside alone causes reflex tachycardia that raises aortic shear stress; it is added only after beta-blockade.
whyNot.E: An oral agent is too slow and too difficult to titrate for an acute dissection.

items.objective: Start an intravenous beta-blocker as first-line medical therapy for uncomplicated type B aortic dissection.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) The same patient's pain settles on intravenous esmolol and nicardipine. On day 3 he develops new severe abdominal pain out of proportion to a soft, mildly tender abdomen. Serum lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (reference 0.5–2.2 mmol/L). Repeat CT angiography shows the false lumen compressing the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, with poor enhancement of the small bowel wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue current therapy and repeat imaging in 48 hours

options.label: C
options.html: Endovascular repair of the descending aorta

options.label: D
options.html: Exploratory laparotomy with bowel resection only

items.explanationHtml:
Mesenteric malperfusion turns this into a complicated type B dissection, which needs urgent repair. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) covers the entry tear, redirects flow into the true lumen and usually restores branch perfusion; laparotomy is added if bowel is already non-viable.

Takeaway: Malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion or refractory pain makes a type B dissection 'complicated' and calls for urgent (usually endovascular) repair.

whyNot.A: More vasodilator does nothing for a mechanically compressed branch artery.
whyNot.B: Waiting with rising lactate and poorly perfused bowel risks infarction and death.
whyNot.D: Resecting bowel without restoring mesenteric flow leaves the cause untreated; bowel surgery may accompany, not replace, aortic repair.
whyNot.E: Heparin does not relieve compression by the false lumen and increases bleeding risk.

items.objective: Recognize complicated type B dissection and choose endovascular repair.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after sudden severe chest pain followed by fainting. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg and pulse 122/min. Neck veins are distended, and there is a soft early diastolic murmur. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes. A chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. Two large-bore intravenous lines are placed and the cardiothoracic surgeon is called. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?

options.label: D
options.html: Transesophageal echocardiography in the operating room

items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension, raised neck veins, low voltage, a widened mediastinum and a new aortic regurgitation murmur suggest a type A dissection complicated by tamponade. An unstable patient should not travel to the CT scanner: transesophageal echocardiography, done in the operating room or at the bedside, confirms the flap, root involvement, regurgitation and pericardial blood while surgery is prepared.

Takeaway: Unstable suspected aortic dissection → TEE where the patient is (ideally the operating room), not a trip to CT.

whyNot.A: Invasive aortography is slow and risky and has been replaced by CT and TEE.
whyNot.B: CT angiography is preferred only in hemodynamically stable patients.
whyNot.C: MR angiography takes too long and isolates an unstable patient in the scanner.
whyNot.E: A V/Q scan is for pulmonary embolism and would delay life-saving surgery.

items.objective: Choose transesophageal echocardiography for an unstable patient with suspected aortic dissection.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily from age 20 to 55 and has hypertension controlled with lisinopril. He has no symptoms. Abdominal examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for this patient?
items.explanationHtml:
Men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked should have a single screening ultrasound for abdominal aortic aneurysm (USPSTF grade B). Ultrasound is safe, cheap and accurate for measuring aortic diameter. If the aorta is normal (under 3.0 cm), no further screening is needed.

Takeaway: AAA screening: one abdominal ultrasound for men 65–75 who have ever smoked.

whyNot.A: Routine ankle-brachial index screening in asymptomatic adults is not recommended because benefit is unproven.
whyNot.B: Screening asymptomatic adults for carotid stenosis is recommended against: it leads to procedures that may cause more harm than benefit.
whyNot.C: CT gives radiation and contrast exposure without advantage over ultrasound for screening.
whyNot.D: Exercise ECG screening of asymptomatic low-risk adults is not recommended.

items.objective: Select one-time abdominal ultrasonography for AAA screening in a man aged 65–75 who has smoked.

items.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old man has an abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening ultrasound. He has no abdominal or back pain. He has hypertension and still smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily. Results of serial ultrasounds are shown:

DateMaximum infrarenal diameter
2 years ago3.9 cm
1 year ago4.1 cm
Today4.3 cm

His blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Start doxycycline to slow aneurysm growth

items.explanationHtml:
The aneurysm is 4.3 cm and growing about 0.2 cm per year, well below repair thresholds (about 5.5 cm in men, or rapid growth of about 0.5 cm or more in a year, or symptoms). Management is surveillance with ultrasound about yearly at this size, plus risk-factor control. Stopping smoking is the most effective measure to slow growth and lower rupture risk; blood pressure control, a statin and antiplatelet therapy address his overall atherosclerotic risk.

Takeaway: Asymptomatic AAA below ~5.5 cm (men) with slow growth → surveillance and smoking cessation, not repair.

whyNot.A: Early endovascular repair of small aneurysms has not improved survival compared with surveillance.
whyNot.B: Open repair carries operative risk not justified at this diameter and growth rate.
whyNot.C: An aneurysm of 4.3 cm needs continued surveillance because it is likely to keep growing.
whyNot.E: Doxycycline has not been shown to slow aneurysm growth in trials.

items.objective: Manage a small, slowly growing abdominal aortic aneurysm with surveillance and smoking cessation.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after the sudden onset of severe left flank and back pain. He fainted at home. He has hypertension and a 60-pack-year smoking history. Blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg and pulse 128/min. He is pale and diaphoretic. A tender, pulsatile mass is palpated above the umbilicus. Two large-bore intravenous lines are placed and blood is sent for crossmatching. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Immediate transfer to the operating room for aortic repair

options.label: C
options.html: Infusion of 4 L of crystalloid to normalize blood pressure

options.label: D
options.html: Non-contrast CT of the abdomen to look for a ureteral stone

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent abdominal ultrasonography to measure the aneurysm

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden flank or back pain, syncope, hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass in an older smoker is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. An unstable patient with this picture goes directly to the operating room (or hybrid endovascular suite) for proximal control and repair; imaging only delays hemorrhage control. Resuscitate with blood products and permissive hypotension rather than large crystalloid volumes.

Takeaway: Hypotension + pain + pulsatile mass in an older smoker = ruptured AAA → straight to repair.

whyNot.A: CT is appropriate only for a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected leak; here it would waste critical minutes.
whyNot.C: Raising pressure to normal with large crystalloid volumes worsens bleeding and dilutes clotting factors; permissive hypotension is preferred until control.
whyNot.D: Renal colic is a classic misdiagnosis of ruptured AAA; hypotension and a pulsatile mass make a stone study inappropriate.
whyNot.E: The pulsatile mass with shock is enough; confirming size with ultrasound does not change the need for immediate surgery.

items.objective: Send a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected ruptured AAA directly for operative repair.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man who has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years has 3 weeks of facial swelling and a feeling of fullness in his head that worsens when he bends over. His face is plethoric, and dilated veins are visible over the neck and upper anterior chest wall. A chest radiograph shows a right upper mediastinal mass. Compression of which of the following structures best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Swelling of the face and upper chest with distended neck and chest-wall veins reflects raised venous pressure in everything that drains into the superior vena cava. A right-sided mediastinal tumor, classically a lung carcinoma or lymphoma, compresses the thin-walled SVC; collaterals through the chest wall and azygos system dilate.

Takeaway: SVC obstruction raises venous pressure in the head, neck and both arms, producing facial plethora and chest-wall collaterals.

whyNot.B: Arterial compression would reduce perfusion to the right arm or head; it would not cause venous engorgement.
whyNot.C: Subclavian vein obstruction causes swelling of one arm only and spares the face.
whyNot.D: IVC obstruction causes leg edema and abdominal-wall collaterals, not facial swelling.
whyNot.E: Thoracic duct injury or obstruction causes chylothorax, not facial venous congestion.

items.objective: Identify superior vena cava obstruction from facial plethora and upper-body venous distension.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension collapses and dies after the sudden onset of severe chest pain radiating to the interscapular area. At autopsy, a 2-cm transverse tear is found in the intima of the ascending aorta, and a blood-filled channel separates the layers of the aortic wall. The pericardial sac contains 400 mL of clotted blood. Which of the following best explains his death?

options.label: D
options.html: Occlusion of the left anterior descending artery

items.explanationHtml:
The findings describe a proximal (Stanford type A) aortic dissection. The false lumen ruptured back into the pericardial space, and a few hundred milliliters of blood in a non-distensible pericardium is enough to compress the heart and stop diastolic filling. Rupture into the pericardium is the leading cause of death in untreated type A dissection.

Takeaway: Ascending aortic dissection most often kills by rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade.

whyNot.A: Dissection of the root causes aortic regurgitation by distorting the valve, not stenosis.
whyNot.B: Free wall rupture follows transmural infarction several days earlier; the aortic tear and false lumen point to dissection.
whyNot.C: Hemothorax follows rupture of the descending aorta into the pleural space; here the blood is in the pericardium.
whyNot.D: When a dissection occludes a coronary ostium it is usually the right one, and the autopsy finding here is pericardial blood.

items.objective: Recognize tamponade from hemopericardium as the fatal complication of type A aortic dissection.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man dies suddenly. He was 196 cm (6 ft 5 in) tall, with long fingers, a pectus excavatum and a history of bilateral lens subluxation. Microscopic examination of his dilated ascending aorta shows fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers with pools of pale basophilic ground substance in the media. A defect in which of the following proteins is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Tall stature with long digits, pectus deformity, lens subluxation and aortic root disease point to Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant defect of FBN1. Fibrillin-1 forms the microfibril scaffold on which elastic fibers are assembled; abnormal microfibrils also fail to hold TGF-β in its latent form, so excess TGF-β signalling adds to medial degeneration. The histology is cystic medial degeneration.

Takeaway: Marfan syndrome = fibrillin-1 defect → cystic medial degeneration of the aortic root → aneurysm and dissection.

whyNot.B: Type III collagen defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with arterial rupture but no lens dislocation or tall habitus.
whyNot.C: Elastin mutations cause supravalvular aortic stenosis (as in Williams syndrome) or cutis laxa, not this phenotype.
whyNot.D: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta (fractures, blue sclerae), not aortic root dilation with lens subluxation.
whyNot.E: Lysyl hydroxylase deficiency causes the kyphoscoliotic form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with hypotonia and scoliosis.

items.objective: Link Marfan syndrome to fibrillin-1 and cystic medial degeneration of the aorta.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman with hypertension has a 5.6-cm ascending aortic aneurysm resected electively. Histologic examination of the aortic wall is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Fragmentation of elastic lamellae with mucoid ground substance in the media

options.label: B
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells in the media

options.label: C
options.html: Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of the intima

options.label: D
options.html: Lipid-laden macrophages forming a necrotic core under a fibrous cap

options.label: E
options.html: Plasma cell cuffs around narrowed vasa vasorum in the adventitia

items.explanationHtml:
Ascending aortic aneurysms in older hypertensive patients are caused mainly by medial degeneration: loss of smooth muscle cells, fragmentation of elastic fibers and accumulation of mucoid ground substance. Atherosclerosis, by contrast, is the dominant association of abdominal aneurysms.

Takeaway: Ascending aortic aneurysm with hypertension or ageing = cystic medial degeneration.

whyNot.B: Granulomatous aortitis with giant cells describes giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis, which are much less common causes.
whyNot.C: Hyaline thickening is the lesion of small arterioles in hypertension and diabetes, not of the aortic media.
whyNot.D: An atheromatous plaque is the classic substrate of abdominal, not ascending, aortic aneurysms.
whyNot.E: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with plasma cells is the lesion of syphilitic aortitis, which is now rare and lacks a hypertension link.

items.objective: Identify cystic medial degeneration as the histology of hypertensive or age-related ascending aortic aneurysm.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has a 4-month history of a hoarse voice. He is a former smoker with hypertension. Laryngoscopy shows a paralyzed left vocal fold. A chest CT shows a 6-cm aneurysm of the distal aortic arch. Stretching of which of the following nerves best explains his hoarseness?

options.label: C
options.html: Left vagus nerve above the aortic arch

items.explanationHtml:
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus in the thorax and loops under the aortic arch, lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum, before ascending in the tracheo-esophageal groove. An arch aneurysm (or an enlarged left atrium or mediastinal tumor) can stretch it, paralysing all intrinsic laryngeal muscles on that side except the cricothyroid.

Takeaway: Hoarseness from a left vocal fold palsy can be the presenting sign of an aortic arch aneurysm.

whyNot.A: Phrenic nerve injury paralyses the hemidiaphragm; it does not affect the voice.
whyNot.B: The superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid and supraglottic sensation; its loss does not paralyse the vocal fold in this way and it lies in the neck.
whyNot.C: The vagus above the arch is not in contact with the arch, and a high vagal lesion would also cause palatal and pharyngeal weakness.
whyNot.D: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian artery, not the aortic arch, and the paralyzed fold is on the left.

items.objective: Relate the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve under the aortic arch to hoarseness from an arch aneurysm.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with a history of untreated genital ulcer disease in his twenties has progressive exertional dyspnea. Examination shows a wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the right sternal border. Imaging shows dilation of the ascending aorta and arch with linear calcification of the wall. Biopsy of the aorta would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Fibrinoid necrosis of the media with neutrophils

options.label: C
options.html: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with plasma cells

items.explanationHtml:
Tertiary syphilis affects the thoracic aorta decades after primary infection. Treponema pallidum provokes an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with plasma cells and lymphocytes; the outer media becomes ischemic, scars and weakens, producing aneurysm of the ascending aorta and arch. Dilation of the root causes aortic regurgitation (wide pulse pressure, early diastolic murmur).

Takeaway: Syphilitic aortitis = endarteritis of the vasa vasorum → ascending aortic aneurysm with aortic regurgitation.

whyNot.A: Fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils describes acute necrotizing vasculitis (for example polyarteritis nodosa) of medium-sized arteries.
whyNot.B: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculous aortitis, a rarity that is not linked to a genital ulcer history.
whyNot.D: Medial calcification sparing the intima is Mönckeberg sclerosis of medium-sized muscular arteries, which does not cause aneurysm.
whyNot.E: Eosinophilic infiltration suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which involves small vessels.

items.objective: Describe the vasa vasorum endarteritis of tertiary syphilitic aortitis and its link to aortic regurgitation.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has an emergency laparotomy after spontaneous rupture of the splenic artery. She has thin, translucent skin through which veins are easily seen, bruises easily, and her mother died at 40 of a ruptured iliac artery. Her large joints have normal mobility. A defect in which of the following is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Arterial, bowel or uterine rupture in a young adult with thin translucent skin, easy bruising and an autosomal dominant family history is vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, caused by mutations of COL3A1. Type III collagen is abundant in the walls of arteries and hollow organs, so they tear, often without prior dilation. Joint hypermobility is usually limited to small joints.

Takeaway: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1, type III collagen) causes spontaneous arterial rupture in young adults.

whyNot.B: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with fractures rather than arterial rupture.
whyNot.C: Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome (nephritis, hearing loss, eye changes).
whyNot.D: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, whose arterial disease is usually aortic root dilation and dissection, with a tall habitus and lens subluxation.
whyNot.E: Loeys-Dietz syndrome causes aggressive aneurysms and tortuous arteries with craniofacial clues such as a bifid uvula; translucent skin is not its hallmark.

items.objective: Recognize vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and its type III collagen defect.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man who has smoked for 50 years has an asymptomatic 4.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm found on ultrasound. Which of the following processes contributes most directly to weakening of the aortic wall in this condition?

options.label: B
options.html: Deposition of amyloid in the media

options.label: C
options.html: Hyperplasia of medial smooth muscle cells

options.label: D
options.html: Matrix metalloproteinase degradation of elastin and collagen

options.label: E
options.html: Thrombosis of the vasa vasorum by septic emboli

items.explanationHtml:
Abdominal aortic aneurysms arise where atherosclerosis is heavy, but the defining process is chronic transmural inflammation. Macrophages and other cells release matrix metalloproteinases that break down elastin and collagen in the media faster than they can be replaced; smooth muscle cells are lost. Smoking promotes this inflammation and is the strongest modifiable risk factor.

Takeaway: AAA = inflammation-driven proteolysis of medial elastin and collagen, promoted by smoking.

whyNot.A: Anti-endothelial antibodies are not the mechanism of degenerative AAA.
whyNot.B: Amyloid in the aortic media occurs with age but is not the cause of aneurysm.
whyNot.C: The media in an aneurysm thins as smooth muscle cells are lost; hyperplasia is the response in hypertensive arterioles.
whyNot.E: Septic emboli cause mycotic aneurysms, which are uncommon, saccular and often in unusual sites.

items.objective: Explain the proteolytic, inflammatory mechanism of abdominal aortic aneurysm.

items.stemHtml: An abdominal aortic aneurysm grows from 4.0 cm to 5.0 cm in diameter while the patient's mean arterial pressure and wall thickness stay the same. By approximately how much has the circumferential wall tension changed?
items.explanationHtml:
The law of Laplace for a cylinder gives wall tension ∝ pressure × radius (and wall stress ∝ pressure × radius ÷ thickness). With pressure and thickness unchanged, tension scales with radius: 5.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.25, an increase of 25%. Because the dilated segment then bears more tension, it stretches further, a feedback loop that explains accelerating growth and why rupture risk climbs with diameter.

Takeaway: Laplace: wall tension rises in proportion to radius, so aneurysms beget further dilation.

whyNot.A: Tension rises, not falls, as the radius increases.
whyNot.B: Tension depends on radius as well as pressure, so it cannot stay the same.
whyNot.D: A 56% rise would follow if tension scaled with the square of the radius (as cross-sectional area does).
whyNot.E: A 95% rise would follow if tension scaled with the cube of the radius, which it does not.

items.objective: Apply the law of Laplace to explain rising wall tension in an enlarging aneurysm.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has sudden severe chest pain radiating to his back. His blood pressure is 176/92 mm Hg in the right arm and 140/80 mm Hg in the left arm. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Echocardiography shows a mobile linear echo in the aortic root and mild aortic regurgitation. Which of the following best explains the ECG findings?

options.label: B
options.html: Dissection flap occluding the right coronary artery ostium

options.label: C
options.html: Embolism from the left atrial appendage to the right coronary artery

options.label: D
options.html: Pericardial inflammation from blood in the pericardial space

options.label: E
options.html: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque in the right coronary artery

items.explanationHtml:
Back pain, an inter-arm pressure difference, a flap in the aortic root and new aortic regurgitation identify a type A dissection. Extension of the flap or false lumen into a coronary ostium causes infarction; the right coronary artery is involved more often than the left because of where proximal dissections usually spiral, so the ECG shows inferior ST elevation. Recognizing this matters because fibrinolysis or anticoagulation for presumed plaque rupture can be fatal.

Takeaway: Inferior STEMI with back pain and an inter-arm pressure gap suggests a type A dissection involving the right coronary ostium.

whyNot.A: Vasospasm can cause transient ST elevation, but it does not explain the flap, the arm pressure difference or aortic regurgitation.
whyNot.C: Coronary embolism needs a source such as atrial fibrillation or endocarditis and would not explain the aortic findings.
whyNot.D: Pericarditis gives diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not a territorial inferior pattern.
whyNot.E: Plaque rupture is the usual cause of STEMI, but it does not explain the aortic root flap or the arm pressure difference.

items.objective: Explain how a proximal aortic dissection can produce an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has 6 months of cramping pain in both calves after walking two blocks; it resolves within 3 minutes of standing still. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia and a 45-pack-year history; he stopped smoking 2 months ago. He takes lisinopril, atorvastatin 80 mg daily and aspirin. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are weak bilaterally. Ankle-brachial index is 0.71 on the right and 0.74 on the left. He has no rest pain or wounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
An ABI of 0.90 or less with typical calf claudication confirms PAD. He already has risk-factor therapy (statin, antiplatelet, blood pressure control, smoking cessation). For claudication, a supervised exercise program of at least 12 weeks is first-line: it increases walking distance through collateral development, better muscle oxygen use and walking economy.

Takeaway: Claudication: optimize risk factors, then a supervised exercise program before drugs or revascularization.

whyNot.A: Revascularization is for lifestyle-limiting claudication despite exercise and medication, or limb-threatening ischemia.
whyNot.B: Pentoxifylline has little proven benefit and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Bypass surgery is not first-line for claudication.
whyNot.E: Full anticoagulation with warfarin does not improve claudication and raises bleeding risk.

items.objective: Prescribe supervised exercise as first-line therapy for intermittent claudication.

items.stemHtml:
A 63-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 18 years and chronic kidney disease has pain in the right calf after walking about 100 meters for 4 months. Foot pulses are difficult to feel. Doppler pressures are shown:

SiteSystolic pressure (mm Hg)
Right brachial134
Left brachial130
Right ankle (higher of DP/PT)> 250 (vessel could not be compressed)
Left ankle (higher of DP/PT)212

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: C
options.html: No further testing; the results exclude peripheral artery disease

items.explanationHtml:
Both ankle-brachial indices exceed 1.40 (right noncompressible; left 212 ÷ 134 ≈ 1.58), which means the tibial arteries are calcified and stiff, common in long-standing diabetes and kidney disease. The ABI is uninterpretable, not normal. Digital arteries are usually spared, so the toe-brachial index (abnormal at 0.70 or less) is the next physiological test to diagnose PAD.

Takeaway: ABI > 1.40 = noncompressible vessels → measure the toe-brachial index.

whyNot.A: Anatomical imaging is for planning revascularization once PAD is confirmed and treatment is considered.
whyNot.B: Exercise ABI helps when the resting ABI is normal or borderline; with incompressible vessels the ankle pressures remain unreliable.
whyNot.C: A high ABI does not exclude PAD; calcification masks it.
whyNot.E: Her symptoms are exertional and arterial, not venous.

items.objective: Interpret an ABI above 1.40 and choose the toe-brachial index.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has calf claudication that limits his walking to one block despite 4 months of a supervised exercise program. He has stopped smoking and takes aspirin, rosuvastatin and amlodipine. Left ventricular ejection fraction measured last year was 60%, and he has no history of heart failure. ABI is 0.68 bilaterally. He has no rest pain or ulcers and would prefer medication before considering a procedure. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to add?
items.explanationHtml:
Cilostazol, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, increases pain-free and maximal walking distance in claudication and is the drug of choice when exercise and risk-factor control are not enough. Check for heart failure first: it is contraindicated in heart failure of any severity. Benefit is assessed after about 3 months.

Takeaway: Persistent claudication after exercise therapy → add cilostazol if there is no heart failure.

whyNot.B: Adding a second antiplatelet agent to aspirin does not improve claudication and increases bleeding; dual therapy is used after stenting.
whyNot.C: Nitrates do not improve walking distance in PAD.
whyNot.D: Beta-blockers are not harmful in PAD but do not treat claudication.
whyNot.E: Pentoxifylline is less effective than cilostazol and is not recommended.

items.objective: Add cilostazol for persistent claudication when there is no heart failure.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking apixaban a month ago has sudden severe pain in her left leg that began 2 hours ago. The leg is pale and cold below the knee. Left popliteal and pedal pulses are absent, and no Doppler signal is heard over the dorsalis pedis artery. She has decreased light-touch sensation over the toes and dorsum of the foot, and toe movement is weak. Pulses in the right leg are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.label: B
options.html: Elevation of the limb and warm compresses

options.label: C
