options.html: Intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus followed by infusion

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, coldness, sensory loss and weakness in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation is acute limb ischemia from an embolus. The leg is immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond the toes and weakness), so after an immediate intravenous heparin bolus and infusion to stop propagation, she needs emergency revascularization (embolectomy).

Takeaway: Acute limb ischemia: give IV heparin at once, then revascularize urgently according to limb viability.

whyNot.A: Antiplatelet loading does not prevent clot propagation in an acute arterial embolus as effective anticoagulation does.
whyNot.B: Elevation lowers perfusion pressure further; ischemic limbs are kept level or slightly dependent.
whyNot.D: Delay risks irreversible ischemia; this is an emergency.
whyNot.E: An oral agent works too slowly and cannot be titrated or reversed before surgery.

items.objective: Start immediate intravenous heparin for acute limb ischemia before urgent revascularization.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man has had pain in his right forefoot for 2 months that wakes him at night and improves when he dangles the foot over the side of the bed. A shallow, painful ulcer on the tip of the right great toe has not healed in 6 weeks. He has a history of claudication and still smokes. The right foot is cool with dependent rubor; there are no palpable pulses below the femoral artery. Right ABI is 0.32. There is no fever or spreading erythema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Rest pain relieved by dependency, a non-healing toe ulcer and an ABI of 0.32 indicate chronic limb-threatening ischemia. The aim is limb salvage: prompt anatomical imaging (duplex, CT angiography or catheter angiography) to plan endovascular or surgical revascularization, together with wound care, smoking cessation, statin and antiplatelet therapy.

Takeaway: Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulcer, gangrene) → urgent imaging and revascularization.

whyNot.A: Amputation is reserved for non-salvageable limbs or failed revascularization.
whyNot.B: Cilostazol helps claudication but does not save a limb with rest pain and tissue loss.
whyNot.C: Hyperbaric oxygen does not restore arterial inflow and is not a substitute for revascularization.
whyNot.D: Exercise therapy is for claudication; it is inappropriate with rest pain and an ischemic ulcer.

items.objective: Recognize chronic limb-threatening ischemia and arrange revascularization.

items.stemHtml: Twelve days after uncomplicated coronary stenting via the femoral artery, a 72-year-old man has bluish discoloration of several toes on both feet and a net-like purple rash on his thighs. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Femoral and pedal pulses are normal. Serum creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no blood or protein. The leukocyte count is 9,800/mm3 with 10% eosinophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Livedo reticularis, blue toes with intact pulses, acute kidney injury that develops over days to weeks, and eosinophilia after an arterial catheter procedure are typical of cholesterol embolization. Treatment is supportive with a statin and control of blood pressure; further instrumentation and new anticoagulation are avoided when possible.

Takeaway: Blue toes with good pulses, livedo, eosinophilia and delayed AKI after catheterization = atheroembolism.

whyNot.B: Contrast-associated kidney injury peaks within a few days and does not cause livedo, blue toes or eosinophilia.
whyNot.C: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia would show a falling platelet count and usually larger-vessel thrombosis.
whyNot.D: Endocarditis would cause fever, a murmur and positive blood cultures; urinalysis often shows hematuria.
whyNot.E: Polyarteritis nodosa is not triggered by catheterization and is not associated with eosinophilia in this way.

items.objective: Diagnose atheroembolic disease after an arterial procedure.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man had 20 minutes of weakness and numbness of the right hand and face with difficulty speaking 5 days ago; symptoms resolved fully. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Neurological examination is now normal. Head MRI shows no infarct. Carotid duplex ultrasonography shows 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery and 30% stenosis of the right. He has good functional status and low surgical risk. He has been started on aspirin and a high-intensity statin. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?

options.label: A
options.html: Left carotid endarterectomy within the next 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
A recent left-hemisphere TIA (right face and hand, aphasia) with 70–99% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery is symptomatic severe stenosis. Carotid endarterectomy, best done within 2 weeks of the event in a patient with good surgical risk, substantially lowers the risk of stroke, together with antiplatelet therapy, a statin and blood pressure control.

Takeaway: Symptomatic 70–99% carotid stenosis → endarterectomy within about 2 weeks (plus best medical therapy).

whyNot.B: Watchful waiting leaves him at high early risk of stroke.
whyNot.C: The right-sided stenosis is mild and asymptomatic; it is not the culprit.
whyNot.D: Anticoagulation is not better than antiplatelet therapy for atherosclerotic carotid disease and raises bleeding risk.
whyNot.E: Stenting is an alternative mainly for high surgical risk patients and is not indicated for the mild right-sided lesion.

items.objective: Choose early carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic severe carotid stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman has 2 years of episodes in which her fingers turn white then blue in the cold. Over the past 6 months she has had heartburn, puffy fingers and tight skin over the fingers, and she now has a small painful ulcer on the tip of the right index finger. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test?

options.label: B
options.html: Arterial duplex ultrasonography of the arms

items.explanationHtml:
Raynaud phenomenon starting in adulthood with digital ulcers, puffy fingers, skin tightening and reflux suggests secondary Raynaud from systemic sclerosis. The first test is an antinuclear antibody assay (with specific antibodies such as anticentromere, anti-topoisomerase I and anti-RNA polymerase III), together with nailfold capillaroscopy.

Takeaway: Raynaud with ulcers, sclerodactyly or late onset → test ANA (and nailfold capillaries) for a connective-tissue disease.

whyNot.B: Arterial duplex looks for large-artery disease, which does not explain sclerodactyly and reflux.
whyNot.C: Cryoglobulins are checked with purpura, hepatitis C or glomerulonephritis, which she does not have.
whyNot.D: An ESR is non-specific and will not establish the diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Endoscopy may later assess esophageal involvement but does not diagnose the underlying disorder.

items.objective: Evaluate suspected secondary Raynaud phenomenon with antinuclear antibody testing.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman has 5 months of crampy mid-abdominal pain that begins about 30 minutes after meals and lasts 1–2 hours. She now eats small amounts because she is afraid of the pain and has lost 9 kg (20 lb). She has smoked for 50 years and has coronary artery disease and claudication. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with an epigastric bruit. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy last month were normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Postprandial pain, food fear and weight loss in a smoker with diffuse atherosclerosis point to chronic mesenteric ischemia, usually from stenosis of at least two of the celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries. CT angiography confirms the stenoses and plans revascularization, typically endovascular stenting.

Takeaway: Postprandial pain + food fear + weight loss in a vasculopath = chronic mesenteric ischemia → CT angiography.

whyNot.A: Biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant pain, not progressive postprandial pain with weight loss and a bruit.
whyNot.C: Gastroparesis causes nausea, early satiety and vomiting rather than ischemic pain.
whyNot.D: Recent endoscopy was normal; the bruit and vascular history point elsewhere.
whyNot.E: Lipase screens for pancreatitis, which does not fit this chronic stereotyped pattern.

items.objective: Diagnose chronic mesenteric ischemia with CT angiography.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy dies in a motor vehicle collision. At autopsy, the intima of the thoracic aorta shows flat, yellow, slightly raised streaks a few millimeters wide. Microscopic examination of these streaks would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Calcified necrotic core with cholesterol clefts

options.label: B
options.html: Concentric smooth muscle proliferation in arterioles

options.label: C
options.html: Organizing thrombus attached to the intima

options.label: E
options.html: Plasma cell infiltrate around the vasa vasorum

items.explanationHtml:
Fatty streaks are the earliest visible lesion of atherosclerosis and are common in adolescents. They consist of lipid-filled macrophages (foam cells), plus some lipid-laden smooth muscle cells, beneath intact endothelium. They do not obstruct flow, and many never progress.

Takeaway: The fatty streak = intimal foam cells; it is the earliest lesion of atherosclerosis.

whyNot.A: A calcified necrotic core belongs to an advanced fibrofatty plaque, not a flat streak in a teenager.
whyNot.B: Onion-skin smooth muscle proliferation is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of malignant hypertension.
whyNot.C: Thrombus forms on a ruptured or eroded advanced plaque.
whyNot.E: Periadventitial plasma cells around the vasa vasorum describe syphilitic aortitis.

items.objective: Identify the fatty streak as intimal foam cells, the earliest lesion of atherosclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A femoral artery plaque removed at surgery has a thick collagen-rich cap over a core of lipid and debris. Which of the following cells is chiefly responsible for synthesizing the collagen in the cap?
items.explanationHtml:
Growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor, released by activated platelets, macrophages and endothelium, draw smooth muscle cells from the media into the intima. There they proliferate and secrete collagen, elastin and proteoglycans that form the fibrous cap. Macrophages, by releasing metalloproteinases, work against the cap and make it thinner and more rupture-prone.

Takeaway: Intimal smooth muscle cells build the fibrous cap; macrophage proteases weaken it.

whyNot.A: Endothelial cells regulate permeability and leukocyte adhesion but do not lay down the bulk of cap collagen.
whyNot.B: Adventitial fibroblasts are outside the intima, where the plaque forms.
whyNot.C: Macrophages take up lipid and secrete proteases that degrade, rather than build, the cap.
whyNot.D: Platelets are anucleate and release growth factors but do not synthesize collagen.

items.objective: Explain the role of migrated smooth muscle cells in forming the fibrous cap of an atheroma.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension for 20 years. A renal biopsy for slowly rising creatinine shows thickened walls of the arterioles with homogeneous, glassy, pink material that narrows the lumen. Which of the following best describes the formation of this material?

options.label: B
options.html: Leakage of plasma proteins across injured endothelium with excess matrix synthesis

options.label: C
options.html: Necrosis of smooth muscle with neutrophilic infiltration

options.label: D
options.html: Proliferation of smooth muscle cells in concentric layers

items.explanationHtml:
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the arteriolar lesion of long-standing hypertension, diabetes and ageing. Hemodynamic and metabolic injury lets plasma proteins leak into the vessel wall, and smooth muscle cells make excess basement-membrane matrix. The lumen narrows, causing diffuse ischemic scarring of the kidney (nephrosclerosis).

Takeaway: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis = plasma-protein leakage plus excess matrix, from chronic hypertension and diabetes.

whyNot.A: Amyloid would stain with Congo red and is not linked to this history.
whyNot.C: Fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils is a feature of malignant hypertension or vasculitis.
whyNot.D: Concentric onion-skin proliferation is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of severe hypertension.
whyNot.E: Immune-complex deposition describes immune-mediated glomerulonephritis or vasculitis.

items.objective: Describe the pathogenesis of hyaline arteriolosclerosis in hypertension and diabetes.

items.stemHtml: An 80-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has foot radiographs after a fall. They show no fracture but do show dense, ring-like calcification outlining the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries along their length, like a pipe. His pedal pulses are palpable. Which of the following best describes this arterial lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation of the arterial wall

options.label: B
options.html: Calcified intimal plaques with critical stenosis

options.label: D
options.html: Calcification of the media that does not narrow the lumen

options.label: E
options.html: Segmental thrombosis with inflammation of the vessel wall

items.explanationHtml:
Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis deposits calcium in the internal elastic lamina and media of medium-sized muscular arteries, especially in older people, diabetes and chronic kidney disease. The lumen is not narrowed, so pulses can be normal, but the stiff arteries resist cuff compression and can give a falsely high ankle-brachial index.

Takeaway: Pipe-stem medial calcification (Mönckeberg) does not obstruct flow but makes arteries noncompressible.

whyNot.A: Granulomatous arteritis affects large vessels in giant cell or Takayasu arteritis and does not cause this radiographic pattern.
whyNot.B: Calcified atherosclerotic plaque is patchy and intimal, and critical stenosis would weaken pulses.
whyNot.C: Intimal hyperplasia after thrombosis does not produce continuous ring calcification.
whyNot.E: Segmental thrombosing inflammation describes Buerger disease in young smokers.

items.objective: Distinguish Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis from atherosclerosis.

items.stemHtml: Ten days after coronary angiography through the femoral artery, a 71-year-old man has painful purple toes, a lace-like violaceous rash on both feet and a rise in serum creatinine from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL. Dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable. The leukocyte count shows 9% eosinophils. A skin biopsy would most likely show which of the following in small arteries?

options.label: E
options.html: Needle-shaped empty clefts within the lumen

items.explanationHtml:
This is cholesterol (atheroembolic) embolization: catheter manipulation dislodged cholesterol crystals from aortic plaques, which lodged in small arteries of the skin, kidneys and other organs. Pulses stay palpable because the emboli are tiny. Eosinophilia and low complement can occur. The crystals dissolve during tissue processing, leaving biconvex, needle-shaped clefts surrounded by inflammation.

Takeaway: Blue toes + livedo + AKI after catheterization, with pulses present → cholesterol emboli (needle-shaped clefts).

whyNot.A: Fibrin thrombi with schistocytes suggest a thrombotic microangiopathy, not a post-procedural embolic shower with eosinophilia.
whyNot.B: IgA vasculitis gives palpable purpura, mainly in children, and is not triggered by catheterization.
whyNot.C: Granulomatous arteritis affects large vessels and does not explain this timing.
whyNot.D: Septic emboli would come with fever and a source such as endocarditis.

items.objective: Recognize atheroembolic disease after vascular procedures and its biopsy finding.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man who smokes 2 packs of cigarettes daily has painful ulcers on the tips of two fingers and the great toe, and tender red cord-like lesions along superficial leg veins. His fingers turn white in the cold. Radial and ulnar pulses are weak; femoral pulses are normal. Biopsy of a digital artery shows a cellular, inflamed thrombus with microabscesses and sparing of the internal elastic lamina. Which of the following is the most important factor in the course of this disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a segmental, inflammatory, thrombosing disease of small and medium arteries and veins of the distal limbs in young heavy smokers. It is tightly tied to tobacco: complete cessation (including smokeless tobacco and nicotine replacement in some cases) halts progression, and continued use leads to amputations.

Takeaway: Buerger disease is driven by tobacco; complete cessation is the only effective treatment.

whyNot.A: Hepatitis B is associated with polyarteritis nodosa, which affects medium arteries of the kidneys and gut, not this picture.
whyNot.C: Cholesterol drives atherosclerosis, which typically affects larger, more proximal arteries in older patients.
whyNot.D: Homocysteine is a vascular risk factor but does not govern the course of Buerger disease.
whyNot.E: Corticosteroids do not alter the course of Buerger disease.

items.objective: Identify tobacco as the driver of thromboangiitis obliterans.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman reports that in cold weather her fingers become white, then blue, then red and painful as they rewarm. Episodes affect both hands symmetrically and last 15–20 minutes. She has no rashes, joint pain or skin thickening, and nailfold capillaries look normal. She is started on a drug that relaxes vascular smooth muscle by blocking L-type voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
items.explanationHtml:
Symmetric triphasic color change in a young woman without features of connective-tissue disease is primary Raynaud phenomenon. When warming measures fail, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as nifedipine or amlodipine is first-line drug therapy. Dihydropyridines act mainly on L-type channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation with little effect on the heart.

Takeaway: Raynaud phenomenon: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (vascular-selective) are first-line drugs.

whyNot.A: Diltiazem blocks L-type channels but acts on the heart as well as vessels and is a weaker vasodilator; dihydropyridines are preferred.
whyNot.B: Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar dilator that does not act by blocking calcium channels.
whyNot.D: Prazosin blocks α1-adrenergic receptors, not calcium channels.
whyNot.E: Verapamil is the most cardioselective calcium channel blocker and is a poor peripheral vasodilator.

items.objective: Choose a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for primary Raynaud phenomenon and explain its vascular selectivity.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with peripheral artery disease is prescribed a drug that improves his pain-free walking distance. It inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates arteries by inhibiting the breakdown of cAMP. This drug is contraindicated if he develops which of the following conditions?
items.explanationHtml:
Cilostazol inhibits phosphodiesterase 3, raising cAMP in platelets (less aggregation) and vascular smooth muscle (vasodilation), and improves claudication. Other phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors (such as milrinone used long term) increased mortality in patients with heart failure, so cilostazol carries a boxed contraindication in heart failure of any severity.

Takeaway: Cilostazol (PDE3 inhibitor) improves claudication but is contraindicated in heart failure.

whyNot.A: Asthma is a caution for non-selective beta-blockers, not cilostazol.
whyNot.B: Gout is a concern with thiazides and low-dose aspirin, not cilostazol.
whyNot.D: Hypothyroidism does not contraindicate cilostazol.
whyNot.E: Diabetes is common in PAD and is not a contraindication; cilostazol is often used in diabetic patients.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of cilostazol and its contraindication in heart failure.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has a femoral stent placed and is started on aspirin and clopidogrel. Six weeks later the stent thromboses despite good adherence. Genotyping shows he is homozygous for a loss-of-function allele of a hepatic enzyme. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

options.label: A
options.html: Faster hepatic clearance of active clopidogrel

options.label: B
options.html: Impaired conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite

options.label: C
options.html: Inherited resistance of COX-1 to acetylation by aspirin

options.label: D
options.html: Mutation of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor

items.explanationHtml:
Clopidogrel is a prodrug. Hepatic CYP2C19 (with other CYPs) converts it to a thiol metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Carriers of loss-of-function CYP2C19 alleles make less active drug and have more stent thrombosis; prasugrel or ticagrelor are not affected in the same way.

Takeaway: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers cannot activate clopidogrel well, so platelet inhibition and protection fall.

whyNot.A: The defect is a loss of enzyme function, which reduces activation rather than increasing clearance.
whyNot.C: Aspirin resistance from COX-1 mutation is not the pharmacogenetic issue tied to a hepatic enzyme.
whyNot.D: GP IIb/IIIa mutations cause Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a bleeding disorder.
whyNot.E: The problem is hepatic bioactivation, not absorption.

items.objective: Explain how CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles reduce the effect of clopidogrel.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has newly diagnosed hypertension of 168/104 mm Hg. She does not smoke and has no family history of hypertension. A bruit is heard in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Renal angiography shows alternating stenoses and dilations of the mid right renal artery, giving a beaded appearance. Which of the following sets of plasma findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory disease of medium-sized arteries, typically in young and middle-aged women; the renal artery shows a 'string of beads'. Stenosis lowers pressure at the juxtaglomerular apparatus, so the kidney releases renin; angiotensin II raises blood pressure and stimulates aldosterone. This is secondary hyperaldosteronism with high renin and high aldosterone.

Takeaway: Renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia) → high renin and high aldosterone.

whyNot.A: Low renin and low aldosterone suggest excess of another mineralocorticoid or Liddle syndrome.
whyNot.B: Low aldosterone with high renin suggests adrenal insufficiency or a block in aldosterone synthesis.
whyNot.C: Low renin with high aldosterone is primary hyperaldosteronism (adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia).
whyNot.E: A hemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis activates the renin system.

items.objective: Predict the renin–aldosterone pattern of renovascular hypertension from fibromuscular dysplasia.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of pain and swelling in her left calf. Three weeks ago she had open reduction and internal fixation of a left ankle fracture, and the leg was in a cast until 5 days ago. She has no chest pain or dyspnea. Pulse is 84/min, respirations 14/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The left calf is 4 cm larger in circumference than the right, with tenderness along the deep veins and pitting edema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Compression ultrasonography of the left leg

options.label: E
options.html: Start warfarin and repeat examination in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
Recent surgery, immobilization in a cast, calf swelling of more than 3 cm, pitting edema and localized tenderness give a high (DVT likely) Wells score. With high pretest probability, a negative D-dimer could not safely exclude DVT and a positive one is expected after surgery anyway, so go directly to compression ultrasonography.

Takeaway: DVT likely → compression ultrasound; DVT unlikely → D-dimer first.

whyNot.A: She has no symptoms of pulmonary embolism; CTPA is not the test for leg symptoms.
whyNot.C: Venography is invasive and has been replaced by ultrasound.
whyNot.D: D-dimer is used to exclude DVT only when pretest probability is low; after recent surgery it will usually be raised.
whyNot.E: Warfarin alone, without diagnosis or heparin overlap, is inappropriate.

items.objective: Use compression ultrasonography directly when pretest probability of DVT is high.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) Compression ultrasonography in the same 52-year-old woman shows a non-compressible left popliteal and superficial femoral vein. She weighs 74 kg. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL and platelet count 248,000/mm3. She has no history of bleeding, cancer or liver disease and is not pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin at prophylactic dose

items.explanationHtml:
She has a proximal DVT with normal renal function, no cancer, no pregnancy and no bleeding risk. A direct oral anticoagulant is preferred for most such patients; apixaban (or rivaroxaban) can be started immediately without initial parenteral therapy, using a higher-dose lead-in phase.

Takeaway: Uncomplicated proximal DVT → a DOAC for most patients.

whyNot.A: Aspirin is far less effective than anticoagulation for treating DVT.
whyNot.B: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is reserved for limb-threatening iliofemoral DVT (phlegmasia), not a popliteal-femoral DVT like this.
whyNot.C: An IVC filter is for patients who cannot be anticoagulated.
whyNot.E: A prophylactic dose is inadequate to treat established thrombosis.

items.objective: Choose a direct oral anticoagulant for uncomplicated proximal DVT.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) The same patient asks how long she will need to take apixaban. She has no other risk factors for thrombosis, and this is her first venous thromboembolism. Her fracture has healed and she is walking normally. Which of the following is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
items.explanationHtml:
A first DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor (surgery with immobilization) that has resolved carries a low recurrence risk after stopping. Three months of anticoagulation treats the clot; extending treatment adds bleeding risk without enough benefit. Unprovoked VTE or VTE with a persistent risk factor such as active cancer is considered for extended therapy.

Takeaway: First VTE provoked by surgery or another major transient factor → 3 months of anticoagulation.

whyNot.A: Two weeks is too short; recurrence is higher when therapy stops before 3 months.
whyNot.B: Six weeks has been associated with more recurrence than 3 months for proximal DVT.
whyNot.D: Twelve months offers no clear benefit over 3 months for a provoked event and adds bleeding risk.
whyNot.E: Indefinite treatment is considered for unprovoked, recurrent or cancer-associated VTE, not a resolved surgical trigger.

items.objective: Set a 3-month duration of anticoagulation for VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has mild aching of the right calf for 2 days after a long day of hiking. She has no recent surgery, travel, cancer or hormone use and no history of VTE. The calves are equal in size, there is no edema, and there is mild tenderness of the gastrocnemius muscle. Her Wells score places her in the DVT unlikely category. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
When the pretest probability is low (DVT unlikely), a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer has a high negative predictive value and excludes DVT without imaging. If positive, compression ultrasonography follows.

Takeaway: Low pretest probability of DVT → D-dimer; a negative result rules DVT out.

whyNot.A: Ultrasound is not needed first when pretest probability is low; D-dimer is efficient and safe.
whyNot.B: CT venography is for suspected pelvic or caval thrombosis.
whyNot.C: Empirical anticoagulation without a diagnosis exposes her to bleeding risk.
whyNot.E: The pretest probability is low but not zero; a simple test is warranted because she has calf symptoms.

items.objective: Use D-dimer testing to exclude DVT when pretest probability is low.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man is admitted with a left middle cerebral artery hemorrhagic stroke. On hospital day 5 his left leg becomes swollen, and compression ultrasonography shows thrombus in the left common femoral vein. Repeat head CT shows the hematoma unchanged in size. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
An acute proximal DVT carries a high risk of pulmonary embolism, but recent intracranial hemorrhage is a contraindication to therapeutic anticoagulation. In this situation a (retrievable) inferior vena cava filter prevents emboli from the legs. Anticoagulation should be started when bleeding risk allows, and the filter removed when it is no longer needed.

Takeaway: Acute proximal DVT + contraindication to anticoagulation → IVC filter; anticoagulate later when safe.

whyNot.A: Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated after intracranial hemorrhage.
whyNot.B: Therapeutic LMWH risks expansion of the hemorrhage.
whyNot.D: Therapeutic heparin, even without a bolus, carries the same bleeding risk.
whyNot.E: A DOAC is still therapeutic anticoagulation and is contraindicated in this acute setting.

items.objective: Recognize when an inferior vena cava filter is indicated for DVT.

items.stemHtml:
A 70-year-old man is receiving subcutaneous unfractionated heparin for VTE prophylaxis after a colectomy. Laboratory results are shown:

DayPlatelets (/mm3)
Admission (day 0)256,000
Day 3231,000
Day 798,000

On day 7 his right leg is swollen and ultrasonography shows a femoral vein thrombosis. He has no bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue heparin at a therapeutic dose

options.label: D
options.html: Switch to enoxaparin at a therapeutic dose

items.explanationHtml:
A platelet fall of more than 50% beginning 5–10 days after starting heparin, with new thrombosis and no other explanation, gives a high 4Ts score for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. All heparin must be stopped, including LMWH and flushes, and a non-heparin anticoagulant started immediately (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC), while PF4 antibody testing is sent.

Takeaway: Suspected HIT: stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant before results return.

whyNot.A: Continuing heparin drives further platelet activation and thrombosis.
whyNot.B: Platelet transfusion may worsen thrombosis and is reserved for bleeding.
whyNot.D: LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and must not be used.
whyNot.E: Warfarin alone during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene; it is started only after platelets recover, with overlap.

items.objective: Manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia by stopping heparin and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman has a tender, red, firm 3-cm cord on the inside of her left forearm at the site where an intravenous cannula was removed 2 days ago. She has no fever. The cord is warm, without fluctuance or purulent drainage, and the arm is not swollen. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Duplex ultrasonography of the arm and therapeutic anticoagulation

options.label: E
options.html: Warm compresses and an oral NSAID

items.explanationHtml:
A short segment of superficial thrombophlebitis at a former cannula site, without signs of infection or deep extension, is managed symptomatically with warm compresses, elevation and an NSAID. It usually resolves within 1–2 weeks.

Takeaway: Small catheter-related superficial thrombophlebitis → warm compresses and NSAIDs.

whyNot.A: Anticoagulation is reserved for longer leg segments or thrombosis near the deep system.
whyNot.B: There is no abscess to drain.
whyNot.C: There is no fever, pus or fluctuance to suggest suppurative phlebitis.
whyNot.D: Excision is only for suppurative thrombophlebitis that does not respond to antibiotics.

items.objective: Manage limited superficial thrombophlebitis conservatively.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer receiving chemotherapy has had 1 day of rapidly worsening swelling and pain of the entire left leg. The leg is massively swollen from the groin to the foot, tense and dusky blue, with blisters on the shin. Pedal pulses are faint by palpation but present on Doppler. Sensation and movement are intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden massive swelling of the whole leg with cyanosis, pain and blistering is phlegmasia cerulea dolens: extensive iliofemoral thrombosis that blocks almost all venous outflow. Rising tissue pressure can impair arterial inflow and lead to venous gangrene. Cancer is a common trigger. Treat with heparin, elevation and urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy.

Takeaway: Massive, blue, painful swollen leg = phlegmasia cerulea dolens (iliofemoral DVT) → urgent clot removal.

whyNot.A: Arterial embolism causes a pale, cold, pulseless leg without massive swelling.
whyNot.B: Cellulitis causes erythema and warmth with fever, not cyanosis and massive swelling over a day.
whyNot.C: Lymphedema develops slowly and is not cyanotic or acutely painful.
whyNot.E: A ruptured Baker cyst causes calf swelling and bruising near the ankle, not cyanosis of the whole leg.

items.objective: Recognize phlegmasia cerulea dolens.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and new heart failure. She is expected to be in bed for most of the next several days. She has no history of bleeding, and hemoglobin is 12.8 g/dL, platelets 210,000/mm3 and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to prevent venous thromboembolism?
items.explanationHtml:
An older, acutely ill medical inpatient with heart failure, infection and reduced mobility is at increased VTE risk and has low bleeding risk. Pharmacological prophylaxis with subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (or unfractionated heparin or fondaparinux) is recommended for the duration of the admission. Mechanical prophylaxis is used instead when bleeding risk is high.

Takeaway: Medical inpatient at increased VTE risk and low bleeding risk → prophylactic LMWH or UFH.

whyNot.A: Aspirin is not recommended for prophylaxis in medical inpatients.
whyNot.B: Ambulation is encouraged but is not enough for a high-risk patient who will be largely bed-bound.
whyNot.C: Filters are never used for primary prophylaxis.
whyNot.E: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation without VTE adds bleeding risk without benefit.

items.objective: Choose pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a high-risk medical inpatient.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has a painful, shallow ulcer above the left medial malleolus that has been present for 3 months. He has had swollen legs for years and had a left leg DVT 8 years ago. The skin around the ulcer is brown and indurated, and there are varicose veins. Pedal pulses are palpable, and ankle-brachial index is 1.02 on the left. Wound culture grows mixed skin flora; there is no surrounding cellulitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Revascularization of the superficial femoral artery

items.explanationHtml:
A shallow ulcer over the medial malleolus with hemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and a history of DVT is a venous ulcer from post-thrombotic venous hypertension. With a normal ABI, multilayer compression bandaging (then stockings) plus elevation and local wound care is the treatment that heals venous ulcers and prevents recurrence.

Takeaway: Venous ulcer with normal ABI → compression therapy (check the ABI first).

whyNot.B: Colonization without cellulitis does not need systemic antibiotics.
whyNot.C: Arterial flow is normal (ABI 1.02), so revascularization is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Grafting without treating venous hypertension usually fails; compression remains essential.
whyNot.E: Topical steroids may help stasis dermatitis but do not heal ulcers.

items.objective: Treat a venous leg ulcer with compression after confirming adequate arterial supply.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has a left femoral vein DVT confirmed by ultrasonography. She has no other medical problems. Platelet count and renal function are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
items.explanationHtml:
Low-molecular-weight heparin does not cross the placenta, is effective and safe, and is the anticoagulant of choice for VTE in pregnancy. It is continued through pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks postpartum (minimum total about 3 months), with planning around delivery and neuraxial anesthesia.

Takeaway: VTE in pregnancy → LMWH; avoid warfarin (teratogenic) and DOACs.

whyNot.A: Apixaban crosses the placenta, and safety data in pregnancy are insufficient.
whyNot.B: Dabigatran is avoided in pregnancy for the same reason.
whyNot.D: Rivaroxaban is avoided in pregnancy because of placental transfer and limited data.
whyNot.E: Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy and fetal bleeding.

items.objective: Choose LMWH for venous thromboembolism during pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma has a right popliteal DVT confirmed by ultrasonography. He is receiving outpatient chemotherapy. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and platelets 180,000/mm3; he has no gastrointestinal bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Warfarin with a target INR of 1.5

items.explanationHtml:
Cancer-associated VTE is treated with low-molecular-weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban), each superior to warfarin at preventing recurrence in this population. Among the options offered, LMWH is correct. Treatment continues for at least 6 months and usually as long as the cancer is active.

Takeaway: Cancer-associated VTE → LMWH or a DOAC, continued while the cancer is active.

whyNot.A: Aspirin does not adequately treat VTE.
whyNot.B: A filter is used only when anticoagulation is contraindicated.
whyNot.D: Observation is not appropriate for a proximal DVT, especially with cancer.
whyNot.E: Low-intensity warfarin (INR 1.5) is inadequate, and warfarin in general is inferior in cancer.

items.objective: Select anticoagulation for cancer-associated deep vein thrombosis.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman develops swelling and pain of the left calf 3 days after a 14-hour flight during which she sat almost continuously. She takes no medications and has no history of surgery or trauma. Ultrasonography shows thrombus in the left posterior tibial and popliteal veins. Which component of the Virchow triad was most likely the principal trigger?
items.explanationHtml:
Prolonged sitting during long travel lets blood pool in the calf veins, especially in the valve pockets, where reduced flow allows activated clotting factors to accumulate and local hypoxia makes the endothelium procoagulant. Stasis is the dominant mechanism in travel-related DVT, immobility, heart failure and paralysis.

Takeaway: Long-haul travel or immobility = stasis, one limb of the Virchow triad.

whyNot.A: Endothelial injury dominates after surgery, trauma or catheter placement, none of which occurred.
whyNot.B: She takes no hormones and is not pregnant.
whyNot.C: An inherited thrombophilia may coexist but is not the trigger suggested by the history.
whyNot.D: Platelet activation drives arterial thrombi; venous thrombi are fibrin- and red-cell-rich.

items.objective: Identify venous stasis as the main mechanism of travel-related deep vein thrombosis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man has an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis of the femoral vein. His father had a pulmonary embolism at 42. Testing shows that his plasma clotting time is prolonged less than normal when activated protein C is added. Genetic analysis is most likely to show a mutation that has which of the following effects?

options.label: A
options.html: Resistance of factor Va to proteolytic inactivation

items.explanationHtml:
Activated protein C resistance is the hallmark of factor V Leiden, an autosomal dominant point mutation (arginine to glutamine at position 506) that removes a cleavage site for activated protein C. Factor Va therefore stays active longer and generates more thrombin, raising the risk of venous thrombosis.

Takeaway: Factor V Leiden: factor Va resists activated protein C → venous thrombosis.

whyNot.B: Protein S deficiency reduces APC cofactor activity but is not detected as resistance of factor Va to APC in this assay.
whyNot.C: Increased prothrombin is the effect of the prothrombin G20210A variant.
whyNot.D: Antithrombin deficiency causes thrombosis and heparin resistance but normal APC resistance testing.
whyNot.E: Resistance of fibrin to plasmin is not a recognized common thrombophilia.

items.objective: Explain the molecular basis of factor V Leiden.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has her second unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. Testing for factor V Leiden, protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiency is negative, and antiphospholipid antibodies are absent. Genetic testing finds a heterozygous single-nucleotide variant in the 3′ untranslated region of the gene for a vitamin K-dependent clotting factor. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this variant?

options.label: A
options.html: Abnormal factor VIII binding to von Willebrand factor

items.explanationHtml:
The prothrombin G20210A variant lies in the 3′ untranslated region of F2. It increases mRNA processing and stability, so more normal prothrombin is made; higher prothrombin levels favor thrombin generation and venous thrombosis. It is the second most common inherited thrombophilia after factor V Leiden.

Takeaway: Prothrombin G20210A (3′ UTR) → more prothrombin → venous thrombosis.

whyNot.A: Defective factor VIII binding to von Willebrand factor (type 2N disease) causes bleeding.
whyNot.B: Failure of γ-carboxylation (as from warfarin or vitamin K deficiency) causes bleeding, not clotting.
whyNot.C: Reduced t-PA release has no common inherited genetic form linked to a 3′ UTR variant.
whyNot.D: Thrombomodulin loss is not an inherited thrombophilia tested this way.

items.objective: Describe how the prothrombin G20210A variant increases thrombotic risk.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is started on warfarin alone for a deep vein thrombosis. On day 4 she develops painful, sharply demarcated purple areas on her thighs and abdomen that become necrotic. Biopsy shows thrombi in dermal venules. Which of the following best explains this complication?

options.label: B
options.html: Faster fall in protein C than in factors II, IX and X

options.label: E
options.html: Rapid fall in factor VII causing bleeding into the skin

items.explanationHtml:
Warfarin reduces synthesis of all vitamin K-dependent proteins, but the effect appears as each protein decays. Protein C has a short half-life (about 8 hours), so its activity falls before that of prothrombin and factor X. For a few days the balance tips towards clotting, and microvascular thrombosis in fatty skin causes necrosis. Underlying protein C deficiency raises the risk; heparin overlap prevents it.

Takeaway: Warfarin skin necrosis: protein C falls before the long-lived procoagulant factors → transient hypercoagulability.

whyNot.A: PF4–heparin antibodies cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; she has not received heparin.
whyNot.C: The lesion is thrombotic, not vasculitic.
whyNot.D: Thromboxane inhibition is the action of aspirin, and it would cause bleeding.
whyNot.E: Factor VII also falls quickly, but the biopsy shows thrombosis, not hemorrhage.

items.objective: Explain warfarin-induced skin necrosis through differential half-lives of vitamin K-dependent proteins.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with a deep vein thrombosis receives intravenous unfractionated heparin by weight-based protocol. After 36 hours and several dose increases, her aPTT remains in the normal range. Platelet count is 240,000/mm3. Her mother and brother have had unprovoked venous thromboses. Deficiency of which of the following proteins is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Heparin has no anticoagulant activity by itself: its pentasaccharide sequence binds antithrombin and accelerates its inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa about a thousand-fold. Inherited antithrombin deficiency (autosomal dominant) causes venous thrombosis and reduced heparin response; options include antithrombin concentrate or a direct anticoagulant that does not need antithrombin.

Takeaway: Heparin needs antithrombin; inherited antithrombin deficiency causes thrombosis with heparin resistance.

whyNot.B: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT and does not cause bleeding or thrombosis to any important degree.
whyNot.C: Protein C deficiency causes thrombosis but does not blunt the heparin effect on the aPTT.
whyNot.D: Plasminogen deficiency impairs fibrinolysis but does not stop heparin prolonging the aPTT.
whyNot.E: TFPI deficiency would not prevent heparin from prolonging the aPTT.

items.objective: Link heparin resistance to antithrombin deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man receives subcutaneous enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis after hip surgery. Compared with unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin has relatively less effect on thrombin. Which of the following best explains this difference?

options.label: A
options.html: Most enoxaparin chains are too short to bind antithrombin and thrombin at the same time

options.label: B
options.html: Enoxaparin does not contain the antithrombin-binding pentasaccharide

options.label: C
options.html: Enoxaparin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase

options.label: D
options.html: Enoxaparin binds thrombin directly without antithrombin

options.label: E
options.html: Thrombin is degraded faster in the presence of enoxaparin

items.explanationHtml:
Both heparins activate antithrombin through the same pentasaccharide sequence. Inhibiting factor Xa needs only that conformational change, but inhibiting thrombin requires a heparin chain long enough (at least 18 saccharides) to bridge antithrombin and thrombin together. Most low-molecular-weight heparin chains are shorter, so their activity is mainly anti-Xa and they barely change the aPTT.

Takeaway: LMWH = mostly anti-Xa because short chains cannot bridge antithrombin to thrombin.

whyNot.B: LMWH does contain the pentasaccharide; that is how it activates antithrombin.
whyNot.C: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase is the action of warfarin.
whyNot.D: Direct thrombin binding without antithrombin describes direct thrombin inhibitors such as argatroban and dabigatran.
whyNot.E: LMWH does not accelerate thrombin degradation.

items.objective: Explain why low-molecular-weight heparin acts mainly against factor Xa.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man receiving intravenous unfractionated heparin after cardiac surgery has a fall in platelet count from 260,000/mm3 to 90,000/mm3 on day 7, and a new thrombus in the right femoral vein. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct toxicity of heparin to megakaryocytes

options.label: B
options.html: IgG antibodies to heparin–platelet factor 4 complexes that activate platelets

options.label: C
options.html: IgM antibodies against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa causing splenic destruction

options.label: D
options.html: Non-immune clumping of platelets by heparin

options.label: E
options.html: Splenic sequestration of platelets after surgery

items.explanationHtml:
This is type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Heparin binds platelet factor 4 and creates a new epitope; IgG antibodies form against the complex. The immune complexes bind platelet FcγRIIa receptors, activating platelets, which release procoagulant microparticles and are cleared. Thrombin generation rises, so patients develop venous and arterial thrombosis despite a low platelet count.

Takeaway: HIT: IgG to heparin–PF4 → platelet activation → thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, 5–10 days after starting heparin.

whyNot.A: Heparin is not toxic to megakaryocytes; the problem is peripheral immune activation.
whyNot.C: Anti-GP IIb/IIIa autoantibodies are typical of immune thrombocytopenia, which causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
whyNot.D: Non-immune heparin-associated thrombocytopenia (type I) is mild, occurs in the first 2 days and causes no thrombosis.
whyNot.E: Sequestration does not cause new thrombosis.

items.objective: Describe the immune mechanism of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old woman taking an oral anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department with a subdural hematoma. Her anticoagulant is reversed with idarucizumab. Which of the following drugs was she most likely taking?
items.explanationHtml:
Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity and neutralizes it within minutes. Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor (a prodrug, dabigatran etexilate). It is the only oral anticoagulant this agent reverses.

Takeaway: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors.

whyNot.A: Apixaban, a direct Xa inhibitor, is reversed with andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate.
whyNot.C: Enoxaparin is partly reversed by protamine.
whyNot.D: Rivaroxaban, a direct Xa inhibitor, is reversed with andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate.
whyNot.E: Warfarin is reversed with vitamin K and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.

items.objective: Match idarucizumab to dabigatran reversal.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man taking apixaban for a recent deep vein thrombosis has life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding. He is given a recombinant protein that resembles human factor Xa but has no procoagulant activity. Which of the following best describes how this agent restores hemostasis?

options.label: B
options.html: It binds and sequesters the circulating anticoagulant

options.label: C
options.html: It enhances hepatic metabolism of apixaban

options.label: D
options.html: It replaces the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors

options.label: E
options.html: It supplies functional factor Xa to the coagulation cascade

items.explanationHtml:
Andexanet alfa is a modified, catalytically inactive factor Xa that acts as a decoy: direct Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban bind it instead of the patient's own factor Xa, so endogenous Xa can work again. It also binds Xa-directed antithrombin complexes from low-molecular-weight heparin.

Takeaway: Andexanet alfa is a decoy Xa that soaks up direct factor Xa inhibitors.

whyNot.A: Activating antithrombin would worsen anticoagulation.
whyNot.C: It does not change drug metabolism.
whyNot.D: Replacing vitamin K-dependent factors is the action of prothrombin complex concentrate.
whyNot.E: The protein is catalytically inactive; it does not act as functional factor Xa.

items.objective: Describe the decoy mechanism of andexanet alfa.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman who works as a cashier has had aching, swollen legs at the end of the day for years. Examination shows dilated, tortuous superficial veins on both legs, pitting edema at the ankles and brownish discoloration of the skin above the medial malleoli. Pedal pulses are normal. Which of the following substances is mainly responsible for the brown discoloration?
items.explanationHtml:
Valvular incompetence of the superficial (and sometimes deep) veins causes venous hypertension in the lower leg. Red cells leak from congested capillaries into the dermis, and macrophages break down their hemoglobin into hemosiderin, which stains the skin brown. Inflammation then causes stasis dermatitis and lipodermatosclerosis, and ulcers may form above the medial malleolus.

Takeaway: Brown skin of chronic venous insufficiency = hemosiderin from extravasated red cells.

whyNot.A: Bilirubin causes generalized jaundice, not localized brown pigment over the ankles.
whyNot.B: Carotene causes diffuse yellow-orange skin, especially palms, with no venous link.
whyNot.C: Melanin increases with sun or hormonal stimulation; post-inflammatory change contributes little compared with hemosiderin here.
whyNot.D: Lipofuscin is an intracellular 'wear and tear' pigment of ageing cells, not visible skin discoloration.

items.objective: Explain the hemosiderin pigmentation of chronic venous insufficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has had tender, red, cord-like lesions appear in superficial veins of his arm, then his chest, then his opposite leg over 6 weeks; each fades as new ones appear. He has lost 8 kg (18 lb) and has new-onset diabetes mellitus. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) is a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state, classically with mucin-producing adenocarcinomas such as pancreatic cancer. Tumor-derived tissue factor and mucins promote clotting. Weight loss and new-onset diabetes in an older adult are warning signs of pancreatic cancer.

Takeaway: Migratory thrombophlebitis + weight loss (± new diabetes) → look for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

whyNot.A: Antithrombin deficiency causes deep vein thrombosis, usually from a young age, not migratory superficial phlebitis with weight loss.
whyNot.B: Buerger disease affects young heavy smokers and causes digital ischemia.
whyNot.C: Factor V Leiden causes deep venous thrombosis and does not explain weight loss or new diabetes.
whyNot.E: Polycythemia vera causes thrombosis with a high hematocrit, pruritus and splenomegaly.

items.objective: Recognize Trousseau syndrome as a sign of occult visceral adenocarcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay 15 minutes after being stabbed once in the left chest. The wound is 2 cm long, just left of the sternum in the fourth intercostal space. He is anxious and pale. Pulse is 132/min, and blood pressure is 80/58 mm Hg. His neck veins are distended. Heart sounds are faint. Breath sounds are present and equal on both sides, and the trachea is midline. Two large-bore IV lines are placed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds (Beck triad) after a parasternal stab wound indicate cardiac tamponade, most likely from a right ventricular laceration. Equal breath sounds and a midline trachea argue against tension pneumothorax.

Takeaway: stab wound in the cardiac box + hypotension + distended neck veins + equal breath sounds → tamponade.

whyNot.A: Tension pneumothorax also causes distended neck veins and shock, but breath sounds would be absent on the affected side, often with tracheal deviation.
whyNot.B: A massive hemothorax causes dullness and absent breath sounds on one side, and flat neck veins from blood loss.
whyNot.C: Pure hemorrhagic shock causes flat, not distended, neck veins; the wound is above the costal margin.
whyNot.E: Contusion results from blunt, not penetrating, trauma and rarely causes this degree of shock.

items.objective: Diagnose cardiac tamponade after penetrating chest trauma.

items.stemHtml: Bedside ultrasound of the patient confirms a pericardial collection with right ventricular diastolic collapse. After 500 mL of crystalloid and 1 unit of blood, blood pressure is 84/60 mm Hg. A trauma surgeon is in the department, and an operating room is available. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the chest with intravenous contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Immediate transfer to the operating room for sternotomy

options.label: E
options.html: Further crystalloid boluses until blood pressure normalises

items.explanationHtml:
Traumatic tamponade from a penetrating wound needs operative repair: relieve the tamponade and suture the cardiac laceration through a median sternotomy (or an anterolateral thoracotomy). Because a surgeon and operating room are available, the patient should go there immediately. Pericardiocentesis is only a temporising bridge when surgery is not immediately available.

Takeaway: penetrating cardiac injury with tamponade → operating room, not a needle.

whyNot.A: An unstable patient should never be sent to CT; the diagnosis is already made at the bedside.
whyNot.B: Breath sounds are equal and there is no pneumothorax or hemothorax to drain.
whyNot.D: Clotted blood is often not aspirable, and the bleeding wound remains; pericardiocentesis is temporary at best.
whyNot.E: Fluids can transiently raise filling pressure, but large volumes delay definitive treatment and dilute clotting factors.

items.objective: Manage penetrating cardiac injury with tamponade by immediate surgical repair.

items.stemHtml: While the operating room is being opened, the patient becomes unresponsive. No carotid pulse is palpable, and the monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 40/min. He had a palpable pulse 2 minutes earlier. Chest compressions are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Left anterolateral (resuscitative) thoracotomy in the trauma bay

options.label: D
options.html: Stop resuscitation because survival is unlikely

options.label: E
options.html: Bilateral needle decompression of the chest

items.explanationHtml:
He has pulseless electrical activity from tamponade after a penetrating chest wound, with signs of life only minutes ago. This is the strongest indication for emergency department (resuscitative) thoracotomy: open the pericardium to relieve the tamponade, control the cardiac wound with a finger or sutures, and give open cardiac massage. Closed compressions cannot fill a tamponaded heart.

Takeaway: penetrating chest trauma with recent loss of pulses → resuscitative thoracotomy.

whyNot.B: Synchronised cardioversion is for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse; this is pulseless electrical activity.
whyNot.C: Atropine does not address the mechanical cause (tamponade) and is no longer part of routine PEA treatment.
whyNot.D: Survival after resuscitative thoracotomy is highest exactly in this group: penetrating cardiac injury with recently lost signs of life.
whyNot.E: Breath sounds were equal and the problem is tamponade; decompression is reasonable only when tension pneumothorax cannot be excluded in traumatic arrest.

items.objective: Identify the indication for resuscitative thoracotomy in penetrating chest trauma.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated after her car struck a pole at moderate speed. The steering wheel hit her chest. She has anterior chest wall tenderness and a non-displaced sternal fracture on CT, with no other injuries. Pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial evaluation for blunt cardiac injury?
items.explanationHtml:
Every patient with suspected blunt cardiac injury should have a 12-lead ECG, and a troponin should be added. If both are normal, significant blunt cardiac injury is effectively ruled out and no cardiac monitoring is needed. A new ECG abnormality or raised troponin calls for admission with continuous monitoring; echocardiography is reserved for hemodynamic instability or unexplained arrhythmia.

Takeaway: screen blunt chest trauma with ECG + troponin; normal both → BCI excluded.

whyNot.A: Echocardiography is not a screening test in stable patients; it is used for instability or arrhythmia.
whyNot.C: CK-MB is released by injured skeletal muscle and does not add to troponin.
whyNot.D: Coronary CT angiography is not part of screening; coronary dissection after trauma is rare and would show on the ECG.
whyNot.E: Cardiac MRI has no screening role in the acute trauma setting.

items.objective: Screen for blunt cardiac injury with an ECG and troponin.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man is admitted after a high-speed motorcycle crash. He has bilateral rib fractures and a sternal fracture. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and stable. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 112/min with frequent premature ventricular complexes and a new right bundle branch block. Troponin I is mildly raised. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
New ECG abnormalities (frequent ectopy and a new right bundle branch block) with a raised troponin after blunt chest trauma indicate blunt cardiac injury. A hemodynamically stable patient should be admitted for continuous ECG monitoring, typically for 24–48 hours, because life-threatening arrhythmias tend to occur early. Echocardiography is added if instability or an unexplained arrhythmia develops.

Takeaway: blunt cardiac injury with ECG changes, stable → monitored bed, not angiography or antiarrhythmics.

whyNot.A: Discharge is unsafe when the screening ECG is abnormal.
whyNot.B: Coronary angiography is for suspected traumatic coronary dissection with a STEMI pattern; this ECG shows ectopy and bundle branch block.
whyNot.D: There is no evidence of tamponade; he is normotensive.
whyNot.E: Premature ventricular complexes alone do not require antiarrhythmic treatment; monitoring and correction of electrolytes come first.

items.objective: Admit stable patients with blunt cardiac injury and ECG changes for continuous monitoring.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a head-on collision at 90 km/h. He has chest pain between the shoulder blades. Pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg in the right arm and 142/86 mm Hg in the left. He responds normally to questions. A supine chest radiograph shows a mediastinal width of 9 cm and an indistinct aortic knob. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Repeat upright chest radiograph in 6 hours

items.explanationHtml:
A high-energy deceleration injury with interscapular pain and a widened mediastinum suggests blunt thoracic aortic injury. In a hemodynamically stable patient, CT angiography of the chest is the diagnostic test of choice: fast, widely available, highly sensitive, and it shows other thoracic injuries. Transesophageal echocardiography is an option for unstable patients in the operating room.

Takeaway: suspected blunt aortic injury in a stable patient → CT angiography of the chest.

whyNot.A: Waiting risks free rupture of a contained tear; a widened mediastinum after this mechanism needs immediate imaging.
whyNot.C: Transthoracic echocardiography cannot see the isthmus well.
whyNot.D: Catheter aortography was the old reference standard but is invasive and slower; CT angiography has replaced it.
whyNot.E: MRI takes too long and is impractical for an acutely injured patient.

items.objective: Choose CT angiography to diagnose blunt thoracic aortic injury in a stable patient.

items.stemHtml: The patient's CT angiography shows a 2-cm contained pseudoaneurysm at the aortic isthmus with a small mediastinal hematoma. He has no other significant injuries. Pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Vascular surgery plans endovascular repair later today. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Anti-impulse therapy lowers the force and rate of rise of aortic pressure to reduce the risk of free rupture before repair. Start with a short-acting IV beta-blocker such as esmolol to slow the heart rate, and add a vasodilator only if blood pressure remains high after beta-blockade. Adequate analgesia also helps. Definitive repair is thoracic endovascular aortic repair when the anatomy is suitable.

Takeaway: contained blunt aortic injury → IV beta-blocker first (esmolol), then a vasodilator if needed, then TEVAR.

whyNot.A: A vasodilator given first causes reflex tachycardia, which increases shear stress on the injured aorta.
whyNot.B: A vasopressor raises pressure and wall stress in a hypertensive patient.
whyNot.D: An oral dihydropyridine acts too slowly and causes reflex tachycardia.
whyNot.E: Fibrinolysis is contraindicated in any acute aortic injury.

items.objective: Begin anti-impulse therapy with an IV beta-blocker in contained blunt aortic injury.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman is brought in after a rollover crash. After 2 L of crystalloid and 2 units of packed red cells, blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg and pulse is 128/min; she responded only briefly to the transfusion. CT obtained during transient stability showed a contained pseudoaneurysm at the aortic isthmus, a grade IV splenic laceration with active contrast extravasation and a large hemoperitoneum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair, then splenic management

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous esmolol infusion to a heart rate below 80/min

options.label: C
options.html: Open repair of the thoracic aorta via left thoracotomy

items.explanationHtml:
She is in hemorrhagic shock with active splenic bleeding and a transient response to resuscitation: the bleeding abdomen is the immediate threat to life. A contained aortic pseudoaneurysm rarely ruptures in the first hours, so it is repaired after the hemorrhage is controlled and she is stable. Anti-impulse therapy is withheld while she is hypotensive and hypovolemic. Use balanced transfusion (massive transfusion protocol) during laparotomy.

Takeaway: with multiple injuries, treat active hemorrhage first; repair a contained aortic tear once the patient is stable, and never beta-block a patient in hemorrhagic shock.

whyNot.A: Repairing the contained aortic injury first delays control of the bleeding that is killing her.
whyNot.B: Beta-blockade blunts the compensatory tachycardia of hemorrhagic shock and can precipitate cardiac arrest.
whyNot.C: Open thoracic repair is a major operation in an unstable patient and does not address the abdominal bleeding.
whyNot.D: Repeat imaging in a patient with ongoing shock delays definitive hemorrhage control.

items.objective: Prioritise control of active hemorrhage over repair of a contained blunt aortic injury.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy collapses on a youth hockey rink seconds after a puck strikes the left side of his chest. A coach reaches him within 30 seconds. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally, and no pulse is felt. An automated external defibrillator is mounted on the wall next to the bench. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin chest compressions and apply the defibrillator as soon as it arrives

options.label: B
options.html: Give a precordial thump and check for a pulse

options.label: C
options.html: Place him in the recovery position and wait for paramedics

options.label: D
options.html: Give rescue breaths only until paramedics arrive

options.label: E
options.html: Immobilise the cervical spine before any other intervention

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden collapse right after a blow to the chest in a young athlete is commotio cordis until proven otherwise, and the rhythm is usually ventricular fibrillation. Survival depends on starting high-quality chest compressions immediately and defibrillating as soon as the AED is attached; each minute of delay sharply lowers survival.

Takeaway: collapse after a chest blow in sport → CPR and AED immediately.

whyNot.B: A precordial thump is unreliable and should not delay compressions or defibrillation.
whyNot.C: The recovery position is for unresponsive patients who are breathing with a pulse; he is in cardiac arrest.
whyNot.D: Rescue breaths without compressions do not circulate blood, and defibrillation is the decisive treatment.
whyNot.E: There is no suggestion of a head or neck injury; cervical precautions must never delay CPR in cardiac arrest.

items.objective: Treat suspected commotio cordis with immediate CPR and defibrillation.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man had a temporary transvenous pacing wire placed through the right internal jugular vein 6 hours ago for complete heart block. He now feels lightheaded. Pulse is paced at 70/min, and blood pressure is 84/62 mm Hg (it was 128/70 mm Hg after the procedure). Systolic pressure falls by 16 mm Hg during inspiration. Jugular venous pressure is 16 cm H2O. Lungs are clear. A chest radiograph shows the lead tip projecting beyond the cardiac apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus hours after a pacing wire was placed, with the lead tip beyond the cardiac silhouette, suggest right ventricular perforation with tamponade. Bedside echocardiography confirms a pericardial effusion and signs of tamponade, and guides urgent pericardiocentesis; the lead is then repositioned under monitoring with cardiac surgery available.

Takeaway: new shock after a pacing lead or catheter procedure → echocardiography for perforation and tamponade.

whyNot.B: Diuretics lower preload and would worsen tamponade physiology.
whyNot.C: A faster pacing rate does not overcome restricted filling and may worsen it by shortening diastole.
whyNot.D: Nitroglycerin lowers preload and can cause collapse in tamponade.
whyNot.E: Pulmonary embolism is possible after immobility, but the lead position and pulsus paradoxus point to perforation; CT would also delay bedside diagnosis in a hypotensive patient.

items.objective: Recognise and confirm tamponade from iatrogenic ventricular puncture.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is stabbed in the chest with a kitchen knife. The entry wound is in the left fourth intercostal space immediately lateral to the sternum, and the blade went straight back. Which part of the heart is most likely to have been injured?
items.explanationHtml:
The right ventricle forms most of the sternocostal (anterior) surface of the heart and lies directly behind the sternum and the medial ends of the left third to fifth intercostal spaces. A blade entering just left of the sternum and passing straight back meets it first.

Takeaway: anterior chest wounds most often injure the right ventricle.

whyNot.A: The left atrium is the most posterior chamber, lying against the esophagus.
whyNot.B: The apex lies further lateral, near the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line.
whyNot.C: The right atrium forms the right border of the heart, to the right of the sternum.
whyNot.E: The ascending aorta lies higher, behind the sternum at about the level of the second and third costal cartilages.

items.objective: Identify the right ventricle as the anterior-most cardiac chamber.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman is the restrained driver in a head-on collision at high speed. CT angiography shows a contained tear of the descending aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, at the attachment of a fibrous cord that connects the aorta to the left pulmonary artery. This cord is derived from which of the following embryonic structures?
items.explanationHtml:
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, which develops from the distal part of the left sixth pharyngeal arch artery. It tethers the aorta at the isthmus, which is why deceleration injuries concentrate there. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it.

Takeaway: isthmus tears occur at the ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the ductus arteriosus (left sixth arch).

whyNot.A: The left fourth arch forms part of the aortic arch itself.
whyNot.C: The third arches form the common and proximal internal carotid arteries.
whyNot.D: The left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver.
whyNot.E: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.

items.objective: Link the site of blunt aortic injury to the embryology of the ligamentum arteriosum.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man falls 8 meters from a scaffold and lands flat on his back. CT angiography shows a pseudoaneurysm at the aortic isthmus. Which of the following best explains why the injury occurred at this site?

options.label: A
options.html: The isthmus has the thinnest media of any segment of the aorta

options.label: B
options.html: Shear between the mobile arch and the tethered descending aorta during sudden deceleration

options.label: C
options.html: Direct compression of the isthmus between the sternum and the vertebrae

options.label: D
options.html: Pre-existing cystic medial degeneration at the isthmus

options.label: E
options.html: Sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure transmitted up the aorta

items.explanationHtml:
During abrupt deceleration, the heart, ascending aorta and arch continue to move forward while the descending thoracic aorta is fixed by the ligamentum arteriosum, intercostal arteries and parietal pleura. The resulting shear and bending stress concentrate at the junction: the isthmus.

Takeaway: blunt aortic injury happens where a mobile segment meets a fixed one.

whyNot.A: The isthmus wall is not intrinsically the thinnest; its location at the mobile–fixed junction explains the tears.
whyNot.C: Direct compression between sternum and spine injures the heart (contusion), not mainly the isthmus.
whyNot.D: Cystic medial degeneration predisposes to spontaneous dissection (Marfan syndrome), not traumatic tears in healthy aortas.
whyNot.E: Raised abdominal pressure is a proposed minor contributor ('water hammer'), but shear at the tether point is the dominant mechanism.

items.objective: Explain why deceleration injures the aorta at the isthmus.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has a stab wound to the chest. Blood pressure is 86/60 mm Hg. During quiet breathing, the systolic pressure falls by 18 mm Hg with each inspiration. Which of the following best explains this inspiratory fall in pressure?

options.label: A
options.html: Inspiratory increase in left ventricular afterload from negative intrathoracic pressure

options.label: B
options.html: Pooling of blood in the pulmonary veins during inspiration

options.label: C
options.html: Increased right ventricular filling shifting the septum toward the left ventricle

options.label: D
options.html: Inspiratory vagal slowing of the heart rate

options.label: E
options.html: Compression of the coronary arteries by the pericardial blood

items.explanationHtml:
In tamponade, the total volume inside the pericardial sac is fixed. Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and increases venous return to the right heart; the right ventricle can only fill by pushing the interventricular septum toward the left ventricle. Left ventricular filling and stroke volume therefore fall during inspiration, exaggerating the normal small inspiratory drop in systolic pressure (pulsus paradoxus: more than 10 mm Hg).

Takeaway: pulsus paradoxus reflects exaggerated ventricular interdependence when the pericardium cannot expand.

whyNot.A: Negative intrathoracic pressure does slightly raise left ventricular afterload, but this is a minor factor compared with septal shift.
whyNot.B: Pulmonary venous pooling contributes to the normal small fall; it does not explain the exaggerated fall in tamponade.
whyNot.D: Sinus arrhythmia changes the heart rate with breathing but does not produce an 18 mm Hg fall in systolic pressure.
whyNot.E: Pericardial fluid does not compress epicardial coronary arteries in a way that varies with each breath.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in cardiac tamponade.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 14-year-old boy playing baseball is struck in the left chest by a pitched ball. He takes two steps and collapses. An automated external defibrillator applied 2 minutes later shows ventricular fibrillation, and he is successfully defibrillated. Echocardiography and coronary imaging later are normal. The impact most likely coincided with which part of the cardiac cycle on the ECG?
items.explanationHtml:
Commotio cordis occurs when a blunt blow to the precordium, without structural injury, lands during a narrow window on the upstroke of the T wave. At that time, myocardial repolarisation is heterogeneous, and the mechanically induced depolarisation (through stretch-activated ion channels) can trigger ventricular fibrillation, much like an 'R-on-T' premature beat.

Takeaway: commotio cordis = chest blow during the vulnerable period of repolarisation → VF; treat with immediate defibrillation.

whyNot.A: A blow during atrial depolarisation does not reach the ventricles at a vulnerable time.
whyNot.B: During the PR segment the ventricles are fully repolarised and not vulnerable.
whyNot.C: During the QRS peak the ventricles are depolarising and refractory; impacts here may cause heart block but rarely VF.
whyNot.D: The early ST segment falls in the absolute refractory period, so a new depolarisation cannot propagate.

items.objective: Relate commotio cordis to the vulnerable period of ventricular repolarisation.

items.stemHtml:
A 29-year-old man has a stab wound to the left parasternal area. He is hypotensive with distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds. Before surgery, a pulmonary artery catheter is briefly placed. Which of the following sets of pressures (mm Hg) is most likely?

Right atrial (mean)RV diastolicPA diastolicWedge (mean)
A2365
B452428
C18181918
D161586
E34308
items.explanationHtml:
In tamponade, the pressure inside the pericardium is transmitted to every chamber during diastole, so right atrial, right ventricular diastolic, pulmonary artery diastolic and wedge (left atrial) pressures rise and become nearly equal. Low cardiac output results because none of the chambers can fill.

Takeaway: equalised, raised diastolic pressures across all chambers = tamponade (constriction can look similar).

whyNot.A: Uniformly low pressures fit hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage without tamponade.
whyNot.B: A high wedge with low right-sided pressures fits left ventricular failure (cardiogenic pulmonary edema).
whyNot.D: High right-sided with low left-sided pressures fit isolated right ventricular failure, such as right ventricular infarction or massive pulmonary embolism with a normal left heart.
whyNot.E: A high pulmonary artery diastolic pressure with a normal wedge and low right atrial pressure is not a coherent shock pattern and does not fit tamponade.

items.objective: Recognise equalisation of diastolic pressures in cardiac tamponade.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman is brought in after a car crash. She has distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds; breath sounds are equal on both sides.
