Pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 82/64 mm Hg. Bedside ultrasound shows a circumferential pericardial collection with diastolic collapse of the right ventricle. Her low blood pressure is most directly due to a decrease in which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Tamponade is obstructive shock: high pressure in the pericardial sac prevents the ventricles from filling in diastole. End-diastolic volume and therefore stroke volume fall (Frank–Starling), and cardiac output drops despite tachycardia and intense vasoconstriction. The right ventricle, with its thin wall and low pressure, collapses first.

Takeaway: tamponade lowers output by restricting diastolic filling, not by weakening the heart.

whyNot.B: Contractility is preserved or increased by sympathetic drive in tamponade; filling is the problem.
whyNot.C: Systemic vascular resistance rises as a compensatory response.
whyNot.D: Heart rate rises (124/min) to compensate for low stroke volume.
whyNot.E: Blood volume may be normal in pure tamponade; the neck veins are distended, not flat.

items.objective: Explain obstructive shock in tamponade as a failure of diastolic filling.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with a large malignant pericardial effusion undergoes subxiphoid pericardiocentesis. The needle is inserted below the xiphoid process and directed toward the left shoulder. Immediately before fluid is aspirated, the needle passes through which of the following layers?

options.label: C
options.html: Endothoracic fascia over the left lung

options.label: D
options.html: Fibrous pericardium fused with the parietal layer of serous pericardium

options.label: E
options.html: Epicardial fat over the left anterior descending artery

items.explanationHtml:
From outside in, the pericardium consists of the fibrous pericardium, which is fused to the parietal layer of the serous pericardium, then the pericardial cavity, then the visceral layer (epicardium) on the heart surface. Fluid lies between the parietal and visceral serous layers, so the needle enters the fluid immediately after crossing the fibrous–parietal layer. Going deeper risks puncturing the right ventricle.

Takeaway: pericardial fluid lies between the parietal (fused to fibrous) and visceral serous layers; the right ventricle is the structure at risk beyond it.

whyNot.A: The visceral layer covers the heart itself; passing it means the needle has gone beyond the fluid.
whyNot.B: Entering right ventricular myocardium is the complication to avoid (ventricular puncture).
whyNot.C: The subxiphoid route stays below and medial to the pleura; crossing the pleura risks pneumothorax.
whyNot.E: Epicardial fat lies under the visceral layer, deep to the pericardial space.

items.objective: Describe the layers crossed during subxiphoid pericardiocentesis.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his car hit a tree at high speed. He is alert, with chest wall tenderness. Pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg in both arms. A supine chest radiograph is obtained. Which of the following findings would most strongly suggest a tear of the thoracic aorta?

options.label: A
options.html: Widened mediastinum with loss of the aortic knob contour

options.label: C
options.html: Fracture of the right ninth rib

options.label: E
options.html: Hyperlucent left hemithorax with a deep sulcus

items.explanationHtml:
A contained aortic tear produces a mediastinal hematoma, seen as a widened mediastinum, an indistinct aortic knob, rightward deviation of the trachea or nasogastric tube, depression of the left mainstem bronchus and a left apical cap. These findings should prompt CT angiography; a normal film does not exclude the injury when the mechanism is high-energy deceleration.

Takeaway: after deceleration injury, a widened mediastinum or obscured aortic knob → CT angiography.

whyNot.B: Free air under the diaphragm suggests a perforated hollow viscus.
whyNot.C: Lower rib fractures raise concern for liver, spleen or kidney injury rather than the aorta.
whyNot.D: Bat-wing opacities suggest pulmonary edema, or contusion if patchy and peripheral.
whyNot.E: A deep sulcus sign on a supine film suggests pneumothorax.

items.objective: Recognise radiographic signs of blunt thoracic aortic injury.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery becomes cyanotic 4 hours after birth. Pulse is 156/min, respirations are 58/min and blood pressure is 68/40 mm Hg in the right arm. Pre- and post-ductal oxygen saturations are both 66%, and they do not rise after 10 minutes of 100% oxygen by hood. There is a single loud S2 and no murmur. A chest x-ray shows a narrow mediastinum and normal lung fields. Echocardiography has been requested but will take 1 hour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen, no murmur and a narrow mediastinum in the first hours of life suggest transposition of the great arteries, a duct-dependent mixing lesion. Start prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) immediately to keep the ductus open and improve mixing; do not wait for echocardiography. Be ready to support breathing, because apnea is a common adverse effect. Balloon atrial septostomy follows if the atrial septum is restrictive, and the arterial switch is done in the first weeks.

Takeaway: suspected duct-dependent cyanotic heart disease → start alprostadil now.

whyNot.A: Indomethacin closes the ductus and would remove a key route for mixing; it could be fatal.
whyNot.B: Inhaled nitric oxide treats persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, in which saturation usually differs pre- and post-ductally and often improves with oxygen; it does not fix parallel circulations.
whyNot.D: The arterial switch is the definitive repair, but it is done after stabilization and imaging, not as the first step.
whyNot.E: He has no pulmonary edema; diuresis would lower preload and worsen hemodynamics.

items.objective: Start prostaglandin E1 in a newborn with suspected duct-dependent cyanotic heart disease.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man has had occasional headaches and leg fatigue when running. Blood pressure is 164/88 mm Hg in the right arm and 112/70 mm Hg by thigh cuff. Radial pulses are strong; femoral pulses are weak and delayed relative to the radial pulse. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard over the left interscapular area. Serum potassium and creatinine are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal arteries

items.explanationHtml:
Upper-limb hypertension with a lower leg pressure, radiofemoral delay and an interscapular murmur in a young adult indicate coarctation of the aorta. Leg fatigue with exercise reflects reduced distal flow. Echocardiography is the initial study, CT or MR angiography defines the anatomy, and treatment is stenting or surgical repair.

Takeaway: in young hypertensive patients, always compare arm and leg pulses and pressures.

whyNot.A: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes renovascular hypertension, usually in young women, with an abdominal bruit but no arm–leg gradient.
whyNot.B: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension, often with hypokalemia, but leg pressures and pulses are normal.
whyNot.C: Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal headaches, sweating and palpitations without a pulse deficit in the legs.
whyNot.E: Takayasu arteritis usually affects young women, involves the aortic arch branches and causes weak arm pulses and arm pressure differences, often with systemic symptoms.

items.objective: Diagnose coarctation of the aorta from an arm–leg pressure gradient and radiofemoral delay.

items.stemHtml: An 18-month-old boy with tetralogy of Fallot awaiting repair becomes agitated and inconsolable after a fall at home. In the emergency department he is breathing deeply at 60/min, and his lips are deeply cyanotic; oxygen saturation has fallen from his usual 86% to 64%. The systolic murmur heard at previous visits is now much softer. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a hypercyanotic (tet) spell: agitation increases infundibular spasm and lowers systemic resistance, so more blood shunts right to left and the outflow murmur fades. First, calm him and place him knee-to-chest (raising systemic vascular resistance and venous return) with oxygen. If the spell continues: IV fluids, morphine, a beta-blocker and phenylephrine.

Takeaway: tet spell → knee-chest and oxygen first; avoid inotropes.

whyNot.A: Dobutamine increases contractility and heart rate, worsening dynamic infundibular obstruction.
whyNot.B: Digoxin is an inotrope and does nothing for a spell; it may worsen obstruction.
whyNot.C: Diuresis reduces preload and worsens right ventricular outflow obstruction.
whyNot.D: He has no tachyarrhythmia; cardioversion is not indicated.

items.objective: Manage a hypercyanotic spell in tetralogy of Fallot.

items.stemHtml: A 6-week-old girl is brought for a well-child visit. She feeds well and has gained weight along the 50th percentile. A grade 4/6 harsh holosystolic murmur with a thrill is heard at the left lower sternal border. Echocardiography shows a 2-mm muscular ventricular septal defect with left-to-right flow, normal chamber sizes and normal estimated pulmonary artery pressure. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Transcatheter device closure in the next month

options.label: C
options.html: Antibiotic prophylaxis before future dental procedures

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical patch closure before 6 months of age

items.explanationHtml:
A small muscular VSD produces a loud murmur (high velocity across a small hole) but little shunt: growth, chamber sizes and pulmonary pressure are normal. Many such defects close spontaneously in the first years. Management is reassurance and periodic follow-up.

Takeaway: the loudness of a VSD murmur does not track its size; small, asymptomatic VSDs are observed.

whyNot.A: Device closure is for hemodynamically significant defects; this one is small and may close by itself.
whyNot.B: There is no heart failure to treat.
whyNot.C: Endocarditis prophylaxis is not recommended for an isolated unrepaired VSD.
whyNot.E: Surgery is reserved for large defects with heart failure, failure to thrive or rising pulmonary pressures.

items.objective: Manage a small asymptomatic ventricular septal defect with observation.

items.stemHtml:
A 34-year-old woman has 1 year of exertional dyspnea and palpitations. Examination shows a fixed split S2 and a soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows an 18-mm ostium secundum atrial septal defect with adequate rims, left-to-right flow and a dilated right atrium and ventricle. Results of right heart catheterization:

MeasurementResult
Pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp:Qs)2.2 : 1
Pulmonary artery pressure34/14 mm Hg (mean 22)
Pulmonary vascular resistance1.6 Wood units (normal < 2)
Systemic arterial oxygen saturation97%

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Open surgical closure through median sternotomy

items.explanationHtml:
A secundum ASD with a significant shunt (Qp:Qs above about 1.5 with right heart enlargement), symptoms and normal pulmonary vascular resistance should be closed. With adequate rims, transcatheter device closure is preferred; it avoids sternotomy and has excellent results. Closure improves symptoms and right heart size and reduces long-term complications.

Takeaway: secundum ASD + RV enlargement + normal PVR → device closure.

whyNot.A: Observation is for small defects without right heart enlargement; she has symptoms and a large shunt.
whyNot.C: Pulmonary vasodilators treat pulmonary arterial hypertension; her pulmonary resistance is normal.
whyNot.D: Anticoagulation is not a treatment for an ASD; it is used only for specific indications such as atrial fibrillation.
whyNot.E: Surgery is reserved for primum, sinus venosus or coronary sinus defects, or secundum defects without adequate rims.

items.objective: Select transcatheter closure for a hemodynamically significant secundum ASD.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has sudden left-sided weakness that resolves over 2 days. MRI shows a right cortical infarct. He has no hypertension, diabetes or tobacco use. CT angiography of the head and neck is normal. Telemetry and a 30-day ambulatory monitor show no atrial fibrillation. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a patent foramen ovale with a large right-to-left shunt on agitated saline injection and an atrial septal aneurysm; there is no thrombus. Hypercoagulability testing is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to reduce his risk of another stroke?

options.label: A
options.html: Lifelong warfarin with a target INR of 3.5 to 4.5

options.label: C
options.html: Placement of an inferior vena cava filter

options.label: E
options.html: Percutaneous closure of the patent foramen ovale

items.explanationHtml:
In adults up to about 60 years with a nonlacunar cryptogenic ischemic stroke and a PFO with high-risk features (large shunt, atrial septal aneurysm), percutaneous PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy lowers the risk of recurrent stroke compared with antiplatelet therapy alone. Closure is considered only after other causes have been excluded, as they were here.

Takeaway: young cryptogenic stroke + high-risk PFO → PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy.

whyNot.A: Anticoagulation at this high intensity is not used for PFO and carries a large bleeding risk; standard-intensity anticoagulation is reserved for a separate indication such as venous thrombosis.
whyNot.B: His carotid arteries are normal on CT angiography.
whyNot.C: An IVC filter is used only for venous thromboembolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated; he has no venous clot.
whyNot.D: Appendage occlusion is for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, which he does not have.

items.objective: Choose PFO closure after a cryptogenic stroke in a younger adult with a high-risk PFO.

items.stemHtml: A girl born at 27 weeks' gestation is receiving mechanical ventilation and surfactant for respiratory distress syndrome. On day 3 her oxygen requirement increases. Pulse is 172/min and blood pressure is 52/24 mm Hg. Peripheral pulses are bounding, the precordium is hyperactive and there is a continuous murmur at the left upper sternal border. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis and its hemodynamic significance?
items.explanationHtml:
Bounding pulses, a wide pulse pressure, a hyperactive precordium and a continuous murmur in a ventilated preterm infant suggest a patent ductus arteriosus with a large left-to-right shunt. Echocardiography confirms the duct, shows the direction of flow and measures its size and effect (left atrial and ventricular dilation, reversed diastolic flow in the descending aorta), and excludes duct-dependent lesions before any closure.

Takeaway: suspect PDA in a preterm infant → echocardiography before treatment.

whyNot.B: Catheterization is invasive and unnecessary for diagnosis; transcatheter closure is a later option in larger infants.
whyNot.C: CT angiography adds radiation and contrast and is not needed to assess a ductus.
whyNot.D: Natriuretic peptides may support the diagnosis but cannot confirm the anatomy or exclude duct-dependent disease.
whyNot.E: An ECG is nonspecific and does not show the ductus.

items.objective: Confirm a suspected PDA in a preterm infant with echocardiography.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) Echocardiography shows a 2.5-mm patent ductus arteriosus with pure left-to-right flow, a dilated left atrium and reversed diastolic flow in the descending aorta; the heart is otherwise structurally normal. She remains ventilator dependent, and the team decides to close the ductus pharmacologically. Platelet count is 210,000/mm3, serum creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL, there is no intraventricular hemorrhage on cranial ultrasound, and abdominal examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
items.explanationHtml:
A hemodynamically significant PDA in a preterm infant can be closed with a cyclooxygenase inhibitor: intravenous ibuprofen or indomethacin (acetaminophen is an alternative). Check first for contraindications: active bleeding, thrombocytopenia, necrotizing enterocolitis, significant renal impairment. She has none. Transcatheter or surgical closure follows if medical therapy fails.

Takeaway: preterm PDA needing closure → ibuprofen or indomethacin if no contraindication.

whyNot.A: Alprostadil keeps the ductus open and is used for duct-dependent lesions, the opposite of the goal.
whyNot.B: Propranolol is used for tet spells and infantile hemangioma, not ductal closure.
whyNot.D: Digoxin does not close the ductus and has a narrow therapeutic window in preterm infants.
whyNot.E: Hydrocortisone treats refractory hypotension or adrenal insufficiency; it does not close the ductus.

items.objective: Choose a COX inhibitor to close a hemodynamically significant PDA in a preterm infant.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is seen for a school physical examination. She is active and well. There is a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. The second heart sound is widely split, and the split does not change between inspiration and expiration. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?
items.explanationHtml:
A wide, fixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmur is the hallmark of an atrial septal defect. The left-to-right atrial shunt keeps right ventricular volume high in both phases of respiration: in inspiration, venous return rises but the shunt falls, so RV stroke volume and pulmonic closure timing change little. The murmur is from increased flow across a normal pulmonic valve, not from the defect itself. Secundum is the most common type.

Takeaway: fixed split S2 = ASD.

whyNot.A: A bicuspid aortic valve causes an ejection click and an aortic-area systolic murmur, with normal splitting of S<sub>2</sub>.
whyNot.B: A PDA causes a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle.
whyNot.C: A VSD causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; S<sub>2</sub> splitting is not fixed.
whyNot.E: Coarctation causes upper-limb hypertension and weak femoral pulses, often with an interscapular murmur.

items.objective: Recognize a fixed split second heart sound as the sign of an atrial septal defect.

items.stemHtml: A 3-month-old boy has episodes during crying in which his lips turn dark blue and he breathes rapidly; the episodes stop when his mother holds him with his knees drawn up to his chest. There is a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border, and the second heart sound is single. A chest x-ray shows an upturned cardiac apex and diminished pulmonary vascular markings. An abnormality in which of the following developmental processes is the most likely cause of his condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral

options.label: B
options.html: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form

options.label: C
options.html: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum

options.label: D
options.html: Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse

options.label: E
options.html: Excessive resorption of the septum primum

items.explanationHtml:
Hypercyanotic spells relieved by knee-to-chest positioning, an outflow ejection murmur and a boot-shaped heart with oligemic lungs indicate tetralogy of Fallot. Its four features follow from one error: anterosuperior (anterior and cephalad) displacement of the infundibular (outlet) septum, which narrows the right ventricular outflow, leaves a malaligned VSD and makes the aorta override it; RV hypertrophy follows.

Takeaway: tetralogy of Fallot = malaligned outlet septum (neural crest/conotruncal defect).

whyNot.A: A septum that does not spiral gives transposition of the great arteries, which causes severe cyanosis from birth and a narrow mediastinum, not a boot-shaped heart.
whyNot.B: Absence of the septum gives persistent truncus arteriosus, with increased (not reduced) pulmonary blood flow.
whyNot.D: Failure of cushion fusion gives an AV septal defect, an acyanotic left-to-right shunt typical of Down syndrome.
whyNot.E: Excess resorption of septum primum gives an ostium secundum ASD, which is acyanotic.

items.objective: Relate tetralogy of Fallot to anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at term to a 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus whose hemoglobin A1c was 9.4% at the first prenatal visit. Two hours after birth he is deeply cyanotic, with an oxygen saturation of 62% that does not improve with 100% oxygen. No murmur is heard; the second heart sound is single and loud. A chest x-ray shows an egg-shaped cardiac silhouette with a narrow superior mediastinum. Which of the following embryologic errors best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Failure of neural crest–derived truncal ridges to spiral

options.label: B
options.html: Anterior displacement of the infundibular septum

options.label: C
options.html: Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets

options.label: D
options.html: Failure of the pulmonary veins to join the left atrium

options.label: E
options.html: Persistence of the left sixth aortic arch after birth

items.explanationHtml:
Profound cyanosis in the first hours without a murmur, unresponsive to oxygen, with a narrow mediastinum, in the infant of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes, is transposition of the great arteries. The truncal and bulbar ridges, populated by migrating neural crest cells, fuse without spiralling, so the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left. The circulations run in parallel, and survival depends on mixing through the foramen ovale and ductus.

Takeaway: a non-spiralling aorticopulmonary septum gives transposition; maternal diabetes is a classic association.

whyNot.B: Anterior displacement of the infundibular septum causes tetralogy of Fallot, which has an outflow murmur and a boot-shaped heart.
whyNot.C: Apical displacement of the tricuspid leaflets is Ebstein anomaly, which causes a massively enlarged right atrium and a large heart on x-ray.
whyNot.D: Anomalous pulmonary venous return causes cyanosis with pulmonary venous congestion; it is not linked to a narrow mediastinum.
whyNot.E: A persistent ductus (from the left sixth arch) causes a left-to-right shunt and a continuous murmur, not cyanosis at birth.

items.objective: Explain transposition of the great arteries as failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral.

items.stemHtml: A newborn girl has upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a single palmar crease and hypotonia. Karyotype confirms the suspected chromosomal disorder. The cardiac defect most characteristic of this disorder results from abnormal development of which of the following structures?
items.explanationHtml:
This infant has trisomy 21. Its most characteristic cardiac lesion is the atrioventricular septal (endocardial cushion) defect: an ostium primum ASD, an inlet VSD and a common atrioventricular valve. The superior and inferior endocardial cushions normally fuse to divide the AV canal and help build the lower atrial septum, the inlet ventricular septum and the AV valves.

Takeaway: Down syndrome → AV septal defect → endocardial cushions.

whyNot.A: A deficient septum secundum contributes to secundum ASD, which is not the signature lesion of Down syndrome.
whyNot.C: Sinus venosus abnormalities produce sinus venosus ASDs, often with anomalous right pulmonary venous drainage.
whyNot.D: Truncal and bulbar ridge (neural crest) defects produce conotruncal lesions such as truncus arteriosus and tetralogy, typical of 22q11.2 deletion.
whyNot.E: The bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow portions of the ventricles; it is not the origin of the AV septal defect.

items.objective: Link Down syndrome to endocardial cushion (AV septal) defects.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 28 weeks' gestation is ventilated for respiratory distress. On day 4 his ventilator requirements rise. He has bounding peripheral pulses, a hyperdynamic precordium and a continuous murmur below the left clavicle; blood pressure is 58/22 mm Hg. Echocardiography confirms the suspected lesion, and the team gives intravenous indomethacin. This drug promotes closure of the lesion by which of the following actions?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of prostaglandin E receptors on ductal smooth muscle

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase, lowering prostaglandin E<sub>2</sub>

items.explanationHtml:
The ductus arteriosus is kept open by prostaglandin E2 and low oxygen tension. Indomethacin (like ibuprofen) inhibits cyclooxygenase, lowering PGE2 so the ductal smooth muscle constricts. Preterm infants respond best because their ducts are more sensitive to prostaglandins.

Takeaway: COX inhibitors close a PDA; PGE1 (alprostadil) keeps it open.

whyNot.A: Activating prostaglandin E receptors is how alprostadil keeps a ductus open in duct-dependent lesions, the opposite of what is wanted here.
whyNot.B: Beta-1 blockade slows the heart and reduces contractility but does not close the ductus.
whyNot.C: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors (milrinone) raise cAMP and dilate vessels; they do not close the ductus.
whyNot.D: Endothelin antagonists dilate pulmonary vessels and are used for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

items.objective: Explain how COX inhibitors close a patent ductus arteriosus.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man who emigrated from a region with limited access to cardiac surgery was told in childhood that he had a "hole in the heart" and a loud murmur. Over the past 2 years he has developed exertional dyspnea and bluish lips. Examination shows digital clubbing and central cyanosis. The second heart sound is loud at the left upper sternal border, and the murmur described in childhood is now barely audible. Hematocrit is 61%. Which of the following best explains the change in his condition?

options.label: A
options.html: The ventricular septal defect has enlarged with age

options.label: B
options.html: Left ventricular systolic failure has raised left atrial pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Pulmonary vascular resistance now exceeds systemic vascular resistance

options.label: D
options.html: Infective endocarditis has destroyed the tricuspid valve

options.label: E
options.html: Right ventricular outflow obstruction has developed below the pulmonary valve

items.explanationHtml:
Years of high pulmonary flow and pressure from a large unrepaired VSD remodel the pulmonary arterioles (medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, plexiform lesions). When pulmonary vascular resistance exceeds systemic resistance, the shunt reverses to right-to-left: Eisenmenger syndrome. Cyanosis, clubbing and secondary erythrocytosis appear; the murmur softens because the pressure gradient across the defect falls; P2 is loud from pulmonary hypertension.

Takeaway: late cyanosis with a softening murmur and loud P2 in an unrepaired shunt = Eisenmenger syndrome.

whyNot.A: VSDs do not enlarge with age; many shrink. A larger defect would also not reverse the shunt by itself.
whyNot.B: Left heart failure causes pulmonary edema, not right-to-left shunting and erythrocytosis.
whyNot.D: Endocarditis causes fever and bacteremia; tricuspid destruction causes regurgitation, not reversal of a VSD shunt.
whyNot.E: Acquired subpulmonary obstruction can occur with VSD, but it would cause a loud outflow murmur, not a barely audible one with a loud P<sub>2</sub>.

items.objective: Explain shunt reversal in Eisenmenger syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 10-week-old girl has had 3 weeks of irritability, pallor and sweating during feeds, and poor weight gain. She was well during the first month. Pulse is 168/min and respirations are 62/min. There is an apical holosystolic murmur and the liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly. An ECG shows deep, wide Q waves with inverted T waves in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?

options.label: A
options.html: Origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk

options.label: B
options.html: Coronary artery aneurysms after a febrile illness

items.explanationHtml:
Heart failure with an anterolateral infarct pattern and ischemic mitral regurgitation in an infant who was well for the first weeks is classic for anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery. In fetal life and just after birth, high pulmonary pressure perfuses the anomalous artery. As pulmonary resistance falls, the left coronary territory receives low-pressure, desaturated blood, and collateral flow from the right coronary artery runs backwards into the pulmonary trunk (coronary steal), causing infarction of the anterolateral wall and papillary muscle.

Takeaway: infant + feeding-related distress + Q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6 = anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery.

whyNot.B: Kawasaki disease causes coronary aneurysms after a febrile illness with mucocutaneous signs, usually in children older than 6 months.
whyNot.C: Myocarditis causes heart failure with low voltage and diffuse ST–T changes, usually after a viral illness, not a regional infarct pattern with deep Q waves.
whyNot.D: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in infancy causes LV hypertrophy voltage and septal Q waves, not an anterolateral infarct pattern with a dilated failing ventricle.
whyNot.E: A large VSD causes heart failure as pulmonary resistance falls, but with a harsh left lower sternal border murmur and no infarct pattern.

items.objective: Recognize anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery as a cause of infant myocardial ischemia.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of chest pain for 1 hour that began after he smoked crack cocaine. He is restless and diaphoretic. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 122/min and blood pressure is 176/104 mm Hg. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST elevation. He has received aspirin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
In cocaine-associated chest pain, benzodiazepines are first-line: they reduce central sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate, blood pressure and agitation, and they reduce the risk of seizures and hyperthermia. Nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers are added for ongoing chest pain or hypertension.

Takeaway: Cocaine chest pain: aspirin plus benzodiazepines first; avoid β-blockers during acute intoxication.

whyNot.A: Fibrinolysis is not indicated without ST elevation, and ST elevation would be treated with primary PCI.
whyNot.C: β-blockade can leave α-mediated coronary vasoconstriction and hypertension unopposed during acute intoxication.
whyNot.D: Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and impairs heat dissipation, which is dangerous in sympathomimetic toxicity.
whyNot.E: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity; this is a sympathomimetic toxidrome with sweating.

items.objective: Use benzodiazepines first in cocaine-associated chest pain.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with newly diagnosed stage II breast cancer that is HER2-negative is scheduled to begin chemotherapy that includes doxorubicin. She has hypertension controlled with lisinopril. She has no cardiac symptoms, and her examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate step before starting chemotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Anthracyclines cause cumulative dose–dependent cardiomyopathy. A baseline assessment of left ventricular function, usually by echocardiography, is recommended before treatment. It identifies patients at high risk, guides the use of cardioprotection (such as dexrazoxane or a liposomal formulation) and provides a reference for later monitoring. Cardiovascular risk factors should also be optimized.

Takeaway: Obtain a baseline echocardiogram before anthracycline therapy.

whyNot.A: Invasive angiography is not indicated without symptoms or signs of coronary disease.
whyNot.B: Biopsy can show anthracycline injury but is invasive and not used as a baseline test.
whyNot.C: Stress testing looks for ischemia, which is not the main concern with anthracyclines.
whyNot.D: Omitting assessment ignores a predictable, dose-related toxicity and leaves no baseline for comparison.

items.objective: Order baseline LV function assessment before anthracycline chemotherapy.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer is receiving adjuvant trastuzumab after completing chemotherapy. She has no dyspnea, orthopnea or edema. Her baseline left ventricular ejection fraction was 64%. Surveillance echocardiography after 3 months of trastuzumab shows an ejection fraction of 46% without regional wall motion abnormalities. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue trastuzumab and repeat echocardiography in 3 months

options.label: B
options.html: Permanently stop trastuzumab and all further cancer therapy

options.label: C
options.html: Hold trastuzumab, start heart failure therapy and repeat echocardiography in 3–4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Her ejection fraction has fallen by 18 percentage points to below 50%, a significant decline even without symptoms. Trastuzumab should be held, guideline-directed therapy (such as an ACE inhibitor or ARB and a β-blocker) started, and function rechecked in about 3–4 weeks. Because trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is usually reversible, the drug can often be resumed once the ejection fraction recovers, preserving its cancer benefit.

Takeaway: A significant asymptomatic EF drop on trastuzumab: hold the drug, treat, reimage in weeks, and consider restarting.

whyNot.A: Continuing despite a large decline below 50% risks progression to symptomatic heart failure.
whyNot.B: Trastuzumab toxicity is usually reversible; abandoning all cancer therapy is unnecessary and harmful.
whyNot.D: Dexrazoxane protects against anthracyclines, not trastuzumab.
whyNot.E: Doxorubicin is not a substitute for HER2-directed therapy and is itself cardiotoxic.

items.objective: Manage a significant LVEF decline during trastuzumab therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old Black woman is admitted with swelling of her tongue and lips that began this morning. She has taken lisinopril for hypertension for 3 years. She is monitored closely, does not need intubation, and the swelling resolves over 36 hours. Her blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg off lisinopril. Kidney function is normal and she has no proteinuria or heart failure. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term antihypertensive therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
ACE inhibitor angioedema can occur after years of uneventful use. All ACE inhibitors must be stopped permanently, as the risk is a class effect of bradykinin accumulation. Neprilysin inhibition in sacubitril-valsartan also raises bradykinin, so it is contraindicated after ACE inhibitor angioedema. A calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine (or a thiazide) is an effective, safe first-line choice for her.

Takeaway: After ACE inhibitor angioedema, never use any ACE inhibitor or sacubitril-valsartan; choose another class.

whyNot.B: Switching to another ACE inhibitor carries the same bradykinin-mediated risk.
whyNot.C: Angioedema is not dose-dependent; any dose can cause recurrence.
whyNot.D: Antihistamines do not prevent bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
whyNot.E: Sacubitril (neprilysin inhibition) raises bradykinin and is contraindicated after ACE inhibitor angioedema.

items.objective: Choose safe antihypertensive therapy after ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a persistent dry, tickling cough for 6 weeks. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus with albuminuria and hypertension and began ramipril 2 months ago. He does not smoke. His lungs are clear, a chest radiograph is normal and there is no postnasal drip or heartburn. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A dry cough beginning weeks after an ACE inhibitor, with no other cause, is most likely bradykinin-mediated ACE inhibitor cough. Because he has diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria, he still needs renin–angiotensin system blockade. An ARB such as losartan provides the same renal protection and rarely causes cough. The cough usually resolves within 1–4 weeks of stopping the ACE inhibitor.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB, especially when RAS blockade is needed (albuminuria, HFrEF).

whyNot.A: He has no asthma or airway inflammation; inhaled glucocorticoids will not stop a drug-induced cough.
whyNot.B: Suppressing the cough leaves the cause in place; switching to an ARB is better.
whyNot.C: A thiazide lowers blood pressure but loses the antiproteinuric benefit he needs.
whyNot.E: Lisinopril is another ACE inhibitor and causes cough just as often.

items.objective: Switch from an ACE inhibitor to an ARB for ACE inhibitor–induced cough.

items.stemHtml:
An 84-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of nausea, vomiting and confusion for 3 days. She takes digoxin, metoprolol and furosemide for heart failure and atrial fibrillation; clarithromycin was started for sinusitis 6 days ago. Pulse is 42/min and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Sodium134 mEq/L
Potassium5.9 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen (BUN)48 mg/dL
Creatinine2.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.2)
Digoxin (8 h after last dose)4.1 ng/mL (therapeutic 0.5–0.9)

An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a regular ventricular rate of 42/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
She has digoxin toxicity precipitated by acute kidney injury and clarithromycin (P-glycoprotein inhibition): gastrointestinal and neurologic symptoms, a very high level, hyperkalemia, and atrial fibrillation with a slow regular ventricular rate (complete heart block with a junctional escape). Symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension, end-organ dysfunction and hyperkalemia are indications for digoxin-specific antibody fragments, which bind digoxin and reverse its effects within an hour. The clarithromycin should be stopped.

Takeaway: Life-threatening digoxin toxicity (bradyarrhythmia, hypotension, hyperkalemia): give digoxin Fab.

whyNot.B: Digoxin has a large volume of distribution, so dialysis removes very little of it.
whyNot.C: Hyperkalemia here reflects pump inhibition; treating the toxin with Fab corrects it. Calcium alone does not reverse digoxin's effects.
whyNot.D: Charcoal is useful soon after an acute ingestion; this is chronic toxicity, and charcoal alone would not treat her instability.
whyNot.E: Pacing can be a temporary bridge, but it does not treat the toxicity and the irritable myocardium may not capture reliably.

items.objective: Recognize chronic digoxin toxicity and its indications for digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man returns for follow-up of hypertension. Three months ago, amlodipine was increased from 5 to 10 mg daily. His blood pressure is now 128/78 mm Hg, but he has had bilateral ankle swelling since the increase. He has no dyspnea. Jugular venous pressure is normal, the lungs are clear and serum creatinine and albumin are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Continue amlodipine and add compression stockings

options.label: D
options.html: Lower amlodipine to 5 mg and add lisinopril

items.explanationHtml:
Ankle edema from dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers is dose-related and results from precapillary arteriolar dilation. Lowering the dose reduces it, and adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB both lowers blood pressure and reduces the edema by dilating the postcapillary venules. Diuretics are largely ineffective for this type of edema.

Takeaway: Treat amlodipine edema by lowering the dose and adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB, not by adding a diuretic.

whyNot.A: Loop diuretics do not correct the capillary pressure gradient and risk volume depletion.
whyNot.B: Spironolactone does not target the mechanism and adds hyperkalemia risk.
whyNot.C: Stockings may help symptoms but leave the cause unchanged when a simple drug change is available.
whyNot.E: Nifedipine is another dihydropyridine with the same edema risk.

items.objective: Manage dose-related dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker edema.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman receiving methadone maintenance therapy for opioid use disorder is found to have chlamydial cervicitis on routine screening. She is not pregnant. She has no allergies. A recent ECG showed sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 510 ms. Serum potassium and magnesium are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her infection?
items.explanationHtml:
Doxycycline for 7 days is the preferred treatment for chlamydial infection in nonpregnant adults and has no meaningful effect on the QT interval. Her QTc is already over 500 ms on methadone, so adding a macrolide or fluoroquinolone, which also block hERG potassium channels, would raise her risk of torsades de pointes. Her methadone should not be stopped abruptly; the prescriber should be informed so the QT can be followed.

Takeaway: When the QTc is already prolonged, choose non–QT-prolonging alternatives; for chlamydia that is doxycycline.

whyNot.A: Azithromycin prolongs the QT interval and is now an alternative rather than the preferred chlamydia regimen.
whyNot.C: Erythromycin prolongs the QT interval, causes more GI upset and is less effective.
whyNot.D: Levofloxacin prolongs the QT interval and is an alternative, not preferred, chlamydia treatment.
whyNot.E: Moxifloxacin is among the more QT-prolonging fluoroquinolones and is not a standard chlamydia regimen.

items.objective: Choose a non–QT-prolonging antibiotic in a patient with methadone-associated QT prolongation.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of progressive exertional dyspnea and leg swelling for 2 months. Three years ago she received chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, including a drug that intercalates into DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II. Jugular venous pressure is elevated and there are bibasilar crackles. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30% and no regional wall motion abnormality. Coadministration of which of the following drugs during her chemotherapy would have been most likely to reduce the risk of this complication?
items.explanationHtml:
Her chemotherapy included an anthracycline (doxorubicin), which causes a cumulative dose–dependent dilated cardiomyopathy that may appear years later. Myocyte injury involves topoisomerase IIβ–mediated DNA damage and iron-catalysed free radical generation. Dexrazoxane chelates iron and interferes with topoisomerase IIβ, lowering the incidence of anthracycline cardiotoxicity.

Takeaway: Dexrazoxane protects against anthracycline cardiomyopathy.

whyNot.A: Amifostine is a free-radical scavenger used mainly to protect the kidneys from cisplatin and the salivary glands from radiation.
whyNot.B: Filgrastim (G-CSF) shortens neutropenia; it does not protect the myocardium.
whyNot.C: Leucovorin rescues normal cells from methotrexate and enhances 5-fluorouracil.
whyNot.D: Mesna binds acrolein and prevents hemorrhagic cystitis from cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.

items.objective: Identify dexrazoxane as the cardioprotective agent for anthracycline therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer receives adjuvant treatment with a monoclonal antibody. Four months later, routine echocardiography shows that her left ventricular ejection fraction has fallen from 63% to 44%. The drug is held. Three months later her ejection fraction is 58%. Which of the following best explains this course?

options.label: A
options.html: Cumulative free radical damage causing myocyte necrosis

options.label: B
options.html: Coronary artery vasospasm causing repeated ischemia

options.label: C
options.html: Interruption of growth-factor receptor survival signalling in cardiomyocytes

options.label: D
options.html: Lymphocytic infiltration of the myocardium from loss of immune tolerance

items.explanationHtml:
Trastuzumab blocks HER2 (ERBB2), a receptor that, with neuregulin, supports cardiomyocyte survival and stress adaptation. Blocking it causes contractile dysfunction without much cell death, so the effect is not cumulative and usually reverses when the drug is held. This contrasts with anthracycline injury, which kills myocytes and is largely permanent.

Takeaway: Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is HER2-mediated dysfunction that usually reverses after the drug is held.

whyNot.A: Cumulative free radical–mediated myocyte death describes anthracyclines and is largely irreversible.
whyNot.B: Coronary vasospasm is typical of 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine, and causes chest pain rather than silent ejection fraction decline.
whyNot.D: Immune-mediated lymphocytic myocarditis is a complication of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
whyNot.E: Repolarization problems cause arrhythmia, not a reversible fall in ejection fraction.

items.objective: Contrast the mechanism and reversibility of trastuzumab cardiotoxicity with anthracycline toxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of crushing chest pain that began shortly after he used an intranasal drug at a party. He is agitated and diaphoretic. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 182/108 mm Hg. Pupils are dilated. An ECG shows ST depression in leads V4–V6, and serum troponin is elevated. The drug most likely responsible acts by which of the following mechanisms?
items.explanationHtml:
Intranasal use, sympathomimetic signs (tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diaphoresis) and myocardial ischemia in a young man point to cocaine. Cocaine blocks reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin at presynaptic terminals. The excess norepinephrine constricts coronary arteries (α1) while raising heart rate and contractility (β1), and cocaine also promotes thrombosis.

Takeaway: Cocaine blocks catecholamine reuptake, causing coronary vasoconstriction and increased myocardial oxygen demand.

whyNot.A: Opioids cause miosis, bradypnea and sedation, not sympathetic excess.
whyNot.B: NMDA antagonism describes PCP and ketamine; PCP is usually smoked and causes nystagmus and violent behaviour.
whyNot.D: MAO inhibitors are prescription antidepressants, not drugs typically used intranasally at parties.
whyNot.E: 5-HT<sub>2A</sub> agonists (LSD, psilocybin) cause hallucinations with only mild sympathetic effects.

items.objective: Recognize cocaine-associated myocardial ischemia and the drug's mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old Black man is brought to the emergency department because of swelling of his lips and tongue that began 3 hours ago. He has no urticaria or itching. He began a new medication for hypertension 6 weeks ago. Blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. Serum C4 concentration is normal. Accumulation of which of the following substances is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Angioedema without urticaria shortly after starting an antihypertensive points to an ACE inhibitor. ACE (kininase II) normally degrades bradykinin. When it is inhibited, bradykinin accumulates and acts on B2 receptors to increase vascular permeability, causing nonpitting swelling of the lips, tongue, face or bowel. The reaction is not IgE-mediated, so antihistamines and glucocorticoids have little effect. Risk is higher in Black patients. A normal C4 argues against hereditary or acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated.

whyNot.A: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II formation.
whyNot.C: Histamine-mediated angioedema usually comes with urticaria and itching, which he does not have.
whyNot.D: Leukotriene excess is associated with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, not ACE inhibitor angioedema.
whyNot.E: Tryptase is a marker of mast cell activation in anaphylaxis, which this is not.

items.objective: Explain the bradykinin mechanism of ACE inhibitor angioedema.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction takes lisinopril, carvedilol, furosemide and spironolactone. He recently began taking ibuprofen for knee pain. Serum potassium is 6.2 mEq/L, and creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.6 mg/dL. Reduced activity of which of the following is the main reason his ACE inhibitor and spironolactone raise serum potassium?

options.label: A
options.html: Apical Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

options.label: C
options.html: Aldosterone-stimulated K⁺ secretion by principal cells of the collecting duct

options.label: E
options.html: Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

items.explanationHtml:
Aldosterone increases ENaC and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity in collecting duct principal cells, creating the lumen-negative potential that drives K⁺ secretion through ROMK channels. ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II–stimulated aldosterone secretion, and spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor, so K⁺ secretion falls. NSAIDs add to the risk by reducing renin release and GFR.

Takeaway: RAAS blockers and aldosterone antagonists cause hyperkalemia by reducing principal-cell K⁺ secretion.

whyNot.A: Loop-segment cotransport is inhibited by furosemide, which lowers potassium.
whyNot.B: Skeletal muscle Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is reduced by digoxin overdose and β-blockade, but it is not the main effect of his ACE inhibitor and spironolactone.
whyNot.D: The intercalated-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase reabsorbs K⁺; reducing it would not raise serum potassium.
whyNot.E: Thiazide-sensitive cotransport inhibition increases distal Na⁺ delivery and lowers potassium.

items.objective: Explain hyperkalemia from renin–angiotensin–aldosterone blockade at the level of the principal cell.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman's hypertension is treated with amlodipine, and the dose was recently increased. She now has bilateral ankle swelling that is worse in the evening. Jugular venous pressure is normal, the lungs are clear and serum albumin is 4.1 g/dL. Adding a thiazide diuretic does not reduce the swelling. Which of the following best explains her edema?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased capillary permeability from endothelial injury

options.label: E
options.html: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from precapillary arteriolar dilation

items.explanationHtml:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate precapillary arterioles much more than venules. More pressure is transmitted into the capillary bed, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration, especially in dependent areas. Because the edema is not caused by salt retention, diuretics help little. An ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates postcapillary venules, lowering capillary pressure and reducing the edema.

Takeaway: Dihydropyridine edema comes from precapillary arteriolar dilation, so it responds poorly to diuretics.

whyNot.A: Her albumin is normal, so oncotic pressure is not reduced.
whyNot.B: There is no inflammation, sepsis or burn to injure the endothelium.
whyNot.C: Lymphatic obstruction causes nonpitting, often unilateral, edema unrelated to a drug dose.
whyNot.D: Calcium channel blockers do not cause meaningful salt retention, which is why the thiazide failed.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of dihydropyridine-induced peripheral edema.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with resistant hypertension and chronic kidney disease begins a new oral vasodilator. Over 2 months his blood pressure improves, but he notices dark hair growing on his forehead and cheeks, gains 4 kg and develops ankle edema. He also takes metoprolol and furosemide. The new drug most likely lowers blood pressure by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: B
options.html: Blocking L-type calcium channels in arterioles

options.label: C
options.html: Increasing cyclic GMP in vascular smooth muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Hypertrichosis with marked fluid retention points to minoxidil, a direct arteriolar vasodilator used for resistant hypertension. Its sulfate metabolite opens ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels in vascular smooth muscle; K⁺ efflux hyperpolarizes the membrane, closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and relaxes the arteriole. The fall in pressure triggers reflex tachycardia and renin release, which is why it is given with a β-blocker and a loop diuretic. It can also cause pericardial effusion.

Takeaway: Minoxidil opens KATP channels; expect hypertrichosis, fluid retention and reflex tachycardia.

whyNot.A: α<sub>1</sub> blockers cause first-dose orthostatic hypotension, not hypertrichosis.
whyNot.B: Calcium channel blockers cause ankle edema but not hair growth.
whyNot.C: Raising cyclic GMP is the mechanism of hydralazine and nitrates; hydralazine causes lupus-like reactions, not hypertrichosis.
whyNot.E: Clonidine causes sedation, dry mouth and rebound hypertension, not hair growth or fluid retention.

items.objective: Identify minoxidil's mechanism from its characteristic adverse effects.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has taken digoxin for 2 years with a stable serum level. Ten days ago, amiodarone was added for rhythm control. She now has anorexia, nausea and blurred vision with a yellowish tint. Her serum digoxin concentration has doubled. Creatinine is unchanged. Which of the following best explains the rise in digoxin concentration?

options.label: A
options.html: Displacement of digoxin from plasma albumin

options.label: B
options.html: Increased oral absorption due to slower gastric emptying

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced glomerular filtration rate from hypotension

items.explanationHtml:
Digoxin is eliminated largely unchanged, partly by P-glycoprotein–mediated secretion in the renal tubule and intestine. Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein, reducing renal and nonrenal clearance and increasing digoxin levels (typically by about 70–100%). When amiodarone is started, the digoxin dose is usually halved and levels are monitored. Verapamil, quinidine and clarithromycin interact in the same way.

Takeaway: Amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine and clarithromycin raise digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein.

whyNot.A: Digoxin is only modestly protein-bound; displacement is not the mechanism of this interaction.
whyNot.B: Amiodarone does not slow gastric emptying, and absorption changes would not double the level.
whyNot.C: Enzyme induction would lower the levels of affected drugs; amiodarone inhibits rather than induces CYP enzymes, and digoxin is not mainly metabolized by CYP3A4.
whyNot.E: Her creatinine is unchanged, so a drop in GFR does not explain the rise.

items.objective: Explain the P-glycoprotein interaction between amiodarone and digoxin.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension takes his first dose of a newly prescribed drug in the morning. Thirty minutes later, he faints after standing up from his chair and recovers within a minute. Lying blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg and standing blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Blockade of which receptor is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
A drug that treats both BPH and hypertension and causes syncope after the first dose is an α1 blocker such as prazosin, terazosin or doxazosin. On standing, α1-mediated constriction of veins and arterioles normally maintains venous return and resistance; blocking it causes orthostatic hypotension, worst with the first dose or a dose increase. Starting with a low dose at bedtime reduces the risk.

Takeaway: First-dose orthostatic syncope is the classic adverse effect of α1 blockers.

whyNot.B: α<sub>2</sub> blockade increases norepinephrine release and would not cause postural hypotension; α<sub>2</sub> agonists (clonidine) lower blood pressure centrally.
whyNot.C: β<sub>1</sub> blockade slows the heart but does not typically cause first-dose orthostatic syncope or improve urinary symptoms.
whyNot.D: Antimuscarinics treat overactive bladder and can cause urinary retention in BPH; they are not antihypertensives.
whyNot.E: ARBs do not treat BPH and rarely cause first-dose syncope.

items.objective: Recognize first-dose orthostatic hypotension from α1-adrenergic blockade.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with metastatic colon cancer develops substernal chest pain 2 days into his first cycle of a continuous infusion of an antimetabolite that inhibits thymidylate synthase. An ECG during pain shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF that resolves within 20 minutes after sublingual nitroglycerin. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive disease. Which of the following best explains his chest pain?

options.label: D
options.html: Myocyte loss from cumulative oxidative injury

items.explanationHtml:
5-Fluorouracil (and its oral prodrug capecitabine) inhibits thymidylate synthase. Its main cardiovascular toxicity is coronary vasospasm, causing chest pain with transient ST changes during or shortly after the infusion, often in patients with normal coronary arteries. It responds to nitrates or calcium channel blockers, and the drug is stopped or changed.

Takeaway: Fluoropyrimidines cause coronary vasospasm with transient ST elevation and normal coronaries.

whyNot.A: Plaque rupture would show an obstructive or thrombotic lesion on angiography.
whyNot.C: Immune-mediated myocarditis is associated with checkpoint inhibitors and does not resolve within minutes after nitroglycerin.
whyNot.D: Cumulative oxidative myocyte injury describes anthracyclines and causes cardiomyopathy, not episodic ST elevation.
whyNot.E: Pericarditis causes diffuse, not regional, ST elevation and is not relieved by nitroglycerin.

items.objective: Recognize 5-fluorouracil–induced coronary vasospasm.
